title: Is this deer going to be the biggest buck shot in Maine this year?
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
A Castle Hill hunter shot a 286-pound buck in Wildlife Management District 6 earlier this month, putting him in contention for the heaviest deer shot in Maine this year. Last year’s heaviest buck weighed 291 pounds.
Eric Argraves shot the buck on Nov. 4 while hunting from a ground blind with a .300 Win. Mag.
The deer weighed 286 pounds on certified scales at The Gateway in Ashland.
His wife, Marci, also had a successful season. She shot a 220-pound buck on Nov. 14 while hunting from a shack along a power line with a .308.
Both deer were harvested in WMD 6.
The couple owns about 1,000 acres in the Castle Hill area, where they have spent the past three years developing food plots and setting up hunting shacks and ground blinds.
Both have taken large bucks in the past, Argraves said. Marci shot a 240-pound buck two years ago.
With deer hunting season still underway, it remains to be seen whether Argraves’ 286-pound buck will finish as Maine’s heaviest this year.

title: Sen. King reacts after Senate passes Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. (WABI) - Senator Angus King is hailing the passage of a bipartisan bill he believes will lower home utility bills, curb emissions, and increase access to renewable energy for Mainers.
The Bipartisan American Affordability & Jobs Act or BAAJA, passed the Senate in a 62-33 vote on Thursday.
King says while he doesn’t agree with everything included in the bill, it was worth the compromise as it deals with affordability and climate change, two of the most pressing issues facing Americans today.
“Is it a perfect bill? No, there’s some things in it that that I don’t like. If I had written it myself, it may have said some other things. But it’s the bill that we can get right now, and there is no clear alternative to it, either now or even in the next Congress. And that’s why I ended up voting ‘yes,’ King said. “It wasn’t an easy choice. I listened to my environmental friends in Maine, many of whom were opposed to the bill, I talked to people in the energy field, particularly in the renewable field, and decided that on balance this bill is a lot better than the status quo.”
There has been a nationwide pushback against the construction of data centers due to the impact they will have on the environment as well as the demand on the electrical grid which will raise the cost of electricity on consumers.
King says the bill also covers this subject.
“It also specifically shifts about $35 billion worth of grid construction costs onto data centers, by making it absolutely clear that they have to pay any costs that they’re imposing on the grid. So, the bill has a lot of very important provisions, and yes, it makes it easier to permit all kinds of energy facilities, and transportation facilities like highways and bridges. But I don’t think it really compromises environmental standards.”
The bill now heads to the House of Representatives for consideration.

title: Family reburies relatives more than 2 years after hurricane washed out cemetery
text:
YANCEY COUNTY, N.C. (WLOS) — More than two years after Hurricane Helene washed away parts of a North Carolina cemetery, a family reburied two relatives whose remains were carried miles away by the storm.
Terry Miller said his grandmother and his aunt were laid back to rest in their original graves.
Miller said his mother, Glessie, has not been found.
“It’s been a long, hard two years,” Miller said.
Storm washed out cemetery
Hurricane Helene tore through Whitson Cemetery in Yancey County in September 2024. Floodwaters carried remains miles away and left the cemetery covered in debris.
“Everything was gone. All the tombstones, all the headstones in the whole cemetery were laying flat on the ground,” Miller said. “The area where my aunt and my mom and my grandparents were, everything was gone.”
Miller said crews had to haul in material to rebuild the cemetery.
“When we rebuilt the cemetery, it took 39 dump truckloads just to rebuild a small area back to the original size,” he said.
Remains found in Tennessee
Miller said answers came from Tennessee after more than two years of searching. He said he gave a DNA sample for a match.
“Finally, after digging through the rubble down in Tennessee, they were able to find my grandmother in Erwin,” Miller said.
His aunt was found in Jonesborough just over a week ago.
“I was happy because I was able to get closure on relocating them,” Miller said.
Miller said the East Tennessee State University forensic team played a significant role in identifying the family members.
Search for mother continues
“She was one of the last ones to wash out of the cemetery, and we still haven’t found her yet,” Miller said.
Miller said his mother, Glessie, remains missing.
“As they find any type of bone or anything, they can do a DNA and hopefully my mom, whether whatever can be found where, we can rebury her at the same time,” he said.
Miller said he hopes to rebury her at the same grave if remains are found.
“My mother, my grandmother, my aunt, they’re physically in heaven, but I’m glad that we can lay them back to rest in the original grave,” Miller said.

title: Thanksgiving get-togethers can reveal changes in older loved ones
text:
(Aging Untold) — Thanksgiving is a time for families to get together, celebrate and enjoy each other’s company.
But gatherings can reveal challenges that older loved ones are facing that are not apparent over the phone.
Problems not apparent by phone
“Thanksgiving is the number one holiday for families to get together and that spurs a huge crisis in the health care industry,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
She said people who may have been talking to their family every single day suddenly realize that things are not going as well as they thought.
Advice for the visit
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said sometimes family members arrive and find that things are not how they thought they would be with the older person.
“Stay out of judgment because it’s easy to do when you’re scared,” O’Rourke said.
She advises not to plan a lot of things so people can relax and be around each other.
Ambrose also said not to go into a holiday with a big agenda.
“Just observing and enjoying each other so you can kind of self-discover what is really going on and then you can make plans later,” Ambrose said.
Resources
Some older adults might hide that they are struggling from their loved ones. This can stem from a fear of losing independence.

title: (Not) up in the air: Travelers' trepidations spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups abound
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.
And for 2026’s busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there’s another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation.
The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She’s pretty sure she’s not the only one.
“For a lot of people, especially as they’re paying attention and because it’s in the news where they’re tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we’re having … I think more and more people are now getting anxious,” said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel.
It’s an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days’ tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it’s a familiar one, too.
Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it’s one they’re likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic.
But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.
“For the most part, air travel still remains strong,” said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People “might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it.”
Air travel is vital — and taken for granted
In some ways, the country’s aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute.
“Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy … and frankly, it is taken for granted,” said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum.
“You’ve got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places,” he said. “But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It’s a commodity. There’s nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that’s a clear sign of its success — that you’re in a bus.”
At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she’s used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she’s not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure issues to the list of potential problems, she’s not rattled by it.
“I literally haven’t had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I’m like, just, okay, here’s another thing,” said Jolene, who lives in Miami.
She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, “the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday.”
And instead of flying this year, they’ll drive to “Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something,” she said. “But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there’s just not much choice. What are you going to do?”
The expense can be as much of an obstacle as the delays
If anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can’t just be stuffed into the overhead compartment.
Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking company Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade.
Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.
It led Jolene, 50, to find a creative way to get her daughter’s flight home to Miami for Thanksgiving: toilet paper.
She saw a promotion on American Airlines’ online shopping portal earlier this year that awarded 10 miles for every dollar spent. She bought 10 boxes of 48 rolls, earning her about 8,500 miles — which was enough to cover the entire flight from Washington, D.C., where her daughter attends college.
The upfront cost was worth it, she said, because it’s a product she would have bought anyway and one that doesn’t go bad. She’s keeping the rolls in her garage
“The funny part,” she said, “is we have to buy toilet paper anyway.”
___
AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat in Las Vegas contributed to this story.

title: School district to close after learning 500 employees didn’t undergo child protective services screenings
text:
ALBEMARLE COUNTY, Va. (WVIR/Gray News) - Citing a years-long issue with the background check process while hiring employees, a Virginia school district announced it would close temporarily.
Albemarle County Public Schools said that schools will be closed to students starting Thursday, November 19, and hopes to reopen after Thanksgiving break on Monday, November 30.
Acting Superintendent Dr. Chandra Hayes sent a message to Albemarle families saying that over the last three years, more than 500 people hired by the division passed their criminal background checks using the State Police criminal history database, but were not checked against the Virginia Department of Social Services’ Child Protective Services Central Registry.
In her message, Hayes said that schools must be closed until the issue is resolved and staff who work directly with children must have their Social Services screening completed before being able to work with students.
Dear Albemarle County Public Schools Community,
When I took on this role, I made a commitment to you to look closely at how our school division operates, to fix what needs fixing, and to tell you what we find. Some of what follows is difficult to share, but you deserve to hear it directly from me.
Immediate Issue Driving the Closure
Every new ACPS employee goes through a rigorous, fingerprint-based criminal background check using the State Police criminal history database. Virginia law and School Board policy also require that new hires be checked against the Child Protective Services Central Registry, which the Virginia Department of Social Services (VDSS) maintains, to confirm they have no founded complaints of child abuse or neglect.
During a review of onboarding procedures, we found that the criminal background checks were administered, but the personnel responsible for submissions to Child Protective Services did not consistently follow established processes. Specifically, over the past three years, there were more than 500 people hired by the division who passed their criminal background checks, but their information was never submitted for the Social Services registry review. We investigated the matter and took immediate action.
Families should not have to accept any uncertainty about the adults working with their children, and I will not risk the safety of our students. Because the affected employees work in schools and departments across the entire division, I made the decision that we must close all schools until we have this issue resolved. We shared our findings with the Virginia Department of Education and they agreed that staff who work directly with children must have their Social Services screening complete before being able to work with students.
What we are doing now
We are working with the Virginia Department of Social Services (VDSS) to complete the screening as soon as possible. Staff who work directly with students will be first to be processed, so that we can reopen schools quickly. The VDSS has prioritized these submissions, and I am grateful for their support.
If the VDSS review shows that any current employee is the subject of a founded complaint of child abuse or neglect, we will act immediately to protect students. School Board Policy GCDA requires that such an employee be dismissed once their appeal rights under state law have been exhausted, and it provides grounds for the division to recommend that the Virginia Board of Education revoke their teaching license.
We also checked whether anyone currently under investigation or facing charges related to abuse, neglect, or failure to report was among the employees not submitted. I can confirm that none of them were.
What families need to know during the closure
School Schedule Through Thanksgiving Break
Trust is built through honesty, especially when the news is hard. I’ll keep you informed as the checks are completed. I will receive a daily report from the Virginia Department of Social Services on the progress of the application review. This will allow me to confirm the reopening date by Nov. 27. With so little notice and the holiday season so close, I know this will be hard on many families, and I am sorry for that disruption. However, the safety of your children must always come first, and I believe this is a necessary action.
I will continue to review processes and procedures and make the changes needed to strengthen and restore Albemarle County Public Schools. Thank you for your continued support in those efforts.
Sincerely,
Chandra Hayes, Ed.D.
Acting Superintendent
Albemarle County Public Schools
Governor Abigail Spanberger said in a statement that Albemarle County Public Schools’ former leadership failed students and families by not conducting legally required background checks. She said state education leaders are assisting the school division’s interim leadership with corrective action, including hiring an outside investigator.
“Albemarle County Public Schools’ prior leadership failed the children and families they serve. They failed to follow the law by not conducting legally-required background checks, and they failed to uphold the trust our Commonwealth placed in them. Virginia Secretary of Education Jeffery Smith and Superintendent of Public Instruction Jenna Conway are assisting Albemarle County Public Schools’ interim leadership in taking swift corrective action, to include hiring an outside investigator. My administration is committed to the education and safety of every child in Virginia, and we will use every available tool to rectify this failure and ensure accountability.”

title: 2 women charged with murder after 3-year-old diagnosed with cancer did not see a doctor for 2 years, authorities say
text:
OZARK, Mo. (KY3/Gray News) — Two women have been charged in connection with the death of a 3-year-old boy who authorities said was diagnosed with cancer but was not taken to the doctor for treatment.
Police responded to a home in Ozark, Missouri, on July 31, where they found the boy dead. Officers wrote in court records that the child appeared undersized and severely malnourished.
Investigators learned the boy had been diagnosed with cancer as a baby but that he had not been seen by a doctor for two years before his death. According to investigators, the boy’s caregivers did not schedule follow-up appointments after he received his cancer diagnosis.
Investigators also described the home as cluttered with animal feces, urine and trash, according to the report.
A cause of death was not released.
The child’s mother, Destiny Schliefert, and another woman, Debbie Potter, who helped care for him, are charged with second-degree murder.
Both women are also charged with child abuse and endangering the welfare of a child.

title: Recurring James Bond Characters (That Are Not James Bond)
text:
10 Recurring James Bond Characters (That Are Not James Bond)
Everyone who loves James Bond movies has “their” James Bond: the Bond they grew up with, the Bond who was Bond when they discovered the franchise, the Bond whose run of movies they love the most. But James Bond isn’t the only James Bond character who shows up again and again in these movies, nor is he the only character who’s been recast more than once. Other familiar faces always appear to flesh out the universe of MI6’s dashing 00, faces almost as iconic as the man himself.
Many of these characters first appear and reappear in Ian Fleming’s series of novels that provide the inspiration for the movies, allowing Bond some regular friends and enemies to meet up with on his many travels. Many of these well-known individuals provide a sense of continuity to the infamously muddled movie series, whose timeline is more convoluted than any bomb Bond ever defused. More than a few of them span multiple Bond eras — while the star may be different, here are a couple of recognizable faces from previous films to remind us that it’s all part of one story.
A few of these characters are just as iconic as Bond. Where would our beloved secret agent be without his steely boss, or his brilliant gadget man? From the halls of MI6 headquarters to the dens of the world’s most infamous supervillains, these friends and foes serve as a reminder that a James Bond movie is never a one-man show — despite how much the guy claims he loves to work alone.

title: AVEC’s furnace program helped about 62 households, but 160 remain on waiting list
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - AVEC Community Action said its Central Heating Improvement Program, known as CHIP, helped about 62 households with furnace replacements and repairs this season, but about 160 households are still on the waiting list.
Hundreds of thousands of dollars in funding helped families repair or replace their furnaces this year. AVEC said it still can’t help everyone on its waiting list.
Waiting list remains
Heidi Rackliffe, AVEC’s chief program officer, said about 160 households are still on the list and the program isn’t able to cover them all.
“There’s no way we’d be able to empty the list of individuals who need a repair and a replacement with the funding that we have, unfortunately,” Rackliffe said.
How to sign up
AVEC is still adding people to the waiting list and encourages those who need help to sign up.
To receive CHIP assistance, households must first be approved for heating assistance, known as HEAP.
Rackliffe said more people could be helped if additional funding becomes available.
More information about the program is available at avecmaine.org.

title: Alone’ Sequel With Macaulay Culkin In Development
text:
‘Home Alone’ Sequel With Macaulay Culkin In Development
Home Alone has evolved past popular kids movie into an all-time holiday classic. Just ask my daughter. She’ll tell you: A little kid bludgeoning two idiot crooks in the groin for 90 minutes? That’s a high-water mark for cinema that has yet to be duplicated.
The enduring power of Home Alone is all around us. McDonald’s just announced they were doing a Home Alone tie-in meal this holiday season — and they got Macaulay Culkin to star in the commercial for the promo as his Home Alone character. Whenever you see an actor do stuff like this you have to wonder: Are they interested in making a whole legacyquel?
Apparently so! Deadline reports that Culkin pitched his own idea for a new Home Alone sequel to Disney, and the film is now “in early works” at the studio.
“As a father now, Culkin had an interesting take as to where his Kevin McCallister would go now that he’s older and wiser, having survived abandonment and burglars as a child,” they write.
(This is absurd. Kevin didn’t survive abandonment and burglars as a child. He survived abandonment and burglars as a child twice.)
Here is that Culkin McDonald’s Home Alone ad, by the way.
READ MORE: Macaulay Culkin Reprises Home Alone Role For McDonald’s Commercial
If the thought of a new Home Alone wasn’t intriguing enough Deadline also reports that Culkin is now working on the project with writer/producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg, the duo behind countless comedies including Superbad, Pineapple Express, and This Is the End, plus the hit TV series The Studio.
Culkin starred in Home Alone and one earlier sequel, 1992’s Home Alone 2: Lost in New York. After that, 20th Century Fox (and later Disney) extended the franchise multiple times without him, bringing in new cute kids to fend off their homes from other clumsy thieves. None of the films without Culkin had anywhere near the impact that the first two did, and continue to have. Disney just recently extended the concept into animation, with a Mickey’s Home Alone debuting later this month on Disney+.
Being left home alone is either a child’s greatest dream, or their worst nightmare. For an adult, that’s just another Tuesday night. But I suppose if Kevin himself is the parent and his own child is the one left home alone that could be interesting. (Although if you were abandoned multiple times by your distracted parents, wouldn’t you be the most overprotective helicopter parent in the history of the world??)

title: East Millinocket’s only police dog could leave with his handler
text:
East Millinocket could be left without a police dog after the resignation of the department’s sergeant and police dog handler.
Sgt. Mallory Clayton, who is partnered with the dog, Derby, has resigned, and her last day is Nov. 26, according to town administrative assistant Celina Charette.
The town has not decided whether Derby will stay in East Millinocket or go with Clayton. If Derby leaves, it was not immediately clear which agency would cover the department’s police dog needs.
Derby’s situation shows how thin police dog coverage can be in rural Maine. In small departments, keeping a dog, which is often paid for by a grant and trained to detect drugs, explosives or missing persons, can hinge on a single handler.
When that officer leaves, the dog can follow, as Holden has seen twice. It’s also unclear how much it would cost East Millinocket to replace Derby if he leaves.
Derby completed training in 2024 and is East Millinocket’s only police dog. He’s helped local and state police track suspects and find drugs in his roughly two years of service, according to Millinocket Town Council meeting minutes. He is a dual-purpose dog, certified for patrol and drug detection.
Police Chief Cameron McDunnah, Cpl. Bradley Fitzgerald, Clayton and the town’s selectmen did not respond to requests for comment.
Clayton pursued the grant that paid for Derby’s training, according to selectmen meeting minutes. She served on the force for about four years after working for the Houlton Police Department. The grant also covered a new cruiser and a specialized cage for Derby, according to a Millinocket Town Council agenda.
East Millinocket police provide 24-hour coverage to about 7,500 residents in East Millinocket, Millinocket and Medway, according to the department’s website. The department handles about 11,000 calls a year.
Police dogs are often funded through grants from groups like the Stanton Foundation, which runs a police dog program for law enforcement agencies throughout New England, according to Maj. Aaron Turcotte, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety. Such grants don’t typically require town money, he said.
From 2013 to 2024, the Stanton Foundation awarded nearly $5 million to establish police dog units in more than 100 departments in Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, New York and Vermont, according to its website.
East Millinocket is among the agencies that have received one of the foundation’s grants to start a police dog unit, which covers buying and training a dog for a department that doesn’t already have one.
In rare cases, Maine State Police will hire a police dog handler and sign a memorandum of understanding with the Stanton Foundation so the dog can come along, Turcotte said. He could recall three times that has happened in the past two decades, in Kennebec, Somerset and Aroostook counties.
In Holden, just east of Bangor, police transferred one dog to state police, Chief Eddie Benjamin said. Its training cost about $3,000 and was covered by the Stanton Foundation.
Holden police then got a second dog, which later left for the Brewer Police Department with its handler, Benjamin said. Brewer reimbursed Holden for the dog’s training.
Holden doesn’t have a police dog now, Benjamin said. When officers need one, they request it through dispatch, which asks neighboring agencies for help, he said.

title: Maine State Library welcomes public back to its renovated home
text:
Following major renovations, the Maine State Library is excited to welcome visitors back to its home in the updated Cultural Building on the Capitol Complex in Augusta on Tuesday, Dec. 8, with a ribbon cutting ceremony at 9 a.m.
Visitors to the Maine State Library will find improved accessibility, updated storage for the Library’s extensive collections, and more flexible spaces for reading, working, and participating in programs. New space-saving shelving on the first floor helps house the Library’s collections, which stretch nearly seven miles if lined up end to end. On the second floor, movable shelving makes it easier to adapt public spaces for seating and events.
The newly renovated Library also includes new spaces for people who need a quiet, private place to work or take meetings and calls. Privacy pods offer visitors a place to participate in telehealth appointments, conduct online job interviews, or take digital meetings.
“We are so excited to welcome the public back into the Cultural Building,” said Lori Stockman, State Librarian. “Our renovated spaces offer new opportunities for people to use the Library in different ways, whether they’re exploring our rich collections, looking for a quiet place to work, seeking assistance with a research question, or simply stopping by while visiting the Capitol Complex. We hope people will come in, take a look around, and make themselves at home!”
The Maine State Library, Maine State Archives, and Maine State Museum moved their staff and collections out of the Cultural Building in June 2020, after a heating system failure and the discovery of asbestos. Over the next six years, the building underwent extensive renovations, creating updated spaces for these three institutions and the people they serve.
The Maine State Library welcomes visitors during the following regular hours:
- Tuesday: 9 a.m.–5 p.m.
- Wednesday: 9 a.m.–7 p.m.
- Thursday: 9 a.m.–7 p.m.
- Friday: 9 a.m.–5 p.m.
The Library is closed on all state and federal holidays. Visitors are encouraged to stop by and discover the renewed spaces and services available at the Maine State Library.
About Maine State Library: Established in 1837, the Maine State Library strives to help people, make Maine libraries stronger, and transform information into knowledge. The services provided by Maine State Library are available to all Maine residents and are free of charge. To learn more, visit https://www.maine.gov/msl/.

title: Court approves $7.25 billion settlement with Bayer over claims Roundup weedkiller caused cancer
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from U.S. cancer patients asserting the company should have warned people that its popular weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved Friday by a Missouri judge.
The nationwide settlement applies both to Roundup users who already are ill and those who become diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in future years. Participants could get an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, depending on how they used the product, how old they were when diagnosed and the severity of their illness.
For Germany-based Bayer, which denies that Roundup causes cancer, the settlement provides some financial certainty against mounting litigation costs that have led it to contemplate pulling the product from U.S. agricultural markets. Bayer already has changed the formula for its Roundup version sold to residential users.
Litigants also faced uncertainty. While the settlement was pending, the U.S. Supreme Court undercut one of the central arguments in the Roundup lawsuits. The high court ruled in June that Bayer cannot be sued in state courts on claims it failed to warn about cancer, because federal regulations don’t require a cancer warning label and states are forbidden from imposing additional labeling requirements.
Though some attorneys for cancer patients contend the settlement payouts are too small, others argue the deal is better than getting nothing — which became a heightened likelihood after the Supreme Court ruling.
In a written judgment granting approval, St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer said the average individual payouts are “fair and adequate” and the total dollar amount is “among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements.” The approved settlement includes $600 million for attorneys’ fees.
The judge said there was a risk Bayer would have filed for bankruptcy protection if the settlement had been rejected.
Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said in a statement that the court-approved settlement is “a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation.”
The decision could be appealed.
Roundup has been used on weeds for over 50 years
Missouri-based Monsanto debuted Roundup weed killer in 1974 with the chemical glyphosate as its active ingredient. The product quickly became one of the most widely used herbicides in agriculture. Roundup is designed to be used with genetically modified seeds that can resist the weed killer’s deadly effect, thus allowing farmers to produce more while conserving the soil by tilling it less.
The product also is commonly applied on lawns and gardens.
Bayer added Roundup to its portfolio when it acquired Monsanto in 2018. With it came a growing number of lawsuits alleging glyphosate causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. But that remains in dispute. The World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer classified the chemical as “probably carcinogenic” in 2015. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has determined that it’s not likely to cause cancer in humans when used as directed.
About 200,000 Roundup-related claims have been made against Bayer, many coming from people who used it on residential lawns and gardens. As a result, Bayer has removed glyphosate from its new versions of Roundup sold for residential markets.
The lawsuits have produced mixed results. Only a couple dozen cases have gone to jurors, some siding with Bayer and others with plaintiffs. In one case, a Georgia jury awarded plaintiffs $2.1 billion.
In the first Roundup verdict since the Supreme Court’s precedent-setting ruling, a Missouri jury in October sided with Bayer in a case alleging design defects, negligence and fraud. The verdict “should send a strong signal” that plaintiffs “will face significant challenges” pursuing Roundup-related cancer claims in the future, said Bill Dodero, Bayer’s U.S. general counsel and global litigation leader.
Attorneys disagree on whether the settlement is fair
Bayer previously set aside $16 billion to cover legal costs related to Roundup cases. The new settlement, which is in addition to that, is designed to address most of the remaining lawsuits, as well as any additional cases brought in the coming years by people who were exposed to Roundup before the settlement was proposed in February.
“Today’s final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice,” said Christopher A. Seeger, a court-appointed counsel for cancer patients in the case.
The settlement calls for Bayer to make annual payments into a special fund for up to 21 years, totaling as much as $7.25 billion. The amount of money paid out to individuals would vary. Agricultural, industrial or turf workers exposed at length to Roundup could receive an average of $165,000 if they were diagnosed with an aggressive form of the illness while younger than age 60. But anyone diagnosed at age 78 or older would get significantly less, with an average of $10,000.
Some attorneys have said the individual settlement amounts are too small and the terms too restrictive.
“This settlement is the scariest, worst future settlement that’s ever been contemplated,” attorney Gerson Smoger said during a September court hearing on whether the settlement was fair. He said it locked in future claimants for decades with no chance at punitive damages yet “kept the product that they were exposed to on the market, allowing the victims to continue to be exposed.”
The settlement was filed in St. Louis Circuit Court in Missouri, home to Bayer’s North America crop science division and the state where many of the lawsuits have been brought.

title: Sen. Warner links recent tech outages to AI, calls for more oversight
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), the Vice Chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said artificial intelligence is responsible for the recent surge in tech outages across the U.S. He said he wants more federal oversight of the industry.
Warner said companies are using AI to prevent AI hacks and are struggling to keep up with the speed of the programs. He said he believes the entire AI field needs more oversight.
Americans have seen tech systems go down over the course of one week, including ground stoppages, Microsoft Outlook and banks. Some Americans have grown suspicious of a cyber attack.
Warner said the Federal Aviation Administration issues had to do with replacing a router. He said the other outages share the same cause.
“All of these are related to AI,” he said.
Warner said the outages are coming from companies using similar software to perform preventative maintenance to avoid cyber attacks.
“AI tools, particularly Mythos that came from Anthropic, are finding a number of vulnerabilities,” he said.
Warner used a pipe leak analogy to explain how AI is shifting security.
“Where it used to be you’d have one leak a month or every three months, you may have 100 leaks in a single day,” he said.
Warner said he believes the government has been too hands off when it comes to the buildout of AI. He said he believes stronger oversight is needed given how large a bet the U.S. economy has made on the technology.
“We are flying blindly with trillions of dollars of investment without the kind of oversight from the regulatory agencies and from the investment community that’s needed,” Warner said.
He’s cosponsoring a bipartisan bill that would require more transparency on AI company investment. It also would require companies with significant AI exposure to provide more information on potential risks.

title: Judge rules that ICE illegally detained an 18-year-old during Maine traffic stop
text:
Judge rules that ICE illegally detained an 18-year-old during Maine traffic stop in Livermore Falls
A federal judge in Maine ordered U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to release a young man from custody after she determined that he was illegally detained.
Court documents state that an 18-year-old was one of multiple people who were detained by immigration authorities Monday morning during a traffic stop in Livermore Falls.
According to the court documents, the detainee entered the United States in or about November 2024 at the age of 16. As an unaccompanied child, he was placed in the custody of the Office of Refugee Resettlement. Within a matter of days, he was released to a sponsor, his brother, who lived in Rhode Island at the time. He graduated high school in June 2025 and in November 2025, he received an I-360 Special Immigrant Juvenile (SIJ) certification after a Massachusetts state court judge found that his father had neglected and abused him.
The court documents go on to state that the young man was a passenger in the vehicle that was stopped by immigration authorities in Livermore Falls. The young man called his brother, who spoke to an ICE agent over the phone and told the agent that the 18-year-old has SIJ certification. According to the court documents, the ICE agent told the young man's brother that the 18-year-old was not in removal proceedings, but immigration officials detained him without a warrant nonetheless.
The young man filed a petition in federal court after he was taken into custody on Monday, claiming that his Fifth Amendment rights were violated and that ICE violated laws regarding the release of unaccompanied noncitizen children.
In a ruling handed down on Wednesday, U.S. District Court Judge Stacey Neumann said that in the two years since the 18-year-old was released from the Office of Refugee Resettlement, he complied with the conditions of his release, graduated from high school and committed no crimes in addition to obtaining SIJ classification. Neumann said ICE seized the young man without first determining that circumstances had materially changed since his release, and without finding that he now posed a danger to the community or a risk of flight.
Neumann also noted that immigration authorities afforded the young man no process before detaining him, and that they have offered no evidence that he is a flight risk or a danger.
An arrest warrant for the 18-year-old was issued, but Neumann said there is no evidence that it was issued before the young man was detained.
"The Border Patrol agent stopped a van because, in his experience, such vehicles 'often transport' noncitizens, and he arrested all passengers," Neumann said. "Petitioner was not a pre-identified target, so no warrant could have been issued as to him after individualized consideration. Where the government cannot show that a warrant preceded the arrest, the court treats the arrest as warrantless."
Neumann ordered ICE to release the young man from detention by 10 a.m. Thursday without any additional conditions or restraints beyond any that may have existed before he was unlawfully detained. ICE was also ordered to return all of the young man's personal belongings to him.

title: Hermon football’s seniors hope to close their careers by winning a Gold Ball
text:
Most years, Hermon football head coach Kyle Gallant said, the Hawks are among the younger teams in their class.
That’s been far from the case in 2026.
With Hermon football just one win away from capturing its first state title in program history, the team’s large senior class has paved the way.
“Our seniors and our six captains are phenomenal,” Gallant said. “It’s helped the mental side of football come a really long way for this group. That senior leadership core is big on learning from mistakes, picking the positives and getting better. I get emotional thinking about them.”
Hermon has 10 seniors on the roster this year, and all 10 have made meaningful contributions on both sides of the ball.
They’re hoping to play one last meaningful part in the program: being the senior class that captures the Hawks’ first state championship.
“The emotions have been high going into this season, knowing we have a team full of seniors,” said Owen Lang, a senior WR/DB. “We wanted our season to end with a state championship from the start.”
Hermon will face off with Leavitt in the Class C State Championship at 2:30 p.m. Saturday in Lewiston. The game will be played at Don Roux Field at Lewiston High School.
This year’s senior class, many of whom were called into action as freshmen because of team injuries in 2023, hopes to hoist the Gold Ball at midfield to cap off their careers.
“In the beginning of the year, the fact this was our last season wasn’t really hitting. Now, it’s all I can think about,” said senior Peyton Tolliver, a right tackle and defensive end. “This is our last game ever.”
Despite the magnitude of the state championship, Gallant said, his seniors are keeping the team focused on its “just another game” mindset.
“They’re teenagers at the end of the day, so it’s hard to get them to buy into that [mindset],” Gallant said. “They aren’t naive to the fact that the stakes are different. But I’m just proud of these [seniors] for who they are and what they’ve done for this program. They’ve done everything it takes to make sure they get every minute out of this football season they possibly can.”

title: A Mainer's Case Against Green Bean Casserole, French-Fried Onions And All
text:
I love many things about Thanksgiving, but one dish doesn't do it for me.
Maine Thanksgivings are Filled With Delicious Fresh Food
Thanksgiving is a feast for any foodie.
So many amazing dishes to enjoy.
I really love cranberries, so whether the sauce is homemade or it's shaped like the can it came in, I'm going to have some on my plate.
READ MORE: Thanksgiving's Best Pie Isn't Apple or Pumpkin: It's a Maine Classic
Turkey is always delicious, especially with a little extra salt.
And no one makes stuffing like my mother-in-law. I could (and have) made an entire meal out of it.
This Mainer Will Pass When Passed the Green Bean Casserole
But when someone passes me the bowl of green bean casserole, I have to pass it along to the next diner without showing how much I dislike it.
Now, I know what you're thinking...I just haven't had YOUR green bean casserole.
Wrong.
Sorry...but I've heard that before.
And I'll admit it's a weird thing.
I love green beans, whether they're canned, frozen, or fresh out of my husband's garden. (The best)
I love cream of mushroom soup in any number of dishes.
And French-fried onion rings? Yes, please!
But put them together, and that becomes a no, thank you.
Maine Green Beans Should Be Crisp, Not Slimy in a Casserole
There's just something about the cream of mushroom soup that makes the green beans slimy, and I greatly dislike that.
It's not just a texture thing...I truly don't like the flavors together.
Dumping a bunch of those crunchy French-fried onions on top won't even save this dish for me.
I can't be the only one who feels this way.
Please, someone, tell me you also hate green bean casserole, so I know I'm not alone.
Happy Thanksgiving, all!
I hope you get all of your favorite dishes!

title: Mamdani sets plan to close NYC's notorious Rikers Island jail
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — New York City’s Rikers Island jail complex would close by 2032 under a plan announced Friday by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose strategy for finally shuttering the notorious facility hinges on substantially reducing the number of people kept behind bars.
The city is all but certain to blow past a legal requirement to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller, more modern jails by 2027.
For years, Rikers Island has stood as a symbol of dysfunction, with the network of jails so plagued by violence and overcrowding that a federal judge, citing “ abnormal and unacceptable ” conditions, appointed an outside manager to restore order and implement reforms.
Mamdani, a Democrat, has been a vocal proponent of closing Rikers, though the longstanding plan to build new jails has met pushback, including from his predecessor, former Mayor Eric Adams, who opposed federal oversight and borough jails.
“It is time to finally close Rikers Island,” Mamdani said in a statement. “For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane.”
The plan hinges on lowering the city’s inmate population from the more than 6,500 people housed at Rikers to around 4,500.
The Mamdani administration is proposing a new slate of diversion and supervised release programs, expanding housing and social services to prevent recidivism, along with restoring an online bail payment system and reducing case delays through various measures.
“We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers. Working alongside the City Council, Courts and nonprofit partners, we will meet it — for the people in our custody, the staff who serve them, victims of crime, and every New Yorker,” Mamdani said.
Instead of housing prisoners at Rikers — an island in the East River near LaGuardia Airport — the city will shift people to jails in the Bronx, Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan, as well as a handful of medical facilities for people who need healthcare or psychiatric treatment. The city also plans to reduce the number of beds for women, diverting them into community-based programs.
The borough jails are expected to open in Brooklyn in 2029; the Bronx and Queens in 2031; and then Manhattan in 2032, according to City Hall.
Criminal justice activists have pushed for decades to close Rikers Island, which has housed jail inmates since the 1930s.
In 2019, the New York City Council voted to close the jail complex and replace it with newer jails located in the city’s boroughs, with local lawmakers invoking the names of former prisoners who died, including Kalief Browder, who took his own life at age 22 after being held for three years at Rikers.
At the time, city officials had also called for shrinking the jail population to accommodate the closure, but ran into opposition from critics who argued doing so would mean more violent criminals on city streets.

title: South Portland library reopens as city works to bring systems back online after cyberattack
text:
South Portland’s library has reopened as officials investigate a cyberattack and work to bring the rest of the city’s systems back online.
City Hall and the assessing office remained closed Thursday due to the outage, but staff “are making good progress” toward reopening them, the city said. Those offices are closed on Fridays as part of the city’s four-day workweek and won’t reopen until Monday at the earliest.
The library expects to be open regular hours moving forward.
City offices have been closed since Monday as the city has worked to address the suspected cyberattack, which officials say was first detected Saturday night.
“While these buildings and the library have been closed to the public this week, staff have continued to work, and many have been working closely with our IT department to bring affected public services back online securely,” the city said in an update Thursday.
LIBRARY REOPENS
In a social media post on Thursday, the library said its main location on Broadway was open and circulation services are up and running, meaning staff can now check items in and out, renew them, or place them on hold. It announced Friday that the branch library on Wescott Road had reopened as well.
However, it’s not all systems go.
The library could not offer public internet access or computer and printing use Thursday. It also does not have phone service and encouraged anyone looking to communicate with library staff to use the “Contact Us” page online.
The library also cautioned that other services may still be limited.
CYBERATTACK INVESTIGATION
The city said Thursday that “the investigation into this cyberattack is ongoing.” Staff members have said they are working with state and federal agencies, as well as forensic examiners and cybersecurity experts.
“While some city data has been impacted, we have confirmed that most of our data was not affected or accessed,” the city said.
The municipality’s computer and phone systems, as well as some online administrative portals and mapping services, have been down since the issues began over the weekend.
The city cautioned that in-person credit card payments and receipts at some city facilities may also be affected. At the community center Wednesday, a notice posted on the front door said the building had no internet or phone service, and patrons could pay with only cash or checks.
The city has said police, fire and EMS services have not been impacted.
“This has been a true group effort that includes you, our community,” the city said. “We thank you for your patience and support at this challenging time, and thank our staff for its hard work and dedication.”

title: Maine report reveals health care and mental wellness struggles for farmers, fishermen, and loggers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine report reveals health care and mental wellness struggles for farmers, fishermen, and loggers
A state report highlights health care delays and mental health concerns among Maine’s heritage industry workers, with recommendations for support programs.
Maine report reveals health care and mental wellness struggles for farmers, fishermen, and loggers
A state report highlights health care delays and mental health concerns among Maine’s heritage industry workers, with recommendations for support programs.
A new state report highlights significant health and wellness challenges faced by Maine’s farmers, fishermen, and loggers, including health care delays and mental health concerns.
The report, based on a survey of nearly 300 workers, found that more than half had delayed seeking health care in the past year due to cost and time away from work.
The working group behind the report has proposed a statewide program to connect workers and their families with mental health support, including short-term counseling and other services. The recommendations include offering low or no-cost services without requiring employer referrals.
Nichole Sargent, owner and co-founder of Southpaw Packing, a slaughter and processing plant in Windham, served on the working group. Her family has deep ties to Maine’s heritage industries.
“A lot of people don’t know how intertwined our heritage industries are and, you know, when we’re not making money at one entity, we’re doing something else within, you know, our heritage industries to try to compensate for that,” Sargent said.
She acknowledged the difficulty of taking time off work and the stigma around asking for help.
“People see loggers, fishermen and farmers and people that are like that strong, burly, you know, persona. And that also goes against us because we’re not by nature going to show that weakness and ask for help,” Sargent said.
Sargent also started an initiative called “Slicing Through the Stigma” after several suicides in the agricultural community. According to the survey, nearly three-quarters of agriculture respondents said mental health was a major or moderate concern in their industry. More than half of forestry and logging respondents shared the same concern.
Dana Doran, executive director of Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast, emphasized the economic pressures facing loggers.
“If we don't take a look at as a state, the economic impact of what's happening to, you know, loggers, fishermen, farmers and their ability to go to work every day. We're going to lose our rural identity,” Doran said.
He added that the financial strain doesn’t end when the workday does.
“You’ve got exceptionally high bills to pay. You’ve got loans on your equipment. And so the bills are always there. The debt is always there,” Doran said.
For fishing families, Monique Coombs of the Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association highlighted the stress tied to the price of the catch and the cost of bringing it ashore.
“It's incredibly stressful. Lobstermen are pretty good at knowing how many lobsters they need to catch in order to make their bottom line. And so right now, a lot of that calculus is just not working for a lot of fishermen. Or it's getting to a point where it might not work,” Coombs said.
The report calls for permanent state funding for the proposed support program but does not specify a cost. As newly elected state lawmakers prepare to convene in Augusta next month, Sargent urged the public to take action now.
“We need you to check in on your neighbor. You know, check in on that farmer. Check in on that logger. A lot of us are isolated,” Sargent said.

title: Former MLB pitcher, ‘Olympus Has Fallen’ actor Lance Broadway dies at 43

title: How rare are 300-pound Maine bucks? This chart shows the biggest recorded
text:
This story was originally published in November 2025.
Many hunters are familiar with the “Big Buck Club,” which recognizes anyone who harvests a buck weighing at least 200 pounds with a patch and the distinction of joining an elite group of Maine deer hunters.
But far fewer realize how rare it is for a Maine deer to top 300 pounds field dressed. Only a handful have ever reached that milestone.
Troy Frye, who compiles and analyzes the state’s harvest records, regularly shares his findings on his Facebook page Maine Hunting History, Statistics and Charts. He also founded the group Allies of Traditional Maine Hunting.
Frye has spent the past 25 years documenting Maine’s deer harvest, and has made much of his work public over the last 12. His findings, shown in the table below, highlight the exceptionally large bucks that surpassed 300 pounds.
He compiled the chart by digging through decades of Maine Fish and Game magazines, which once published annual lists of the biggest bucks before The Maine Sportsman took over that tradition.
“There will always be people who say there were other 300-pound deer,” Frye said. While he doesn’t doubt those claims, he said he can only include deer verified in the Big Bucks of Maine Club list because otherwise there’s no proof. The club, founded in 1949, requires deer to be field dressed and weighed on a certified scale to qualify.
Frye notes that his statistics for the 2025 season are unofficial until the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife releases its final numbers in late spring 2026. His current figures come directly from the department’s dashboard — he’s simply presenting them in a more accessible format.
Based on the numbers so far, Frye believes Maine is on track for the highest deer harvest ever recorded.

title: Patriots QB Drake Maye has fractured right fibula
text:
Patriots quarterback Drake Maye doesn’t need surgery but still could miss the rest of the regular season because of a fractured right fibula, two people with knowledge of the injury told The Associated Press on Friday.
The defending AFC champion Patriots (5-5) also won’t have wide receiver A.J. Brown for several games because of a hamstring injury, a third person with knowledge of his injury told the AP.
All the people spoke on condition of anonymity because the team hasn’t provided details.
Tests revealed Maye didn’t sustain ligament damage in the ankle, one of the people said. He was injured on a sack by Aidan Hutchinson in New England’s 35-10 loss to Detroit in Germany. Hutchinson tore his ACL after the play when he jumped up to celebrate.
Maye, who was runner-up to Matthew Stafford for the AP NFL MVP award last season, has thrown for 2,330 yards, 18 touchdowns, and 11 interceptions with a 65.6% completion rate and 97.0 passer rating. He has 230 rushing yards and three rushing TDs.
Brown, who was acquired from Philadelphia for a 2028 first-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick, was expected to be New England’s No. 1 receiver. He missed four games with a high ankle sprain suffered in Week 1 and two more games with a knee injury. Brown has 11 catches for 128 yards in four games.

title: Affordable housing project breaks ground in Windham
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Developers broke ground this week on Pettingill Pines, a 48-unit affordable housing community in Windham aimed at older adults.
All 48 apartments at Pettingill Pines are reserved for people age 55 and older earning 60% or less of the median area income, with rents set well below market rates for North Windham. The income and age restrictions will be locked in for a minimum of 45 years.
Amenities at the complex include a community room that opens onto an outdoor patio, raised garden beds, fitness room, laundry facilities and easy access to businesses in North Windham.
Meg Robinson, a project manager at Developers Collaborative, said Pettingill Pines has been in development since early 2022, when the Roman Catholic Diocese of Portland expressed interest in selling church-owned land in North Windham. This was part of the Yes In God’s Backyard movement, in which religious organizations convert underused land for affordable housing projects.
One of the most significant challenges the project faced was dealing with requirements set by the Build America Buy America Act, which requires that certain materials used in construction, such as iron and steel, be manufactured in the United States. Robinson said the law presents substantial challenges for affordable housing development, as certain essential building materials are not readily available in the United States. Developers Collaborative applied for a waiver to use foreign-made heating and cooling equipment, which was granted in May.
At the groundbreaking, Tom Bartell, Windham’s economic development director, praised the perseverance of the developers in bringing the project to life, and noted that Pettingill Pines is part of the town’s larger vison for its 21st Century Downtown Plan. The plan was conceived in 2013, and seeks to improve transportation and economic development in North Windham.
Pettingill Pines is one of several housing projects in the works in Windham, including a 172-unit development on Tandberg Trail and an apartment complex adjacent to Dormir hotel.
Construction on the development is expected to take 14 months, with the first residents ariving in early 2028. The total budget for the project is roughly $17.3 million.
Correction: An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated the name of the developer, Developers Collaborative.

title: Scammers target Noah Kahan fans with a fake show at L.L.Bean’s Maine campus
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
L.L.Bean is known for its summer concerts, which draw national musical acts to its Freeport store each year.
So when Lauren Libby, of Brunswick, saw an Eventbrite listing in her Facebook feed for a June 12 performance by singer-songwriter Noah Kahan outside the L.L.Bean flagship store, she bought two tickets.
Then she had second thoughts.
“I was impulsive and foolish and I fell for it, and now I’m living with embarrassment,” she said.
Libby contacted Eventbrite through its live chat, called L.L.Bean to report what had happened and canceled the credit card she had used. Her bank helped her file a claim, and a refund was issued.
She wasn’t the only one who fell for the scam. The event, called Summer Camp featuring Noah Kahan, was promoted through a Facebook post that included a link to buy tickets for $50 each. The post quickly gained traction.
The scam was exposed about 24 hours later. There was no Kahan concert at L.L.Bean. In fact, he’s scheduled to perform at a sold-out show in Buffalo, New York, on June 12.
On Nov. 14, the L.L.Bean Flagship Store Facebook page posted a warning that the company was aware of the fraudulent Eventbrite listing. L.L.Bean has hosted free outdoor summer concerts for years, featuring national acts, and does not sell tickets for those shows.
“The listing has no affiliation with L.L.Bean and no such event is occurring at our Flagship campus. Once it was discovered we immediately notified Eventbrite and they have disabled the listing,” the statement said.
The post encouraged people to check L.L.Bean’s website to verify events before registering through third-party posts or links.
According to a statement an Eventbrite spokesperson made to Rolling Stone magazine, the listing was removed, the organizer was identified as an unauthorized seller and the account was locked. The spokesperson also said no money was paid to the fake organizer and that everyone who purchased a ticket had been refunded. The timing of refunds may vary depending on the buyer’s bank.
Kahan and L.L.Bean have collaborated before, lending some credibility to the idea that the popular singer might show up on the store’s front lawn. The two released a line of apparel and accessories in 2025.
The closest Kahan will actually get to Maine while he’s on the tour is Fenway Park in Boston, where all six of his concerts scheduled for May and June are sold out.
Going forward, Libby said, she’ll be more cautious. She does take some comfort in the fact she bought real tickets to one of Kahan’s Boston shows.
Linda Carrigan Chaisson, of Poland, was also scammed into buying two tickets to the fake show.
She knew about L.L.Bean’s free summer concerts, but wasn’t initially suspicious that this particular show carried a price tag.
“I thought ‘Wow,’ that’s really nice of them to do this since nobody can get tickets to his shows,” she said.
Carrigan Chaisson logged into her Eventbrite account and found the tickets waiting for her.
“Everything looked normal,” she said.
Once she realized Kahan would be performing elsewhere on that date, she called her bank to report the suspected scam. A few days later, after the charge went through, she disputed it and received a refund.
Even so, the experience left her feeling embarrassed.
“I worked in IT for 30 years, so I felt really stupid,” she said. “I spent years teaching people how not to get scammed.”

title: Vigil held for 17-year-old killed in Waldoboro hit-and-run
text:
Vigil held for 17-year-old killed in Waldoboro hit-and-run on Friendship Road
Brody Sawyer had a love for family, friends, and fishing, according to his grandfather
Vigil held for 17-year-old killed in Waldoboro hit-and-run on Friendship Road
Brody Sawyer had a love for family, friends, and fishing, according to his grandfather
Dozens gathered for a vigil on Thursday to remember Brody Sawyer, the 17-year-old killed in a Waldoboro hit-and-run on Friendship Road. The crowd said prayers, shared memories, and called for justice.
"We have never seen anything like this here. I am just in shock," said Jennifer Powers, a family friend and organizer of the vigil.
Sawyer was killed when Gifford Campbell, 53, veered into the right lane where Sawyer was walking. Investigators said Campbell did not stop and kept on driving after hitting Sawyer with his pickup truck.
"I have a lot of memories that I can't put into words right now without tearing up," said Chris Collins, Sawyer's grandfather.
Collins said he and his grandson loved to fish and hang out together, and got out on the water a few times this past summer. Collins also said Sawyer loved his family, girlfriend, and cat. Friends at the vigil also shared memories and spoke about how much Sawyer will be missed at school and around town.
"It's worse when it is a child, and seeing his friends all so young saying this person was taken from the Earth way too soon," Powers said.
Campbell has been charged with manslaughter, operating under the influence of drugs resulting in death and leaving the scene of an accident resulting in death. He is being held at the Two Bridge Regional Jail and is scheduled to appear in court on Friday.
"I hope that guy gets what he deserves," Collins said.
A GoFundMe page has been set up for Sawyer's family to help them cover funeral expenses.

title: A Maine district is releasing students early Wednesdays because of teacher cuts
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Augusta students will be released early from school on Wednesdays for the rest of the year.
That’s because the Augusta School Department has cut 39 positions over the last two years to reduce the impact on taxpayers, according to Superintendent Michael Tracy.
“It was a thoughtful effort, but we have come to see that the reductions have stretched our staff very thin,” Tracy said in a letter to the school community. He noted that the staffing cuts have led to “real fatigue and burnout.”
The Augusta school board this week approved a plan to release students early on Wednesdays beginning Dec. 9 and doing so for the rest of the year.
“Our teachers need our support to do their best work for your child, and the most meaningful way we can give it is by giving them more time: time to plan, to collaborate, and to meet the needs of every student in their classroom,” Tracy wrote.
Maine has been facing a yearslong shortage of teachers, as well as other staff, including bus drivers. A shortage of bus drivers has prompted the Bangor School Department to cut bus routes recently.
In Augusta, a conservative-led City Council has pushed for deep cuts to reduce the tax burden in the capital city. Earlier this year, after pressure from the City Council, the school board proposed $2.5 million in cuts that would eliminate several teaching, social work and administrative positions and introduce a “pay to play” system for athletes on the hockey team.
Tracy told the board during a June meeting that, even before the newest proposed cuts, “I already think we’ve gone too deep.”

title: Would Ed Muskie have voted for BAAJA? No.
text:
If Maine’s legendary environmental champion, Sen. Ed Muskie, were still serving in Congress, would he vote for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA)? I think the answer is “No.”
Muskie understood that economic prosperity and environmental protection aren’t competing goals. As the principal architect of the Clean Air Act and a driving force behind the Clean Water Act, he helped establish a simple but powerful principle: America’s natural resources should be protected for future generations, not sacrificed for short-term economic gains. BAAJA, however, would dramatically weaken the Clean Water Act by severely limiting state and tribal rights to protect their own local waters. It would also weaken the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act, limiting opportunities for public input and reducing safeguards for wildlife and public health.
Muskie was a bipartisan legislator who believed in finding practical solutions, but he also understood that environmental laws must have teeth. He would likely support making permitting more efficient, but not at the expense of the protections he spent his career building. It’s possible to build the infrastructure we need without damaging the bodies of water we love. Clean energy and grid investments must preserve safeguards for clean water, wildlife and the communities affected by development.
Maine should expect better than a bill that trades away environmental safeguards in the name of expediency. I believe Ed Muskie would agree.
Ivy Frignoca
Portland

title: Fighting human trafficking while supporting brides on a budget
text:
BEAVERTON, Ore. (InvestigateTV) - Fighting human trafficking one wedding dress at a time. That is the mission of Adorned in Grace.
Berg is the Oregon Regional Director for Compassion Connect, Inc., the nonprofit oversight and resource center for Adorned in Grace.
For soon to be bride Marina Rael, it was the affordability that brought her through the doors, but it was the mission that made leaving with her perfect dress even more special.
“It’s definitely a plus to get something for such a special day but also have it go towards a great cause,” said Rael. “This place is open to every budget too, so it’s a really accessible location for all brides.”
The average cost of a wedding dress in 2026 is $2,250 according to analysis from wedding planning website Zola. That price doesn’t include alterations, undergarments, accessories, and cleaning, which can add an additional $800-1,200 to the total cost.
“Some just can’t afford these elaborate weddings. They are here because they also have a need. They only have a certain budget,” said Mardie Figueroa, volunteer developer and store manager.
Figueroa has been with Adorned in Grace since 2022 and is just one of many volunteers that without, the boutique would not be able to run.
“It’s not about selling a dress; it’s about making them feel wonderful in the dress they have selected,” said Figueroa. “When you see a bride that smiles, when you see the party and they all start crying, you know you took part in that. That’s what we are all about.”
Adorned in Grace has dresses of every style and every size, with new dresses arriving daily. And it’s not just bridal gowns, you can also find bridesmaid dresses, flower girl dresses, mother of the bride dresses, and dresses for any other formal occasion.
“I have some beautiful dresses that I wore to my daughter and son’s weddings, and I didn’t want them to go to just anywhere. I wanted it to be purposeful,” said Dawn Staoffel.
Staoffel loaded her dresses into the car and drove from Northern California with her dog to donate her dresses to Adorned in Grace.
“I love it and I would love for somebody else to have the joy that I did,” said Staoffel. “I had a lot of help getting the dress with support from the family and making sure it was the right choice for the weddings I wore them at so hopefully someone else will find the same excitement and joy of that.”
Adorned in Grace also carries veils, belts, shoes, jewelry, and other wedding accessories. There are two bridal boutique locations in Beaverton, Oregon and Mesa, Arizona. Then in Gresham, Oregon, another boutique specializing in formalwear.
From shopping, to donating, and volunteering, there are plenty of ways to get involved with Adorned in Grace.
