title: Ski mountains wait for colder temperatures before firing up snow guns
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ski mountains wait for colder temperatures before firing up snow guns
Mt. Abram says that they typically don't open until mid-December, but they like to have started making snow by now.
Ski mountains wait for colder temperatures before firing up snow guns
Mt. Abram says that they typically don't open until mid-December, but they like to have started making snow by now.
Looking up at Mount Abram from the main ski cabin, there's no snow as far as the eye can see. On Thursday, temperatures reached 60 degrees.
"If we had the temperatures, we would probably be making snow right now," said Allie Masten, the director of marketing for Mount Abram Ski Area & Bike Park.
For the last several years, the mountain has had its opening day the week before Christmas. Despite the warm temperatures, staff aren't worried about missing that timeframe this year.
They usually don't get worried until around Thanksgiving if they haven't fired up the snow guns yet.
"We don't try and fight against Mother Nature. We will wait patiently for her to decide it's time," Masten said.
Other mountains, like Sugarloaf and Sunday River, typically aim for earlier start times around mid-November or earlier. However, both mountains appear not to be opening quite yet, with high temperatures in the forecast until next week.
New England Ski History is a site that keeps track of the opening and closing days for ski resorts in the area. According to its data from the past 20 years, the latest Sunday River has opened is Nov. 23 in 2016. For Sugarloaf, it was Nov. 29 in 2008. Sunday River has typically opened the earliest, with some years getting chairlifts running around mid-October.
Mt. Abram, which nearly always starts in mid-December, has been keeping busy this month on its warm days.
Snow makers have been making sure the system is ready to go for when it's really needed. Veteran snow makers have also been training new recruits on how to make sure the system is running properly and avoiding any leaks.
On a warm day like Thursday, crews will walk up and down the mountain blowing water and compressed air through the pipes of the snow-making equipment.
"[They're] making sure everything is clean," Masten said. "It's literally blowing the cobwebs out."
Masten says it not only needs to be cold to run the snow guns, but ideally it also needs to be dry to get fluffy snow.
"We're hoping that next week it'll cool off and we can really get everything going, but ideally, it would be now," she said.

title: Ex-gun parts maker settles with family in fatal Brooks shooting
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A California company that made gun parts has settled with the family of a man who was fatally shot in Brooks in 2022.
MDX Corp. was one of three defendants in a lawsuit by Billi-Jo Cluney on behalf of her deceased husband James Cluney Sr., who was killed May 6, 2022, in Brooks by Atilio Delgado.
Delgado, who was 16 at the time, had been taken in by the family. He was tried as a teen, pleaded guilty to murder in 2025 and was sentenced to 25 years in prison.
Billi-Jo Cluney subsequently filed a wrongful death lawsuit against gun parts makers MDX and Brownells, Inc., and FedEx, who delivered the parts to Delgado.
MDX, which operated as MDX Arms before closing in May, made parts for so-called “ghost guns,” which are assembled from unregistered components.
Delgado allegedly bought the gun parts online from MDX and Brownells for around $600, using prepaid gift cards, according to the lawsuit, which accused the companies of selling the gun parts to Delgado without verifying he was legally allowed to buy guns.
The court dismissed MDX from the case with prejudice on Tuesday, Nov. 17. The amount the company paid to Cluney in settlement is confidential, according to attorney Peter Richard of Garmey Law, who represents Billi-Jo Cluney and her husband’s estate.
“For the Cluney family, knowing that the company that sold the components used to
build the gun that killed James is no longer in business brings some measure of
comfort,” Richard said in a statement Friday. “But the settlement with MDX resolves only one part of this case.”
The lawsuit continues against the two remaining defendants, Richard said.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Extreme Drought Conditions Expand Across The County, Rain Chances Increase for Monday
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Thursday. It was certainly another enjoyable day across Northern Maine and Western New Brunswick, especially when you consider we’re now just a week away from Thanksgiving! We’ve still got a few more days of above-average temperatures to enjoy before we see some significant changes in our weather pattern early next week. Unfortunately, the latest drought monitor report released this morning wasn’t all that encouraging, although our chances of seeing some beneficial rainfall early next week are beginning to look a little better than they did yesterday.
Heading into the overnight hours tonight, we’re looking at another fairly mild night across the region with partly cloudy skies. Temperatures will generally settle into the mid to upper 30s and lower 40s, with overnight lows of 39 degrees in Caribou, 41 degrees in Presque Isle, and 37 degrees in Houlton. Once again, we’re looking at overnight low temperatures in some communities that are actually warmer than where our afternoon high temperatures should be for this time of year! Winds will be out of the southwest at around 5 to 10 mph, with occasional gusts up to 20 mph.
We’ll see another nice day across the region on Friday, with plenty of sunshine and temperatures climbing into the lower to upper 50s. I’m forecasting a high of 55 degrees in both Caribou and Presque Isle, with 57 degrees in Houlton. Some of our communities in Western New Brunswick could even approach 60 degrees. The one difference from what we experienced today will be the return of some breezier conditions, with winds out of the west at around 10 to 15 mph and gusts up to 25 mph. A weak cold front will be working its way through the region during the afternoon hours, although I don’t expect we’ll see any precipitation associated with its passage.
We will notice the passage of that cold front as we head into Friday night, with temperatures falling back below the freezing mark across much of Northern Maine. Most communities will see overnight lows in the upper 20s and lower 30s, with some additional cloud cover developing later in the night. We’ll also need to watch for some patchy fog developing after midnight and lingering into the early morning hours on Saturday.
While Saturday will be a little cooler than what we’ve been experiencing over the past couple of days, we’re still going to be looking at temperatures that are well above average for this time of year. Afternoon highs will generally range from the mid to upper 40s to around 50 degrees, with a mixture of sunshine and clouds expected throughout the day. Temperatures will climb back into the lower to mid 50s on Sunday, with another decent amount of sunshine expected before cloud cover begins to build back into the region Sunday night.
Unfortunately, there was some disappointing news in this morning’s drought monitor update. We continue to see extreme drought conditions expanding across northwestern portions of Aroostook County, with those conditions now extending farther east and encompassing a larger portion of the North Maine Woods. Severe drought conditions remain in place across much of the rest of The County, with moderate drought conditions confined to portions of southern Aroostook County.
To give you an idea of just how much things have changed over the course of the past week, 19.11% of Aroostook County was classified as being in an extreme drought last week. As of this morning’s report, that number has increased to 38.13%, essentially doubling the amount of The County experiencing extreme drought conditions in just one week’s time. Another 46.12% of The County remains in a severe drought, meaning more than 84% of Aroostook County is now experiencing severe or extreme drought conditions. As much as I’ve been enjoying this stretch of warmer weather and sunshine, we really do need to see a change in this pattern. Fortunately, there are some slightly more encouraging trends in our forecast guidance for early next week.
I’m continuing to monitor the development of a coastal low pressure system that will be working its way up the eastern seaboard late this weekend and into Monday. Over the past 24 hours, some of our forecast guidance has been trending farther west with the track of that system, which would allow more moisture to work its way into Northern Maine. The latest outlook from the Weather Prediction Center suggests the potential for around half an inch to three-quarters of an inch of precipitation across portions of eastern and central Aroostook County, with amounts approaching an inch across some of our southern communities. Unfortunately, some of the areas across northwestern Aroostook County that need the precipitation the most are still looking at considerably lower amounts.
There’s still some uncertainty regarding exactly how close that system will track to the region, so I wouldn’t get too attached to any particular rainfall totals just yet. However, I’m a little more optimistic about our chances of seeing some beneficial rainfall on Monday than I was earlier this week. It’s certainly not going to bring an end to our drought, but at this point, we’ll take whatever precipitation we can get!
I’d certainly take advantage of the warmer weather we’ve got sticking around through the weekend while we have it! For a closer look at the forecast, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening everyone!

title: Support for Pan Am pilots shows how Susan Collins has fought for ‘forgotten Americans’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Ron Fitch of Poland is a senior pilot who flew for the military before spending more than 23 years flying for Pan Am.
I believe Sen. Susan Collins cares and has a legacy of fighting for the “forgotten American.” She has consistently demonstrated her support for justice for Mainers and those who support our country’s values.
She has led the Senate effort to pass the Justice for the Living Victims of Lockerbie Act. I am a proud Maine resident and a member of a group of 50 senior Pan Am pilots who lost our careers, pensions, healthcare and savings when the airline went bankrupt following Libya’s terrorist bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland on Dec. 21, 1988.
Following the bombing, people stopped flying Pan Am, forcing its closure. We’d spent an average of 23 years with Pan Am following military service. Airline seniority rules and the then federal requirement that pilots retire at 60 kept us from finding jobs as pilots elsewhere — the only career for which we were trained.
My family and others in our group lost everything they’d saved. Some families lost their homes. Children were pulled out of college. Our families were left without the security we had spent decades working to achieve.
For years, we have been trying to recoup a fraction of our losses from funds paid by Libya to compensate victims of its terrorism. The legislation spearheaded by Collins has been our last hope for what is left in the Libya paid humanitarian fund. The funds left over, all other claims having been paid, should not be expropriated by the government.
Our group is eternally grateful to Sen. Collins for her continued advocacy on our behalf. Collins and her team helped pass this bill unanimously in the Senate in the last days of an earlier session of Congress. Unfortunately, the bill passed on the last day of that Congress, too late to be considered in the House. In the remaining legislative days in the 119th Congress, we hope to finally take our bill across the finish line, led by Collins.
We believe this legislation is a win for Collins and all of us in Maine for important reasons: It is humanitarian and bipartisan, it includes no taxpayer funds, and it uses only what is left over from the humanitarian fund paid by Libya — all other claims having been paid. It supports seniors and veterans and delivers justice and recognition to “forgotten Americans” victimized by state-sponsored terrorism.
Our group is now elderly and deserves to be recognized by our country for what terrorism stole from us. If justice is further delayed, it will be denied. The senior Pan Am pilots and so many others in our great state, thank Sen. Collins for her unwavering advocacy for Americans otherwise forgotten by their country.

title: Possible gunman on campus at Quinnipiac University
text:
Campus alert sent out for possible gunman at Quinnipiac University
Quinnipiac University in Hamden, Connecticut, sent a campus alert for a possible gunman on campus around 9 p.m. on Thursday.
The university urged students to stay indoors as police patrolled the area on its social media accounts.

title: How to keep the peace when grandparents don’t get along
text:
(Aging Untold) — Not every set of grandparents will naturally get along. Different backgrounds, beliefs or old conflicts can create tension, especially during holidays, birthdays and major family events.
There are ways that families can manage those relationships while keeping the child’s well-being at the center.
Keep the child’s well-being first
“That’s the key right there. Keep the child’s well-being at the center,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said. “You can keep your opinions to yourself long enough to get through a birthday party, or a wedding or an event or a holiday.”
Cradduck said children learn from how adults behave around them.
“The only way they’re going to see good role modeling is for you not to go into battle, even if it’s your divorced spouse,” Cradduck said. “You just don’t have to get into family issues right there in front of them.”
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said this is about everyone, including the children.
“Let’s have some peace. Let’s have some grace. Let’s be mature adults. Have some emotional intelligence for heaven’s sake and get along,” Ambrose said.
Set ground rules for tough topics
Grandparents do not have to get along to be good grandparents, aging expert Amy O’Rourke said. If certain conversations create tension, she said, families can agree on topics that are allowed and topics that are not.
“Let’s keep food recipes on the table. Let’s keep birthday parties on the table. But religion, politics, anything that escalates, just keep it off the table,” O’Rourke said. “So set up some ground rules that make it work for everybody.”
Show children what respect looks like
Children notice when adults are not getting along, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
“They know what’s going on and they know that you’re not getting along. They hear the comments,” Rogers said. “One of the greatest gifts that you can give them is to show them what respect looks like when you get along with someone that you don’t agree with.”
Cradduck said differing belief systems can exist side by side.
“Maybe if you would just open up your mind a little bit and listen to somebody else’s belief systems, you might grow to respect that person a little bit more,” she said.
Split holidays and weekends if needed
If conflict continues after families have tried to resolve it, O’Rourke said, separate arrangements can help.
“If it’s just not working, make arrangements that holidays or weekends are separate,” O’Rourke said. “If you’ve done everything you can and it’s not getting any better, then just say OK this weekend’s going to be open for this set, this weekend’s going to be open for another set.”
Grandparents can create smaller, more intimate celebrations if large holiday gatherings feel too big, O’Rourke said. She gave the example of a grandparent telling grandchildren that Christmas with them will be in July.
Ambrose said she would not wait until July to celebrate with family.
“I would just rather get along with everybody and blend our families together,” she said. “When it really counts, when we’re doing deathbed vigils and things like that, we have to support each other.”
Keep the parents’ marriage separate
Cradduck added that grandparents’ disagreements should not affect their children’s marriages.
“Don’t cause your children’s marriage to have issues because you don’t get along with their parents or with who they married,” Cradduck said.
Include others and let families build traditions
Ambrose encouraged families to combine gatherings when possible and include widows and others who may be left out of holiday meals.
“Be inclusive and let’s bring families together,” she said.
Cradduck said to let your children develop their own traditions.
“Allow your children to develop their traditions with their kids,” Cradduck said. “If those traditions are to follow yours, great. That’s fine, let them come on over and let them be part of that, but if they choose to stay away and to have traditions and time with just their children, go over and see them. Don’t exclude yourself because they want to do something different than you always did.”
Cradduck said not to make your angst someone else’s issue.
Key takeaways
- Grandparents don’t have to agree on politics or parenting, but the grandchild should never become the battleground.
- Focus on shared love for the child rather than being right.
- Establish clear ground rules that leave sensitive topics at the door.
- Keep disagreements between grandparents separate from the grandchild’s parents’ marriage.
- Split holidays when keeping the peace matters most.

title: Top Maine football state championship storylines to follow
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
We’ve reached the end of the line. State championship weekend is here for 11-man football, and eight teams that are a combined 75-8 this season should provide us with some great action.
There’s plenty to discuss ahead of the games Saturday at Fitzpatrick Stadium in Portland and at Don Roux Field in Lewiston. So, let’s dive into some of the biggest storylines ahead of four Gold Ball games.
CLASS A
Bonny Eagle (10-1) vs. Oxford Hills (9-1)
at Fitzpatrick Stadium in Portland
11 a.m. Saturday
• Bonny Eagle has big-play ability. And it’s not just from quarterback Lucas Klehn, who ran for 170 yards and four TDs on only 10 carries when the Scots played arguably their most complete game of the season in a 45-6 romp against Oxford Hills in Week 6. In that game, Bonny Eagle had eight plays of at least 20 yards and went to a hurry-up offense early, putting extra stress on Oxford Hills’ big linemen. It worked to the tune of 497 yards. Bonny Eagle and coach Kevin Cooper are 7-0 in state championship games. The Scots haven’t been there since 2019.
• Keegan Ridley (854 yards, 10 touchdowns) only played defense against Bonny Eagle when the two teams met last month. Given how much the junior running back has impacted his team’s offensive success, especially in its last two games against Bangor and Windham where he’s tallied five touchdowns, the Vikings may have a chance against the Scots with him playing on both sides of the ball.
CLASS B
Marshwood (9-1) vs. Cony (9-1)
at Fitzpatrick Stadium in Portland
2:30 p.m. Saturday
• Marshwood and first-year coach Andrew Elwell are looking to etch themselves into the school’s rich football history. The Hawks have won 22 state football championships. Rod Wotton, the first coach to win a Lobster Bowl, led Marshwood to 16 titles across all four classes from 1966-89. Alex Rotsko, who retired in June, won six crowns in seven seasons from 2014-21. Fullback Greg Castoras can stake a legitimate Fitzpatrick Trophy claim with a big game. Castoras, also an outside linebacker, has rushed for 1,795 yards and 26 touchdowns despite missing the regular-season finale because of an injury. Those numbers compare favorably to Marshwood’s three previous Fitzy winners who finished as champions: Steve Knight (1989, 1,454 yards), Brett Gerry (2014, 2,263 yards) and Justin Bryant (2019, 1,522 yards).
• In a state championship game, you want a player who doesn’t make mistakes. Cony quarterback Drew Lindquist fits that description. The junior has thrown only one interception this season compared to 27 touchdown passes. With star running back Anderson Noyes again injured, you can expect the Rams to go to the air. If Cony’s receivers can make the plays they did against Fryeburg Academy in the North final, the Rams could have a successful formula.
CLASS C
Hermon (9-2) vs. Leavitt (11-0)
at Lewiston High School
2:30 p.m. Saturday
• Leavitt’s 14-10 win over Hermon on Oct. 23 was the closest game of the season for both teams. The Hawks held a 10-0 lead at halftime. Both teams feature players who have previously competed in a state championship game. Leavitt lost to Greely in last year’s Class C final, and Hermon fell to Fryeburg in 2024.
• The Hornets have been run-heavy all season, and they’ll likely lean on the ground game against the Hawks, especially with freshman Jamison Hutchinson taking over for injured starting quarterback Landon Marquis. Expect a high-volume day for Jeremiah McKenzie (872 yards rushing, 10 touchdowns). He and Darren Flagg (681 yards rushing, 564 yards receiving, 16 total touchdowns) are Leavitt’s offensive workhorses.
• Hermon’s running game is just as good. Making the other team pass will be the clear indicator of superiority. The Hawks, whose loss in the 2024 state final is their only other championship game appearance, are a very experienced team that plays with poise and purpose. Senior running back Sam Hopkins leads the way, and switching former wideout Griffin Dunton to a run-first QB has given Hermon an added weapon in the ground game. The defensive line is stout, led by Noah Romsberg on the edge and Hunter McDonald up the middle, and the back seven can fly to the ball.
CLASS D
Winthrop/Monmouth/Hall-Dale (9-1) vs. Winslow (9-1)
at Lewiston High School
11 a.m. Saturday
• This is a rematch of last year’s title game, won 41-14 by Winthrop — and if you’ve followed Class D football over the years, you’ve gotten used to state final rematches. Before the Ramblers and Black Raiders, Wells and Foxcroft battled for the Gold Ball in 2023 and 2024. Those teams also met in 2017 and 2018. Oak Hill and Maine Central Institute faced off in 2014 and 2015.
• You can expect these two teams to run the ball. In fact, by the time this game concludes, it’s possible that Winslow and Winthrop will each have two players with more than 1,000 rushing yards for the season. Michael Loubier (1,604 yards) and Isaac Bulger (1,255) have already surpassed that milestone for the Winslow. Carter Rand (1,073) has reached the mark for the Ramblers and Tristyan Ortiz (965) is close.
• Could Winthrop flip the script again? In last year’s state final, the run-happy Ramblers found a weakness in the Winslow secondary and exploited it. Quarterback Jacob Feith was 4 of 5 passing for 167 yards and two touchdowns, all in the first half. Don’t be shocked if Winthrop throws a curveball. Junior quarterback Porter Lavigne (86 of 142, 1,128 yards, 11 touchdowns, 6 interceptions) has the skills to distribute the ball in the air, with Lucas Rice (33 receptions, 597 yards, 5 touchdowns) and Clyde Moody (17 receptions, 281 yards, 5 touchdowns) the main targets.
• Winslow and Winthrop have both dealt with injuries but have gotten healthy at the right time. Senior defensive back Alyx Hardy returned to practice this week for Winslow after missing the North final, and junior lineman Noah Harding should also return. Senior running back and linebacker Ross Fichthorn, likely Winthrop’s best all-around player, returned two weeks ago against Morse.

title: How did a hat get into Fiona’s habitat, and why wasn’t surgery an option?
text:
CINCINNATI (AP) — Fiona, the hippo whose premature birth and fight for survival at the Cincinnati Zoo turned her into a global sensation nearly a decade ago, died Thursday from complications after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure. She was 9 years old.
Fiona swallowed the hat about 12 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air. A ceiling fan caught and deflected the hat into the hippo enclosure through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows.
It was an accident, zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley said.
Before Fiona died, Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health, said veterinarians had sedated her twice to evaluate her condition.
An ultrasound on Tuesday showed some bunching of her intestines, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy using a 9-foot (2.7-meter) scope but were unable to detect anything, he said.
The Association of Zoos and Aquariums, the accrediting body for facilities, said in a statement Thursday that the Cincinnati Zoo provided “extraordinary 24/7 care for Fiona throughout this heartbreaking event.”
Surgery would have been challenging
Surgery would have been a major logistical challenge — multiple incisions would have been needed during a very long surgery, as hippos are notoriously difficult to anesthetize and have thick skin, said Jack Kottwitz, assistant professor at Michigan State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine.
The hat and its blend of fibers posed a particular danger despite its relatively small size.
Experts said hippos have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants, and the system makes for a very large gastrointestinal tract through which anything would have to travel.
Jan Hawkins, doctor of veterinary medicine at North Carolina State University, said Fiona’s situation was difficult because it would have been hard to tell where in her body the hat was.
“You can’t do the normal imaging and things that you can do in some of the smaller animals, or even horses,” Hawkins said.
Zoos around the world have warned for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats. Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.

title: Aging Untold: How to keep the peace when grandparents don’t get along
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore how families can navigate conflict between grandparents on both sides, keep the peace and focus on what’s best for the grandchildren.
Then we look at how planning for aging can ease uncertainty and help protect independence.
Plus, we decode emoji and texting slang so parents and grandparents can better understand kids’ online conversations and support their safety.
When grandparents don’t get along, it can create tension, especially during holidays, birthdays and major family events.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said children learn from how adults behave around them. Families can manage those relationships by keeping the child’s well-being first, gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.
The Aging Untold experts are offering advice on how to do that along with setting ground rules for tough topics and showing children what respect looks like.
If conflict continues after families have tried to resolve it, aging expert Amy O’Rourke said separate arrangements can help.
Aging is normal. It is not a crisis, but it can become one without preparing for the help you or a loved one will need in the future.
The Aging Untold experts said everyone is aging, and a fall, hospitalization, new diagnosis or sudden need for care can quickly expose the lack of conversations about money, housing, insurance, caregiving and independence.
Learn what families can do ahead of time to ease into the care that comes with aging.
You might be familiar with LOL, BRB and many emojis, including hearts and thumbs-up. But some emojis and acronyms have hidden meanings that parents and grandparents might not know.
Jill Story said it is tough to stay on top of the abbreviated language her three daughters use.
“They have a whole language that they use that I’m constantly having to, like, figure out,” she said.
Story said some of the acronyms her daughters use are even more difficult to decipher.
The founder of For Working Parents, a former vice principal, detailed what he described as sinister emojis, symbols that could represent something different from what parents might think. The meanings range from drugs to sex to extremism.
Larry Coffin is a former history teacher. The 82-year-old is also a living link to the history of his town, Bradford, Vermont.
He serves as the curator of the Bradford Historical Society and writes about the history of the town and surrounding communities.
“To me, is like he’s still teaching,” Carolyn, his wife of 57 years, said.
Coffin said he does it because it keeps his brain active.

title: Northeastern Florida now under flood threats from storms that have devastated coastal communities
text:
Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday as forecasters warned flooding threats could stretch into next week when a major river is expected to crest well above record levels.
The National Weather Service posted flood warnings and watches stretching around 200 miles (320 kilometers) from just south of Melbourne to the Jacksonville area. Additional rainfall of 2 to 6 inches (5 to 15 centimeters) was expected through Saturday, while some areas could see an extra 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 centimeters).
“Severe, widespread flash flooding is expected,” the weather service said in a Friday morning forecast. “In addition, areas that normally do not experience flash flooding will flood. Furthermore, lives and property (are) in great danger.”
The St. Johns River, Florida’s longest, rose above a record level Thursday near Cocoa that was set in 1953. The river is forecast to stay at least 2 feet (61 centimeters) above flood stage through early next week, the weather service said.
Also Friday, a nontropical low-pressure system was expected to form and could become a subtropical or tropical storm along the southeastern U.S. coast, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said. The southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts should expect strong winds, dangerous surf and coastal flooding into early next week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
Parts of Florida’s east coast have been deluged with rainfall totaling more than 17 inches (43 centimeters) in some spots since Tuesday, according to preliminary totals by the weather service. That’s in addition to heavy rains that fell earlier this month. Several places have already seen their wettest November on record.
The storms shifted north to the Space Coast on Thursday, sending rivers over their banks and prompting water rescues of people and horses during what is supposed to be Florida’s dry season that runs from October to May.
“Never seen such a thing like this in Florida,” said Jazmin Foster, whose Melbourne home was inundated with water for the second time in two weeks.
In Brevard County on Thursday, people with trailers braved knee-deep water to rescue dozens of horses and other animals at the Blue Lake Equestrian Center, an animal hospice and boarding facility in Cocoa. The animals were taken to a dry pasture elsewhere.
First responders conducted nearly 100 high-water rescues across the county, and those numbers continued to climb, Sheriff Wayne Ivey said. The city of Palm Bay conducted mandatory evacuations for some residents of a mobile home community. Shelters were opened for residents forced from their homes.
Nearly 200 Florida National Guard personnel with 50 high-water vehicles have been deployed to help up and down the coast, the Division of Emergency Management said. Other responding agencies included about 235 officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.
This week’s storms have been fueled by persistent high pressure over Virginia and a low-pressure system and an associated stationary front in the Gulf, which together have pushed a steady onshore flow across the Florida Peninsula. They’re an offshoot of El Niño, the natural warming of the Pacific near the equator that warps weather patterns worldwide.
Forecasters said El Niño conditions are expected to persist through the spring, meaning the soggy extreme weather in Florida and California will likely continue through the winter.
The California coast, from the Los Angeles to San Francisco areas, was also swamped with flooding in many areas this week, leaving neighborhoods under water and forcing some drivers to abandon stalled vehicles in floodwaters. A long stretch of the coastal Highway 1 was closed south of the Monterey Peninsula due to rock and mud slides.
___
Associated Press writers Amy Taxin in Santa Ana, California, and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report.

title: Belmont Volunteer Fire Department receives donated truck from Boston Fire Department
text:
BELMONT, Maine (WABI) - The Belmont Volunteer Fire Department has a donated truck from the Boston Fire Department after losing a truck in the Robbins Lumber fire in May.
Belmont has been leaning on mutual aid since losing the truck, but the new to them truck will get the department back onto the front lines.
“We picked it up on July 3, and we’ve been working on it, getting it into service,” Ron Wellman, deputy chief of the Belmont Fire Department, said
As of two weeks ago, the truck is in service 200 miles from where it once served in Boston.
“It’s a big city truck. To bring it up here in little Belmont, Maine, is quite an honor to have a truck,” Wellman said.
Boston Fire Department donated the truck for free after hearing about Belmont losing the truck.
“We walked into the garage. They said, there it is. And take it home. And we did,” Ron Harford, chief of the Belmont Fire Department, said.
Harford said all of the stickers will stay on the truck even though it is no longer in Boston. He said that is a nod to the support the Boston Fire Department gave the department beyond the truck donation. That support included Boston traveling for Searsmont assistant fire chief Wayne Woodbury.
“Boston has been amazing. As you probably remember, A.C. Woodbury was actually a chief here before. He was on this department. He was the captain. The day that I joined, he welcomed me in. Just grew up with him. They brought up that amazing flag. The color guard units come up, did the service with us,” Harford said.
A few changes are being made to the decals. Harford said the tweaks will honor the trucks previous life.
“All of the Boston rigs have Boston written up there. So we thought it was only appropriate that we have a little bit of added to it. It just says, from Boston, and thank you,” Harford said.
The thank you will be on the front of the truck, but the back of the truck will have a subtle nod to the incident that destroyed the first truck. Harford said the ‘stay back 300 feet’ on the back of the truck will honor the date of the Robbins Lumber fire.
“In the city, it’s only 300 feet, because 500 could be two city blocks. This is going to be changed out to keep back 515 feet in honor of May 15, the day it all happened,” Harford said.
Harford said things may not be normal again after Searsmont, but getting the truck is a step in the right direction.
“It’ll never be normal. It will never, ever be normal. But yes, to that point, yes. I mean, the station, around the station and during meeting nights and training nights is a lot more active,” Harford said.

title: Lewiston taps public input to help shape city's future
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The nonprofit Downtown Lewiston Association is hosting a series of conversations with residents and business owners to help shape how the city can build on its strengths and expand its economy.
The first session, held earlier this week, focused on what Lewiston should be known for. Breakout groups discussed what makes the city unique and what it should be known for, particularly as it seeks to encourage people to visit, start a business or make Lewiston their home.
Samantha Herriot, director of engagement for the Lewiston Auburn Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce, said the conversations highlighted a wide range of strengths and opportunities, including Lewiston’s arts and cultural community, its diverse restaurant scene, its affordability and its history and architecture.
Participants also noted “the grit, resilience and strong work ethic of its people,” she said.
The listening sessions are part of the Downtown Lewiston Association’s mission to bring the community together and celebrate the downtown’s assets. Sessions are set to be held quarterly.
The association invites business owners, residents, employees and anyone who lives, works or spends time downtown to participate. The next session will be in February, with the date to be confirmed.
‘Collaborative efforts’
Lewiston’s downtown has been designated as a Maine Downtown Affiliate Community through the Maine Development Foundation’s Maine Downtown Center.
The downtown association is now organizing around the four pillars of the nationally recognized Main Street America approach: economic vitality, design, promotion and organization.
Each pillar has a committee focused on advancing Lewiston’s downtown revitalization.
“Right now, the entire board and all committee members are volunteers, so the DLA welcomes community members who want to get involved and volunteer to be part of the effort,” Herriot said.
“The goal is to turn these conversations into collaborative efforts that support downtown businesses, celebrate Lewiston’s identity and encourage investment and activity downtown.”

title: Merchant mariners of the Vietnam War deserve full veteran status
text:
Capt. Roger E. Haines, a graduate of Maine Maritime Academy in Castine, served as third mate and second officer aboard the SS Exton, chief replenishment officer aboard USNS Marias, LTJG USNR (Ret.), and retired as a Panama Canal pilot, senior port captain and canal operations captain.
Sixty years ago, in June 1966, a total of 102 young men graduated from Maine Maritime Academy in Castine. Armed with U.S. Coast Guard licenses and commissions in the U.S. Naval Reserve, my classmates and I stepped directly from the commencement stage into the dangerous machinery of wartime logistics.
This past July, 13 surviving members of our class gathered at Castine for our 60th reunion. We remembered those who could no longer make the journey, and those who have passed away. As has been true for decades, our conversation inevitably turned to an unresolved piece of history: the long-overdue formal recognition of civilian merchant mariners who served under fire in the combat zones of the Vietnam War.
When the military sealift required rapid expansion, the National Shipping Authority reactivated World War II-era Victory ships and placed them under general agency agreements. Deck officers like myself were required to hold naval commissions to sign on. As third mate and later second officer aboard the SS Exton, I completed four supply runs into the Vietnam combat theater between 1966 and 1968.
Our cargo was not routine freight. We loaded high explosives at Military Ocean Terminal Sunny Point, North Carolina — bombs, artillery shells, landmines, and white phosphorus incendiary devices. We circumnavigated the globe via the Suez Canal shortly before its historic closure during the 1967 Arab-Israeli War, navigated the Panama Canal, and brought volatile ordnance directly into hostile waters.
In South Vietnam, we took fully loaded ammunition ships up the winding, narrow Long Tàu River through the Rung Sat Special Zone — a waterway infamous for Viet Cong riverbank ambushes and mines.
In 1968, aboard the Exton, we delivered the mobile equipment for the U.S. Army’s 458th Transportation Company to establish a new outpost at Vung Ro Bay. We dropped anchor in an unsecured, enemy-controlled bay, drawing small-arms rifle fire from the shore while waiting days for security forces and landing craft to offload our cargo.
Later in my career, I served as chief replenishment officer aboard the USNS Marias, refueling U.S. Navy warships at sea in the Persian Gulf and Mediterranean, before serving as a Panama Canal pilot, senior port captain and canal operations captain.
A small detachment of active-duty military personnel sailed aboard our vessels alongside us. They performed their duty honorably and earned full veteran status, military healthcare and GI Bill benefits for their service in the combat zone. Yet the civilian mariners standing the exact same watches, carrying the exact same high explosives and drawing the exact same enemy fire were classified strictly as civilian employees.
A clear national precedent exists for righting this wrong. Decades after World War II concluded, Congress and the Department of Defense recognized the extraordinary sacrifices of World War II merchant mariners, finally granting them full veteran status. The mariners who crewed sealift vessels during the Vietnam War answered the same call, operated under the same military oversight, and faced the same operational hazards.
Our mariner brothers of WWII waited four decades for full recognition for their service.
We have been waiting for six decades.
I am fortunate to enjoy good health and a comfortable pension. But as president of the Maine Maritime Academy Class of 1966, I speak for those classmates who are no longer here and those surviving mariners who have struggled without the recognition and care they earned.
We urge Maine’s congressional delegation, the Department of Transportation and the Maritime Administration to support legislation extending full veteran status to the merchant mariners of the Vietnam War. Maine has always sent her finest to sea in times of national crisis. It is time our nation fully honors the mariners who carried the line in Southeast Asia.

title: Famed Marine Corps veteran under federal investigation over undisclosed allegations
text:
LAS VEGAS (AP) — A celebrated Marine Corps veteran who became famous for his heroism during the Iraq War is under criminal investigation for undisclosed allegations, the Naval Criminal Investigative Service confirmed Friday.
CBS News first reported that retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal is under investigation over allegations stemming from his time as an ROTC assistant at a high school in Henderson, Nevada. The Naval Criminal Investigative Service, which is the Navy’s lead for felony-level criminal investigations, declined to provide further details to The Associated Press.
Kasal is a well-known veteran who earned the Navy Cross — the second-highest award for heroism for members of the Navy and the Marines — for his actions during combat operations in Fallujah, Iraq. Kasal was wounded in 2004 while fighting and shielding an injured Marine from a grenade. An iconic photo capturing the moment that soldiers helped carry Kasal inspired sculptures that were displayed at Marine Corps base camps.
The Clark County School District, which oversees hundreds of schools in the Las Vegas area, confirmed that Kasal worked at the Basic Academy of International Studies as an ROTC assistant. He was hired in August 2018 and resigned in August 2025, the district said.
In an email to Basic Academy families, the district said it was aware of the investigation into the former employee and said the former employee is no longer on campus. The district added that it will “cooperate fully with any investigation.”
The AP left text and voicemail messages Friday at a cellphone number for Kasal. CBS News said he did not respond to its own attempts to seek comment.
Some former students interviewed by CBS News praised him as a caring instructor who devoted time, energy and resources to his students. Other cadets claimed to the outlet that Kasal would take a select group of female cadets to get Starbucks.
Damien Greenwell, a 22-year-old who participated in the program from 2018 to 2022, told CBS News that he questioned some of Kasal’s conduct over the years and his behavior toward students could be interpreted as inappropriate by an outside observer.
Estella Deleon, a cadet who graduated in 2022, told the AP she was “baffled” by the investigation into Kasal and she never witnessed inappropriate behavior by him. Kasal always made himself available to cadets if they needed someone to talk to, she said, and he taught them important life lessons she still thinks about.
Deleon, 22, said Kasal would take everyone to get coffee or bring it to cadets if they were staying late after school or arriving early in the morning. One day he brought everyone in the class tamales, she said.
Deleon said she can understand the thinking that he should have kept a more professional relationship, “but he was like a father figure to a lot of us, and he was a great role model.”

title: Fighting human trafficking while supporting brides on a budget
text:
BEAVERTON, Ore. (InvestigateTV) - Fighting human trafficking one wedding dress at a time. That is the mission of Adorned in Grace.
“We walk with young women, and we hope to show them that there are always opportunities for second chances and the story to continue,” said Kaitlin Berg.
Berg is the Oregon Regional Director for Compassion Connect, Inc., the nonprofit oversight and resource center for Adorned in Grace.
The Bridal and Formalwear boutique is filled with donated dresses, some brand new from boutiques across the country, and others worn just once by another bride. All are under $1,000 with nearly 70% of every sale going directly to the mission – funding prevention, awareness, and survivor support.
For soon to be bride Marina Rael, it was the affordability that brought her through the doors, but it was the mission that made leaving with her perfect dress even more special.
“It’s definitely a plus to get something for such a special day but also have it go towards a great cause,” said Rael. “This place is open to every budget too, so it’s a really accessible location for all brides.”
The average cost of a wedding dress in 2026 is $2,250 according to analysis from wedding planning website Zola. That price doesn’t include alterations, undergarments, accessories, and cleaning, which can add an additional $800-1,200 to the total cost.
“Some just can’t afford these elaborate weddings. They are here because they also have a need. They only have a certain budget,” said Mardie Figueroa, volunteer developer and store manager.
Figueroa has been with Adorned in Grace since 2022 and is just one of many volunteers that without, the boutique would not be able to run.
“It’s not about selling a dress; it’s about making them feel wonderful in the dress they have selected,” said Figueroa. “When you see a bride that smiles, when you see the party and they all start crying, you know you took part in that. That’s what we are all about.”
Adorned in Grace has dresses of every style and every size, with new dresses arriving daily. And it’s not just bridal gowns, you can also find bridesmaid dresses, flower girl dresses, mother of the bride dresses, and dresses for any other formal occasion.
“I have some beautiful dresses that I wore to my daughter and son’s weddings, and I didn’t want them to go to just anywhere. I wanted it to be purposeful,” said Dawn Staoffel.
Staoffel loaded her dresses into the car and drove from Northern California with her dog to donate her dresses to Adorned in Grace.
“I love it and I would love for somebody else to have the joy that I did,” said Staoffel. “I had a lot of help getting the dress with support from the family and making sure it was the right choice for the weddings I wore them at so hopefully someone else will find the same excitement and joy of that.”
Adorned in Grace also carries veils, belts, shoes, jewelry, and other wedding accessories. There are two bridal boutique locations in Beaverton, Oregon and Mesa, Arizona. Then in Gresham, Oregon, another boutique specializing in formalwear.
From shopping, to donating, and volunteering, there are plenty of ways to get involved with Adorned in Grace.

title: Here’s how you can live on a beautiful island for free
text:
(Gray News) - SyroCats, a non-profit cat rescue on the Greek island of Syros, is looking for volunteers, who can live on the island and help take care of cats.
In exchange for noms and lodging, volunteers care for cats on the island. They feed clowders, or feral cat colonies, across the island, plus they support around 70 “long-term residents” at their facility.
The shelter also provides medical care for sick or injured cats and runs a trap-neuter-return program to help control the cat population.
Volunteers must be able to commit to at least one month of service, be self- sufficient, and able to perform daily duties that include cleaning, lifting, and handling cats.
No previous experience is needed, but any training or veterinary experience is a plus. Interested people can apply here.
Voluntourism
SyroCats is one example of a growing trend of voluntourism, where travelers pitch in for a cause at their travel destination.
Grand View Research estimates the current market size of about $1 billion to grow to over $1.5 billion by 2033.
Many well know organizations, such as Habitat for Humanity, the American Red Cross and the https://www.peacecorps.gov/ offer opportunities both in country and abroad.
What to know before planning a volunteer trip
The U.S. Department of State has advice for Americans considering voluntourism. Some of the suggestions include:
- Always research any organization before committing
- Make sure passports and other travel documents are up to date before planning a trip
- Look for organizations that provide in-country support, preferably 24 hours a day, for volunteers

title: Hermon council approves zoning change for trucking location on Coldbrook Road
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HERMON, Maine (WABI) - The Hermon Town Council has approved a zoning change that will likely bring a new trucking location to Coldbrook Road.
Residential zone becomes commercial
The change converts a residential zone to a commercial one, making way for Northeast Transport.
The company is looking to buy the property at 861 Coldbrook Road. The sale is scheduled for Friday and was contingent on the zoning change.
Residents opposed the change
Some nearby residents opposed the change and signed a petition to stop it.
“From my perspective, it’s mostly a traffic situation. The guys down the street opposite, that would have obviously some noise pollution and light pollution,” one of the residents said. “But I’m not just concerned about that, but the eight acres could be developed over the next five to ten or fifteen years into a huge commercial project, which would really increase traffic and make things really worse here in that respect,” said local resident David Sleeper.
Company owner responds
Ricky Hughes, the owner of Northeast Transport, said he is committed to doing everything possible to be a good neighbor, keep noise and traffic to a minimum, and listen to feedback from the community.

title: Trump says he plans to penalize US tech companies that build AI data centers in other countries
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump says U.S. tech companies will face “a tremendous tax” if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries.
Trump did not provide details Friday and he said he hadn’t yet told his own officials about his plan. The Republican president urged Americans to welcome data center construction in their communities and extract concessions from the developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
Trump says, “You ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off.”
The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train its best artificial intelligence models.
With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses.
The new raft of promises from the world’s richest companies came as anti-data center sentiment was a potent issue in the midterm elections, in which Democrats took control of Congress.
After a campaign season filled with outrage against artificial intelligence data centers, the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.
A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if Trump — perhaps the industry’s biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown.
Despite backing from Trump, the data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom have become politically toxic.
The tech industry says it has gotten the message. In addition to ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build.
Companies are also making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment and offering assurances that data centers will boost local property values — all while maintaining AI is a positive force for the American economy, despite its skeptics.

title: White House replaces national cyber director as nation reels from tech outages
text:
White House replaces national cyber director as nation reels from tech outages
The White House named a new national cyber director Thursday after a series of widespread service outages disrupted life and unnerved many Americans.
Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Defense Department, will fill the role, according to social media posts by several members of Trump's Cabinet. She will replace Sean Cairncross as the administration's top cybersecurity official.
“Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected,” Davies wrote in a post on X. “Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future.”
President Donald Trump faced a groundswell of criticism as Americans grappled with a cascade of service outages that snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications.
Video below: How to protect yourself against cyber outages
Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause of the disruptions. Over the past week, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there’s “zero” information that the technical failures are related to each other or to a malign actor.
The White House made the change as Trump returned from a three-day trip to Asia.
“She has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump’s America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote in a post on X congratulating Davies.

title: Prosecutors: Men charged in $22M train cargo thefts shared videos of themselves from heists
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — More than a dozen people were charged Thursday with allegedly orchestrating a massive train heist operation to steal over $22 million in cargo — from popular shoes to power tools — from major retailers.
A federal indictment unsealed on Thursday paints a picture of an organized group that targeted more than three dozen trains carrying Nike sneakers, Crocs footwear, power tools and other consumer goods that were imported into the United States through Los Angeles and Long Beach, which are home to the busiest ports in the country.
Trains that shuttle goods to stores and customers around the country have become a prominent target for large-scale theft in recent years, especially at large ports in the U.S. that receive hundreds of millions of dollars of shipments every day. The relatively low-tech robberies have demanded attention from the world’s largest retailers, including the likes of Amazon.
The men would disable the trains at a planned location by busting the brakes, the indictment alleged, at which point the goods would be offloaded onto trucks. The goods were then peddled to an unnamed company that would resell the stolen merchandise for profit.
“The scale of the theft is staggering,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli, promising to prosecute any future efforts to steal the merchandise.
In group chats, the men shared numerous photos and videos of themselves busting into the hulking train cars, and posing with wads of cash and stolen merchandise. They also shared AI photos of themselves captioned “Los Trenes,” which means the trains in Spanish, beneath glamorized photos of men throwing boxes of shoes off trains into nearby cars while police helicopters descended overhead.
The 13 men were indicted for conspiracy and theft of interstate railroad cargo. Two were also charged with violence against railroad carriers.
If convicted, the men could face anywhere from five to 20 years in federal prison.

title: Pentagon puts Iran war cost at $48.3 billion, excluding base damage
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The costs of the Iran war have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13, but because that total does not include damage to U.S. bases attacked in the Middle East, lawmakers are pushing for the Pentagon to provide those figures.
Arthur Miller, a Pentagon budget official, provided the latest overall cost estimate Thursday to the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is considering his nomination to be Navy comptroller. The $48 billion figure includes the costs of military operations, as well as for replacing equipment and munitions.
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut pressed Miller for an estimate on damage to U.S. installations, which Miller said he didn’t have. Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, the committee’s chair, directed Miller to try to provide an answer as soon as possible.
An Associated Press analysis found that Iran attacked aircraft hangars, systems that detect incoming strikes, warehouses, troop housing and more, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage.
The war’s price tag has been a flashpoint in Congress, with debates over costs intensifying as the Trump administration asks lawmakers to pass a $1.5 trillion defense budget. After the unpopular war and its economic effects contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections, financial battles over the conflict will only escalate once Democrats take control of Congress in January for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term.
The Pentagon has faced growing calls from Democrats to release estimates on the damage Iran has done to American bases in the Middle East through missile and drone attacks.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on the costs of the war at his confirmation hearing Tuesday for the permanent job.
Citing independent estimates and media reports, Warren said the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian shipping costs about $32.5 million a day, while an Iranian attack on the Navy’s regional headquarters in Bahrain did at least $400 million in damage.
Cao confirmed the figure for the blockade but said he could not offer a full damage assessment in Bahrain because “it’s a nonpermissive area for us to go.” Cao told a reporter months ago that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain.”

title: Orland may need $14.3M for new dam to hold back mercury-tainted tides
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The town of Orland on Thursday chose a design for a new dam and fishway at its village center needed to hold back tides that are contaminated with mercury and improve its commercial alewife harvest.
The selected design is an early step in a project that’s expected to take many years and an estimated $14.3 million in outside funding.
The mercury contamination stems from the former Holtrachem plant in Orrington, which illegally discharged between six and 12 tons into the Penobscot River in the late 1960s and early ’70s.
The tides have essentially trapped the mercury from washing out to sea, and appear to have begun carrying it up the Orland River, which empties into the Penobscot — held back only by a nearly century-old dam. Without it, officials expect the toxic mercury would spread through the watershed.
“Keeping that dam in place is unfortunately critical,” Select Board member Gina Bushong said Thursday after a unanimous board vote to choose the design.
Orland’s situation shows another way industrial contamination in the lower Penobscot still has significant and costly effects on the area, permanently shaping the landscape. Early court-ordered work to clean up some of the contamination further upriver in Orrington also began this summer.
The dam at Orland’s village center was built to support papermaking for Bucksport’s paper mill but never used. Orland residents voted to take ownership of it in 2010.
The tide now regularly washes over the top, longtime local Fish Warden Pete Robshaw said this summer, and mercury has been found in smaller amounts above it.
The fishway allows migratory fish — primarily alewives — to swim up the river each spring as they return from the ocean to spawn, but Robshaw previously said the current design limits their passage.
Orland is one of a few Maine towns that has kept a commercial alewife harvest for decades, though harvests have increased elsewhere in recent years as dams are removed and fish passages improved.
Alewives are used as lobster bait and also fill a key role in the food chain, feeding other fish and birds. Fishway improvements for easier passage would benefit them primarily, according to Robshaw, but elvers are also harvested in the river, and he sees occasional brown trout and bass.
He also manually opens and closes the dam gates by hand to maintain water levels, and said in June they are in bad shape.
The town completed a feasibility study this summer on options for replacing or shoring up the dam and associated fishway, using funds from one of two trusts created from a long-fought court settlement over the Holtrachem contamination.
An engineer’s inspection of the dam in April revealed no immediate issues, but found it was in fair to poor condition, particularly around the concrete gate area.
A town steering committee worked with the Select Board and the Maine Department of Marine Resources to recommend the option the Select Board decided on Thursday.
It would build a new concrete dam reinforcement abutting the downstream face of the current structure to stabilize it, add a vertical slot fishway for better passage for more species of migratory fish, and add hinged electric gates atop the dam to stop high tides from washing over it. A vertical slot fishway is a concrete channel that creates a kind of ramp.
The early cost estimate is $14.3 million, according to a summary document, with $10.1 million for the dam with the gate and $4.2 million for the fishway. That’s at the high end of the options, which started at $12.7 million.
Completing it will depend on outside funding for the small town, Bushong said. Next would come a detailed design and evaluation phase followed by extensive permitting work before construction could start.
Bushong emphasized that Thursday’s vote is just the start of a long process that will include public participation throughout.
“We’re not ready to go out and build a dam,” she said.
Correction: A previous version of this story contained incorrect information about the amount of mercury discharged into the Penobscot River.

title: Camden-based Bookclubs platform adds social features to rival Goodreads
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bookclubs, a Camden-based platform serving more than 1.5 million book club members, has introduced a suite of social features designed to connect more bibliophiles with one another and challenge Amazon-owned Goodreads.
The new tools expand Bookclubs’ reach beyond club management. Now, users can get a personalized home feed showing nearby and online clubs, discussions about books they’ve read and recommendations from friends.
Readers can also create shareable profiles and join conversations with people outside their clubs on the platform, where most clubs have 10 to 20 members.
“We wanted to create more opportunities for readers to connect outside of their existing club, with thousands more ‘book clubbers,’ especially if they read a book outside of their book club that they’re dying to talk about,” Anna Ford, co-founder and CEO of Bookclubs, told Mainebiz.
The startup also sees an opportunity to distinguish itself from Goodreads by offering tools to organize and sustain reading communities.
“Bookclubs offers community-organizing features for book clubs and reading groups — something that Goodreads doesn’t,” Ford explained “This allows us to be a one-stop shop for readers in a book club,” she added.
Amazon, the online seller of books and other merchandise, launched Goodreads in 2006 for readers to track books they and their friends are reading, have read or want to read, write reviews and get personalized recommendations. Bookclubs, especially now with its new social features, aims to offer readers another option.
“It’s our goal to be the Goodreads alternative for readers who want to connect with others and support a woman-owned, independent literary company,” Ford said.
In the first few days after the social features were introduced, 12,000 members started following friends, noted Ford, who formerly worked in public health policy and advocacy. She launched Bookclubs while leading a bookclub that grew to 40 members and finding the logistics becoming increasingly complicated, as she shared with Mainebiz in a 2024 “On the Record” interview.
Backers and employees
Bookclubs, founded in 2019, is backed by Maine Technology Institute; Maine Venture Fund; Blue Collective, Brooklyn, N.Y.-based venture capital firm; and several angel investors in Maine and beyond.
The company has three full-time and three part-time employees, along with five full-time engineering contractors.
Next chapters
Over the next year, Bookclubs hopes to strengthen its marketing and partnership development capabilities to accelerate growth.
The company is also developing additional reading challenges, improved reading-progress tracking, curated book lists and a revamped public club directory to help readers find local groups. Other planned features include on-demand virtual meetups, one-on-one video discussions and voice dictation to make it easier to add titles to users’ “Want to Read” shelves.

title: Patrick Stewart's cause of death confirmed by actor's death certificate
text:
Patrick Stewart's cause of death confirmed by actor's death certificate
Patrick Stewart died from Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, the actor's death certificate confirmed.
Video above: Steps to reduce risk of dementia and Alzheimer's disease
The "Star Trek" and "X-Men" actor's death certificate lists cardiopulmonary arrest and a neurocognitive disorder as the cause, according to documents obtained by TMZ.
The acclaimed English actor died on Oct. 28. His publicist said he died after a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. He was 86.
Stewart, whose career spanned more than six decades in theater, television and film, had not publicly disclosed his diagnoses prior to his death.
The two conditions can overlap
Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia are different conditions, but both can affect memory, thinking and everyday life.
Lewy body dementia can also cause changes in alertness, visual hallucinations, sleep problems and movement difficulties, according to the National Institute on Aging.
The conditions can occur together. When a person has brain changes linked to more than one type of dementia, it is called mixed dementia, according to the Alzheimer's Association. Alzheimer's-related changes are often found alongside Lewy bodies, though having one condition does not necessarily mean a person has the other.
What is Lewy body dementia?
Lewy body dementia is linked to abnormal protein deposits in the brain, called Lewy bodies. Named after the scientist who discovered them, Lewy bodies can disrupt brain functions that affect thinking, movement, behavior, mood and sleep.
Common signs include changes in attention, seeing things that are not there, and stiffness or difficulty walking.
The condition drew wide public attention after CNN founder Ted Turner revealed his diagnosis in 2018. Robin Williams' autopsy later found Lewy body disease, although his condition was not publicly diagnosed while he was alive.
Lewy body dementia is the second most common type of dementia after Alzheimer's disease, according to Mayo Clinic.
What is Alzheimer's disease?
Alzheimer's is the most common form of dementia. It gradually damages parts of the brain involved in memory and thinking.
Memory problems are often an early sign, but the disease can also affect language, judgment and reasoning, according to the Alzheimer's Association.
Over time, these changes can make everyday tasks harder.
Both Lewy body dementia and Alzheimer's are devastating conditions.
A statement posted to Stewart's Instagram page reads in part, "He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace."

title: Alex Murdaugh retrial moves forward after South Carolina judge refuses to toss murder indictments
text:
Alex Murdaugh retrial moves forward after South Carolina judge refuses to toss murder indictments
A South Carolina judge on Friday refused to dismiss the original murder indictments against Alex Murdaugh in the killings of his wife and son.
Judge Debra McCaslin’s ruling came after a hearing on Nov. 13, when Murdaugh’s attorneys argued for nearly an hour that the chief investigator lied to a Colleton County grand jury in 2022 about blood spatter being found on Murdaugh’s T-shirt. Prosecutors say they have plenty of evidence supporting the charges.
The ruling clears the way for the disgraced lawyer’s April retrial on the murder charges. The South Carolina Supreme Court threw out his convictions and life sentence in May, ruling a court clerk improperly influenced jurors during his 2023 trial.
Chief investigator’s testimony led to indictment questions
The chief investigator in the case, former State Law Enforcement Division agent David Owen, was central to Murdaugh’s arguments.
McCaslin wrote in her order that any mistakes by Owen were not intentional and that other evidence was enough to support the indictments. Still, she said she was disappointed that Owen failed to read a report saying there wasn’t blood on the T-shirt before making his presentation to the grand jury.
“Law enforcement bears a fundamental duty to thoroughly review and accurately represent the complete evidentiary record,” the judge wrote. “Oversights of this nature undermine public confidence in the integrity of the criminal justice system.”
Any issues about inconsistencies in evidence are matters for the trial and cross- examination, McCaslin said.
Prosecutors said Murdaugh, 58, killed his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, on their sprawling property in the South Carolina Lowcountry in 2021. Murdaugh is spending decades in prison for stealing millions of dollars from clients, and has admitted in court that he is a thief, insurance cheat, bad lawyer and longtime opioid addict. But he denies being a killer.
Defense questioned blood spatter conclusions
Defense lawyer Jim Griffin said at the Nov. 13 hearing that when prosecutors sought the indictments, Owen told the Colleton County grand jury that blood spatter was found on a T-shirt Murdaugh was wearing the night of the killings. An earlier report from state agents said there were no blood stains, and no such evidence was introduced at trial.
The false claim about the blood spatter was the only thing anyone heard that could link him to the place and time of the killings, Griffin said.
“A phone call doesn’t put him there. The video doesn’t put him there,” Griffin said. “The blood from his murdered son sprang through the air — it’s raining back on him — puts him there.”
Owen also told grand jurors that the same ammunition load of buckshot in one chamber and large birdshot in the other that was used to kill Paul Murdaugh was found loaded in weapons all over the Murdaugh property. This was not the case.
Video below: Watch the moment Alex Murdaugh was sentenced to life in prison
Prosecutors cited other evidence they said incriminates Murdaugh
Prosecutors wrote that “a single mistake is not bad faith” and that other evidence supports the charges.
Owen, who abruptly retired in 2024, told grand jurors about the video Paul Murdaugh recorded in which Alex Murdaugh’s voice could be heard at the scene, contradicting his denials. Owen also told them about the family’s mounting debts and how Murdaugh’s schemes to steal from clients and his law firm were close to being discovered.
Prosecutors said Murdaugh killed his wife and son because he thought the sympathy generated by the killings would buy him time to cover up his thefts.

title: Maine students take the lead in building a greener future
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine students take the lead in building a greener future
More than 140 students attended the event.
Maine students take the lead in building a greener future
More than 140 students attended the event.
More than 140 Maine students gathered at Gilsland Farm in Falmouth to share ideas, discuss environmental challenges and explore ways to build a more sustainable future.
Organizers initially expected about 70 students to attend, but turnout more than doubled, bringing together students interested in making a difference in their schools and communities.
Students broke into smaller groups, leading discussions about some of the biggest environmental challenges facing Maine. One topic that stood out was the impact of large institutions, including schools, hospitals and the military, which can be significant sources of pollution.
Students also came up with ideas for solutions, including offering more locally and school-grown food, creating composting programs and giving students hands-on opportunities to maintain gardens and compost bins.
Lucy Griset, a student at Brunswick High School who is involved with the Green Schools Network, says Maine has a unique opportunity to build on its natural resources while doing more to address climate change.
“I think Maine people, we are lucky enough to have such an amazing natural environment around us and a lot of access to the outdoor space. But I also think that we can be a little bit behind on some of the policy aspects of climate education, and in general climate mitigation, so I would really like to see some more growth in that area,” Griset said.
The gathering is part of Maine's Green Schools Program, a partnership between the Maine Department of Education and the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future.
The program works with public schools across the state to advance sustainability through four key areas: leadership, facilities, curriculum and career pathways.
Its goals include helping school districts save money, improving energy efficiency, reducing pollution and creating healthier learning environments for students and staff.
The program also focuses on connecting students with emerging career opportunities in Maine's growing green economy, including clean energy, environmental engineering, sustainable land management, recycling and waste reduction.
In 2025, Maine's Green Schools Program received the Green Difference Makers Award from national organization Project Green Schools. The award recognized the state's innovative partnership between education and climate policy, described as the first of its kind in the nation.
With more than twice the expected number of students attending the Falmouth gathering, the event offered an opportunity for young people to share their perspectives and help shape what sustainability could look like in Maine schools and communities.
Organizers hope those conversations will continue beyond the gathering, turning student ideas into meaningful changes across the state.
