title: AP reporter says Texas execution was like no other he's witnessed before
text:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — After covering capital punishment for The Associated Press in Texas since 1983 — and witnessing nearly 500 lethal injections — I’ve become accustomed to a certain routine in the procedure, although I’m reticent to describe any execution as “routine.”
It was 6 p.m. Thursday — a bell from a nearby church tolling the hour — when I and other witnesses climbed the concrete steps into the more than century-old Huntsville Unit of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice. We were led into a reception office for what normally is a very brief period to await the short trek to the death chamber to watch condemned killer Reinaldo Dennes die.
A large state of Texas clock on a wall ticked off the moments. By about 6:20 p.m., we still hadn’t moved.
I knew one of two situations was likely: Dennes was resisting the execution team’s attempts to insert a pair of intravenous needles into his arms, or the execution team was having difficulty finding a suitable vein for the needles.
Thirty minutes later, as we were led into the chamber by corrections officers, Dennes appeared docile. His eyes were closed and his head was pointed toward the ceiling. His white prison garb was not disheveled and no additional restraints were applied to his head, meaning no evidence of a struggle.
Now I’ve seen over the years any number of final statements and reactions from condemned inmates who spoke in foreign languages, prayed, recited poetry, sang, cursed, expressed love, insisted on their innocence or acknowledged their crime and one who even told a joke.
Dennes was like no other.
Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Dennes talked about being “extremely blessed” by the love of “the father” and hoped his family and loved ones “get to know this great gift and great grace of God the father.”
He told the warden: “Go.” Almost immediately as the procedure began, his demeanor changed.
“The pain!” he exclaimed. “Go! Go!”
For nearly three minutes — and standing there furiously scribbling notes, I thought it seemed much longer — Dennes repeatedly moaned.
“Take me father! … Take me into your arms! … Take me father!” He occasionally interjected his cries with obscenities, a grunt and then groans. His right leg was “killing me,” he said, likening the sensation to a cramp.
“I don’t think this is normal,” he said at one point.
On that, he was right. I’ve heard inmates say the lethal drug was hot or cold, that they could smell or taste it, or that it hurt. No one I can recall went to such drama as Dennes.
At 7:08 p.m., after being examined by a physician, he was pronounced dead.
Texas prison officials said the execution team had difficulty finding suitable veins. Spokeswoman Amanda Hernandez said after repeated unsuccessful attempts — she couldn’t say how many — the technicians found a vein in Dennes’ left foot and another on the left side of his neck that were receptive to the IV needles.
I couldn’t see. His feet were covered by a sheet and only the right side of his neck was visible to those of us who were witnesses.
The injection sites were in line with the prison system’s procedures, Hernandez added. The alternate sites have been used in previous executions, although the need to do so is relatively rare.
Hernandez also suggested Dennes may have been faking, saying he had been complaining about pain from areas where no injections were attempted.
As a reporter, I’d like to find out the truth about the matter. But there’s no way to know for sure.
Dennes himself, as reporters are known to say, wasn’t available for further comment.

title: Obituary: Eric “Rick” Lee Plummer
text:
GEORGETOWN – Eric “Rick” Lee Plummer, on Nov. 7, 2026. Rick went to be with Ma, Farv, and Sarg. He was born on Nov. 24, 1956, in Bath. Here are a few words that best describes Rick.
Happy – Always Smiling
Friend – Everybody’s buddy
Worker – He worked right along side of mother, father, brothers, uncles, whoever needed help.
Company – Went everywhere with everyone.
Townie – “Me”
Comic – Always made you laugh,
Smart – The smartest
Memory – Once he met you, he never forgot you.
Boundaries – “Mine”
Leadership – He ran the program.
Truth – He held the truth and wasn’t afraid to use it.
Confidant – Advisor, his opinion was often sought and mostly used.
And Yes, puzzles he had a million of them
Rick knew everyone, you couldn’t go anywhere without someone knowing him.
Magnetic – Always making you laugh and feel good.
Thanks, are many, so is family, everyone was family to him. and somehow, we should thank Rick for being in our life.
We will think of you often. There will be no services. Condolences can be made online at http://www.DaigleFuneralHome.com.

title: Hundreds mourn Fiona the hippo at Cincinnati Zoo as memorial grows
text:
CINCINNATI (WXIX/Gray News) - Hundreds of people visited the Cincinnati Zoo on Thursday night to mourn Fiona, the hippopotamus who died after ingesting a visitor’s hat that accidentally entered her habitat.
Flowers, handmade cards and stuffed animals were left at a growing memorial near a statue of Fiona.
“We love our Cincinnati Zoo. Fiona we will miss you always,” 10-year-old Mikey read from a card.
Fiona’s final days
Fiona ingested the hat on Nov. 8. Her care team worked around the clock in the days that followed, but she died despite their efforts.
“I can’t imagine what her caretakers are going through, everything they’ve done in the past 10 days,” one visitor said.
Fiona’s birth in 2017
Fiona captured the world’s attention in 2017 when she was born six weeks prematurely, weighing 29 pounds.
Millions followed her journey as she grew from a newborn into a hippo who drew families to the zoo.
“I remember when she was born. I remember the fight, all of the nurses from Cincinnati Children’s feeding her around the clock,” another visitor said. “I started buying our family season passes because of Fiona.”
For one parent, Fiona’s story was connected to memories of watching a child grow up.
“I watched him kind of grow with Fiona because I was staying at home with him, and she was born a month later,” the parent said.
Visitors remember Fiona
Another visitor reflected on Fiona’s fight to survive and the impact of her death.
“It’s just so sad with her story and how hard she fought and how long she made it and then to lose her tragically. It’s heartbreaking for us and the whole city,” the visitor said.
“We will miss her very much,” Mikey added.

title: Make an owl ornament at the Gilley
text:
SOUTHWEST HARBOR — Let your holiday spirit take wing at the Gilley in this ornament-making class. Use carving tools and wood-burning to create a snowy owl ornament in a workshop at the Wendell Gilley Museum. The class is suitable for beginners, but carvers of all levels are welcome. Participants will start with a pre-cut wooden blank, then shape and wood-burn it. Students must be at least 12 years old.
The workshop will be offered three times: Saturday, Nov. 28 from noon to 3 p.m.; Saturday, Dec. 5 from noon to 3 p.m.; and Friday, Dec. 11 from 5 to 8 p.m. It will be led by Lynda Millar, who teaches woodburning, carving and papercutting at the Gilley. The cost is $36 for museum members and $45 for nonmembers. All materials and tools are supplied. Class size is limited. Sign up at www.wendellgilleymuseum.org/calendar.

title: Mild Friday, pleasant weekend, rain Sun night
text:
Mild Friday, pleasant weekend, rain Sun night
Mild Friday, pleasant weekend, rain Sun night
Temperatures are running well above average for late November, with highs in the low to mid 60s for most on Friday afternoon.
It will be slightly cooler on Saturday and Sunday, but still warmer than average, with highs in the mid to upper 50s. Plentiful sunshine is expected Saturday, with more clouds rolling in Sunday ahead of our next round of rain.
A storm moving up the East Coast this weekend brings a quick round of beneficial rain to Maine Sunday night into Monday morning. 1 to 2 inches of rain are possible across southern and central Maine, with less than an inch likely up north. Shifts in the storm's track could mean even higher rainfall for Maine, a trend which will be monitored closely as it develops.
The storm will be fast-moving, with a majority of the rain falling overnight Sunday night. Rain ends from west to east Monday morning, with cold air flowing in on breezy northwest winds in the afternoon.
Turning much colder for the rest of next week with highs in the 30s to mid-40s. Maine's Total Weather is watching another storm riding up the coastline that could impact Thanksgiving and Black Friday. With the cold air in place, snow, ice, and rain are all possible should the storm track close enough to New England.

title: Somerset County to receive $3.1M federal grant to expand addiction treatment
text:
MADISON, Maine (WABI) - Somerset County expects to receive $3.1 million over five years from the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration to continue addiction treatment and expand recovery support.
The grant aims to make sure people with substance use disorders do not face the transition out of jail alone.
Treatment at the jail
Since 2022, the Somerset County Jail has offered a monthly injection of buprenorphine to treat opioid use disorder. The medication can help manage withdrawal and cravings, including after someone is released.
“So this gives them the medication coverage they need when they depart to really save their life, frankly, and also to get connected to services. It just kind of buys them more time,” Dr. Alane O’Connor, director of addiction medicine at the jail, said.
Somerset County Sheriff Dale Lancaster said treatment is part of the job.
“I truly believe that part of our job is to save lives. And if we can do that, and this program shows that it does, I think we’d be remiss not to do that,” Lancaster said.
Outreach, referrals and stimulant program
The grant also will support outreach and referrals, as well as the development of a program to address stimulant use disorder.
Grant manager LeeAnna LaVoie said the team is focused on making connections to care that last.
“How are we all working together to make sure that we’re connecting them while they’re here? And then how do we bring them out into the community and working with our community partners?” LaVoie said.

title: Mamdani sets plan to close NYC's notorious Rikers Island jail
text:
Mamdani sets plan to close NYC's notorious Rikers Island jail
New York City's Rikers Island jail complex would close by 2032 under a plan announced Friday by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose strategy for finally shuttering the notorious facility hinges on substantially reducing the number of people kept behind bars.
Video above: NY Mayor Mamdani watches World Cup semifinal match with Rikers Island prisoners in July
The city is all but certain to blow past a legal requirement to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller, more modern jails by 2027.
For years, Rikers Island has stood as a symbol of dysfunction, with the network of jails so plagued by violence and overcrowding that a federal judge, citing "abnormal and unacceptable" conditions, appointed an outside manager to restore order and implement reforms.
Mamdani, a Democrat, has been a vocal proponent of closing Rikers, though the longstanding plan to build new jails has met pushback, including from his predecessor, former Mayor Eric Adams, who opposed federal oversight and borough jails.
“It is time to finally close Rikers Island,” Mamdani said in a statement. “For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane."
The plan hinges on lowering the city's inmate population from the more than 6,500 people housed at Rikers to around 4,500.
The Mamdani administration is proposing a new slate of diversion and supervised release programs, expanding housing and social services to prevent recidivism, along with restoring an online bail payment system and reducing case delays through various measures.
“We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers. Working alongside the City Council, Courts and nonprofit partners, we will meet it — for the people in our custody, the staff who serve them, victims of crime, and every New Yorker,” Mamdani said.
In 2019, the New York City Council voted to close the jail complex and replace it with newer jails located in the city's boroughs, with local lawmakers invoking the names of former prisoners who died, including Kalief Browder, who took his own life at age 22 after being held for three years at Rikers.

title: Trump warns U.S. companies against building data centers overseas

text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump warned U.S. companies that want to build data centers overseas that they will face what he called a “tremendous tax.”
Data centers have become one of the biggest hot-button issues in the country. Trump gave his support to data centers at a Friday press conference, amid protests against construction in many communities around the country.
“We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they’re great places. They have energy, and they have everything. They’re tremendous assets,” Trump said.
Trump also said he opposes any U.S. company building a data center overseas that uses AI chips.
“They can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them,” Trump said.
Numerous American-based tech companies, including Microsoft, Amazon and Oracle, have already built data centers in foreign countries. It is not clear if the president’s tax threat applies to them.

title: Susan Collins will have options to explore come January
text:
Most people who get fired after they reach retirement age choose the obvious next step: they retire.
But I have a hard time imagining Sen. Susan Collins, following her ouster by an angry electorate, sitting on a rocker watching the world go by. Though she may feel like hunkering down, she’s shown us for years that she’s just not that way.
Unlike most of us, the go-getters who hold Senate seats are unlikely to embrace a low-key life focused on family, friends and perhaps some travel.
Sometimes it happens.
Republican Sen. Frederick Payne, who lost his 1958 reelection in Maine, stepped back from public life and simply went home to Waldoboro. He spent his last two decades in poor health, working on a book he never finished.
Payne’s predecessor, Republican Owen Brewster, who lost a 1952 primary to Payne, also lived quietly after departing the Senate.
Maine’s subsequent senators proved far busier after moving out of their Capitol Hill offices than Payne and Brewster.
Republican Margaret Chase Smith, who lost in 1972, lectured extensively, chaired Freedom House and established the Margaret Chase Smith Library in Skowhegan to house her papers.
The man who defeated her, Democrat William Hathaway, served a single term before his ouster. He stayed in Washington to practice law, lobby his former colleagues and eventually serve on the Federal Maritime Commission.
Former Sen. Edmund Muskie, a Democrat, resigned his office to become secretary of state during the Carter administration. He later practiced law and was a member of the Tower Commission that investigated the Iran-Contra affair in 1987.
The senator who succeeded Muskie, Democrat George Mitchell, took on the job of U.S. special envoy for Northern Ireland and played a key role in brokering the 1998 Good Friday Agreement that ended decades of strife. Mitchell, a lawyer, also led the probe into steroid use in Major League Baseball and founded the Portland-based Mitchell Institute to support Maine college students.
Sen. William Cohen, a Republican who beat Hathaway in 1978, served as U.S. secretary of defense in the Clinton administration and later founded a business focused on consulting and strategic advice. He also wrote novels and other books.
Republican Sen. Olympia Snowe, who stepped down in 2013, worked for political reform and bipartisanship in Washington. She also formed the Olympia Snowe Women’s Leadership Institute, a nonprofit focused on helping high school girls in Maine become leaders.
Sen. Collins obviously has many models she could follow, but I think she’ll find her own path. It could prove significant that before she won her Senate seat, Collins served as executive director of the Center for Family Business at Husson University — she is familiar with academia and overseeing an educational program.
I suspect Sen. Collins will look closely at the widely admired post-Senate careers of the two Maine women who preceded her. After all, one way to put an exclamation point on the best elements of her tenure in the Senate would be to keep pushing for the bipartisanship she always insisted was important to her.

title: 3D Printing Club Donates Wheelchair to Family
text:
WOODLAND, Maine (WAGM) - One family’s life is a little easier thanks to the 3D printing club at Woodland Consolidated School. For the past few months, club members have been working on a 3D-printed wheelchair for a toddler with a disability.
Students in Woodland’s 3D printing club have spent months building a wheelchair for a 2-year-old girl. Club members say all that hard work was worth it when they saw her in the finished chair. “I feel like it was very exciting. We worked really, really hard on that wheelchair, and I feel like her inside of it made it 10 times better than just the wheelchair itself,” said Tabitha Scherer, a 7th Grader in the school’s 3D Printing Club.
The idea for the project came after one of the club’s founders built a wheelchair for his own daughter, who has cerebral palsy. The club decided to make another one to donate to a family in need. “Most conventional strollers they’re kind of laid back. They can’t really... babies and children under 2 can’t really look around as well in a stroller type setting. I mean, strollers are fine, but when you have a child with a disability something like this is kind of a god send,” said Cameron Poussard, the 3D Printing Club’s founder and volunteer.
After months of work, the club had just one minor challenge during the build. Zech Arce, an 8th Grader in the 3D Printing Club said: “One piece was defective while we were building it. So, we had to like emergency print it.”
“It felt like I was putting together a masterpiece. We got to fit each piece together and there was some hammering involved,” added Tabitha.
Students say being part of a project that helped a family has been rewarding. “It feels like the work is very rewarding after we see how much help we’re doing,” said Zech.
“When you help out somebody it helps a lot with the parent’s life and also the child’s life. We she gets to grow up she gets to have easier access to places, and she gets to grow up in the wheelchair because of the way it’s built, and it will be a piece of her life that she can remember forever,” added Tabitha.
The family receiving the wheelchair asked to remain anonymous. Club members say many people and organizations helped make the project possible. MakeGood Inc. provided the wheelchair design, and the Woodland School PTO funded the project. David and Sandy Perloff and the UMPI Maine Educational Talent Search Program provided the 3D printers. Holland Moms connected the club with the family receiving the chair. For these students, a project built piece by piece became a way to make a difference in a young girl’s life.

title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.
Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.
Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.
With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a “testament of the hard work” his team put into the case. He said he was “intimately familiar” with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.
Rinderknecht’s attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.
“After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration,” Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.
Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.
Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht’s first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren’t presented as evidence during the trial.
Juror says Rinderknecht’s own testimony pointed to a guilty verdict
Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.
“It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise,” he said. “After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he’s guilty.”
Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a “lack of information” presented to the jury about the technical review.
In the end, it was Rinderknecht’s own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.
“Stating that he was up on the hill, didn’t smell a fire, didn’t see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night,” Cameron said.
Prosecutors say Rinderknecht had been ‘mad at everything’
During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht’s state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by “societal revenge” like they previously did.
Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire’s origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.
“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.
After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?”
These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.
They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.
Defense argues fire’s origin is unproven
Haney cast doubt on the government’s case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.
The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.
Prosecutors attacked the fire investigator during cross examination and at one point accused him of perjury, alleging he did not disclose all records related to the case. The judge ultimately rejected prosecutors’ request to strike his testimony.
Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor’s testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht’s character, such as his angry text messages, because they were “evidence of the man, not evidence of the act.”
Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.
In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

title: Pentagon puts Iran war cost at $48.3 billion, excluding base damage
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The costs of the Iran war have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13, but because that total does not include damage to U.S. bases attacked in the Middle East, lawmakers are pushing for the Pentagon to provide those figures.
Arthur Miller, a Pentagon budget official, provided the latest overall cost estimate Thursday to the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is considering his nomination to be Navy comptroller. The $48 billion figure includes the costs of military operations, as well as for replacing equipment and munitions.
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut pressed Miller for an estimate on damage to U.S. installations, which Miller said he didn’t have. Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, the committee’s chair, directed Miller to try to provide an answer as soon as possible.
An Associated Press analysis found that Iran attacked aircraft hangars, systems that detect incoming strikes, warehouses, troop housing and more, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage.
The war’s price tag has been a flashpoint in Congress, with debates over costs intensifying as the Trump administration asks lawmakers to pass a $1.5 trillion defense budget. After the unpopular war and its economic effects contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections, financial battles over the conflict will only escalate once Democrats take control of Congress in January for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term.
The Pentagon has faced growing calls from Democrats to release estimates on the damage Iran has done to American bases in the Middle East through missile and drone attacks.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on the costs of the war at his confirmation hearing Tuesday for the permanent job.
Citing independent estimates and media reports, Warren said the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian shipping costs about $32.5 million a day, while an Iranian attack on the Navy’s regional headquarters in Bahrain did at least $400 million in damage.
Cao confirmed the figure for the blockade but said he could not offer a full damage assessment in Bahrain because “it’s a nonpermissive area for us to go.” Cao told a reporter months ago that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain.”

title: Man who filed for divorce 2 weeks ago now accused of killing his wife, police say
text:
GRAND ISLAND, Neb. (KSNB/Gray News) - A Nebraska man who had filed for divorce is accused of killing his wife Wednesday night.
Police arrested 43-year-old Luis Gutierrez after officers were called to the couple’s home. His wife, Connie Gutierrez, was 36.
What police found
Police received several 911 calls from the home at 4117 Michigan Ave., according to an affidavit. The first caller hung up.
As officers headed to the home, a woman called 911 and asked for police. During the call, a loud noise that sounded like a door slamming could be heard, followed by a man yelling and asking what he had just done, the affidavit says.
Another 911 call was traced to Luis Gutierrez. During that call, he said he had shot his wife, according to the affidavit.
When officers arrived, Luis Gutierrez came out the front door holding a phone, with his hands raised. Inside, police found Connie Gutierrez sitting on a couch with a gunshot wound to her head. A handgun was on the coffee table in front of her.
She was taken to a hospital, where she died.
The couple’s two children were inside the home when the shooting happened, according to the affidavit. Neither child was harmed.
Suspect charged
Gutierrez was arrested and taken to the Hall County Department of Corrections. He is charged with five felonies, including first degree murder.
Grand Island Police Division Chief Dean Elliott said officers had responded that home several times before the shooting.
“We’ve had calls for service there, nothing physical in nature, but for a pattern that we sometimes see when parents are not getting along,” Elliott said. “A ‘he said, she said’ situation between the two of them, nothing where criminal charges were filed, more like safety of the children at that point in time.”
Elliott also said the investigation is still in the early stages, with the autopsy playing an important role.
Elliott encouraged anyone who sees domestic violence happening to call police so officers can respond, help stop it and connect those involved with resources.
At a hearing Thursday morning in Hall County Court, a judge set Gutierrez’s bond at $10 million, with 10% required. A probable cause hearing is scheduled for Dec. 22.
Divorce filing
Court records show Luis Gutierrez filed for divorce on Nov. 3, 2026.
In the filing, his attorney said the marriage was “irretrievably broken and all efforts at reconciliation have wholly failed.”
The two had been married since January 2023. Gutierrez requested custody of the two teenage children living in the home.

title: Meet the Four 2026 Aroostook County Athletes of the Fall
text:
Querze, Cyr, Graves and Gorneault Named 2026 Athletes of the Fall
Nine weeks of Athlete of the Week, a full postseason and more than 18,000 votes cast have brought the 2026 fall sports season to its final awards.
Josh Querze of Madawaska, Madisyn Cyr of Wisdom, Emma Graves of Caribou and Pierce Gorneault of Caribou have been selected as the 2026 Aroostook County Athletes of the Fall.
This year's season-ending awards were divided into four categories for the first time, with separate Large School and Small School boys and girls divisions.
The winners are:
Large School Boys Athlete of the Fall: Pierce Gorneault, Caribou
Large School Girls Athlete of the Fall: Emma Graves, Caribou
Small School Boys Athlete of the Fall: Josh Querze, Madawaska
Small School Girls Athlete of the Fall: Madisyn Cyr, Wisdom
Large School Boys Athlete of the Fall: Pierce Gorneault, Caribou
Pierce Gorneault put together a championship cross country season from beginning to end.
The Caribou standout won the PVC Championship, Northern Maine Class B Regional Championship and Class B State Championship, becoming Caribou's first boys individual state champion in 30 years.
Gorneault also recorded a 16:01 personal best, qualified for the New England Championships and helped Caribou capture conference and regional team championships before finishing third at states.
It was a season defined by consistency and championship performances.
Congratulations to Pierce Gorneault, the 2026 Large School Boys Athlete of the Fall.
Large School Girls Athlete of the Fall: Emma Graves, Caribou
Emma Graves was one of Northern Maine's top runners throughout the fall.
Graves won the PVC individual championship and continued her outstanding season through the championship meets, eventually finishing second at the Class B State Cross Country Championship.
She also earned Athlete of the Week honors during the season while consistently racing among the top competitors in the region.
Congratulations to Emma Graves, the 2026 Large School Girls Athlete of the Fall.
Small School Boys Athlete of the Fall: Josh Querze, Madawaska
Josh Querze closed his high school soccer career with another outstanding season while helping lead Madawaska all the way to the Class D State Championship game.
Querze finished his career with more than 120 goals, earned All-Aroostook and regional recognition and remained one of the area's most dangerous offensive players throughout the fall.
But his impact went beyond scoring.
Querze served as a captain and helped lead a Madawaska team that captured the Class D North regional championship and represented Northern Maine in the state final.
Congratulations to Josh Querze, the 2026 Small School Boys Athlete of the Fall.
Small School Girls Athlete of the Fall: Madisyn Cyr, Wisdom
Madisyn Cyr helped Wisdom complete one of the most memorable seasons anywhere in Aroostook County this fall.
Cyr delivered important goals during Wisdom's postseason run, scoring in consecutive tournament victories as the Pioneers advanced through the playoffs.
The run eventually ended with Wisdom capturing the state championship, completing a historic season for the program.
Cyr also earned Week Nine Athlete of the Week honors during that postseason run before finishing the year as an Athlete of the Fall winner.
Congratulations to Madisyn Cyr, the 2026 Small School Girls Athlete of the Fall.

Making the Athlete of the Fall ballot required more than one great performance.

title: Texas says an execution went as planned. A witness says screams showed 'tremendous distress'
text:
A Texas official on Friday defended how the state carried out the execution of a 70-year-old man who loudly insisted he was in pain and pleaded, “Don’t let me suffer like this,” during a lethal injection that followed a struggle to find a suitable vein.
Yet Reinaldo Dennes’ spiritual adviser, who had his hand on Dennes’ shoulder inside the death chamber in Huntsville, said he felt like he was holding a bucking bronco Thursday.
“Twice he said, ‘It’s not working. It’s not working. It’s not going how it’s supposed to go. This isn’t right.’ Those types of words kept coming,” said the Rev. Jeff Hood, a death penalty opponent.
Dennes was “clearly in tremendous distress,” said Hood, who called it torture.
It was the ninth execution this year in Texas, which has a long history of using the death penalty as punishment for murder. Executions across the U.S. have garnered more attention since Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital in Tennessee in September. The drug didn’t enter her bloodstream correctly.
State says execution worked ‘as planned’
Amanda Hernandez, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, said initial attempts to place two IV lines into Dennes’ hands and arms were unsuccessful.
Dennes was strapped to the gurney at 6:04 p.m. Hernandez said an IV was successfully placed in the left side of his neck 16 minutes later at 6:20 p.m., followed by another line in his left foot at 6:38 p.m.
Witnesses, including Hood and an Associated Press reporter, were escorted into the death chamber before Dennes began his final statement at 6:52 p.m. Lethal drugs began flowing less than a minute later, Hernandez said.
Almost immediately, Dennes exclaimed: “The pain! Go! Go!” He uttered an expletive and implored “the father” to “take this pain.”
He subsequently shouted: “My right leg is killing me!” and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, “I don’t think this is normal. Take me, father. Don’t let me suffer like this. C’mon.”
The drugs were stopped at 7:07 p.m., and he was declared dead a minute later, slightly more than an hour after he was restrained in the death chamber, Hernandez said.
“We feel that all of our processes and procedures were followed and that it was carried out as planned,” she told the AP.
Hernandez said she didn’t know how many attempts were made to place IV lines.
“It’s not a race — it’s not how quickly can we get this done,” she said. “It’s something you want to do correctly. There is no normal time limit. It’s what it takes for it to be successfully done.”
In May, Tennessee called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers after failing for over an hour to establish an IV line. Idaho, in 2024, tried eight times to establish a line to execute Thomas Creech before stopping. Republican Gov. Brad Little subsequently signed a law making a firing squad the primary method of execution.
Advocate says Dennes would not fake pain
As for Dennes’ claims of extreme pain, Hernandez said the state plans no additional inquiry. She said there were reasons to suspect he was exaggerating, adding that he complained even before the lethal drugs were given and grumbled about pain in a leg that didn’t have an IV line.
Hernandez said “it makes you wonder” if the high-profile Pike case has influenced death row inmates to act out.
“They watch the news. He was aware of the other executions,” Hernandez said.
Dr. Paul Wax, executive director of the American College of Medical Toxicology, said he couldn’t think of any reason why an injection of pentobarbital into the left foot or left side of the neck would cause pain in the right leg.
Michael Graczyk, The AP reporter who attended the execution, said witnesses can’t see when the drug starts to be administered. Dennes’ foot was covered by a sheet, and the IV in the left side of his neck wasn’t visible from their position.
It’s not possible to definitively know what caused him to scream in pain. Hernandez said the lethal drugs had not passed their expiration date, though she didn’t know the date.
Hood, the spiritual adviser, said assertions that Dennes was faking pain were “disgusting.”
“We have heard them say repeatedly since last night that this was not botched. That is absolutely, unbelievably absurd,” Hood said.
Dale Baich, an Arizona lawyer who has represented death row inmates and witnessed 17 U.S. executions, said the latest Texas lethal injection raises concerns.
“Calling a prisoner’s screams an act is not a medical finding. It is an accusation, and the state should be required to produce evidence to support it,” Baich said.
___
Associated Press reporter Kate Brumback in Atlanta contributed to this story.

title: Florida, Texas execute 2 men on same day; Florida sets yearly record
text:
RAIFORD, Fla. (AP) — Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year Thursday on a man convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion, while Texas put to death a man for a jeweler’s killing during a $3.6-million diamond heist.
Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. EST following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple’s home and attacking them, saying, “I never killed anyone.”
Soon after, Texas conducted the day’s second execution. Reinaldo Dennes, 70, became the ninth Texas inmate executed this year, receiving a lethal injection at the penitentiary in Huntsville. He was pronounced dad at 7:08 p.m. CST. The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population.
Overton was convicted of killing Michael and Susan MacIvor and their unborn child during an August 1991 break-in at their Florida Keys home. Dennes was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996.
Florida has now carried out more than half of the nation’s 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. The executions follow renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike in September.
DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who’ve waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. After a record-setting Thursday, Florida is planning two more executions in December.
Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.
Florida husband and wife were strangled
In Florida, Overton was strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the death chamber curtain lifted at 6 p.m.
“I’ve never sexually assaulted anyone. I never killed anyone,” Overton said, denying ever having been in the MacIvors’ home or gated community. “I didn’t kill the MacIvors.”
The injection began immediately afterward with Overton panting and breathing heavily before all movement ceased. A warden then shook Overton and shouted his name without answer before a medic declared the inmate dead.
The MacIvors’ bodies were found in their Tavernier, Florida, home on Aug. 22, 1991, court records show. Autopsies determined they were strangled and that Susan MacIvor, eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.
Investigators collected DNA evidence but found no match with the state’s database. But when Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors’ home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996, his DNA sample matched one from the MacIvors’ home.
Overton was subsequently convicted in 1999 of two first-degree murder counts and received a death sentence for each.
Michael MacIvor’s sister, two brothers and cousin witnessed the execution. The man’s sister, Sharon MacIvor, said watching Overton die gave her a sense of relief but not satisfaction.
“One of the hardest things I have ever had to hear was how my brother Michael fought to stay alive,” Sharon MacIvor said. “Michael was my little brother. He was loved, he had a family, and he had a lifetime ahead of him.”
Diamonds missing in jeweler’s killing were never recovered
Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes arranged for her to open the building’s back door after hours, allowing Dennes and his brother entry the night of the shooting. Records showed she also distracted the security guard at Dennes’ request.
The guard was shot twice but recovered and identified Dennes as his assailant.
Police found the jeweler’s body in his office, but his safe was empty with no sign of the diamonds or some $200,000 in cash he supposedly kept there, court filings indicated. Authorities said the diamonds were never located.
Dennes’ attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove he killed Szucs.
A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.
___
Corrects that the failed Tennessee execution was in September, not October.
___
Stengle contributed to this report from Dallas and Graczyk from Huntsville, Texas.

title: Lobstermen deserve access to USDA loans
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
If anyone still wonders whether the aquaculture industry is working alongside Maine’s traditional fishing industry, a recent fight over federal lending offers a telling example.
On Oct. 13, the National Aquaculture Association (NAA) urged lawmakers to oppose a Farm Bill provision that would extend access to certain U.S. Department of Agriculture operating loans to commercial fishermen. The provision would help fishermen finance the purchase, operation, and repair of their vessels. The NAA argues that these resources should remain reserved for agricultural and aquaculture producers.
The NAA’s president, Sebastian Belle, is also executive director of the Maine Aquaculture Association whose board of directors includes representatives of Cooke Aquaculture, the New Brunswick-based seafood corporation with extensive international aquaculture operations, including salmon net pens in Maine’s coastal waters. Cooke has faced loads of accusations over environmental, animal welfare, and other issues concerning its aquaculture operations worldwide, and the Conservation Law Foundation is pursuing litigation alleging violations of the federal Clean Water Act at Cooke’s Maine salmon farms. Owner Glenn Cooke, meanwhile, has acknowledged publicly that his company earns $4 billion a year.
These connections matter because the NAA’s position raises a fundamental question: Whose interests are being advanced when an industry association seeks to deny American seafood producers access to federal financing?
For years, Maine lobstermen have reported concerns to Protect Maine’s Fishing Heritage Foundation about escaped farmed salmon, fish die-offs, and noxious odors near some Cooke-owned net pens. Now, many are understandably frustrated by an industry association’s effort to prevent commercial fishermen from accessing a federal loan program that could help sustain their businesses.
In his letter opposing the Farm Bill provision, Belle wrote that aquaculture farmers “grow a renewable crop that they own and manage from start to finish,” while commercial fishermen “harvest a wild, public trust resource that they do not own, cultivate, or replenish through their own labor or capital investment.”
That characterization is both dismissive and misleading.
First, Maine’s lobster industry is built on generations of investment, knowledge, and stewardship. Lobstermen and women invest in vessels, gear, licenses, and their communities. They also participate in conservation practices, including v-notching egg-bearing female lobsters and returning them to the water, as well as measures designed to protect the long-term health of the fishery. It is a livelihood that depends on maintaining a productive fishery for future generations.
Second, the fact that Maine’s wild fisheries depend on a public trust resource does not make the people who harvest it any less deserving of access to government financing. Nor does the fact that aquaculture operations cultivate a crop give them a superior claim to public support.
Finally, the NAA frames this as a competition for a limited pool of money, arguing that allowing commercial fishermen to access USDA loans would leave less support for farmers and aquaculture businesses. But limited funding does not justify categorically excluding an entire class of American food producers. If the concern is that existing resources are inadequate to meet demand, the answer should be to address that shortfall. At a time when significant public funding is being invested in aquaculture research and development, it is particularly troubling that the industry’s national association is working instead to shut commercial fishermen out of a federal lending program.
At public hearings throughout Maine, Protect Maine has heard the aquaculture lobby speak about the importance of being good neighbors. Yet good neighbors do not insist that shared resources and public support belong exclusively to them. Maine’s waters are a public trust, and the people who earn their living from them deserve a fair opportunity to participate in programs that support American seafood production.
Maine’s fishing heritage was built by independent fishermen and fishing communities, not by multinational seafood corporations. Maine should not accept a vision of the future in which industrial aquaculture is prioritized over traditional fishermen who are told that the public resources they steward and the financing they need to work are not meant for them.
Maine’s identity, economy, and coastal communities have been built over generations on the hard work of lobstermen and women. Our state’s fishing heritage is rooted in independent fishermen and the communities they sustain, not in a foreign corporation headquartered in Canada. State and federal policies should honor that legacy and protect the livelihoods that have defined our coast for generations, rather than allow the interests of industrial aquaculture to come at their expense.
Crystal Canney is executive director of Protect Maine’s Fishing Heritage Foundation.

title: Crews battle growing woods fire in Woodstock
text:
WOODSTOCK —A woods fire on the eastern shore of North Pond was about 25% contained Saturday morning after crews fought the blaze until late Friday night, according to Woodstock Fire Chief Kyle Hopps.
Fire crews from several towns returned to the area on Saturday morning to fight the blaze, which still covered about 7 acres, Hopps said at about 9:30 a.m. More than 10 acres had burned as of 5 p.m. Friday, according to a firefighter at the scene.
Hopps said fire crews fought the blaze until about 11 p.m. Friday because it had spread to within about 100 yards of residences on Mann Road. He said landowners would be contacted if need be.
The Maine Forest Service sent a helicopter to the scene Friday, as well as several rangers who were assisting on the ground. Firefighters from various towns, including Bethel, West Paris, Greenwood, Newry, Sumner, Paris and Norway were also sent to the area.
A request was sent Friday for a CMP worker after power lines were discovered down on Mann Road near where it is believed the blaze began.
It’s possible the downed lines had sparked the blaze, although that could not be confirmed Friday. The cause is expected to be investigated once the fire is under control.
Some customers were without power Friday due to the downed lines, CMP said.
Mann Road runs along the eastern shore of North Pond in the area of Buck’s Ledge Community Forest, a popular hiking spot that encompasses roughly 640 acres. Smoke was drifting up the side of the mountain, toward the ledge, over steep and rugged terrain.
On nearby Route 26, several cars had stopped along the road as their occupants viewed the progress of the blaze. Drivers have been asked not to pull over to watch the fire to reduce traffic issues and risks of an accident.
By 4:30 p.m. Friday, heavy smoke was billowing over Buck’s Ledge. Crews from more than a dozen fire trucks were battling the blaze.
By early evening, a light wind was blowing in from the west at 5 mph in the area of the fire. The fire at that time appeared to be at least halfway up the mountain.
A short time later, fire crews began calling some firefighters back due to the dangers of battling a woods fire at night. The Forest Service helicopter also left the area shortly before 5 p.m.
Most of the state has been in severe drought since mid-August. At the start of November, the U.S. Department of Agriculture designated seven Maine counties as natural disaster areas due to the ongoing drought, unlocking relief for farmers, businesses and nonprofits throughout most of the state.
Oxford County was not among those counties. However, some areas bordering the most troubled zones might also be eligible for federal relief.
Earlier this month, a wildfire in the White Mountain National Forest, just over the Maine border in Coos County, New Hampshire, consumed over 800 acres. First reported on Nov. 1, it took roughly 10 days to halfway contain it. The U.S. Forest Service estimated in its latest update on Tuesday that the Wild River Fire had burned 817 acres and was 59% contained.
The ongoing drought, which has impacted parts of New Hampshire, was a key factor in the fire’s rapid growth, a White Mountains National Forest Service representative said.
This story will be updated.

title: Trump administration official jailed for reckless driving defended his speeding on Reddit
text:
(CNN) - A senior deputy to Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte has defended driving at excessive speeds.
Aaron Kofsky was pulled over in Virginia in April for allegedly driving 109 miles per hour.
In August, he was sentenced for misdemeanor reckless driving to 90 days in jail, with 86 of those days suspended.
He also paid a fine and court costs and lost his license for 6 months.
A CNN review of his posts to Reddit after that incident revealed he wrote that speed is not inherently dangerous and that excessive speed isn’t the same as distracted driving.
Kofsky was previously fired from then-senator JD Vance’s team after he posted to Reddit about taking illegal drugs and how to sneak them through airports.
Neither Kofsky nor the Federal Housing Finance Agency has commented.

title: Man in ICU after 7-foot plank flies off pickup, crashes through windshield
text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily/Gray News) - A Phoenix man has spent eight days in intensive care after a 7-foot wood plank flew off a pickup truck and crashed through his windshield on an interstate, his mother said.
Lisa Hughes said her 35-year-old son, DJ Hughes, was driving near Jackrabbit Trail around 1:20 p.m. Nov. 10 when the wood came from a white pickup truck hauling lumber on Interstate 10 in Buckeye.
The plank slid across the hood of his car before striking him in the face, she said.
Family seeks pickup driver
DJ Hughes’ family is looking for the pickup driver and hopes anyone who saw what happened or has information will come forward.
Injuries and surgeries
“Broke every bone in his, from his eyes down. Split his chin in half,” Lisa Hughes said.
She said her son’s skull was fractured in several places. He has undergone three surgeries and will likely need more, she said.
“It’s tough seeing your baby. I know he’s 35, but seeing him laying like that in pain,” she said.
Lisa Hughes described the incident as a near-death experience and said she has thought about what could have happened to someone else.
“Heartbreaking. In a way, I’m thankful that it was him and not a young kid or a young girl,” she said.
Recovery and securing loads
A GoFundMe campaign has been set up to support DJ Hughes’ recovery.
As DJ Hughes faces a long recovery, his mother hopes other drivers will take a moment to make sure their loads are secure.
“Just take the extra two seconds to secure it. It’s not that much time to save a life,” Hughes said.

title: Total number of jobs in Maine holds steady as unemployment rate streak sets record
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Total number of jobs in Maine holds steady as unemployment rate streak sets record
According to a new report from the Maine Department of Labor on Friday, the unemployment rate in Maine in October held steady at 3.3%. The unemployment rate for the state has been below 4% for 58 consecutive months, the longest stretch on record.
The report shows there were about 679,400 people in Maine who had jobs in October, about 7,000 fewer than in October of 2025. The total number of unemployed people in Maine, according to the report, was down by about 1,500.
The unemployment rate was highest in Piscataquis and Washington counties and lowest in Sagadahoc and Cumberland counties.
The Department of Labor says Maine’s unemployment rate has been below the U.S. average for more than 18 years and remains below the long-term average of 5.4% for the state since 1976. Unemployment averaged 4.1% for New England and the U.S. in the month.
The labor force participation rate averaged 58.5% over the last three months, which is slightly lower than during the three month period ending in July.
The department blamed the lower labor force participation rate on a decreasing employment-to-population ratio.
The report shows that the number of nonfarm wage and salary jobs was basically the same as a month ago, and that there was little or no net job change across all sectors. Job estimates have stayed within a narrow range near 660,000 for 30 consecutive months.
Among jobs in the private sector, the workweek averaged 33.3 hours and earnings averaged $34.14 per hour in October. The report shows that average hours changed little, and hourly earnings increased 4.1% from one year ago.

title: A Mainer's Case Against Green Bean Casserole, French-Fried Onions And All
text:
I love many things about Thanksgiving, but one dish doesn't do it for me.
Maine Thanksgivings are Filled With Delicious Fresh Food
Thanksgiving is a feast for any foodie.
So many amazing dishes to enjoy.
I really love cranberries, so whether the sauce is homemade or it's shaped like the can it came in, I'm going to have some on my plate.
READ MORE: Thanksgiving's Best Pie Isn't Apple or Pumpkin: It's a Maine Classic
Turkey is always delicious, especially with a little extra salt.
And no one makes stuffing like my mother-in-law. I could (and have) made an entire meal out of it.
This Mainer Will Pass When Passed the Green Bean Casserole
But when someone passes me the bowl of green bean casserole, I have to pass it along to the next diner without showing how much I dislike it.
Now, I know what you're thinking...I just haven't had YOUR green bean casserole.
Wrong.
Sorry...but I've heard that before.
And I'll admit it's a weird thing.
I love green beans, whether they're canned, frozen, or fresh out of my husband's garden. (The best)
I love cream of mushroom soup in any number of dishes.
And French-fried onion rings? Yes, please!
But put them together, and that becomes a no, thank you.
Maine Green Beans Should Be Crisp, Not Slimy in a Casserole
There's just something about the cream of mushroom soup that makes the green beans slimy, and I greatly dislike that.
It's not just a texture thing...I truly don't like the flavors together.
Dumping a bunch of those crunchy French-fried onions on top won't even save this dish for me.
I can't be the only one who feels this way.
Please, someone, tell me you also hate green bean casserole, so I know I'm not alone.
Happy Thanksgiving, all!
I hope you get all of your favorite dishes!

title: Commanders QB Sam Hartman says he's going on 'The Bachelor' for the chance 'to find somebody'
text:
Commanders QB Sam Hartman says he's going on 'The Bachelor' for the chance 'to find somebody'
For the first time in his football career, Sam Hartman hasn't watched film.
The Washington Commanders quarterback says he's never seen an episode of “The Bachelor,” but the 27-year-old is set to star in the upcoming season of the long-running reality show.
“The opportunity to find somebody,” Hartman said Thursday, explaining why he pursued going on the show. “I think that’s a really rare experience and I think just a really unique opportunity to experience ... the traveling of the world and also to experience the idea of finding your future teammate.”
Related video in player above: Sam Hartman named as next star on 'The Bachelor'
Hartman, signed as an undrafted free agent in 2024 out of Notre Dame, has yet to play in a regular-season game for the Commanders. He's currently on the team's practice squad. When this season ends for Washington, he'll begin shooting the 30th season of “The Bachelor,” which premieres on March 21. The Commanders' last regular-season game will be played either Jan. 9 or Jan. 10.
The decision to cast Hartman is not entirely new; Jesse Palmer, now the show’s host, was a quarterback for the New York Giants when he appeared in the fifth season.
Hartman said it's an exciting opportunity to showcase himself. His experiences as a starting QB at Wake Forest and Notre Dame, he said, will help him deal with both the criticism and praise “The Bachelor” has brought his way.
“It’s awesome,” Commanders right guard Sam Cosmi said, laughing. “It’s not a distraction, first and foremost. We're rooting for the guy, we're rooting for Sam. I had a group of guys at O-line house (in college). We used to watch ‘The Bachelorette.’ O-linemen, we'd bring wide receivers, we had my girl and the volleyball girls come over. We had a whole thing. We watched ‘The Bachelorette’ and it was just our thing. We had a great time with it. You think it’s shocking, but there’s a lot of guys out there that do that.”
Cosmi said that if there are teammates around in the offseason, he wouldn't mind getting together to watch Hartman on the show.
“They got a heck of a guy for that show,” he said.
Hartman said people in the building were supportive of his decision to become “The Bachelor” during the offseason.
Football “is my first love and always [has] been my first love,” Hartman said. “And so I’m hoping to find the second love, and then also continue to show my second love, my first love.”

title: Chef gives tips on how to avoid getting sick at Friendsgiving potlucks
text:
Chef gives tips on how to avoid getting sick at Friendsgiving potlucks
Chef and culinary instructor Anna Banda shares advice on food safety for Friendsgiving gatherings, focusing on food temperature, handwashing, and asking questions.
Chef gives tips on how to avoid getting sick at Friendsgiving potlucks
Chef and culinary instructor Anna Banda shares advice on food safety for Friendsgiving gatherings, focusing on food temperature, handwashing, and asking questions.
As Friendsgiving potlucks approach this weekend, culinary instructor Anna Banda is offering practical tips to help guests and cooks stay safe and avoid foodborne illness.
“If you walk in and you think it doesn't look right, don't eat it,” Banda said.
Banda, a chef and culinary instructor at Francis Tuttle in Oklahoma with three decades of experience, highlighted the importance of food temperature as a key indicator of safety.
“If something is supposed to be served hot. If it's not hot, I wouldn't eat it. If something is supposed to be served cold and it's not cold, I wouldn't eat it,” she said.
She also advised guests to consider how long food has been sitting out before going back for seconds.
“Four hours is a maximum. We always talk about it in class. We always try to on the side of like 2 to 3 maximum,” Banda said.
While food temperature is important, Banda emphasized that handwashing is the most critical safety measure.
“The number one safety is wash your hands, wash your hands, wash your hands, wash your hands,” she said.
Finally, Banda encouraged guests to ask questions about the food they’re eating.
“I don't think there's anything wrong with asking, you know. Hey, who brought this and what's in it?” she said.
According to Banda, asking questions may be the last line of defense against getting sick.

title: Trump says he plans to penalize US tech companies that build AI data centers in other countries
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump says U.S. tech companies will face “a tremendous tax” if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries.
Trump did not provide details Friday and he said he hadn’t yet told his own officials about his plan. The Republican president urged Americans to welcome data center construction in their communities and extract concessions from the developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
Trump says, “You ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off.”
The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train its best artificial intelligence models.
With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses.
The new raft of promises from the world’s richest companies came as anti-data center sentiment was a potent issue in the midterm elections, in which Democrats took control of Congress.
After a campaign season filled with outrage against artificial intelligence data centers, the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.
A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if Trump — perhaps the industry’s biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown.
Despite backing from Trump, the data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom have become politically toxic.
The tech industry says it has gotten the message. In addition to ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build.
Companies are also making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment and offering assurances that data centers will boost local property values — all while maintaining AI is a positive force for the American economy, despite its skeptics.

title: How conservation efforts helped bison recover from near extinction
text:
JAMESTOWN, N.D. (InvestigateTV) — More than 100 years of conservation efforts have helped keep bison from disappearing, and the population is now nearly half a million and growing, according to Ilana Xinos, executive director of the North American Bison Discovery Center.
Bison once roamed North America in the tens of millions. They became a critical part of Native American culture, which used the animal for food, shelter, tools, clothing and jewelry.
In the 1800s, the westward expansion of European settlers, along with railways, rifles and an international market for hides, led to the bison’s rapid decline.
Xinos called the story of American bison conservation is “the greatest success story.”
“Before the 20th century, right when bison got down to a population, I would say under a thousand, people went out to try to gather them up and save them,” Xinos said. “And there were ranchers. There were indigenous people. There were — one of them was a taxidermist, and he said, you know, these bison are going to go extinct, and I’m going on a journey to collect them for taxidermy so people can at least even know what they looked like. He changed his mind. He wanted to save them.”
Xinos said the story of American bison conservation is “the greatest success story.”
Bison are still considered “near threatened,” but enough exist that they can be found on dinner tables everywhere.
“They think, you know, if you eat a bison steak, like you’re contributing to their demise,” Xinos said. She said “people who are ranching bison love bison.”
Xinos said many people still think bison are extinct. Conservation of the national mammal can take different forms. “We don’t say your way is right, your way is wrong.”
She said the animal is meant to be wild, but human development makes that virtually impossible.
The animal’s spiritual importance to Native Americans, economic importance to ranchers and symbolic importance to the nation led to the National Bison Legacy Act of 2016, which made the bison the national mammal.
“This is an animal. It represents us. And look what it did and look how it keeps going,” Xinos said.
Yellowstone National Park is the only place where bison have lived continuously since prehistoric times, according to the National Park Service.
The National Park Service reports bison weigh more than 1,000 pounds, are agile and can reach speeds of up to 35 mph.
Bison can be aggressive, and rangers suggest staying at least 25 yards away. That is about two standard school bus lengths.

title: Trump speaks after meeting with Xi, Putin at APEC summit
text:
SHENZHEN, China (AP) — Results matter in the international arena, but so do optics.
This week’s high-level meetings in China’s tech hub gave President Xi Jinping a win, reinforcing his image as a central player in global diplomacy and demonstrating the nation’s superpower status.
As host of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday and Thursday, Xi welcomed the leaders of 21 economies that account for about 60% of global economic activity. He also convened the first formal gathering of the three biggest nuclear powers: the United States, Russia and China.
“History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace, and when they engage in confrontation the world is thrown into turmoil,” Xi said Thursday before starting closed-door discussions with U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“Our three countries should set an example by working together to address global challenges, jointly safeguard world peace and stability and make greater contributions to human progress,” he added.
Summit images were a diplomatic win despite lack of substance
Although the trilateral meeting produced no major breakthroughs, the image of Xi, Trump and Putin seated at an enormous round table with Xi at the center will become part of diplomatic history.
“For most, the image was a suggestion that the world increasingly revolves around Beijing’s power and preferences,” Rush Doshi, director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in an article. “And for U.S. allies in particular, it was unsettling because it suggested that Washington will prioritize engagement with the other great powers over that with its own partners.”
“Xi’s clearest diplomatic gain in Shenzhen was bringing Trump and Putin to the same table,” said Yaqi Li, a Chinese foreign policy researcher at Singapore’s ISEAS — Yusof Ishak Institute.
China has positioned itself as a force for global stability in recent years. Xi started the meeting with Trump and Putin with a reminder of how the three countries fought together in World War II.
“History is the best textbook,” Xi said, presenting the talks as a way to push for peace for humanity. “We must remember history, learn from it and work together to shape the future.”
The meeting resulted in a joint declaration that was light on commitments and did not tackle major issues in a substantive way.
“They’re using this opportunity … to highlight that China is a great power, and they’re in a different status relative to other countries,” said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.
On Friday, meetings between Xi and other foreign leaders continued. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim congratulated him.
“You were successful in handling President Trump and President Putin together. That takes only President Xi, I don’t know anyone else who can do that,” he said.
Relationship with US appears stable but issues remain
Xi and Trump held their third meeting this year, highlighting the personal rapport they have built that both men said was important to the bilateral relationship between their nations. China’s government highlighted the “constructive strategic stability” of the relationship, while Xi commended the U.S. president for his role.
“The efforts you have made are there for all to see and will go down in history,” Xi told Trump.
There were no announcements about existing trade tensions between the countries, such as U.S. complaints that China has not fulfilled its commitment to buy from U.S. farmers and export more rare earth materials. Nor were there announcements about the Board of Trade and the expected framework to allow trade in nonsensitive goods worth $30 billion on each side.
It was unclear if officials taking part in a diplomatic channel to discuss artificial intelligence issues met in Shenzhen, said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
However, “AI seems to be the one area where some progress has been made, with China affirming its concerns about safety and security and welcoming bilateral work,” Cutler said.
Whether the personal rapport between Xi and Trump can persist will be tested soon, according to Craig Singleton, senior fellow and senior director of the China Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
“Xi treated Trump with respect in Shenzhen. He will test his resolve in Miami next month, when the bill for Beijing’s trade commitments comes due,” Singleton said in an email.

title: Crunchy, chewy and charitable, the Girl Scout cookie is an emblem of empowerment
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Ding dong — the Girl Scout cookies are here!
Whether delivered door to door, sold outside a grocery store or even dropped by drones, the arrival of Girl Scout cookie season is a time-honored tradition that people anticipate for months.
More than century ago, a simple idea of a bake sale run by a Muskogee, Oklahoma, troop of Girl Scouts spread in a grassroots way across the country. In a few years, troops were sharing homemade recipes for shortbread cookies that could be easily baked, wrapped in wax paper and sold for a quarter a dozen. Today hundreds of thousands of scouts sell cookies each year, giving them entrepreneurial experience and money to fund troop activities.
As a former scout and scout leader, the cookies were a staple in my house: stacked up by the hundreds in our hallway, hauled from one Kmart to another, peddled and pushed at every shopper or distant relative or random passerby.
Through sleet, snow, wind and rain, I would be out selling cookies multiple nights and weekends, often poorly calculating change by doing math on my mittened fingers. These days, scouts are more often swiping a credit card or holding up a QR code. No more counting out quarters from a cash box.
As a leader, I watched scouts learn to find their voice when approaching an adult with a box or an order sheet. Some kids just enjoyed counting sales and inventory or competing for who could sell the most. A portion of each sale helps fund camps, trips, community projects and other activities. I could rely on cookie sale proceeds to make sure everyone in our troop got an opportunity to go camping, even if their family couldn’t afford it.
Wanna start a lively discussion? Ask a crowd which is the best Girl Scout cookie flavor. People hold steadfast to the cookies they grew up eating, whether it’s the hugely popular Thin Mints, the shortbreads perfect for a cup of tea, the chocolate-covered peanut butter cookies or the caramel and coconut circles. My favorite has always been the Tagalongs, so don’t come at me.
Today there are more ways to enjoy Girl Scout cookies. They’ve had gluten-free, nut-free and vegan versions and even ones that dogs can enjoy. Plenty of other brands have tried to jump aboard the train with products like cookie-scented candles, Thin Mint-flavored coffee, Lemon-Up doughnuts and yes, even a line of shampoo, deodorant and body washes that smells remarkably like Do-si-dos.
The secret to the cookie success was only marginally about the crumbly, crunchy treat that keeps people buying them. The true pleasure was a little charitable giving, packaged in a reward for yourself.
