title: Planned Brunswick airport customs facility sparks immigration enforcement fears
text:
BRUNSWICK — At a tense meeting Thursday night, some Brunswick residents voiced fears that a planned Customs and Border Protection facility at Brunswick Executive Airport could lead to increased immigration enforcement, though the entity that owns the airport says that is not the case.
The packed meeting was intended to review the airport master plan, a Federal Aviation Administration requirement that lays out options for the next 20-plus years of development at the Brunswick Executive Airport, or BXM.
Recommendations in the plan include rehabilitating one of the airport’s runways and shortening the other, as well as allowing for several new aircraft hangars. It also includes plans for a customs facility to be built sometime around 2029.
“We know that Customs and Border Protection works hand-in-hand with ICE, and they are both part of the Department of Homeland Security,” said Catherine Whitaker, who stood outside Town Hall Thursday night with signs reading “MRRA lies” and “No BXM expansion.”
“They have proven themselves to be an unruly, out of control agency, and to invite them into our community is absolutely uncalled for,” Whitaker said.
Midcoast Regional Redevelopment Authority, a quasi-governmental organization that oversees the redevelopment of the former Navy air base, says the planned CBP facility would allow customers to fly in and out of the country without stopping at larger airports like Portland International Jetport.
“There’s no inference that it would somehow become a de facto ICE facility,” Jim Nall, Brunswick airport manager, said in an interview Thursday.
Some at the meeting Thursday night questioned any development on the former air base, which was the site of an August 2024 spill of 1,450 gallons of aqueous film-forming foam, or AFFF, containing a toxic PFAS chemical known as PFOS, mixed with 50,000 gallons of water.
The spill drained harmful chemicals through the sewer and stormwater systems and into surrounding ponds, streams and rivers, and became the largest foam spill in Maine history.
“Do we really want to start messing with concrete saturated with PFAS and other toxins before we know what we’re dealing with?” Brunswick resident Ralph Keyes asked at Thursday’s meeting.
Tests conducted by the Friends of Merrymeeting Bay this summer showed high levels of PFAS in the airport hangar oil-water separators, which feed into the sewer system. MRRA Director Dan Stevenson said the authority is looking into filtration systems for the oil-water pits.
CUSTOMS FACILITY
A social media post circulated by the Maine Democratic Socialists of America drew attention to Thursday’s meeting by claiming that the customs facility “could effectively give Immigration and Customs Enforcement a new home-away-from-home in Midcoast Maine.”
MRRA denies that ICE would have any involvement in the planned $6.5 million customs facility, which is expected to process 145 aircraft annually. The facility would be owned and funded by MRRA, not the federal government, Stevenson said Thursday. It would likely employ one CBP agent.
Town Councilor Ramona Thieme, who is endorsed by the Maine DSA, said in an email Wednesday that it’s “naive” to ignore the possibility of the facility being used for immigration enforcement, since ICE and CBP often collaborate.
“Although the proposed customs facilities do not have a listed intent of assisting with enforcement actions against residents, it is naive to ignore this possibility,” Thieme said. “The risks of housing CBP here are especially significant due to the potential to move people out of state via our airport and the airport’s proximity to where most residents have been taken within our community.”
In a memo to MRRA board members this week, Stevenson wrote that the facility “was not conceived, proposed, or designed as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility, detention center, or immigration enforcement operation.”
“Part of CBP’s requirement is a detention cell, if they have to detain a pilot that, for example, flies in and there’s an active warrant on that pilot … or, a plane shows up with a bunch of drugs in the plane or something, they need the ability to detain that person until either local or state law enforcement can take that on,” Nall said Thursday.
Nall and Stevenson stressed that the master plan is only for planning purposes, and that all projects would require proper regulatory approvals.
“In the plan, there’s space for numerous hangars. Does that mean we’re going to put all those hangars there? It doesn’t,” Nall said.

title: Woman admits to using Meta glasses to secretly record witnesses in federal drug trial
text:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) — An Alabama woman who was upset about the prosecution of a now-convicted drug “kingpin” admitted Thursday that she used special glasses to secretly record witnesses who testified at the trial in January.
Tierra Shatalia “Badd Twin” Douglas, 35, of Mobile, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to retaliate against a witness.
Recording inside the courthouse
Recording devices are prohibited in federal court.
Douglas admitted that she used Meta glasses inside the courthouse to secretly record three witnesses during the January trial of Glennie “Little Man” McGee and his wife and sister-in-law.
Douglas also admitted that she communicated with co-conspirators to obtain personal information about the witnesses.
Harassment after the trial
Douglas’ written plea agreement indicates her harassment continued for months after the trial. In one case, according to the plea document, she asked ChatGPT in August to make a flyer identifying one of the witnesses as a “snitch.” The chatbot responded that it could not create a flyer accusing a real person of being a confidential informant but could produce an image that clearly was labeled as a fictional character or parody.
One of the witnesses reported that on Jan. 16, he received a video from a friend showing him exiting the courtroom, where he had just testified. Douglas admitted that she disseminated a flyer with a picture of the witness, labeling him as a “snitch.” She also admitted that she sent Discord messages identifying one of his minor children and where the child went to school.
In February, according to the plea agreement, Douglas sent text messages to the same witness. He was identified in her phone contacts as “The Rat.” She sent numerous messages taunting him for testifying.
Sentencing
Confronted with evidence that included internal surveillance video from the courthouse, Douglas confessed, according to the plea document.
A federal judge set Douglas’ sentencing for Feb. 19. The maximum sentence is life in prison, but prosecutors have agreed to recommend leniency.

title: ‘This program saved my life’: veteran credits horse therapy
text:
Folsom, La. — Some veterans and first responders in Louisiana are finding peace at New Heights Therapy Center, the only equine-assisted therapy center of its kind in the state. Participants do not ride the horses. They groom and lead them, building trust, reducing stress and regulating emotions.
Coast Guard veteran Juliet LeBlanc, who says she struggles with PTSD, said horses were the key to her healing. “This program saved my life,” LeBlanc said. She has graduated from the program and still volunteers at the center.
Program Director Vicki Eiland said most people find the center through word of mouth. “So we saw that need and developed a program to help them build resilience and connect with other veterans,” Eiland said.
Adam Shields, a fire prevention captain with St. Tammany Fire District Five, said the program helps him reset without saying a word. “I’m not familiar with horses, but I’m much better now,” Shields said. Folsom police officer Patrick Fair said it took four weeks to get comfortable with the horses. He has since built a relationship with Pete.

title: Fans near and far mourn Fiona the hippo after her death at the Cincinnati Zoo
text:
CINCINNATI (AP) — Fans of Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s hippo, draped a hippo statue with flowers and notes written in crayon Friday, a day after she died from complications caused by swallowing a knit hat accidentally flung into her enclosure.
A little girl held up a drawing of Fiona while a woman left behind a watermelon, one of Fiona’s favorite treats.
“She brought so much love in her lifetime,” said one note.
Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many — from teachers to parents to children.
“I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle,” Thayne Maynard, the zoo board’s executive chair, said in a statement. “And, she will be remembered and beloved many years from now.”
Zoo officials have yet to release the specific medical cause of Fiona’s death or details surrounding her final hours. Fiona was 9 years old.
“Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore,” zoo director Dave Jenike said.
Zoo worked around the clock to save Fiona
At first, Fiona showed no signs of distress after swallowing the hat 11 days before her death. A zoo visitor tossed the hat, which a ceiling fan caught and flung into the hippo habitat.
But a few days later, her appetite started to decline, zoo officials said. By Monday, the zoo announced Fiona was undergoing veterinary care.
The zoo’s animal care team gave her fluids through an IV, conducted a colonoscopy and tried to shake the obstruction loose with a vibration table borrowed from a horse farm.
They said they were cautiously optimistic she could pass the hat.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.
The zoo’s director said Fiona’s death came as a shock. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore,” Jenike said.
Fiona is mourned by many worldwide
Fiona captured the hearts of millions in her first months and final days, uniting people across all boundaries and political spectrums.
Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, posted a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through the glass wall of her enclosure.
Former first daughter Chelsea Clinton posted photos of her behind-the-scenes encounter with Fiona, writing that she would treasure “the smiles she gave me.”
Speaking outside the zoo Thursday, Amy Haacke, a teacher from Dayton, said that she was a “huge fan” of Fiona because she likes underdogs. She said she uses the Fiona book series in her classroom.
“It kind of means a lot to be here,” she said.
Fiona wasn’t expected to survive her first weeks
Fiona was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), far below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time.
The zoo’s staff went to extraordinary lengths to keep her alive, raising her by hand. She couldn’t nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother to feed her.
She became a celebrity during her nine years. Hippos typically live 40 to 50 years in zoos.
Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the 2016 shooting of Harambe. The gorilla became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.

title: Here’s how you can live on a beautiful island for free
text:
(Gray News) - SyroCats, a non-profit cat rescue on the Greek island of Syros, is looking for volunteers, who can live on the island and help take care of cats.
In exchange for noms and lodging, volunteers care for cats on the island. They feed clowders, or feral cat colonies, across the island, plus they support around 70 “long-term residents” at their facility.
The shelter also provides medical care for sick or injured cats and runs a trap-neuter-return program to help control the cat population.
Volunteers must be able to commit to at least one month of service, be self- sufficient, and able to perform daily duties that include cleaning, lifting, and handling cats.
No previous experience is needed, but any training or veterinary experience is a plus. Interested people can apply here.
Voluntourism
SyroCats is one example of a growing trend of voluntourism, where travelers pitch in for a cause at their travel destination.
Grand View Research estimates the current market size of about $1 billion to grow to over $1.5 billion by 2033.
Many well know organizations, such as Habitat for Humanity, the American Red Cross and the https://www.peacecorps.gov/ offer opportunities both in country and abroad.
What to know before planning a volunteer trip
The U.S. Department of State has advice for Americans considering voluntourism. Some of the suggestions include:
- Always research any organization before committing
- Make sure passports and other travel documents are up to date before planning a trip
- Look for organizations that provide in-country support, preferably 24 hours a day, for volunteers

title: How to make sure your business shows up in Google AI searches
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Your customers have changed the way they search online. Instead of typing “plumber Portland,” more of them type a full question, such as “Who can fix a frozen pipe in Portland tonight?” or “Do I need a lawyer to set up an LLC in Maine?”
Google now answers many of those questions with an AI Overview, a written summary at the top of the results that sometimes names specific businesses. Most owners have never checked whether their company appears in those answers. At the same time, vendors have started pitching “AI optimization” packages to small businesses, often with little explanation of what the work involves.
Google’s own guidance for site owners is a good place to start. It says there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode and that the best practices for SEO (Search Engine Optimization) remain relevant for its AI features. The fundamentals still decide who shows up. Here are some tips to find out where you stand and what to fix.
Search the questions your customers ask. Write down five to 10 questions you hear on the phone or at the counter. Search each one on your phone and laptop. Note whether an AI Overview appears, which businesses or websites it mentions and whether yours is among them. When a competitor is named and you aren’t, open its website and Business Profile and compare. Look for what AI Overview covers that you leave out. Results can change over time, so repeat the exercise every few months and keep your notes.
Audit your Google Business Profile. Google lists keeping your Business Profile information up to date among its best practices for its AI features. Check your hours, holiday hours, categories, service area, services and photos. Make sure your business name, address and phone number match your website exactly. Owners who set up a profile years ago and never revisited it often find outdated hours or a missing service. While you’re there, ask a few recent customers to leave a review. A profile with current feedback gives searchers more of a reason to call.
Answer questions directly on your website. If customers regularly ask how much a septic inspection costs or how long a kitchen remodel takes, your site should address the topic in plain language near the top of a relevant page. A short list of common questions on a service page is one simple way to do this, as long as the answers are specific to your business. A clear answer in the first sentence or two helps the person reading and makes the page easier for any search tool to understand. A page that only says “contact us for details” offers potential customers and search tools very little to work with.
Be skeptical of special tricks. Google says you don’t need to create AI text files, new machine-readable files or special schema markup to appear in its AI features. If a proposal centers on a secret technique, ask the vendor which Google documentation supports it. Structured data can still help search engines read a page, but Google says it should match the visible text on that page.
Measure what you can. Google counts clicks from AI Overviews and AI Mode in the Performance report in Google Search Console, within the overall Web search numbers. Search Console is free, and if no one has set it up for your website, that is worth doing first. Pair that data with your manual checks and track the outcomes that matter most to a small business: phone calls, form submissions and booked jobs.
The takeaway
None of these steps requires a large budget. An afternoon of searching, an hour on your Business Profile and a few rewritten pages can help you figure out where you stand.
Google has been clear that the basics still apply. Accurate information and clear answers serve your customers whether they find you in an AI Overview, a map listing or a regular search result.

title: Local MMA fighters win championships at NEF 69: Crossfire
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Two local MMA fighters won championships at Saturday’s NEF 69: Crossfire in Bangor.
Bucksport’s Jayce Murphy submitted Eric Checinski with an armbar to take Checinski’s amateur bantamweight championship in the second round.
Then in the main event, Holden’s Ed Davis beat CJ Ewer by technical knockout in the second round to win the vacant professional welterweight title.
“I started Jiu Jitsu when I was eight years old. I just kind of wanted to be doing that for as long as I can remember. title: A Maine girl shot her 1st buck at just 5 years old
text:
At just 5 years old, Maisey Philbrick has already shot her first deer. She killed a buck Tuesday from about 80 yards away while hunting with her father, Brady, in Wildlife Management District 16.
Maisey used her father’s Remington .308 from their hunting shack. Brady had taken her out of school that day to hunt.
The two sat together for a while, watching several does move through the area. Maisey eventually fell asleep, but Brady woke her when he noticed the deer becoming more active. He suspected a buck might be nearby.
A buck the family had nicknamed “Nine Lives” soon appeared. Several family members had previously tried to shoot the deer without success.
With her father’s help, Maisey got the buck in her scope and fired. The deer dropped where it stood.
She excitedly called her mother, Hope, who initially thought the call was about picking Maisey and her younger sister up from daycare.
Instead, Maisey wanted Hope to bring the family’s “by-and-side” — their side-by-side — so they could retrieve the deer.
Maisey Philbrick, 5, celebrates her first deer (left) and gets an early introduction to processing wild game (right) at her family’s butcher shop, B&H Meat Cutting. Credit: Courtesy of Hope Philbrick
The family tagged the buck and brought it to B&H Meat Cutting, their family butcher shop, where it was caped for a shoulder mount.
Maisey has grown up around the wild game business, and longtime customers of the shop came to celebrate her first deer.
Although this is her first year interested in hunting, Maisey has been practicing with a .22 rifle since last year. She and Brady began preparing for deer hunting over the summer.
She is already looking ahead to her next hunt. Maisey hopes to fill her doe tag during Thanksgiving break. She and her father also have a list of hunts in other states they hope to do together someday.

title: Midcoast couple creates lobstering board game inspired by Penobscot Bay
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The board game Corker started as a map.
“Almost every house in Maine that’s been around for a long time will have this Penobscot Bay chart on the wall … One day I walked past that thing and thought, ‘This is a perfect game board,’” Corker co-creator Greg Birgfeld said.
That was over a year ago. Now, it’s a fully-fleshed out board game. A trailer of the first 1,000 copies arrived Wednesday at Birgfeld and co-creator Cindy Wren’s home in Swanville.
Corker is a strategy game based on Penobscot Bay lobster fishing. The game is played with two to six players, and can take one to three hours depending on the number of players.
“Corker” is a British slang term to refer to something striking. In the 1830s, it was also used to mean something that could settle a debate. The creators chose the name for its old-fashioned, distinctive sound.
Wren and Birgfeld aimed to capture the uncertainty faced by lobstermen, with game mechanics simulating changing markets and unpredictable weather. The element of luck also makes for more enjoyable play, Wren said.
“Every time we play-tested, even with the same group of friends, a different person wins every time, so I don’t have to feel insecure about, ‘Well, I’m just bad at this game,’” Wren said.
The game went through several rounds of play-testing and redesign. Some of those rounds were with lobstermen, allowing Wren and Birgfeld to assess whether their game accurately captured the experience of lobster fishing. The first play-test took place at Vinalhaven Community Brewery, where many nearby residents are in the lobster industry.
Birgfeld was excited whenever a player would say, “You know, that happened to me just last week,” he said.
Players select fishing locations within Penobscot Bay, claiming them with tokens of boats and buoys. The tokens were 3D-printed by Wren and Birgfeld, who had a 3D printer in their basement from Birgfeld’s Etsy business selling fantasy miniatures for tabletop games and collectibles.
The choice to self-produce the tokens was cost-saving but time-consuming, Wren said. Over the past five months, the pair have spent two hours a night 3D-printing. They have enough tokens now for 400 games.
The tokens were too much of a selling point to be removed from the game, Wren said.
“Everybody kind of fell in love with the boats … It was really important that we keep that for the game,” she said.
Wren marketed the game through word-of-mouth and social media. Copies of the game have been pre-ordered across the country, particularly in Maine and the Pacific Northwest.
Corker is Anchor Point’s first board game. Birgfeld and Wren have several ideas for their next game: a collaborative game based on the logging industry in 1830s Maine, for example, or a simulation of sheep farming.

title: 9-year-old taken to ER after eating THC gummy that friend gave her at school, mom says
text:
LINCOLN, Neb. (KOLN/Gray News) - A 9-year-old Nebraska girl was taken to the emergency room after eating a THC gummy a friend gave her at elementary school, according to her mom.
Kala Strow said she got a call from her daughter Eleanor’s school last week saying that she wasn’t feeling well.
“She said she felt like her head was caving in. Her head was heavy,” Strow said. “And everything was spinning. She said she felt like it wasn’t the same world.”
Strow said Eleanor had eaten what she thought was candy from a friend at lunchtime. She rushed her daughter to the emergency room.
After the incident, Strow said the other student’s parent reached out and apologized. The parent told her the child was afraid to return to school after a suspension and that the family had received threats.
Strow said she has been disappointed by some parents’ reactions, including people laughing about the incident and making assumptions she said were untrue.
“When things do happen to our children it’s not because of where I live, or the school that my daughter went to, or because of my past, or our skin color, or who we are,” she said. “It has nothing to do with that. It could have happened to any of these children.”
Strow said she wants the community to focus on preventing another incident.
“Why are we pointing fingers and blaming rather than doing what we can to make sure that no other child in the community has to go through this?” she said.
Strow said the other student and the student’s parent told her the gummy came from Halloween, but Lincoln police said they have not been able to confirm where it came from.
Police said the case is inactive and no citations have been issued. If new information becomes available, they will continue investigating.

text:
GORHAM, N.H. (WCAX) - The Wild River wildfire in the White Mountain National Forest has now been burning for several weeks.

Firefighters remain focused on suppressing hot spots and conducting monitoring, patrol and mop-up operations. The blaze has not spread and remains under 1,000 acres.
Full containment is not expected until there is significant precipitation.

title: Prosecutors: Men charged in $22M train cargo thefts shared videos of themselves from heists
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — More than a dozen people were charged Thursday with allegedly orchestrating a massive train heist operation to steal over $22 million in cargo — from popular shoes to power tools — from major retailers.
A federal indictment unsealed on Thursday paints a picture of an organized group that targeted more than three dozen trains carrying Nike sneakers, Crocs footwear, power tools and other consumer goods that were imported into the United States through Los Angeles and Long Beach, which are home to the busiest ports in the country.
Trains that shuttle goods to stores and customers around the country have become a prominent target for large-scale theft in recent years, especially at large ports in the U.S. that receive hundreds of millions of dollars of shipments every day. The relatively low-tech robberies have demanded attention from the world’s largest retailers, including the likes of Amazon.
The men would disable the trains at a planned location by busting the brakes, the indictment alleged, at which point the goods would be offloaded onto trucks. The goods were then peddled to an unnamed company that would resell the stolen merchandise for profit.
“The scale of the theft is staggering,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli, promising to prosecute any future efforts to steal the merchandise.
In group chats, the men shared numerous photos and videos of themselves busting into the hulking train cars, and posing with wads of cash and stolen merchandise. They also shared AI photos of themselves captioned “Los Trenes,” which means the trains in Spanish, beneath glamorized photos of men throwing boxes of shoes off trains into nearby cars while police helicopters descended overhead.
The 13 men were indicted for conspiracy and theft of interstate railroad cargo. Two were also charged with violence against railroad carriers.
If convicted, the men could face anywhere from five to 20 years in federal prison.

title: Photos and videos show multiacre forest fire burning in Woodstock
text:
Multiacre forest fire burning on Bucks Ledge in Woodstock, Maine
Crews continue to fight a forest fire that is burning multiple acres in the Oxford County town of Woodstock.
Shortly before 5:45 p.m. Friday, the Greenwood Fire and Rescue Department told Maine's Total Coverage that the fire on Bucks Ledge was nowhere near extinguished, and that firefighters are expected to be in the Mann Road area for a few more hours.
Fire officials did note, however, that the number of departments at the scene has been scaled back from the height of the fire Friday afternoon.
Shortly before 6:50 p.m., the Greenwood Fire and Rescue Department shared an update to Facebook, saying the fire was still spreading and that multiple towns were working to extinguish the fire. Firefighters also asked the public to refrain from blocking traffic on Route 26.
The Maine Forest Service confirmed a forest ranger and a helicopter responded to assist crews at the scene. Viewers shared video of the helicopter dumping water on the fire from above.
Multiple photos shared with Maine's Total Coverage also showed the scope of the fire that broke out in the woods on Bucks Ledge.
The Maine Forest Service's wildfire danger map indicates that there was moderate fire danger for the Woodstock area on Friday.
As of 3:41 p.m. Friday, Central Maine Power (CMP) reported that there were 37 power outages in the town of Woodstock, all along roadways surrounding the shore of North Pond, which is next to Bucks Ledge.
But by 4:04 p.m., CMP had removed Woodstock from its power outage list.

title: Wisdom Girls Finish Historic Season With First Soccer Gold Ball
text:
The Fall Five and Five No. 1: Wisdom Girls Finally Bring the Gold Ball Home
There really wasn’t much debate for me about what belonged at No. 1.
Wisdom had been here before.
The Lady Pioneers had reached the state championship three previous times, including 2025, when Bangor Christian beat them 3-0.
Then Bangor Christian beat Wisdom twice more during the 2026 regular season. Those were Wisdom’s only two losses all year So when the two teams met again in the state championship, there really couldn’t have been a more fitting way for Wisdom to finally finish the job.
One More Shot
Wisdom came into the state final at 15-2 after scoring goals at an incredible pace all season.
The Lady Pioneers finished the year with 102 goals, but Bangor Christian had been the one team they hadn’t figured out.
For a while, it looked like that might continue.
Bangor Christian led 1-0 at halftime in Presque Isle, leaving Wisdom 30 minutes away from another state-final disappointment.
Then the game changed.
Emma Soucy tied it in the second half, and Ellie Cyr scored twice late to give Wisdom a 3-1 lead.
When Cyr’s second goal went in with just 1:13 remaining, the Gold Ball was finally within reach.
Mikayl Michaud finished with eight saves, and Wisdom walked away with the first girls soccer state championship in school history.
A Long Wait Ends
That championship carried a little more history with it, too.
Wisdom’s girls had not won a state championship in any sport since the girls basketball team brought home the Class D Gold Ball in 1998.
Twenty-eight years later, another Wisdom girls team finally did it.
It was also the fourth state-final appearance for the girls soccer program, following trips in 1997, 2021 and 2025.
The fourth time was the one that ended with the Gold Ball. Wisdom finished 16-2, scored 102 goals and won four straight tournament games to close the season. And after losing three straight meetings with Bangor Christian going back to the 2025 state final, Wisdom finally beat them when there was no next game left.
That’s about as good an ending as you can ask for.
Family, Then Champions
Wisdom High School was named such in 1965. Sixty-one years later, the girls soccer program finally had its first Gold Ball.
And after hearing “1, 2, 3, family” at ever Wisdom game the better part of a year and a half, this group gets to add one more word to it.
Champions.
That’s why Wisdom girls soccer is No. 1 in my five moments that defined the fall of 2026.

title: Lawsuits allege corner cutting and ignored warnings led to fatal Brooklyn building collapse
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — As investigators probe what caused a New York City building collapse that killed eight people, workers and residents are painting a portrait of two trouble spots side-by-side: the apartment house that fell down and the construction site being excavated next door.
Lawsuits filed since the Nov. 11 disaster in Brooklyn cast blame in multiple directions: at the construction site owner and contractors; at an engineering firm that drew up the excavation plan; and at the owner of the building that collapsed. Several injured workers have also taken steps toward suing the city agency that polices construction safety.
A key question for investigators is whether work underway to dig a deep pit for a new building undermined the foundation of the three-story building next door at 1321 Flatbush Ave., causing it to topple into the jobsite.
A lawsuit filed by five injured construction workers said the dig at 2625 Bedford Ave. lacked adequate retaining walls, shoring and underpinning to keep the adjoining building safe, and that excavation work continued even after the building’s facade began to crack.
“The shoring that they were planning to keep the collapsed building up was severely insufficient,” said lawyer Jonathan Damashek, who has sued on behalf of injured workers. He questioned whether the city should have approved the plans, and whether contractors’ work was negligent.
Damashek’s lawsuits accuse defendants, including construction manager Townhouse Homes, of failing “to consider public safety above their own concern of keeping down costs.”
The litigation comes as families mourn the dead — among them two children. City officials said Wednesday that another building adjoining the one that crumbled will have to be demolished after the collapse peeled off an outer wall.
Tenant says construction work next door led to cracks
Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani vowed to do “everything we can to understand exactly how this collapse occurred, so that the responsible parties can be held to account.” His department is hiring an independent engineering consultant to help. Brooklyn prosecutors also are investigating.
The Buildings Department said by email Friday that it reviewed the excavation and support plans and found they complied with city requirements. As for examining what actually got installed, the agency noted that the city requires private inspectors — hired by developers — to check some stages of construction.
The agency didn’t answer a question about whether it responded to a preconstruction survey that found the adjoining wall of the now-collapsed building “in poor condition with noticeable cracks.”
That three-story brick structure, erected nearly a century ago, had its own woes — over 90 unresolved citations for exposed wiring, roof leaks, faulty doors and other alleged housing code violations.
Conditions worsened once construction ramped up next door, tenant Dengane Omari Jack said in a lawsuit.
Jack, who lost his extensive record collection and other personal effects, said he was rebuffed when he tried warning the landlord about cracks he noticed near the building’s entrance. After providing photos of the damage, Jack was told it wasn’t the landlord’s fault and couldn’t be fixed, the lawsuit said.
Builder and excavation engineer have faced lawsuits
While the investigation proceeds, the city is checking out over 160 construction sites tied to companies involved in the project at 2625 Bedford Ave., a planned apartment and commercial building.
Townhouse, which also operates as Promont, has been heavily involved in New York’s construction scene over the last three decades.
In 2016, it was accused in lawsuits of damaging an adjacent building during a Manhattan renovation project, which it denied, and compromising the structural integrity of adjacent structures while performing excavation, pile driving and steel beam installation for a Brooklyn hotel. The company’s lawyers haven’t addressed the allegations in the lawsuit involving the hotel.
Principals in Townhouse, other firms named in this report and the property owners haven’t responded to The Associated Press’ requests for comment.
The Bedford Avenue project’s excavation engineer, Jieming Wang, has also faced lawsuits. At least a dozen have blamed excavation plans designed by his firm, New Jersey-based LMW Engineering Group, for damage at adjacent properties, court records show.
A 2015 lawsuit alleged that LMW’s work on a Manhattan excavation site caused sloping floors, damaged doors and windows and destroyed utility pipes at an adjacent building.
In 2016, the wall of a building next to a Queens excavation project was undermined by soil removal, another lawsuit said. A 2020 lawsuit accused the firm of skipping required testing and monitoring at another Queens project. A neighboring building’s foundation was left unstable, its gas and hot water systems were damaged and an architectural arch partially separated from the structure, the lawsuit said.
The company, which has worked on bridges, airports and other projects since its 1998 founding, denied the allegations in the 2015 and 2016 cases but hasn’t responded to the 2020 lawsuit. Other litigation was resolved out of court.
City fined project during demolition phase
The Bedford Avenue project ran afoul of the Buildings Department in March for starting to demolish an existing structure without installing enough netting and other protections from flying debris.
Demolition contractor N Tech Design of America was ordered to stop the work — but continued, got caught again in April, admitted both violations and paid a total of $12,500 in fines, city records show.
N Tech representative Aramis Brown told local news outlet The City Reporter that the company finished its work at the site in May and had nothing to do with the excavation or the collapse.
The excavation work started, with city permission, in September.
Collapsed building owner was on “worst landlords” list
The owner of the building that collapsed, Olufemi Falade, has held a slate of Brooklyn buildings under various corporate names — and has been listed on the city public advocate’s “100 worst landlords” roster six times in the last decade.
Falade, a licensed professional engineer, was jailed for 12 days in 2006 for failing to fix violations in a dozen buildings. Then-Housing Commissioner Shaun Donovan called him “one of the most egregious examples we’ve seen citywide of flouting the law and forcing his residents to live in horrible conditions.”
Falade told the Village Voice after his release that tenants weren’t paying rent. “People want something for nothing,” he fumed.
He hasn’t responded to the AP’s requests for comment since the collapse.
At a vigil near the collapse site on Wednesday, housing activists, faith leaders and others called for Falade and the developers to be held accountable.
“New housing cannot come at the expense of tenants’ lives,” said Judith Douglas, a tenant advocate who lives in Flatbush.

title: InvestigateTV+: Protecting young athletes in the NIL era
text:
(InvestigateTV) — High school players are starting to cash in on Name, Image, Likeness (NIL) deals, and InvestigateTV+ explores how some states are trying to protect young athletes by regulating who gets a cut.
Then, we take an in-depth look at a tool some say can help protect people with dementia, when they wander off.
Plus, the biggest land animal in North America was once pushed to near extinction. We’ll explain how different communities fought to keep it part of our future.
Protecting young players
Name, image and likeness, or NIL, continues to dominate headlines and forever change the game for student athletes.
While the federal government tackles the college landscape, some states have enacted laws to protect high school students and their families.
In Louisiana, lawmakers recently passed legislation seeking to protect K-12 student athletes interested in signing NIL deals. Young players in the state can legally enter into big money contracts, but the new laws also look to add transparency and accountability.
Keeping track of family
Walking off alone can put people living with cognitive impairments in life-or-death situations.
Experts encourage families to make sure their loves ones have identifying information on them at all times. This can include caregiver contact and potentially GPS-enabled tracking tools.
In the summer of 2026, the Huntington Police Department rolled out the “Blue Lights the Way” program, aimed at protecting those who have a tendency to wander away from home.
Bison success story
Bison once roamed North America in the tens of millions. They became a critical part of Native American culture, which used the animal for food, shelter, tools, clothing and jewelry.
In the 1800s, the westward expansion of European settlers, along with railways, rifles and an international market for hides, led to the bison’s rapid decline.
Ilana Xinos called the story of American bison conservation is “the greatest success story.”
Supporting brides on a budget
Fighting human trafficking one wedding dress at a time. That is the mission of Adorned in Grace.
“We walk with young women, and we hope to show them that there are always opportunities for second chances and the story to continue,” said Kaitlin Berg.
The Bridal and Formalwear boutique is filled with donated dresses, some brand new from boutiques across the country, and others worn just once by another bride. All are under $1,000 with nearly 70% of every sale going directly to the mission – funding prevention, awareness, and survivor support.

title: Public decries California owner of Lewiston hospital during state hearing
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUBURN — Patients, community members, elected officials, and current and former workers delivered searing rebukes of the California-based owner of Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston during a state hearing attended by 250 people Friday afternoon.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services held the hearing to determine whether Prime Healthcare Foundation is complying with commitments it made to the state as conditions for its acquisition of the health system. The system includes critical access hospitals in Bridgton and Rumford, and several long-term care facilities and physician practices.
Prime committed to maintain operations at the hospitals and practices, including general surgery, general medicine, emergency department services, maternity services and family medicine residency. The state asked for testimony regarding any reductions to those operations and other essential services.
The state could impose penalties and withhold financial reimbursement if it rules the owner has not complied with the commitments it made.
More than 120 people filled the rows at the Kirk Hall Auditorium at Central Maine Community College in Auburn, while another 140 attended online. More than a dozen gave testimony; dozens more held printed speeches or handwritten notes.
One attendee was Jennifer Bodger, who said she resigned as senior vice president of operations for Central Maine Healthcare on Thursday “because we need to do better.”
“I live in this community, my children go to this hospital,” Bodger said. “And I understand the need to make changes, to be sustainable — hard decisions — but I want us to do it right.”
Rep. Julie McCabe, D-Lewiston, opened the hearing with testimony about care delays and training gaps that she said have worsened since CMMC fired or suspended 20 nurses during their campaign to unionize in September. She was followed by Lewiston Mayor Carl Sheline and several former hospital workers, including some of the discharged nurses.
“Prime increased the nurse-patient ratios across the hospital to one nurse to six patients on almost every unit of our hospital,” said Katie Grinnell, a registered nurse who was among the nurses fired in September. “Since Prime acquired CMMC, the cuts to services and the quality of care are growing exponentially.”
Fred Ortega, vice president of external affairs at Prime Healthcare Foundation, said the health system has maintained all key services, in keeping with the state’s requirements.
The state also requested testimony on CMMC’s progress to reestablish level three trauma center status, an American College of Surgeons designation that requires hospitals to provide around-the-clock trauma surgery, overseen by a trauma manager. The Lewiston hospital’s status lapsed in December 2025 after Prime applied for a certificate of need to acquire Central Maine Healthcare — a process required by the state Division of Licensing and Certification.
Prime committed to regaining CMMC’s trauma center certification by 2028 and hiring a trauma manager by October, among other steps to rebuild.
Meredith Kennedy, the director of emergency services at CMMC, took the podium to share that she is acting as the interim trauma manager until the hospital recruits and hires a permanent manager.
“Our goal is to strengthen trauma care and ensure that patients continue to receive appropriate, timely care within Central Maine’s capabilities, with access to higher levels of care when needed,” Kennedy said. “We understand that the certificate of need approval represents more than just a regulatory obligation: It represents a commitment to the state of Maine.”
Since Prime’s acquisition, she said the health system has treated more than 40,000 emergency department patients and delivered 542 babies.
“Bring back our nurses,” a few members of the crowd shouted after she finished speaking.
While CMMC’s nurses voted overwhelmingly to unionize in late September, the health system has challenged the election result with the National Labor Relations Board that oversees elections. Union representatives have said their first action at the bargaining table will be to bring back the 19 nurses who remain suspended or fired.
Many of the speakers at the hearing were patients with personal stories about the care they or a loved one received at a Central Maine Healthcare facility. Robert Hack, of Turner, said he is grieving the loss of his wife, who died in the inpatient care unit after an emergency department visit on Oct. 12.
“My wife paid the ultimate price for poor health care and the cuts that CMMC has made,” he said.
The crowd seemed to draw in a collective breath.
Only testimony related to the conditions of the certificate of need will be used to make a determination, said Jonathan Leach, a Division of Licensing and Certification representative who moderated the hearing. He said comments related to quality of care would be passed on to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services or another accreditation agency.
Applicable testimony will be compiled for Sara Gagné-Holmes, the commissioner of Maine DHHS, to make a determination in the coming weeks.
If Gagné-Holmes determines Prime’s conduct is in violation of certificate of need approval, she could decide to prohibit ongoing conduct, impose civil penalties or withhold reimbursement from state agencies, according to Maine law regarding the certificate of need and subsequent review process.
Prime Healthcare Foundation has spent $26 million on facility and technology improvements at Central Maine Healthcare, according to news release issued Thursday by the foundation.

title: Necropsy shows hat Fiona the hippo ate was so far into her intestine that supportive care couldn’t save her, zoo says
text:
CINCINNATI (AP) — A necropsy on Fiona the hippo showed that the hat she swallowed nearly two weeks ago was caught in the middle of her small intestine, causing her death this week, the Cincinnati Zoo said Friday.
Fiona, whose premature birth and fight for survival captured hearts nearly a decade ago, died Thursday after an attempt to locate the blockage. She was 9 years old.
The hat Fiona ate after it was accidentally flung into her enclosure was so far into her digestive system that no supportive care could have saved her, the zoo said in a statement.
Since her death, Fiona’s fans have covered a hippo statue at the zoo with flowers and notes written in crayon. Others left behind watermelons and pumpkins, some of her favorite treats. “She brought so much love in her lifetime,” said one note.
Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many — from teachers to parents to children.
During her visit to the zoo Friday morning, Jessica Grieshop, who often brought her daughters to see Fiona, called the hippo an inspiration for “anyone that was going through hard times.”
Zoo leaders said Fiona will be remembered for many years.
“The support that we’re feeling from all over the world reminds me of the time when everyone pulled together to root for her to survive,” said Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike. ”She did, and she gave us almost a decade of smiles.”
One of Fiona’s keepers, Jenna Wingate, posted a heartbreaking message on Instagram, saying it was like losing a family member.
“It has always felt like we grew up together, and I often used to smile thinking about growing old with her and her still being around when I retire,” Wingate wrote. “We lost her in the most horrific and tragic way.”
She ended: “She was our family. I love you Fiona and I am so sorry.”
Another hippo died similarly a century ago
Fiona wasn’t the first hippo to die at the zoo after ingesting a foreign object.
In 1923, a hippo “came to an untimely death due to a small boy who threw a rubber ball into its mouth,” according to records at the Field Museum in Chicago, which confirmed Friday that it received that hippo’s remains from the Cincinnati Zoo.
The Cincinnati Enquirer reported at the time that Zeekoe had a habit of opening his mouth wide to chomp cake and other treats tossed by guests. He died after swallowing a tennis ball, which zoo officials believed a child had dropped into the hippo’s mouth without realizing the harm it could cause.
The zoo’s team couldn’t reach the hat in Fiona
Unlike the watermelons and pumpkins she easily devoured, Fiona’s digestive system wasn’t meant to break down synthetic fibers, experts said.
Hippos have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants and a very large gastrointestinal tract that swallowed material must pass through.
Blood work showed her health was failing Thursday, so the zoo’s animal care team tried to locate the hat using a scope and an ultrasound, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health. Removing the hat surgically was impossible based on its location and the hippo’s anatomy, he added.
Fiona died during recovery from the procedure, he said.
The necropsy found the hat was 25 feet (7.6 meters) beyond her final stomach compartment and 50 feet (15.2 meters) from the end of her intestines.
“No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked,” Wenninger said.
Jenike called the zoo’s staff heroic in their efforts to save her. borrowed from a horse farm.
Zoo worked around the clock to save Fiona
At first, Fiona showed no signs of distress after swallowing the hat 11 days before her death. A zoo visitor tossed the hat, which a ceiling fan caught and flung into the hippo habitat.
But a few days later, her appetite started to decline, zoo officials said. By Monday, the zoo announced Fiona was undergoing veterinary care. Officials were cautiously optimistic she could pass the hat.
The zoo’s animal care team gave her fluids through an IV, conducted a colonoscopy, and tried to shake the obstruction loose with a vibration table borrowed from a horse farm.
Fiona is mourned by many worldwide
Fiona inspired millions in her first months and final days, bringing people together across political divides and other boundaries.
Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, posted a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through the glass wall of her enclosure.
Former first daughter Chelsea Clinton posted photos of her behind-the-scenes encounter with Fiona, writing that she would treasure “the smiles she gave me.”
Fiona wasn’t expected to survive her first weeks
Fiona was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), far below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time.
The zoo’s staff went to extraordinary lengths to keep her alive, raising her by hand. She couldn’t nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother to feed her.
She became a celebrity during her nine years. Hippos typically live 40 to 50 years in zoos.
Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the 2016 shooting of Harambe. The gorilla became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.
___
Associated Press journalists Holly Ramer in Concord, New Hampshire, and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed.

title: Driver charged in Waldoboro hit-and-run that killed teen appears in court
text:
Driver charged in Waldoboro hit-and-run that killed 17-year-old appears in court
The Maine man charged in a hit-and-run crash that killed a teenage boy in Waldoboro made his first court appearance on Friday.
Gifford Campbell, 53, of Waldoboro, appeared in West Bath District Court over Zoom from the Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset.
Campbell is charged with manslaughter, operating under the influence and leaving the scene of an accident resulting in death in connection with the pedestrian crash, which happened shortly after 3 p.m. Wednesday.
Police said Campbell was high on drugs when he fatally struck 17-year-old Brody Sawyer with his pickup truck. Sawyer was walking along Friendship Road when he was hit.
Campbell drove away from the scene of the crash as the teen lie dying on the front lawn of a nearby home, according to investigators.
Authorities caught up with Campbell just down the road and arrested him, officials said.
Campbell's niece, Harley Richards, spoke with Maine's Total Coverage outside the courthouse about her mission to bring attention to drug use in her community, pleading with law enforcement to do something.
"It is important for me to be here because I made a promise to Brody's grandfather, Charlie, that I would be Brody's voice. And if that means standing against my own family and the wrong that has been done, that is exactly what I'm going to do," Richards said. "That means that I am going to make it my number-one priority to clean up narcotics, drug use, needles, you name it. It is my goal."
A candlelight vigil in Sawyer's honor was held Thursday night in Nobleboro, where friends and family gathered to remember Sawyer. Among the crowd that gathered was Sawyer's grandfather, Charles Collins.
"I loved him very much and I hope that guy gets what he deserves," Collins said.
Campbell is due back in court on Jan. 25, 2027, unless a grand jury indicts him before that.
The judge set bail at $150,000. Campbell remains held at the Two Bridges Regional Jail. If Campbell is convicted of manslaughter, he could face up to 30 years in prison.

title: Indianapolis Colts release starting QB Daniel Jones as offensive woes continue
text:
Colts decide to make quarterback change and will release Daniel Jones as offensive woes continue
The Indianapolis Colts decided to release starting quarterback Daniel Jones on Friday and will turn to Anthony Richardson as the starter for next week's game against the New York Giants.
Coach Shane Steichen announced the decision less than 24 hours after yet another abysmal offensive performance in a 26-3 loss at Houston.
It's the second time in three years Jones has been released, though this one was apparently not of his choosing. He sought and received his release from the New York Giants in November 2024 and then joined the Minnesota Vikings practice squad before signing a one-year deal with the Colts. Indy re-signed Jones to a two-year deal worth $88 million in March.
"This was a decision that was made for, you know, the best interests of both parties," Steichen said, explaining Jones had not asked for his release this time. "It's just where we're at in our season. That's just the situation we're at right now."
Indy (3-8) has struggled mightily on offense most of this season and it was on full display for a national television audience Thursday night when they finished with only a field goal and 167 total yards as they dropped to 3-15 since Jones was diagnosed with a broken bone in his left leg. Jones also tore his Achilles tendon in December, ending his season.
But after a promising first 10 games with the Colts, Jones struggled.
His completion percentage this season, 58.4%, and passer rating, 65.4, are among the worst of all NFL starters. And he followed a season worst single-game passer rating, 41.9, in a victory over Miami, with his second worst rating of the season, 45.9, on a night he went 11 of 27 for 144 yards with one interception. He also was sacked for a safety.
Richardson replaced Jones in the fourth quarter and now the No. 4 overall pick in the 2023 draft and one-time future face of the Colts will get a second chance to prove himself.

title: Plastic surgeon convicted of killing lawyer in Florida is sentenced to death
text:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — A judge in Florida on Thursday sentenced a plastic surgeon to death for killing an attorney in a law office bathroom and then dumping his body in a trash bin in the Everglades, where it was never found.
Dr. Tomasz Kosowski killed attorney Steven Cozzi in the bathroom of Cozzi’s law office in March 2023, moments after both participated in a conference call about a lengthy, acrimonious legal battle over medical billing, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors said Kosowski took the call from a Toyota pickup truck outside the office and that he had supplies to commit the killing, including trash bags, a syringe containing a paralyzing drug and a wagon to haul the corpse out.
Investigators used cellphone records and surveillance video to track Kosowski to a remote area west of Miami on the Tamiami Trail, also known as U.S. Highway 41. That’s where they believe Kosowski tossed the body into a Dumpster that was eventually emptied by a garbage truck. The driver noticed an unusually “vile” smell at the stop, authorities said.
Trash from the route is typically hauled to a Collier County landfill, but authorities who searched the property for Cozzi’s body said the facility routinely compacts its trash, making recovery efforts nearly impossible. In addition, investigators said, Cozzi’s blood and DNA were found in the law office bathroom and in the garage at Kosowski’s home.
Kosowski was convicted in September, following a trial in which he represented himself and presented no defense beyond making a closing argument in which he said prosecutors had not proved their case.
Pinellas Circuit Judge Joseph Bulone was tasked with deciding whether to sentence Kosowski to death or to life in prison without the possibility of release.
Kosowski declined to present any mitigating evidence on his own behalf, but a special counsel appointed by the court highlighted his lack of criminal history and his medical work. A graduate of Dartmouth College medical school, Kosowski specialized in reconstructive breast surgery.
The judge acknowledged in court that there were several mitigating factors, but said none outweighed the aggravating factors — most importantly, that the crime was committed in a “cold, calculating and premeditated manner, without any pretense of moral or legal justification.”
“The court concludes that the defendant, under the laws of the State of Florida, has forfeited his right to live,” Bulone said.
Investigators said that when they arrested Kosowski, he had $280,000 in cash, masks, duct tape, firearms, a ballistic vest with “EMS” written on it, law enforcement patches and a vial of succinylcholine, which is a paralyzing drug. A search of his home turned up about 200 guns, according to court documents.
Cozzi, meanwhile, seemingly disappeared without a trace. His keys, wallet and cellphone remained on his law office desk and a work file was open on his computer. His husband never heard from him.
The missing lawyer represented a Dunedin, Florida-based medical practice that Kosowski alleged had shorted him thousands of dollars in billings and damaged his reputation as a doctor.
Bulone appointed the public defender’s office to represent Kosowski in his appeals.

title: Maine Celtics surge past Capital City
text:
The Maine Celtics ended the first half with a 23-2 run and maintained a double-digit lead for almost the entire second half on their way to a 114-102 win over the Capital City Go-Go in an NBA G League game Friday night at the Portland Expo.
Amari Williams led the Celtics (4-1) with 25 points on 11-for-16 shooting and also grabbed 12 rebounds.
Maine trailed 30-15 in the first quarter but outscored the Go-Go 49-24 for the remainder of the first half, building a 64-54 lead. The Celtics were 25 for 31 on 2-point attempts in the first half and shot 50 percent from the field overall, despite going just 7 for 31 from 3-point range.
Caleb Grill added 16 points off the bench, Hank Morgan scored 14, Milos Uzan finished with 12, and Tucker DeVries and Steven Jamerson II had 10 apiece.
The teams play again Sunday at 1 p.m.

title: Former manager sentenced for contaminating coworker’s mug with bodily fluid
text:
PITTSBURGH, Pa. (WPXI) – A former healthcare company manager was sentenced Tuesday to one to two years in jail after pleading guilty to a stalking charge as part of a plea deal.
Prosecutors said Timothy Haver contaminated a Highmark Health coworker’s drink with his own bodily fluids.
Haver was taken out of the Allegheny County Courthouse in handcuffs.
Details of the case
Prosecutors said Haver put his bodily fluids into a female coworker’s mug at least five times.
Highmark detectives set up a sting to catch him on surveillance. When he was questioned, Haver told detectives he wanted to get close to the victim.
Victim impact statements
The victim and her husband each read victim impact statements Tuesday.
She told the judge it has been “the worst year of her life.” She said Haver was her direct manager.
The victim said she now suffers from PTSD and becomes anxious when accepting a cup of coffee from someone.
Her husband called Haver a criminal.
Defense attorney comments
Haver’s defense attorney, Casey White, spoke after the plea.
“He feels remorse for everyone involved, including his family, her family, and he’s hopeful she’s able to put this behind her,” White said.
White said the biggest goal for Haver was to keep him off the Megan’s Law registry.
“He’s sitting in the county jail, so it’s certainly not a win. Is it a win that he’s not going to be on the Megan’s Law registration? Yes, candidly, but he’s got a lot to deal with. Sitting at the county jail is certainly not sitting at a Hilton hotel for a year. He’s sitting in the county jail,” White said.
Haver’s statement in court
Before he was sentenced, Haver turned around to look at the victim and her husband and apologized.
“I wish I had an exact answer as to why I did this. Part of my brain didn’t signal that this was wrong,” Haver said.
During the hearing, the judge asked Haver how he would feel if someone did to his wife what he did to the victim.
“He’s been contrite. He’s upset. He still doesn’t understand why he did what he did. He’s embarrassed,” White said.

title: Còig holiday concert Dec. 5
text:
Còig is one of Atlantic Canada’s most exciting Celtic traditional groups made up of accomplished multi-instrumentalists. With the fiery Celtic high-energy style as its musical core, Còig easily shifts between century-old tunes of past generations to original and upbeat compositions. On Saturday, Dec. 5, the band arrives to perform a holiday-infused concert on the decked out and dazzling holiday stage at the Boothbay Harbor Opera House.
The band includes musicians Darren McMullen, Rachel Davis, Thierry Phillipe Clouette and Margie Beaton performing on the band's range of over a dozen instruments including vocals, fiddles, piano, guitars, banjo, mandolin, viola, bouzouki, whistles, and more. With driving tunes, haunting songs and infectious energy, Còig is an unparalleled music force.
Opera House Director Cathy Sherrill says, "The band is one of the most frequently requested acts but they don’t travel to Maine often enough!” The band has just finished a tour in the United Kingdom, and their holiday show in Boothbay Harbor is their only concert appearance in Maine this season.
The Cape Breton band has earned rave reviews from audiences around the world and an impressive list of credits for their recordings, ”Rove” (2017), “Carols” (2015) and “Five” (2014) including a Canadian Folk Music Award, a JUNO Award nomination and multiple East Coast Music Awards and Music Nova Scotia Awards. title: 9-year-old taken to ER after eating THC gummy that friend gave her at school, mom says
text:
LINCOLN, Neb. (KOLN/Gray News) - A 9-year-old Nebraska girl was taken to the emergency room after eating a THC gummy a friend gave her at elementary school, according to her mom.
Kala Strow said she got a call from her daughter Eleanor’s school last week saying that she wasn’t feeling well.
“She said she felt like her head was caving in. Her head was heavy,” Strow said. “And everything was spinning. She said she felt like it wasn’t the same world.”
Strow said Eleanor had eaten what she thought was candy from a friend at lunchtime. She rushed her daughter to the emergency room.
After the incident, Strow said the other student’s parent reached out and apologized. The parent told her the child was afraid to return to school after a suspension and that the family had received threats.
Strow said she has been disappointed by some parents’ reactions, including people laughing about the incident and making assumptions she said were untrue.
“When things do happen to our children it’s not because of where I live, or the school that my daughter went to, or because of my past, or our skin color, or who we are,” she said. “It has nothing to do with that. It could have happened to any of these children.”
Strow said she wants the community to focus on preventing another incident.
“Why are we pointing fingers and blaming rather than doing what we can to make sure that no other child in the community has to go through this?” she said.
Strow said the other student and the student’s parent told her the gummy came from Halloween, but Lincoln police said they have not been able to confirm where it came from.
Police said the case is inactive and no citations have been issued. If new information becomes available, they will continue investigating.

title: Former MLB pitcher, ‘Olympus Has Fallen’ actor Lance Broadway dies at 43
text:
DALLAS (AP) — Lance Broadway, a major league pitcher who became an actor following his baseball career, has died. He was 43.
His cause of death was not immediately clear. The report posted Thursday by the Dallas County Medical Examiner’s Office said Broadway died Tuesday in a stairwell at an apartment complex near Love Field Airport.
Dallas Police did not immediately respond to an open records request for reports involving Broadway’s death.
Broadway pitched in college at Dallas Baptist and Texas Christian. He was taken in the first round of the 2005 draft by the Chicago White Sox and appeared in a total of 27 games for them and the New York Mets from 2007-09.
He made his movie debut in “Olympus Has Fallen” in 2013 and appeared in several television series.

title: After mass shootings, whole communities need help healing
text:
Rebecca Swanson Conrad served as voluntary chair of the Broad Recovery Efforts and Organizations Fund, administered by the Maine Community Foundation. Her nephew, Tommy Conrad, was murdered at Just in Time Recreation in Lewiston on Oct. 25, 2023.
Living in Lewiston-Auburn since 1978, I have witnessed our community’s strength during many tragedies. That resilience was never more evident than on Oct. 25, 2023, when in a few short moments folks enjoying an evening out changed to carnage, fear and desperation, followed by a two-day lockdown tracking a mass shooter.
The number of mass shootings in America should infuriate us. And that Lewiston is among the data is heartbreaking. But our community’s response of collective capacity, rooted in our deep relationships, did not surprise me.
I watched support begin immediately for the victims’ families, the survivors and those who witnessed the murders. Their trauma is nearly immeasurable.
But the larger community was also stunned and needed help.
In addition to direct medical and mental health support, our local nonprofit agencies fed children who could not get school meals; translated public safety information into multiple languages; added counseling shifts so re-experiencing trauma did not cause more aggressive actions, including domestic violence; implemented activities for kids to not feel helpless; provided gathering spaces for grieving; and created tributes to victims and first responders.
There is research on community impact. The journal Health Affairs finds, “Mass shootings have significant detrimental effects on the health of the people who witness them, and those who live in the communities surrounding them.” Philanthropic Response to Disasters states, “In the affected communities, normal citizens and organizations also become responders, assisting those in their community who need help.” Neighbors, government, businesses and nonprofits across our community cared for each other in a time of crisis, fear and overwhelming grief. People wanted to help in any way possible and many were moved to donate money.
There were several funds and most supported victims’ families and survivors. The Maine Community Foundation voluntarily administered two funds: The Victims and Families Fund and the Broad Recovery Efforts and Organizations Fund. The Chamber of Commerce led an economic recovery fund for local businesses. And Lewiston’s delegation leveraged state funds to create Maine’s Mass Violence Care Fund for ongoing medical costs after a victim exhausts their benefit from the Maine Victims’ Compensation Fund.
But only the Maine Community Foundation’s Broad Recovery Efforts and Organizations Fund has been called into question. Specifically grants to immigrant-led nonprofits, questioning their contribution to rebuilding community resilience.
The Maine Community Foundation was advised by an expert on mass shooting community response to give donors an option to support nonprofits. Nonprofits develop solutions that reflect the unique characteristics of the community they serve and address the gaps government and private business cannot or will not fill. Many donors see great value in that work.
A community committee was asked to distribute the funds. The committee required the nonprofit be located in Lewiston/Auburn and list what they did or would continue to do for community recovery. The grant amount was the total donor-designated dollars in the fund divided equally among those applicants that met the criteria. Nonprofits had no idea how much the grant might be.
I was on the first flight out of the Portland Jetport to NYC following 9/11. What struck me across the city were the signs for help: help search, feed, transport, give blood, identify, interpret, stand vigil. HELP. And every flyer, poster and leaflet was by a local New York nonprofit organization.
And around the recent Lewiston anniversary, there were interviews with community members still traumatized by the shooting. Nonprofits were noted as doing the work on the journey of healing in the aftermath of such a profound tragedy.
I stand by the Maine Community Foundation allowing donors the choice for broad community recovery. And I stand by the committee’s process to ensure our ongoing collective community healing can continue.

title: How police are using this device to help track people with dementia
text:
HUNTINGTON, W.Va . (InvestigateTV) - Walking off alone can put people living with cognitive impairments in life-or-death situations.
For a person with dementia, any stage of the disease can be at risk for wandering, according to the Alzheimer’s Association. Many will do so repeatedly as symptoms include losing their ability to recognize familiar places and faces.
Experts encourage families to make sure their loves ones have identifying information on them at all times. This can include caregiver contact and potentially GPS-enabled tracking tools.
In the summer of 2026, the Huntington Police Department rolled out the “Blue Lights the Way” program, aimed at protecting those who have a tendency to wander away from home.
Families anywhere in Cabell and Wayne counties can apply to receive an AngelSense watch or fob tracking device for their loved one from HPD, free of charge.
“[Families] can set up a geofence that would let them know if the person has traveled outside of that area,” HPD Lt. Matt Null explained. “Or it can work like a two-way radio device that you could actually contact them, even has an SOS feature if someone was to fall.”
HPD is launching the program after a WSAZ investigation into Charles “Chuck” Carroll’s death. Carroll, who had dementia, was dropped off at Cabell Huntington Hospital on Dec. 30, 2021, before wandering off on his own.
Carroll was missing for 53 days before being found dead in an outbuilding blocks from the hospital.
“I was at home in Huntington and I started getting text messages from a lot of my classmates from Ravenswood, and they said Chuck is missing,” Caroll’s lifelong friend Debbie Holmes recounted. “And I said, ‘well, sometimes he’s always missing, because he kind of did his own thing and then he’d pop up every now and then.’ And so they said, ‘no, they have on WSAZ where he is missing from the hospital.’”
Caroll believes if Chuck had been wearing one of the devices now offered by HPD, he would have survived.
“I just couldn’t believe what had happened to him, that he was so close to the hospital,” she said. “He was so close to me, where I lived. He was pretty close to me. I wouldn’t have known to look for him there.”
Several changes have been inspired by Carroll’s death, including by the hospital and by Mingo Central students.
Lt. Dunn said the program, which is fully funded by a grant from the Department of Justice, is in the department’s mission to protect, serve, and better the community.
“Other than family, there’s very little that’s more important than that,” he said. “So if you’re already working through, if you have someone who’s having cognitive problems or they’ve been diagnosed with an illness, you’ve already got obstacles. If this can help alleviate some of those obstacles, and it’s exactly what we want to do. We want to make sure that everyone’s safe, that we don’t have any tragic stories.”
Holmes implored those with loved ones like Chuck to reach out for the program, so their loved ones can avoid what happened to Chuck.
“Don’t be apprehensive at all, because you’re saving a life,” she said. “Everybody’s family is going to be affected with dementia, one way or the other. My own family was. And it’s so sad to think that little things that we can do can make a difference. All it takes is effort.”
Lt. Null said there are only 100 devices available, and demand is already high, saying his phone has been “ringing off the hook.”
He also emphasized that the devices aren’t just for people with dementia, but can be used for people of any age with mental disabilities that might make them wander off, like autism.

title: Maine's heating oil prices have fallen nearly 6% over the past 3 weeks
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s heating oil prices have fallen 6% over the past three weeks.
The average price for a gallon of heating oil is now $5.71, down from last week’s average of $5.84, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
In eastern and Down East Maine, prices range from a low of $5.20 to a high of $6.05.
Despite prices falling over the past two weeks from a record high of $6.05, that statewide average is 66% higher than this time last year, when heating oil went for $3.44 a gallon.
Mainers will still have to spend an additional $624.25 to fill a standard 275-gallon tank.
Energy prices have been climbing globally since February when President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched a surprise war against Iran. Although Trump said that the war would last only weeks, it has dragged on for more than eight months.
That war effectively halted fuel shipments out of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s natural gas and oil passes, for much of the year. The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine also has strained global fuel supplies as both sides have traded blows on each other’s energy infrastructure, and Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have attacked Saudi energy sites and seized territory along the Red Sea coast, another key trade route.
Last month, the Trump administration released about $37 million in low-income heating assistance for Maine. An additional $1.4 million was awarded to the state’s four federally recognized tribes. The administration also is tapping the Northeast heating oil reserves for the first time since 2012 when Hurricane Sandy devastated the northeastern U.S.
About half of Maine households ( more than 300,000) rely on heating oil to stay warm during the winter, and consumption can average 2 to 7 gallons a day, depending on how cold it is outside. That means the 13.2 million gallons flowing from the Northeast stockpile would amount to approximately nine days of consumption at a rate of five gallons a day.
Gov. Janet Mills has renewed calls for Congress to increase federal low-income heating assistance, saying the program should be bolstered with $3 billion in additional funding to offset rising energy costs that are eating away at the aid’s purchasing power.
Rising energy costs and anger over the Iran war contributed to heavy losses for Republicans in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, including the ousting of U.S. Sen. Susan Collins after three decades representing Maine in Washington.
It’s unclear whether the election results will deliver any meaningful relief from high oil prices.
Despite declaring the Iran war “militarily effectively over” last week, White House insiders told Axios that Trump is considering more joint military strikes with Israel targeting Iranian nuclear facilities, as well as possibly power plants and bridges.
Gulf allies are urging Trump to avoid actions that could restart a regionwide conflagration.
That may not be imminent, however, with Trump telling Fox News that the timeline for such strikes is early next year, according to Axios.

title: Firefighters save cat from Aroostook house fire
text:
Firefighters saved a cat from a Madawaska Lake Township house fire early Friday morning.
The fire broke out about 4:58 a.m. at the New Sweden Road home, according to Maj. Aaron Turcotte, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
When they arrived, firefighters found flames around the rear of the home and smoke coming from inside.
Both occupants safely escaped the flames.
Firefighters saved a cat from the fire.
The fire caused significant damage to the rear of the home, including portions of the basement and attic, Turcotte said Friday.
Investigators believe the fire was started by burned wood discarded in shrubs and landscaping mulch at the rear of the house.
It was ruled accidental.
Madawaska Lake Township is south of Madawaska.
