title: Court approves $7.25 billion settlement with Bayer over claims Roundup weedkiller caused cancer
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from U.S. cancer patients asserting the company should have warned people that its popular weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved Friday by a Missouri judge.
The nationwide settlement applies both to Roundup users who already are ill and those who become diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in future years. Participants could get an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, depending on how they used the product, how old they were when diagnosed and the severity of their illness.
For Germany-based Bayer, which denies that Roundup causes cancer, the settlement provides some financial certainty against mounting litigation costs that have led it to contemplate pulling the product from U.S. agricultural markets. Bayer already has changed the formula for its Roundup version sold to residential users.
Litigants also faced uncertainty. While the settlement was pending, the U.S. Supreme Court undercut one of the central arguments in the Roundup lawsuits. The high court ruled in June that Bayer cannot be sued in state courts on claims it failed to warn about cancer, because federal regulations don’t require a cancer warning label and states are forbidden from imposing additional labeling requirements.
Though some attorneys for cancer patients contend the settlement payouts are too small, others argue the deal is better than getting nothing — which became a heightened likelihood after the Supreme Court ruling.
In a written judgment granting approval, St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer said the average individual payouts are “fair and adequate” and the total dollar amount is “among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements.” The approved settlement includes $600 million for attorneys’ fees.
The judge said there was a risk Bayer would have filed for bankruptcy protection if the settlement had been rejected.
Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said in a statement that the court-approved settlement is “a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation.”
The decision could be appealed.
Roundup has been used on weeds for over 50 years
Missouri-based Monsanto debuted Roundup weed killer in 1974 with the chemical glyphosate as its active ingredient. The product quickly became one of the most widely used herbicides in agriculture. Roundup is designed to be used with genetically modified seeds that can resist the weed killer’s deadly effect, thus allowing farmers to produce more while conserving the soil by tilling it less.
The product also is commonly applied on lawns and gardens.
Bayer added Roundup to its portfolio when it acquired Monsanto in 2018. With it came a growing number of lawsuits alleging glyphosate causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. But that remains in dispute. The World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer classified the chemical as “probably carcinogenic” in 2015. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has determined that it’s not likely to cause cancer in humans when used as directed.
About 200,000 Roundup-related claims have been made against Bayer, many coming from people who used it on residential lawns and gardens. As a result, Bayer has removed glyphosate from its new versions of Roundup sold for residential markets.
The lawsuits have produced mixed results. Only a couple dozen cases have gone to jurors, some siding with Bayer and others with plaintiffs. In one case, a Georgia jury awarded plaintiffs $2.1 billion.
In the first Roundup verdict since the Supreme Court’s precedent-setting ruling, a Missouri jury in October sided with Bayer in a case alleging design defects, negligence and fraud. The verdict “should send a strong signal” that plaintiffs “will face significant challenges” pursuing Roundup-related cancer claims in the future, said Bill Dodero, Bayer’s U.S. general counsel and global litigation leader.
Attorneys disagree on whether the settlement is fair
Bayer previously set aside $16 billion to cover legal costs related to Roundup cases. The new settlement, which is in addition to that, is designed to address most of the remaining lawsuits, as well as any additional cases brought in the coming years by people who were exposed to Roundup before the settlement was proposed in February.
“Today’s final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice,” said Christopher A. Seeger, a court-appointed counsel for cancer patients in the case.
The settlement calls for Bayer to make annual payments into a special fund for up to 21 years, totaling as much as $7.25 billion. The amount of money paid out to individuals would vary. Agricultural, industrial or turf workers exposed at length to Roundup could receive an average of $165,000 if they were diagnosed with an aggressive form of the illness while younger than age 60. But anyone diagnosed at age 78 or older would get significantly less, with an average of $10,000.
Some attorneys have said the individual settlement amounts are too small and the terms too restrictive.
“This settlement is the scariest, worst future settlement that’s ever been contemplated,” attorney Gerson Smoger said during a September court hearing on whether the settlement was fair. He said it locked in future claimants for decades with no chance at punitive damages yet “kept the product that they were exposed to on the market, allowing the victims to continue to be exposed.”
The settlement was filed in St. Louis Circuit Court in Missouri, home to Bayer’s North America crop science division and the state where many of the lawsuits have been brought.

title: Mamdani sets plan to close NYC’s notorious Rikers Island jail
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — New York City’s Rikers Island jail complex would close by 2032 under a sweeping plan announced Friday by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose strategy for finally shuttering the notorious facility hinges on substantially reducing the number of people kept behind bars.
The mayor, a Democrat, unveiled the plan as the city is all but certain to blow past a legal requirement to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller, more modern jails by 2027.
For years, Rikers Island has stood as a symbol of dysfunction, with the network of jails so plagued by violence and overcrowding that a federal judge, citing “abnormal and unacceptable” conditions, appointed an outside manager to restore order and implement reforms.
Mamdani has been a vocal proponent of closing Rikers, though the longstanding plan to build new jails has met fierce pushback, including from his predecessor, former Mayor Eric Adams, who opposed federal oversight and borough jails.
At a celebratory news conference at City Hall, Mamdani said the extended timeline was needed because of resistance from the previous administration, calling Rikers “a place we have long turned our eyes away from rather than confront head on.”

title: Reporter who witnessed nearly 500 lethal injections says Texas execution was like no other he’s seen
text:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — After covering capital punishment for The Associated Press in Texas since 1983 — and witnessing nearly 500 lethal injections — I’ve become accustomed to a certain routine in the procedure, although I’m reticent to describe any execution as “routine.”
It was 6 p.m. Thursday — a bell from a nearby church tolling the hour — when I and other witnesses climbed the concrete steps into the more than century-old Huntsville Unit of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice. We were led into a reception office for what normally is a very brief period to await the short trek to the death chamber to watch condemned killer Reinaldo Dennes die.
A large state of Texas clock on a wall ticked off the moments. By about 6:20 p.m., we still hadn’t moved.
I knew one of two situations was likely: Dennes was resisting the execution team’s attempts to insert a pair of intravenous needles into his arms, or the execution team was having difficulty finding a suitable vein for the needles.
Thirty minutes later, as we were led into the chamber by corrections officers, Dennes appeared docile. His eyes were closed and his head was pointed toward the ceiling. His white prison garb was not disheveled and no additional restraints were applied to his head, meaning no evidence of a struggle.
Now I’ve seen over the years any number of final statements and reactions from condemned inmates who spoke in foreign languages, prayed, recited poetry, sang, cursed, expressed love, insisted on their innocence or acknowledged their crime and one who even told a joke.
Dennes was like no other.
Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Dennes talked about being “extremely blessed” by the love of “the father” and hoped his family and loved ones “get to know this great gift and great grace of God the father.”
He told the warden: “Go.” Almost immediately as the procedure began, his demeanor changed.
“The pain!” he exclaimed. “Go! Go!”
For nearly three minutes — and standing there furiously scribbling notes, I thought it seemed much longer — Dennes repeatedly moaned.
“Take me father! ... Take me into your arms! ... Take me father!” He occasionally interjected his cries with obscenities, a grunt and then groans. His right leg was “killing me,” he said, likening the sensation to a cramp.
“I don’t think this is normal,” he said at one point.
On that, he was right. I’ve heard inmates say the lethal drug was hot or cold, that they could smell or taste it, or that it hurt. No one I can recall went to such drama as Dennes.
At 7:08 p.m., after being examined by a physician, he was pronounced dead.
Texas prison officials said the execution team had difficulty finding suitable veins. Spokeswoman Amanda Hernandez said after repeated unsuccessful attempts — she couldn’t say how many — the technicians found a vein in Dennes’ left foot and another on the left side of his neck that were receptive to the IV needles.
I couldn’t see. His feet were covered by a sheet and only the right side of his neck was visible to those of us who were witnesses.
The injection sites were in line with the prison system’s procedures, Hernandez added. The alternate sites have been used in previous executions, although the need to do so is relatively rare.
Hernandez also suggested Dennes may have been faking, saying he had been complaining about pain from areas where no injections were attempted.
As a reporter, I’d like to find out the truth about the matter. But there’s no way to know for sure.
Dennes himself, as reporters are known to say, wasn’t available for further comment.

title: Necropsy shows hat Fiona the hippo ate was so far into her intestine that supportive care couldn’t save her, zoo says
text:
CINCINNATI (AP) — A necropsy on Fiona the hippo showed that the hat she swallowed nearly two weeks ago was caught in the middle of her small intestine, causing her death this week, the Cincinnati Zoo said Friday.
Fiona, whose premature birth and fight for survival captured hearts nearly a decade ago, died Thursday after an attempt to locate the blockage. She was 9 years old.
The hat Fiona ate after it was accidentally flung into her enclosure was so far into her digestive system that no supportive care could have saved her, the zoo said in a statement.
Since her death, Fiona’s fans have covered a hippo statue at the zoo with flowers and notes written in crayon. Others left behind watermelons and pumpkins, some of her favorite treats. “She brought so much love in her lifetime,” said one note.
Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many — from teachers to parents to children.
During her visit to the zoo Friday morning, Jessica Grieshop, who often brought her daughters to see Fiona, called the hippo an inspiration for “anyone that was going through hard times.”
Zoo leaders said Fiona will be remembered for many years.
“The support that we’re feeling from all over the world reminds me of the time when everyone pulled together to root for her to survive,” said Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike. ”She did, and she gave us almost a decade of smiles.”
One of Fiona’s keepers, Jenna Wingate, posted a heartbreaking message on Instagram, saying it was like losing a family member.
“It has always felt like we grew up together, and I often used to smile thinking about growing old with her and her still being around when I retire,” Wingate wrote. “We lost her in the most horrific and tragic way.”
She ended: “She was our family. I love you Fiona and I am so sorry.”
Another hippo died similarly a century ago
Fiona wasn’t the first hippo to die at the zoo after ingesting a foreign object.
In 1923, a hippo “came to an untimely death due to a small boy who threw a rubber ball into its mouth,” according to records at the Field Museum in Chicago, which confirmed Friday that it received that hippo’s remains from the Cincinnati Zoo.
The Cincinnati Enquirer reported at the time that Zeekoe had a habit of opening his mouth wide to chomp cake and other treats tossed by guests. He died after swallowing a tennis ball, which zoo officials believed a child had dropped into the hippo’s mouth without realizing the harm it could cause.
The zoo’s team couldn’t reach the hat in Fiona
Unlike the watermelons and pumpkins she easily devoured, Fiona’s digestive system wasn’t meant to break down synthetic fibers, experts said.
Hippos have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants and a very large gastrointestinal tract that swallowed material must pass through.
Blood work showed her health was failing Thursday, so the zoo’s animal care team tried to locate the hat using a scope and an ultrasound, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health. Removing the hat surgically was impossible based on its location and the hippo’s anatomy, he added.
Fiona died during recovery from the procedure, he said.
The necropsy found the hat was 25 feet (7.6 meters) beyond her final stomach compartment and 50 feet (15.2 meters) from the end of her intestines.
“No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked,” Wenninger said.
Jenike called the zoo’s staff heroic in their efforts to save her. borrowed from a horse farm.
Zoo worked around the clock to save Fiona
At first, Fiona showed no signs of distress after swallowing the hat 11 days before her death. A zoo visitor tossed the hat, which a ceiling fan caught and flung into the hippo habitat.
But a few days later, her appetite started to decline, zoo officials said. By Monday, the zoo announced Fiona was undergoing veterinary care. Officials were cautiously optimistic she could pass the hat.
The zoo’s animal care team gave her fluids through an IV, conducted a colonoscopy, and tried to shake the obstruction loose with a vibration table borrowed from a horse farm.
Fiona is mourned by many worldwide
Fiona inspired millions in her first months and final days, bringing people together across political divides and other boundaries.
Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, posted a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through the glass wall of her enclosure.
Former first daughter Chelsea Clinton posted photos of her behind-the-scenes encounter with Fiona, writing that she would treasure “the smiles she gave me.”
Fiona wasn’t expected to survive her first weeks
Fiona was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), far below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time.
The zoo’s staff went to extraordinary lengths to keep her alive, raising her by hand. She couldn’t nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother to feed her.
She became a celebrity during her nine years. Hippos typically live 40 to 50 years in zoos.
Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the 2016 shooting of Harambe. The gorilla became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.
___
Associated Press journalists Holly Ramer in Concord, New Hampshire, and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed.

title: UMF student selected as Peace Corps Campus Ambassador by national program
text:
FARMINGTON — Maygin Leighton, a University of Maine at Farmington junior from Baileyville, has been selected by the national Peace Corps program to serve as UMF’s Peace Corps Campus Ambassador. Leighton is a biology major with minors in climate change solutions and international & global studies.
Campus ambassadors are degree-seeking students who have been selected to raise the Peace Corps’ profile on campus and introduce the agency’s mission to student groups. They serve as local points of contact for students, faculty, and campus organizations and share information about Peace Corps opportunities and benefits.
Leighton has always been interested in helping people. She comes from a small town in Maine where community is a shared set of values that connect you with your neighbor. It was only natural that she would be interested in learning more about the Peace Corps program and how her concern with helping people could impact an even wider community.
“Coming from a small town, I’m very community-minded,” Leighton said. “One person can have a huge impact in this world. My high school experiences helped me to be more confident and outspoken, and I have brought those strengths with me to my UMF experience.”
In addition to being named a Campus Peace Corps Ambassador, Leighton has also been admitted to the Peace Corps Prep certificate program at UMF. As Maine’s only Peace Corps Prep program, UMF prepares students for international development fieldwork and service with interrelated coursework, hands-on experience and professional development support.
The program is available to undergraduates, regardless of their major, and requires that they complete courses related to one of six Peace Corps service sectors, gain practical experience through volunteering or internships, develop intercultural competence and strengthen their leadership and professional skills. Upon completion of the program, students receive a certificate from the Peace Corps that recognizes their preparation for international service and gives them a competitive edge when pursuing Peace Corps service.
In addition to her Peace Corps involvement, Leighton also worked with several other UMF students to create the UMF to create the UMF Global Connections Club to promote global service on campus. She currently serves as the club president.

title: Bangor cancels school bus routes as Maine’s driver shortage goes uncounted
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Megan Anderson’s minivan was more full than usual this week.
The Bangor parent drove extra kids to school, along with her own, after the city’s bus contractor canceled three routes serving eight schools for most of the week because it didn’t have enough drivers. In local Facebook groups, other parents offered rides to children they’d never met.
“I’m concerned that there are families just opting out of school because they’re too overwhelmed to make alternate arrangements,” Anderson said.
This is the latest flare-up of a problem Maine schools have fought for nearly a decade, and one the state isn’t even measuring. Schools aren’t required to report how many bus drivers they’re missing. The Maine Department of Education doesn’t track it, and the secretary of state’s office, the Maine Education Policy Research Institute, or the association that represents pupil transportation managers don’t either.
The state’s best estimate, that there are about 80 open bus driver jobs statewide, is a year old and came from informal reports at a training session. Nobody can say whether the shortage is improving or worsening. About 80% of Maine students take the bus to and from school, according to the Department of Education.
Cyr Bus Line, the contractor that operates Bangor’s public school buses, canceled two buses starting Monday afternoon and a third bus for Wednesday and Thursday. Drivers were out because of illness and medical needs, and the contractor had no one to cover for them, according to school department spokesperson Ray Phinney. Each bus makes multiple rounds of pickups and serves three to four schools, so one driver being out affects several schools at once.
Cyr has notified the department of cancellations repeatedly over the last three weeks, Phinney said. A representative for Cyr’s Bangor division declined to comment.
As of September, Cyr had 25 drivers for Bangor routes but needed 30, the school department’s business services director, Heather Hale, told the school committee that month. Two more were in training, she said, but it could take several months before they’re on the road.
“If you can imagine being short five bus drivers, that’s quite a bit,” Hale said. “There are no substitute bus drivers. So, if one is out sick or something of that nature, that can create quite a chaotic event.”
Phinney did not provide the current number of drivers, and Hale did not respond to an email requesting updated figures.
“It’s just, unfortunately, a statewide problem,” Hale said in September.
But nobody can say how big that problem is. Schools aren’t required to report driver staffing to any state or federal agency, and the Department of Education doesn’t track it, according to department spokesperson Melissa White.
“We can attempt to collect anecdotal information, but that is not an exact data collection, and we could not require schools to report these data without statutory authority,” White said.
White did not answer questions about the reasons for the shortage or whether the DOE is doing anything to address it.
The problem is nationwide and getting worse. School bus driver employment fell 5% over the past year and is now 15% below 2019 levels, according to a recent analysis by the left-leaning Economic Policy Institute, which tied the drop to falling inflation-adjusted wages. News stories going back to 2017 describe chronic driver shortages in Maine, and a Swanville elementary school canceled classes for a day in 2019 for lack of drivers.
“Nobody knows what the actual problem is,” said Chris Pasciuto, vice president of the nonprofit Maine Association for Pupil Transportation and transportation manager for Kennebunk-based RSU 21.
The shortage has been particularly severe across the state since around 2023, Pasciuto said. Many factors could be contributing, he said, including a wave of retiring drivers, the difficulty of the job, the unusual hours, drug testing requirements, and the three to four months it can take to get certified.
The effects on families reach far. Inconsistent busing can upend work schedules, create extra hardship for guardians who can’t drive or don’t have cars, and disrupt extracurriculars and the support services some kids rely on at school, like meals or laundry, Pasciuto said.
His district has made some progress on driver retention by offering paid training, benefits and bonuses, he said, “but it hasn’t put us over the hump.”
In Bangor, Phinney said he was unsure whether other routes would be affected. Families are notified of cancellations by text, email and app, and can use a mapping tool on the school department’s website to find another nearby bus stop.
One of the cancelled buses goes back in service Friday, and the other two are expected to return to normal on Monday. But there’s no sign of a fix for the statewide shortage, or even a count of how big it is.
“It’s an immediate need in almost every town,” Pasciuto said. “I don’t think there’s any town that would turn anybody away at this point.”

title: Beautiful Fall Weather Continues Through The Weekend... Much Needed Rain Arrives Sunday Night
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Our stretch of beautiful fall weather continues today. We’ll see plenty of sunshine for our Friday with a few clouds mixed in across the north this afternoon as a cold front approaches. Mild temperatures will continue with afternoon highs in the mid-50s to near 60° north and upper 50s to low 60s elsewhere... some 15°-20° above average for this time of year. A cold front moving into Northern Maine tonight will bring a few clouds into the state... mainly across the north. Expect clear to partly cloudy skies for the nighttime hours with temperatures dropping to the 30s to near 40°.
Our weekend weather looks awesome as well with mostly sunny skies to start the weekend Saturday. The aforementioned cold front moving into the state will allow for some slightly cooler air to move in as well... keeping temperatures in the 50s for highs Saturday afternoon. Clouds will be on the increase Sunday as our next weathermaker approaches. Highs on Sunday will top off in the mid-50s on average.
We’ve been watching the potential for some much needed rain in the Sunday night-Monday timeframe... all dependent on the track of low pressure moving toward the region. Computer models have been trending further north and west with this system and are coming into better agreement with tracking the system near the Maine coastline... leading to a more widespread... heavier rainfall. That being said... low pressure developing off the Carolina coastline this weekend will strengthen as it heads northward along the East Coast toward New England Sunday then along the Maine coast Monday. This will spread rain into the state Sunday night... near or after midnight for most locales. Rain could be moderate to heavy at times with the heaviest rain (possibly 1″+) falling south of Greenville and Millinocket. The rain is forecast to taper off from west to east by late morning into the afternoon with drier weather expected Monday afternoon as the system moves to our east. Despite the clouds and rain Monday... temperatures will remain on the mild side with highs in the upper 40s to mid-50s.
As the system moves to our east later Monday... winds will shift out of the northwest Monday night and become gusty... bringing our mild stretch to an end as it ushers much colder air into the state for Tuesday. We’ll see a mix of sun and clouds Tuesday with temperatures about 20° colder than Monday with highs only in the 30s to near 40°. The pressure gradient will tighten up over the area Tuesday too leading to a gusty northwest breeze which will make things feel even colder. It looks like that colder weather will stick around through the remainder of next week. And... we’re keeping an eye on your Thanksgiving forecast as it could be a bit messy with another storm system bringing the chance of some rain and snow for the holiday. It’s still a long way out... so stay tuned for updates.
Rest of Today: Partly to mostly sunny. Highs in the mid-50s to low 60s. West wind 5-15 MPH with gusts to 20-25 MPH possible.
Tonight: Clear to partly cloudy. Lows in the 30s to near 40°. Light and variable wind.
Saturday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s to near 60°. Light and variable wind.
Sunday: Increasing clouds. Highs in the 50s.
Monday: Mostly cloudy with rain likely... mainly during the morning. Highs in the upper 40s to mid-50s.
Tuesday: Mix of sun and clouds. Breezy and much colder. Highs in the 30s to near 40°.

VIDEO: Rare greater one-horned rhino calf born at Chester Zoo
A rare greater one-horned rhinoceros has been born at Chester Zoo in England, the zoo announced.
See video of the baby rhino in the video player above.
The rhino was born on Nov. 11 to its mother, Asha. The zoo said the two are both in good health. The calf's father, Beni, died earlier this year from a sudden illness, according to the zoo.
Video posted by the zoo shows the baby rhino, who has not yet been named, taking its first steps.
The birth "marks a significant milestone" for conservation efforts to protect the rare species, Chester Zoo said on its website.
The zoo said the greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds, and the largest adults can weigh more than 4,400 pounds, which is as much as an average car.

title: Obituary: James “Jim” Clarence Hathaway
text:
NAPLES – James “Jim” Clarence Hathaway, 86, of Naples passed on Thursday Nov. 5, 2026, with loved ones by his side.
Jim was born in Biddeford, on Sept. 1, 1940, son of the late Alice (Leavitt) Hathaway and James Percy Hathaway. He graduated from Scarborough High School in 1959. Following high school, he attended Maine Maritime Academy, graduating in 1962. He met his wife Vivian there and married her in Castine in June of 1962.
He joined the Navy in March of 1963, earning an Antarctica Medal of Honor. Jim spent a majority of his career as a merchant marine and chief engineer. He would later inspect ships before retiring from the merchant marines. After traveling the world on oil tankers for over 30 years, Jim retired in Naples. In his retirement, he spent time building the docks at Lake Sebago Estates, fishing, hunting, and supporting a variety of local clubs.
Jim was a Master Mason, member of the Kora Shrine Temple, and Scottish Rite. He was a past treasurer of the Sebago Lake Anglers, member of Songo Garden Club, along with both the Biggest Bucks, and One That Didn’t Get Away club from The Maine Sportsman. Jim was a past officer at the American Legion Post 155 in Naples. He spent several years volunteering to support events, donate to special programs, and enjoying the company of his friend Barbara.
He is survived by his three children, Jennifer Huber and her husband Frederick of Gulfport, Mississippi, J. David Hathaway and his wife Laura of Bowdoinham, and Elizabeth Urquhart and her partner Todd Simond of Monmouth. He also leaves four grandchildren, Victoria Pickreign and husband Josh of Gorham, Alexandria Huber of Topsham, and Fred Huber of Freeport, Florida, and Lanayria Urquhart of Monmouth as well as four great grandchildren Liam and Ria Pickreign, Jackson Psonak, and Molly Huber.
There will be a celebration of life on November 22, from 1-4 p.m., at the American Legion Post 155 in Naples. Relatives and friends are invited to share memories and stories in Jim’s honor. He will be interned at the Veterans Cemetery in Augusta.
Please visit http://www.advantageportland.com to view Jim’s online memorial.
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Maine Department of Inland
Fisheries and Wildlife.

title: Saco Santa Claus Moonlighting as a Crossing Guard
text:
At a Saco crosswalk, you can find Santa Claus helping kids year-round
It's Christmas all year long at a crosswalk in Saco, Maine, where a real-life Santa Claus brings children joy as they come and go from school.
Rick Banks, who is a full-time Santa, also works as a part-time crossing guard. Most weekday mornings and afternoons, Banks can be found at the corner of Beach and Middle streets in Saco, ensuring students at the Burns and Fairfield schools are safe.
Banks, 68, said he heard about the job from his neighbor, a crossing guard who was about to retire.
"She said, 'You should be a crossing guard. It's in the morning. It's in the afternoon, it's pretty flexible,'" Banks recalled.
Banks' house is painted Christmas red, he drives a red pickup truck featuring a decal of Santa's sleigh and reindeer on the side, and his license plate reads: "SANTAH."
Banks and his wife, who have been married for 34 years, moved to Saco from central New Hampshire two and a half years ago to be closer to their two sons. They have a 2-year-old granddaughter named Summer.
So how does Banks' wife feel about him being a full-time Santa?
"Oh, my wife is Mrs. Claus," Banks said.
No matter the season, Banks is always Santa and his favorite place to be is at the corner of Beach and Middle.
"It's amazing. I really like crossing with him," said Saco student Piper Murray.
Banks said there is one particular group of students that is always excited to see him.
"There's bus No. 702. They're nuts. They are just crazy," he said. "Because the bus driver will beep — all of the bus drivers beep their horn, and we wave — but Bus No. 702, those kids are, and I think the bus driver is also, very much into Christmas. They just wave and scream, 'Hey, Santa!' And we do the six-sevens, and we have a great time."
Banks said he has never had a bad day at work as a crossing guard.
"What is not great about it?" he asked. "I deal with children. I make people happy. I hope that I can give people a really good feeling and my goal — Santa's goal — is always to deliver joy and to preserve the wonder of Christmas."
"It all starts with children. I want them to be happy. I want them to be good people," Banks added. "The best part about a child is they're going to grow up to be a respectful adult, and I'd like to be a part of that."
After spending even a few minutes with Banks, you start to believe he is the real Santa Claus and not one of Santa's helpers.
"The fact that I look like this, I'm this all the time. In the middle of summer, I'm this," Banks said. "I'm not not Santa. I'm always Santa."
There are five Christmas trees inside Banks' house, including one that sings.
When Banks is not at the crosswalk helping to keep the kids of Saco safe, he can be found at various community events throughout the month of December.

title: With an eye toward pedestrian safety, Portland may try to set its own speed limits
text:
Officials in Portland have asked city staff to identify a legislative pathway for lowering speed limits on major arterials like Forest and Brighton avenues ― a decision now made at the state level.
The move, coming this week out of the sustainability and transportation committee, is the latest in a City Hall effort to reduce pedestrian fatalities and serious injuries in Portland. It could also have statewide implications for how speed limits are set.
Portland’s bicycle and pedestrian advisory committee, which has advocated for several initiatives in the wake of five pedestrian deaths in 2025, has driven much of the discourse over speed limits, arguing that lowering vehicle speeds is the most cost-effective and impactful way to address road safety.
The group believes Portland, like other major municipalities including New York City, should set a citywide speed limit of 25 mph — unless otherwise posted, as with 15 mph school zones — and local officials appear to agree that the most impactful change would be reducing speeds on major roads like Franklin Street and Forest and Warren avenues, where the bulk of serious injuries and deaths occur.
The power to set speed limits on those roads, however, lies with the Maine Department of Transportation, which is reluctant to change how it approaches setting speeds.
Under state law, MaineDOT is the controlling authority for state-owned highways, major-minor arterials, and collector roads, which are ranked 1-4 in the department’s five-priority classification system.
State law allows local speed-setting authority for priority 5 roads, which are neighborhood streets that are mostly already set at 25 mph.
Priority 1 roads in Portland include Interstate 295 and corridors like Brighton and Forest avenues, while priority 2 includes roads like Congress Street and Warren Avenue. According to city data for 2025-26, nearly 70% of traffic fatalities and serious injuries occurred on priority 1-2 roads.
According to a staff memo, MaineDOT leadership has communicated a willingness to support statutory changes that would give municipalities speed setting authority for priority 3-4 roads (places like Marginal Way and Veranda Street), but would not support any statutory changes related to priority 1-2 roads.
In a statement Friday, MaineDOT reiterated this position, saying it is open to working with Portland to discuss the potential for giving the city the authority to set speed limits on priority 3 and 4 roads.
“These roads are considered collector roadways and generally connect local streets with major transportation roads (priority 1-2) that move people and goods regionally or statewide,” the statement said. “We welcome additional conversation to determine how this might work in practice.”
Councilor Anna Bullett, who made the motion Tuesday to direct staff to pursue legislative avenues, acknowledged that the effort is a “much more uphill challenge,” but said “it makes the most sense if what we’re trying to do is stop pedestrian fatalities from occurring.”
Bullett also said that although she is interested in potential changes to state law around speeds on state roads, she is sensitive to the city’s partnership with MaineDOT on several ongoing projects, including the Franklin Street redesign.
Assistant City Manager Greg Jordan said if the city does pursue a legislative pathway for priority 1-2 roads, MaineDOT would not support it, and he believes it would have a tough time making it through the Legislature.
The last time there was an attempt to change the law, which was spearheaded by Sen. Rick Bennett in 2023, MaineDOT opposed a bill that would have given municipalities the authority to lower speed limits to 20 mph on a single street without taking speed-setting responsibility for all roads in the municipality.
The bill was supported by several organizations, but the city of Portland was the only municipality that testified in favor of it.
Myles Smith, chair of the city’s bicycle and pedestrian committee, said in the end, he doesn’t care who holds the authority to set speed limits. He just wants the decisions to be based on best practice and available data, and he believes MaineDOT’s system is extremely flawed.
“(MaineDOT) has chosen to implement an opaque, onerous, slow, and ineffective policy which takes years to enact,” Smith said, referring to the multi-year speed studies required for changing a speed limit.
He said the state’s system uses an algorithm that still classifies some roads in the urban core as suburban, making them eligible for speeds of up to 45 mph. These include western Commercial Street, outer Congress Street, Marginal Way, Franklin Street, and Riverside Street, several of which have seen recent fatalities.
Other streets classified as urban, which are supposed to have maximum speed limits of 30 mph, are set at 35 mph. They include Baxter Boulevard, Canco Road, Allen Avenue and Auburn Street.
The committee says there is now solid evidence to support lower default speed limits based on data from places like New York City, Seattle, Madison, Wisconsin and Somerville, Massachusetts, which have had similar default limits in place for years.
Smith said based on guidance from the National Association of City Transportation Officials, which is recognized by the federal government as a valid basis for state DOT’s and municipalities, the recommended speed limits on almost all Portland streets would be 25 mph or 20 mph.
Portland has seen three pedestrian deaths this year. In June, Jason Ayers was struck and killed at the intersection of Preble Street and Marginal Way. Nichele Roakes, 57, was killed Aug. 25 in a hit-and-run on outer Forest Avenue, and Abdulrahman Mohammed, a 13-year-old Scarborough student, was killed on Warren Avenue in September.
Under MaineDOT’s system, Warren Avenue is considered a “suburban minor arterial,” which is eligible for a 45 mph speed limit, but it’s currently posted at 35 mph. Smith and the committee believe it should be 25 mph.
During Tuesday’s meeting, city staff said they are developing a list of streets that should have reduced speed limits, which could be used as a template for future changes with or without changes to the state law.
If the city were to proceed with setting new speeds on several roads, the final cost is uncertain. City staff told the committee that changing most residential streets from 25 mph to 20 mph would cost about $750,000 to install about 1,400 signs, and that’s after conducting required speed studies.
Jeremiah Bartlett, a traffic engineer for the city, said another complication would be that Portland would be making these changes outside of what neighboring municipalities are doing, meaning motorists could have conflicting rules across city lines.
“It would have to be set up in such a way that it’s clear to the traveling public what these speeds are and what the expectation is,” he said.

title: Trump administration moves to have lawsuit dismissed in challenge to Alaska’s US Senate race
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — The Trump administration on Thursday moved to effectively drop its lawsuit that sought to block the certification of Democrat Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race, ending a much-criticized gambit by the president to prevent one of his political rivals from taking office.
The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court already ruled that the second Sullivan’s candidacy is legal and that he could be on the ballot.
Attorneys for the state, which is currently controlled by Republicans, also objected to the administration’s move, calling it legally “meritless” and filing papers to help get the initial case dismissed. The administration moved Thursday to have an appeals court declare its case moot, two days after the race was decided.
In their filing, Justice Department attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn the lower court’s dismissal of the case to erase the loss, but then dismiss the case anyway. They said the court “should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground.”
That decision comes after Peltola won an outright majority in the race to become Democrats’ 56th senator, the ninth Senate pickup for the party in its midterm blowout. Peltola won by more votes than were taken by the other candidate, Dan J. Sullivan.
In a statement responding to the filing, Peltola said it was time to move on: “Now that the election is over and the voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in, I’m eager to move forward and get to work on behalf of all Alaskans.”
Messages seeking comment also were left with Sen. Sullivan’s campaign and the Alaska Department of Law.
The Department of Justice filed the lawsuit at President Donald Trump’s direction, saying that a Peltola win should not be certified until an investigation can determine if voters were confused. The administration never explained how such an investigation could take place given the secrecy of the ballot.
The case was filed before The New York Times reported on texts and other documents that appeared to show Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting the retired schoolteacher from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg. He was listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot, with no party preference, to distinguish him from the senator, who was identified as a Republican and the incumbent. Dan J. Sullivan has long insisted he ran on his own and Peltola has denied any involvement.
Trump also has demanded that Peltola be prosecuted for the scheme, and federal investigators swarmed into Alaska before Election Day. Tricks involving decoy candidates such as the second Sullivan have been a staple of U.S. politics for decades, and Trump’s allies have also used them, though occasionally the schemes do lead to criminal charges.
It was at least the second time since the Nov. 3 election that the Department of Justice has acted to dismiss one of its high-profile lawsuits interfering in states’ handling of their elections.
Just days after the election that saw Democrats flip control of Congress and peel off big wins in races for governor and state legislatures, the Justice Department moved to drop a lawsuit seeking to prevent California officials from counting roughly 20,000 ballots. The Trump administration alleged the ballots belonged to suspected noncitizens, but election officials questioned the validity of the data and said the government’s list contained many U.S. citizens.
___
Riccardi reported from Denver.

title: Love isn't in the air, it's at baggage claim during ground stop at Denver International Airport
text:
Love isn't in the air, it's at baggage claim during ground stop at Denver International Airport
Airports across the country were filled with frustration this weekend as flight delays and cancellations left travelers stranded.
For Brelyn Bowman, it meant missing a conference, KCNC reports.
"I was on the airplane for over four hours," Bowman said. "Everybody was grounded."
Jake Hinson and Chelsey Rogers were also stuck, but they were trying to make it to Las Vegas for their wedding.
The couple watched as their flight kept getting pushed back.
"We kept getting notifications on the app. It's delayed. Oh, it's delayed again," Rogers said.
Eventually, the notification they had been dreading came through: their flight was canceled.
"There's nothing that's available that's gonna get us there in time for the ceremony," Rogers said.
Their checked bags had already been sent without them. With no way to make it to Las Vegas in time for the ceremony, the couple headed to leave the airport with little more than a wedding veil in their carry-on.
"I'm crying at this point. I was so hopeful. I really thought we'd make it," Rogers said.
But then they struck up a conversation with Bowman, who just happened to be an ordained minister.
"I made the joke of, like, hey, you know, we can wrap this up now," Bowman said. "But I never imagined that they would actually say yes."
They did.
And shortly after saying yes, Hinson and Rogers said, "I do."
"At first it was just the three of us, yeah, and then another woman ran up," Rogers said. "And then as the trains were letting people off, people were kind of gathering."
The airport tram station by baggage claim became an unexpected wedding venue, with the sound of arriving trains serving as wedding bells.
"You have those moments where time just stands still, you know? And you're just in a moment in space where humanity really connects the way we're supposed to connect," Bowman said. "Nobody was concerned about the flight at that point. Nobody."
After 13 hours at the airport, what began as a miserable travel day became something the couple says they will never forget.
"Thirteen hours in an airport. That's a bad day," Hinson said. "And so that just made what had been a really awful experience a highlight of our life."
And the connection didn't end with the ceremony.
Bowman said she and the couple have stayed in touch. "Yes, yes. So at this point, I am the godmother to their children," Bowman said. "We plan to get together a year from now to celebrate."
Their story proves that even when love isn't in the air, sometimes it's waiting at baggage claim.

title: Why the bricks around Bangor’s Hannibal Hamlin statue are suddenly blacktop
text:
Pedestrians walking by Bangor’s Hannibal Hamlin statue Friday might notice a change of scenery: the brick pavers around the statue and through the surrounding park have been paved over with asphalt.
The asphalt is a temporary fix to prevent tripping hazards over the winter before the historic park undergoes a fuller revamp next year, which will include taking out the old pavers and putting down new ones, according to the city.
“Those pavers are all old and broken up, and there were a lot of tripping hazards,” City Engineer Jeff Davis said.
The pavers will be replaced as part of a larger project to rebuild the retaining wall between the park and Kenduskeag Stream, Davis said. The Bangor City Council authorized a contract for the project in October. A site evaluation report found structural problems with the wall, which was built in the 1930s, that leave it more vulnerable to tides.
The rebuild is slated to cost about $3.8 million. Construction is expected to begin in the spring and wrap up in late fall 2027, Davis said.
The entire park will be dug up during construction, and new pavers will go in after the new wall is finished, Davis said.
Hannibal Hamlin Park honors the country’s 15th vice president, who lived in Bangor and served under President Abraham Lincoln. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1984.

title: New video shows Brooklyn building collapse in real time
text:
NEW YORK (Gray News) – New video shows the moment a building in Brooklyn collapsed last week.
The video, provided by the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, was taken through a window of a New York City bus that was stopped at a red light.
Shortly after the light turns green, the building can be seen collapsing into a construction site.
Eight people were killed, including two children, ages 9 and 10, according to city officials. Another 18 people were injured, including four firefighters.
Many families were left homeless.
New York officials, from building inspectors to prosecutors, say they’re investigating what caused the three-story building to come crashing down as workers were digging at an adjacent construction site.
The city has ordered inspections at more than 160 sites in New York that are associated with six entities linked to the construction and demolition site next to the fallen building, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.
“I think it is always an outrage when eight New Yorkers lose their lives, when 18 New Yorkers are hospitalized, and when families are shattered as a result of all of this,” Mamdani said.
If investigators uncover “any evidence of criminality,” Mamdani said, “it is one that we follow through to the fullest extent of the law.”

title: What does Project 2025 say about the FAA and banking?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
What does Project 2025 say about the FAA and banking?
After widespread technology disruptions to banking and air travel, some people are pointing to Project 2025.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
“Just a reminder that what’s happening with the (Federal Aviation Administration) is planned and deliberate,” a TikTok narrator said.
A Facebook page from a group called The Democratic Coalition shared a photo of people lining up at what looks like an airport with text that said, “Remember, destroying the FAA is part of Project 2025.” Other posts on Facebook and Instagram make similar claims.
When major U.S. banks experienced widespread outages Nov. 16, social media users again invoked Project 2025.
“The bank outages make sense after the FAA grounding if you are aware of project 2025,” said David Ross Lawn, a digital creator with more than 600,000 followers, in a Nov. 16 Facebook post. “Banks were next in line on the agenda. They’re doing a speed run of Project 2025 because of the Blue Tsunami,” a reference to Democratic wins in the 2026 midterm elections.
Project 2025 was a presidential transition project led by the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank. The 900-page manual recommends detailed policies following a 2024 Republican presidential victory.
While some Project 2025 goals line up with descriptions in the social media posts, the posts also overstate what the project proposed. These goals do not have much to do with explanations offered for outages and the ground stop.
The nationwide ground stop, and what Project 2025 says about the FAA
The FAA’s Nov. 13 ground stop, which lasted about five hours, stemmed from the deployment of a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas, that caused “excessive data flooding the systems,” the FAA said.
Project 2025 would not “destroy” the FAA, as social posts claimed, but it would fundamentally reshape it. It recommends that the agency operate more like a business, reshape its funding sources and run separately from the Transportation Department.
The Trump administration hasn’t proposed restructuring the agency as the project outlines.
After the recent tech disruptions, multiple social media videos also pointed to pages 632 to 635 as evidence that Project 2025 aims to privatize certain parts of the FAA.
Aviation expert Edward Booth told PolitiFact that air traffic control services are already significantly privatized, with more than 50% of U.S. control towers run by private contractors. Booth drew a distinction between privatization and user fees for air traffic control services, which Project 2025 proposes.
“For nearly 100 years, all pilots in the U.S. have received (air traffic control) services free of charge,” Booth said. “Fuel and airline ticket taxes fund the system. Project 2025 urges charging fees for use of the system.”
Project 2025 says that at a minimum, the Air Traffic Organization should be separated from the FAA. The ATO is in charge of providing airspace navigation services to all of the U.S. and large portions of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans and the Gulf of Mexico.
“Organizations such as the FAA whose sole responsibility is public safety should be fully auditable and led by experts in their field or industry with oversight from DOT leadership,” page 633 of Project 2025 says.
It also calls for “completely restructuring the FAA’s funding system.” Instead of using taxes from aviation users, as it currently does, Project 2025 proposes that the FAA charge fees for air traffic services and issue long-term revenue bonds for major projects. Currently, the majority of the FAA’s funding comes from a trust fund that draws from taxes on domestic flight tickets, air cargo, plane fuel and other things.
Booth said Congress has consistently rejected direct user fees for air traffic control services. He predicted that if such fees are imposed, many general aviation pilots would not pay the fees and would fly without the air traffic control services.
After the ground stop, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, such as upgrading the telecommunication systems; the Trump administration said Nov. 17 it is seeking $50 billion more, on top of $12.5 billion that Congress approved in 2025.
Project 2025 aim to restructure the U.S. banking system?
JPMorgan Chase said it had longer than usual service times on Nov. 16 because of technical issues. A Chase spokesperson told CBS News that its services experienced a technical bug, not a cyber issue.
Bank of America customers also reported technical issues that day, but the bank told CBS the system was operating normally.
After the tech outages impacted banks and the FAA, a social media user connected the disruptions with Project 2025’s proposals. He said Project 2025 wants to “reshape federal banking oversight, consolidate regulatory functions and roll back major financial regulations.”
Project 2025 calls for restructuring the financial regulatory system. Chapter 22 supports legislation to merge the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the National Credit Union Administration and the Federal Reserve’s non-monetary supervisory and regulatory functions. It also calls for policymakers to create new charters for financial firms that reduce regulations, with these charters replacing government regulation.
In chapter 24, it recommends that neither interest rates nor the supply of money be controlled by the government. The Federal Reserve would be effectively abolished, and the Department of the Treasury would largely limit itself to handling the government’s money.
Will Ragland, vice president of research for the advocacy department at the left-leaning Center for American Progress, told PolitiFact that Project 2025 sought to restructure banking in the U.S., including eliminating some Dodd-Frank protections; Fannie and Freddie conservatorships, the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate and lender of last resort lending, and eliminating the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
“However, from what I’ve observed the Trump administration has really only made progress to date on gutting the (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau) and a more lenient approach to regulatory enforcement and investigations writ large,” Ragland said. “While I think Project 2025 sought to restructure banking in a big way, I don’t think it or the (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau) being gutted had anything to do with the outages we’re seeing.”
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.

title: Senator proposes select committee on AI as Democrats hope to move quickly to regulate it
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Democrats are debating the best way to try to quickly establish guardrails around artificial intelligence in the next Congress, with one senator pushing the two candidates for Senate majority leader to create a new committee.
Colorado Sen. John Hickenlooper said this week that the person leading their majority next year should have a “day one plan for responsible regulation” on AI as he has so far withheld an endorsement in the race between Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen.
Hickenlooper said Friday that there hasn’t been enough progress in Congress since Democrats formed a working group on AI three years ago and convened tech leaders from across the country to figure out next steps. While Republicans who have led the House and Senate for the last two years have said that AI should be a priority, they have focused mostly on innovation and there has been no major push to establish safeguards or increase monitoring of the technology.
“There’s a perception that we haven’t done anything,” Hickenlooper said.
Democrats have been publicly and privately discussing what their first steps could be on artificial intelligence when they take the majority in January. Top policy proposals could be regulating data centers, safety standards and stepping up monitoring and research. Hickenlooper said his priorities are robust third-party evaluation requirements, mitigation of national security challenges and “clear rules of the road to hold AI companies accountable.”
A spokeswoman for Schumer, who is favored to win reelection in the closed-door Dec. 1 caucus leadership vote, said he has been working closely with the incoming heads of committees to “develop an ambitious AI agenda and hit the ground running in January.”
“Senate Democrats will make AI a top priority of the new Democratic majority and are working to deliver comprehensive legislation that addresses the serious risks AI poses to our national security, workers, and consumers while keeping America at the forefront of innovation,” said Schumer spokeswoman Allison Biasotti.
Some Democrats support a separate committee
Hickenlooper said that he proposed a select committee on artificial intelligence to consolidate the conversation.
“With the presidential election two years away, we have a two-year audition to show Americans we can deliver on three priorities: affordability, accountability, and AI safety,” Hickenlooper wrote in letters to both Schumer and Van Hollen.
Van Hollen said he supports the idea. “I do think we need a joint committee,” he said. “AI covers so many different areas that are impacting our lives.”
Still, it’s unclear if other Democrats — especially the heads of committees who are already working on AI proposals — will support it.
Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the incoming chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, said he would “want to see the specifics” and what topics would be covered in the committee. Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who is expected to become the chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, also did not immediately endorse the idea.
Democrats have to make it a priority “no matter what particular way we end up approaching it,” Sanders said. “Congress has been way, way, way behind where it should be in protecting the American people.”
Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, the current Republican chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, said a plan to take the issue out of his committee and others “makes no sense.” But he said that there were already bipartisan conversations about the issue looking forward to next year.
“I hope in the next Congress we can see Republicans and Democrats finding common ground on addressing catastrophic risk,” said Cruz.
Little action in Congress
President Joe Biden’s administration called on lawmakers to develop policies after a 2023 executive order on AI oversight, which President Donald Trump rescinded soon after returning to office. And the bipartisan working group on artificial intelligence formed by Schumer released a report in 2024 recommending the U.S. spend at least $32 billion over the next three years to develop artificial intelligence and implement safeguards around it.
But even as the technology has progressed at a rapid clip, Trump — who will hold the power of the veto — has repeatedly maintained that little regulation is needed.
House Democrats have also been discussing a way forward on AI and have proposed a robust package of proposals. This week, three Democrats announced the launch of the House AI Safety and Innovation caucus to address security risks.

title: Coastal storm races toward Maine early Monday

A storm moving up the East Coast this weekend brings a quick round of beneficial rain to Maine Sunday night into Monday.
The storm will be fast-moving, with a majority of the rain falling overnight Sunday night. The rain may be heavy at times with breezy, but not damaging, winds. Rain ends from west to east Monday morning, with cold air flowing in on a northwest breeze in the afternoon.
Southern and central Maine could pick up 1 to 2 inches of rain, although the exact track of the storm will determine where the heaviest amounts fall. A narrow band of higher rainfall totals is a possibility, a trend which will be monitored closely as the storm develops.
Turning much colder for the rest of next week with highs in the 30s to mid-40s. Maine's Total Weather is watching another storm riding up the coastline that could impact Thanksgiving and Black Friday. With the cold air in place, snow, ice, and rain are all possible should the storm track close enough to New England.

title: Obituary: Cheryl L. Coy
text:
RICHMOND – Cheryl L. Coy, 78, was reunited with her youngest daughter, Trina, when she passed away peacefully on Nov. 15, 2026, surrounded by her loving family, following a stroke.
Born on March 21, 1948, in Bath, Maine, Cheryl was a warm and spirited woman who knew how to enjoy life’s simple pleasures. In her younger years, she was an avid bowler who loved the fun and camaraderie of the lanes. Later in life, one of her favorite pastimes was going out for a good dinner followed by a relaxing evening drive through the Maine countryside to count deer.
Above all else, Cheryl cherished the family she built over six decades. She is survived by her beloved husband of 60 years, Charles A. Coy; her children, Debra and her husband Kevin, Darla and her partner Stephen, and Sherry; her grandchildren, Kevin Jr. and his wife Alex, Veronica, Derek and his wife Emily, Moriah, and Tyler and his wife Miranda; and her great-grandchildren, Aria, Nora, Sawyer, and Savannah. She was predeceased by her loving parents Frank and Gladys Johnson.
The family wishes to extend their heartfelt gratitude to the compassionate nurses, doctors, and palliative care team on Terrace West at MaineGeneral’s Alfond Center for Health for the comfort and dignity they provided Cheryl and her family.
There will not be any services held at this time.
Arrangements are under the care of Kincer Funeral Home 130 Pleasant St. Richmond, Me 04357.

title: 14-year-old’s death ruled homicide after alleged online manipulation and extortion, authorities say
text:
FORT WAYNE, Ind. (WPTA/Gray News) - The death of a 14-year-old Indiana girl has been ruled a homicide after authorities said she was subjected to psychological manipulation and extortion by an outside actor.
Brynlee Jo Stempa’s death was ruled a homicide following an autopsy, toxicology testing and an “extensive review of digital and investigative evidence,” according to the Allen County Coroner’s Office.
The coroner’s office said evidence provided by Fort Wayne police, the FBI and international law enforcement partners showed that Stempa’s death was “directly orchestrated and compelled through severe psychological manipulation and extortion by an outside actor.”
The office explained that, under forensic pathology standards, a homicide ruling means a death resulted from the intentional, coercive or culpable actions of another person.
The FBI said German authorities arrested a man in connection with her death. German broadcaster NDR reported that the suspect was 17 at the time of the alleged crime, according to the Hamburg Public Prosecutor’s Office.
Prosecutors said the suspect allegedly demanded that Stempa harm herself and later tried to obtain recordings of her death, NDR reported.
The broadcaster also reported that investigators found references to a group known as the “Nefarious Maniac Cult” in Stempa’s recordings.
Last month, Fort Wayne police warned families and educators about online networks that target children and other vulnerable people.
Police said perpetrators use platforms including Discord, Roblox and Telegram to build relationships with potential victims.

title: Brewer woman pleads guilty to depositing counterfeit government checks
text:
A Brewer woman has pleaded guilty to depositing counterfeit government checks.
Michelle Sands, 40, entered her plea Thursday in U.S. District Court in Bangor, according to the U.S. attorney’s office.
Sands deposited five counterfeit U.S. Treasury checks totaling $23,675 at her credit union, the U.S. attorney’s office said Thursday.
The serial numbers and amounts on the checks matched genuine tax refunds the Internal Revenue Service issued to other people. Sands changed the payee and address to make them payable to herself.
When confronted by IRS agents, Sands claimed to have received the checks in the mail from the IRS, according to prosecutors.
She faces up to 20 years in prison, a $250,000 fine and up to three years of supervised release.
Sands will be sentenced at a later date after a judge consults the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other factors.

title: Injuries piling up for Patriots as bye week arrives
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — With the Patriots sitting at 5-5, Mike Vrabel believes his team can still find a way over its final seven games to make it back to the playoffs.
But the availability of key players — or lack thereof – has put New England in a tough position as it looks to avoid becoming the third straight Super Bowl runner-up to not make the playoffs the following year.
“We’re grown men. We all have to recognize what it is we need to do better and improve. That’s what winners do,” Vrabel said. “Winners figure out ways to help the team win. They don’t (moan) and complain. They try to find ways to help the team.”
There’s little doubt that injuries have hindered Vrabel’s team from doing that.
Entering the bye week, New England’s Week 1 starters have missed a total of 49 games, the most in the NFL to this point in the season. Second is the Carolina Panthers with 48 games missed.
Prominent players from last year’s Super Bowl run to miss multiple games because of injuries include right guard Mike Onwenu (broken ankle, eight games), wide receiver Mack Hollins (four games, calf) and cornerback Christian Gonzalez (two games, shoulder). Their absences have played roles in the Patriots’ lack of consistency.
On Friday, the Associated Press learned quarterback Drake Maye could miss the rest of the regular season because of a fractured right fibula and wide receiver A.J. Brown will miss several weeks with a hamstring injury.
Gonzalez struggling
In Gonzalez’s case, his injury has coincided with a big drop in his production.
In the 14 regular-season games he appeared in last season, he was targeted 84 times and allowed 45 receptions for 482 yards. Through eight games this season, he has already been targeted 48 times and has allowed 31 receptions for 472 yards.
According to Pro Football Focus, he ranks 53rd out of 67 cornerbacks who have played at least 50% of their team’s defensive snaps.
It’s not the production the Patriots were hoping to see from him after signing him to a four-year, $135 million contract extension, making him the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history.
Maye latest to join injury list
Maye became the latest to go down, suffering his injury in the first quarter of a 35-10 loss to the Detroit Lions in Germany last weekend.
Tests revealed Maye didn’t sustain ligament damage in the ankle, one of the people said.
New England also has 18 players on the injured reserve or physically unable to perform lists, which is tied with Houston for the third-most in the league behind Green Bay (20) and Arizona (19).
That, combined with a team that is regressing offensively while giving up 30 or more points on defense in each of its last three losses, has left the defending AFC champions trying to stitch things back together.
Vrabel said it’s no time to dwell on what’s gone wrong.
“Every year is different. Every game is different,” Vrabel said. “It’s a different team, different time. We’ve got to focus on what our team is and who we want to be.”
Newcomers haven’t avoided injury bug
What might be most striking is the number of Patriots players from this offseason’s free agency class that have been sidelined.
Wide receivers A.J. Brown (six games, ankle and knee injuries) and Romeo Doubs (four games, shoulder), fullback Reggie Gilliam (four games, knee, ankle) and left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (four games, hamstring) have missed multiple games.
And with all four of those players having already done a stint on injured reserve, options will soon be exhausted for any future players to return if they must go on IR.
NFL teams can designate up to eight players to return from IR during the regular season (and up to 10 if they make the postseason). An individual player can be so designated twice.
“The injuries and the injured reserve, I mean, if you pay attention,” Vrabel said, “we don’t have too many spots left here to bring guys back on injured reserve.”
Still, linebacker Christian Elliss said even with all disruptions to the roster, he believes increased effort and finishing plays can go a long way for the players that are available each week.
“The frustrating part is you see it. You see the effort and finish and then it’s just one play here, one play there,” Elliss said. “Down-in, down-out type of thing that we’ve got to really look at ourselves in the mirror and you fix yourself first and then you drag other people along.”

title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ sets record with $3.79B in first-day retail sales, Rockstar Games reports
text:
‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ sets record with $3.79B in first-day retail sales, Rockstar Games reports
Sales of “Grand Theft Auto VI” generated a record with $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales, maker Rockstar Games said Friday, underscoring the enormous demand for the first new installment in the blockbuster series in 13 years.
The worldwide figure was based on company estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game launched. Rockstar also said in a release that it sold 32.5 million units prerelease, setting a record across platforms.
“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a release.
A launch far bigger than “GTA V”
The launch far eclipsed that of its predecessor.
“Grand Theft Auto V," released in 2013, generated $1 billion in retail sales in its first three days. It went on to become one of the bestselling video games of all time, accounting for more than 230 million of the franchise's more than 470 million units sold globally, according to publisher Take-Two Interactive.
Earlier Friday, market research firm Sensor Tower estimated that “GTA VI” had generated $2.36 million in revenue on approximately 24.6 million units sold. Rockstar's figures, released later in the day, were based on the company's own estimates of worldwide day-one retail sales.
The standard edition of the game retails for around $80 in the U.S.
Earlier this month, the PlayStation blog said that “GTA VI” was the most preordered game in the history of its namesake store. Due to the demand, PlayStation said that it was teaming with Rockstar Games to allow players to start preloading the game nine days early, so that they'd be ready to play on launch day.
Thirteen years of anticipation
"GTA VI” is the latest installment in the hyperviolent, open-world video game series that has skewered American culture with fictionalized versions of New York and Los Angeles and is now returning to its sun-baked version of Miami — Vice City.
It's the first new “GTA” game in 13 years, with the story of “GTA VI” centered on Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple trying to improve their circumstances through crime across the fictional state of Leonida.
Early reviews for the game have noted a greater emphasis on relationship building that goes beyond the violent stickups, bank robberies and mayhem that have long defined the franchise.
The game's release also ended years of secrecy around its cast. Manni L. Perez plays Lucia and Dylan Rourke portrays Jason, while Bobby Moynihan, Stephen Root, Taryn Manning, Roselyn Sanchez and rapper Denzel Curry are among the familiar names in Rockstar’s sprawling credits.
The enormous launch comes after more than a decade of anticipation around a series that has become one of the biggest properties in entertainment.

title: Man who filed for divorce 2 weeks ago now accused of killing his wife, police say
text:
GRAND ISLAND, Neb. (KSNB/Gray News) - A Nebraska man who had filed for divorce is accused of killing his wife Wednesday night.
Police arrested 43-year-old Luis Gutierrez after officers were called to the couple’s home. His wife, Connie Gutierrez, was 36.
What police found
Police received several 911 calls from the home at 4117 Michigan Ave., according to an affidavit. The first caller hung up.
As officers headed to the home, a woman called 911 and asked for police. During the call, a loud noise that sounded like a door slamming could be heard, followed by a man yelling and asking what he had just done, the affidavit says.
Another 911 call was traced to Luis Gutierrez. During that call, he said he had shot his wife, according to the affidavit.
When officers arrived, Luis Gutierrez came out the front door holding a phone, with his hands raised. Inside, police found Connie Gutierrez sitting on a couch with a gunshot wound to her head. A handgun was on the coffee table in front of her.
She was taken to a hospital, where she died.
The couple’s two children were inside the home when the shooting happened, according to the affidavit. Neither child was harmed.
Suspect charged
Gutierrez was arrested and taken to the Hall County Department of Corrections. He is charged with five felonies, including first degree murder.
Grand Island Police Division Chief Dean Elliott said officers had responded that home several times before the shooting.
“We’ve had calls for service there, nothing physical in nature, but for a pattern that we sometimes see when parents are not getting along,” Elliott said. “A ‘he said, she said’ situation between the two of them, nothing where criminal charges were filed, more like safety of the children at that point in time.”
Elliott also said the investigation is still in the early stages, with the autopsy playing an important role.
Elliott encouraged anyone who sees domestic violence happening to call police so officers can respond, help stop it and connect those involved with resources.
At a hearing Thursday morning in Hall County Court, a judge set Gutierrez’s bond at $10 million, with 10% required. A probable cause hearing is scheduled for Dec. 22.
Divorce filing
Court records show Luis Gutierrez filed for divorce on Nov. 3, 2026.
In the filing, his attorney said the marriage was “irretrievably broken and all efforts at reconciliation have wholly failed.”
The two had been married since January 2023. Gutierrez requested custody of the two teenage children living in the home.
