title: Trump administration moves to have lawsuit dismissed in challenge to Alaska’s US Senate race
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — The Trump administration on Thursday moved to effectively drop its lawsuit that sought to block the certification of Democrat Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race, ending a much-criticized gambit by the president to prevent one of his political rivals from taking office.
The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court already ruled that the second Sullivan’s candidacy is legal and that he could be on the ballot.
Attorneys for the state, which is currently controlled by Republicans, also objected to the administration’s move, calling it legally “meritless” and filing papers to help get the initial case dismissed. The administration moved Thursday to have an appeals court declare its case moot, two days after the race was decided.
In their filing, Justice Department attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn the lower court’s dismissal of the case to erase the loss, but then dismiss the case anyway. They said the court “should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground.”
That decision comes after Peltola won an outright majority in the race to become Democrats’ 56th senator, the ninth Senate pickup for the party in its midterm blowout. Peltola won by more votes than were taken by the other candidate, Dan J. Sullivan.
In a statement responding to the filing, Peltola said it was time to move on: “Now that the election is over and the voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in, I’m eager to move forward and get to work on behalf of all Alaskans.”
Messages seeking comment also were left with Sen. Sullivan’s campaign and the Alaska Department of Law.
The Department of Justice filed the lawsuit at President Donald Trump’s direction, saying that a Peltola win should not be certified until an investigation can determine if voters were confused. The administration never explained how such an investigation could take place given the secrecy of the ballot.
The case was filed before The New York Times reported on texts and other documents that appeared to show Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting the retired schoolteacher from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg. He was listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot, with no party preference, to distinguish him from the senator, who was identified as a Republican and the incumbent. Dan J. Sullivan has long insisted he ran on his own and Peltola has denied any involvement.
Trump also has demanded that Peltola be prosecuted for the scheme, and federal investigators swarmed into Alaska before Election Day. Tricks involving decoy candidates such as the second Sullivan have been a staple of U.S. politics for decades, and Trump’s allies have also used them, though occasionally the schemes do lead to criminal charges.
It was at least the second time since the Nov. 3 election that the Department of Justice has acted to dismiss one of its high-profile lawsuits interfering in states’ handling of their elections.
Just days after the election that saw Democrats flip control of Congress and peel off big wins in races for governor and state legislatures, the Justice Department moved to drop a lawsuit seeking to prevent California officials from counting roughly 20,000 ballots. The Trump administration alleged the ballots belonged to suspected noncitizens, but election officials questioned the validity of the data and said the government’s list contained many U.S. citizens.
___
Riccardi reported from Denver.

title: 'The most effective ambassador': Fiona the hippo's death sparks grief and talk about famous animals
text:
Why do we mourn famous animals we don’t even know? Maybe it’s because the media — and, increasingly, social media — makes us feel like we know them intimately.
Millions of people watched footage of Fiona the hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo wiggle out of her mom and into the world in 2017, struggle to survive as a preemie — and then thrive with the help of dedicated staff into a playful beast weighing more than a ton. When she died Thursday after swallowing a child’s hat in an apparent accident, Cincinnati wept. People around the world demanded explanations. Some sought to cast blame.
“I miss her so much already,” said an emotional Zee Azari, an admirer who, like many others visiting the zoo Friday, brought Fiona’s favorite food and smell. “I brought a watermelon and some coffee today to remember her, so that she knew how much I loved her.”
People often are surprised by the level of grief they feel when a beloved pet dies, and research has shown that it can be experienced equally intensely whether the deceased is human or not — and even if it’s a famous animal they’ve watched from afar.
That loss can be felt via a virtual experience, too — such as following online as an animal is born, fights to survive and grows to adulthood, like Fiona. Put them together, and they add up to a phenomenon known as disenfranchised grief — the experience of meaningful loss when culture and society do not recognize or support it.
‘It just weighs so heavy’
Fiona would not likely have survived without the zoo staff’s care. And her death, according to the zoo, was truly accidental. A child tossed a hat into the air; a ceiling fan blade catapulted it through a foot-wide gap near the ceiling and into Fiona’s pen. The hippo swallowed it and could not pass it out of her body, the zoo said.
“It just weighs so heavy when we love these animals, even if we haven’t met them,” posted a woman who identified herself to The Associated Press as Alice, from Wales, on Reddit. “Their individual personalities shine through.”
Alongside the love for innocent animals and the need for conservation, though, complicated questions arise about other institutions that have kept wild animals through history. About exploiting the animals as well as the human need for connection with them. About ethics and myth- and profit-making that can be hard to tell from genuine efforts to raise money for conservation.
And money has been raised. Animals like giant pandas, tigers, polar bears, and elephants act as “mascots” for conservation groups, drawing public donations that often support wider habitat protection.
So while Fiona’s death gives parents a chance to talk with children about love and the end of life, it also perhaps provides the opportunity to discuss the ongoing debate over keeping animals in captivity.
“There’s all kinds of narratives at play here: Politics and privilege and visual culture and profit as much as agency on the part of the individual animals themselves. And animals don’t have agency, ” said Huw Lewis-Jones, an associated professor of environment and culture at Falmouth University in Cornwall, England. “We want to look at them, we want to think about them. We certainly want to tell stories about them.”
There’s a long history of animal celebrities
The history of creating animal celebrities goes back centuries. Some of the stories are complicated.
For starters, Fiona has always been connected with Harambe.
The year before Fiona’s birth — in 2016 — zoo officials shot to death the beloved endangered gorilla after a small boy fell into his exhibit. Fiona’s birth six weeks early, and her unlikely survival, did much to quiet the backlash over the zoo’s choices. But for many, her unrelated death this week at the same zoo revived the horror.
Think, too, of Koko, the gorilla fluent in sign language who loved cats, understood death and could rate her own pain on a scale of one to 10. When she died in 2018 at age 46, people around the world mourned her as a bridge between species. But questions also lingered about exploitation and the ethics of making animals perform for public attention.
The original Shamu, the killer whale, died in 1971. But SeaWorld continued to use her name until, under pressure from animal rights groups and environmentalists, it announced in 2016 it was phasing out its killer whale program.
But some animal ambassadors are apparently adorable. Punch, the Japanese macaque orphaned in 2025, marked his first birthday with a flood of well-wishing messages from his fans around the world — even though he now has friends and is no longer holding on to the toy.
Ask anyone in Southern California about P-22 and they’ll know: He was the region’s most famous mountain lion, named for being the 22nd puma in a National Park Service study. Wildlife cameras tracked his search for a mate over a decade before he was found injured and euthanized in 2023. He inspired a wildlife crossing over a Los Angeles-area highway.
There’s no doubt that the connection with celebrity animals can be enduring for humans. In Knautschke the hippo’s case, the appeal was also diplomatic.
Knautschke was a famous male hippopotamus at the Berlin Zoo who survived World War II and became a symbol of resilience. He remains popular even now. During a specialized tour of the zoo earlier this year for people who live with dementia, several participants recognized the late hippo’s bronze statue outside the current hippo habitat.
Fiona was the “most effective zoo ambassador I believe there has ever been,” Jenna Wingate, her longtime keeper, wrote on Instagram on Friday.
“She was magic,” Wingate wrote, “wrapped in a hippo.”

title: Meet the Four 2026 Aroostook County Athletes of the Fall
text:
Querze, Cyr, Graves and Gorneault Named 2026 Athletes of the Fall
Nine weeks of Athlete of the Week, a full postseason and more than 18,000 votes cast have brought the 2026 fall sports season to its final awards.
Josh Querze of Madawaska, Madisyn Cyr of Wisdom, Emma Graves of Caribou and Pierce Gorneault of Caribou have been selected as the 2026 Aroostook County Athletes of the Fall.
This year's season-ending awards were divided into four categories for the first time, with separate Large School and Small School boys and girls divisions.
The winners are:
Large School Boys Athlete of the Fall: Pierce Gorneault, Caribou
Large School Girls Athlete of the Fall: Emma Graves, Caribou
Small School Boys Athlete of the Fall: Josh Querze, Madawaska
Small School Girls Athlete of the Fall: Madisyn Cyr, Wisdom
Large School Boys Athlete of the Fall: Pierce Gorneault, Caribou
Pierce Gorneault put together a championship cross country season from beginning to end.
The Caribou standout won the PVC Championship, Northern Maine Class B Regional Championship and Class B State Championship, becoming Caribou's first boys individual state champion in 30 years.
Gorneault also recorded a 16:01 personal best, qualified for the New England Championships and helped Caribou capture conference and regional team championships before finishing third at states.
It was a season defined by consistency and championship performances.
Congratulations to Pierce Gorneault, the 2026 Large School Boys Athlete of the Fall.
Large School Girls Athlete of the Fall: Emma Graves, Caribou
Emma Graves was one of Northern Maine's top runners throughout the fall.
Graves won the PVC individual championship and continued her outstanding season through the championship meets, eventually finishing second at the Class B State Cross Country Championship.
She also earned Athlete of the Week honors during the season while consistently racing among the top competitors in the region.
Congratulations to Emma Graves, the 2026 Large School Girls Athlete of the Fall.
Small School Boys Athlete of the Fall: Josh Querze, Madawaska
Josh Querze closed his high school soccer career with another outstanding season while helping lead Madawaska all the way to the Class D State Championship game.
Querze finished his career with more than 120 goals, earned All-Aroostook and regional recognition and remained one of the area's most dangerous offensive players throughout the fall.
But his impact went beyond scoring.
Querze served as a captain and helped lead a Madawaska team that captured the Class D North regional championship and represented Northern Maine in the state final.
Congratulations to Josh Querze, the 2026 Small School Boys Athlete of the Fall.
Small School Girls Athlete of the Fall: Madisyn Cyr, Wisdom
Madisyn Cyr helped Wisdom complete one of the most memorable seasons anywhere in Aroostook County this fall.
Cyr delivered important goals during Wisdom's postseason run, scoring in consecutive tournament victories as the Pioneers advanced through the playoffs.
The run eventually ended with Wisdom capturing the state championship, completing a historic season for the program.
Cyr also earned Week Nine Athlete of the Week honors during that postseason run before finishing the year as an Athlete of the Fall winner.
Congratulations to Madisyn Cyr, the 2026 Small School Girls Athlete of the Fall.

Making the Athlete of the Fall ballot required more than one great performance.

title: Trump administration moves to have lawsuit dismissed in challenge to Alaska's US Senate race
text:
Trump administration moves to have lawsuit dismissed in challenge to Alaska's US Senate race
The Trump administration on Thursday moved to effectively drop its lawsuit that sought to block the certification of Democrat Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, ending a much-criticized gambit by the president to prevent one of his political rivals from taking office.
The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court already ruled that the second Sullivan’s candidacy is legal and that he could be on the ballot.
Attorneys for the state, which is currently controlled by Republicans, also objected to the administration's move, calling it legally “meritless” and filing papers to help get the initial case dismissed. The administration moved Thursday to have an appeals court declare its case moot, two days after the race was decided.
In their filing, Justice Department attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn the lower court's dismissal of the case to erase the loss, but then dismiss the case anyway. They said the court “should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground.”
That decision comes after Peltola won an outright majority in the race to become Democrats' 56th senator, the ninth Senate pickup for the party in its midterm blowout. Peltola won by more votes than were taken by the other candidate, Dan J. Sullivan.
In a statement responding to the filing, Peltola said it was time to move on: "Now that the election is over and the voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in, I’m eager to move forward and get to work on behalf of all Alaskans.”
Messages seeking comment also were left with Sen. Sullivan's campaign and the Alaska Department of Law.
The Department of Justice filed the lawsuit at President Donald Trump’s direction, saying that a Peltola win should not be certified until an investigation can determine if voters were confused. The administration never explained how such an investigation could take place given the secrecy of the ballot.
The case was filed before The New York Times reported on texts and other documents that appeared to show Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting the retired schoolteacher from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg. He was listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot, with no party preference, to distinguish him from the senator, who was identified as a Republican and the incumbent. Dan J. Sullivan has long insisted he ran on his own and Peltola has denied any involvement.
Trump also has demanded that Peltola be prosecuted for the scheme, and federal investigators swarmed into Alaska before Election Day. Tricks involving decoy candidates such as the second Sullivan have been a staple of U.S. politics for decades, and Trump’s allies have also used them, though occasionally the schemes do lead to criminal charges.
It was at least the second time since the Nov. 3 election that the Department of Justice has acted to dismiss one of its high-profile lawsuits interfering in states' handling of their elections.
Just days after the election that saw Democrats flip control of Congress and peel off big wins in races for governor and state legislatures, the Justice Department moved to drop a lawsuit seeking to prevent California officials from counting roughly 20,000 ballots. The Trump administration alleged the ballots belonged to suspected noncitizens, but election officials questioned the validity of the data and said the government's list contained many U.S. citizens.

title: How to keep the peace when grandparents don’t get along
text:
(Aging Untold) — Not every set of grandparents will naturally get along. Different backgrounds, beliefs or old conflicts can create tension, especially during holidays, birthdays and major family events.
There are ways that families can manage those relationships while keeping the child’s well-being at the center.
Keep the child’s well-being first
“That’s the key right there. Keep the child’s well-being at the center,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said. “You can keep your opinions to yourself long enough to get through a birthday party, or a wedding or an event or a holiday.”
Cradduck said children learn from how adults behave around them.
“The only way they’re going to see good role modeling is for you not to go into battle, even if it’s your divorced spouse,” Cradduck said. “You just don’t have to get into family issues right there in front of them.”
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said this is about everyone, including the children.
“Let’s have some peace. Let’s have some grace. Let’s be mature adults. Have some emotional intelligence for heaven’s sake and get along,” Ambrose said.
Set ground rules for tough topics
Grandparents do not have to get along to be good grandparents, aging expert Amy O’Rourke said. If certain conversations create tension, she said, families can agree on topics that are allowed and topics that are not.
“Let’s keep food recipes on the table. Let’s keep birthday parties on the table. But religion, politics, anything that escalates, just keep it off the table,” O’Rourke said. “So set up some ground rules that make it work for everybody.”
Show children what respect looks like
Children notice when adults are not getting along, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
“They know what’s going on and they know that you’re not getting along. They hear the comments,” Rogers said. “One of the greatest gifts that you can give them is to show them what respect looks like when you get along with someone that you don’t agree with.”
Cradduck said differing belief systems can exist side by side.
“Maybe if you would just open up your mind a little bit and listen to somebody else’s belief systems, you might grow to respect that person a little bit more,” she said.
Split holidays and weekends if needed
If conflict continues after families have tried to resolve it, O’Rourke said, separate arrangements can help.
“If it’s just not working, make arrangements that holidays or weekends are separate,” O’Rourke said. “If you’ve done everything you can and it’s not getting any better, then just say OK this weekend’s going to be open for this set, this weekend’s going to be open for another set.”
Grandparents can create smaller, more intimate celebrations if large holiday gatherings feel too big, O’Rourke said. She gave the example of a grandparent telling grandchildren that Christmas with them will be in July.
Ambrose said she would not wait until July to celebrate with family.
“I would just rather get along with everybody and blend our families together,” she said. “When it really counts, when we’re doing deathbed vigils and things like that, we have to support each other.”
Keep the parents’ marriage separate
Cradduck added that grandparents’ disagreements should not affect their children’s marriages.
“Don’t cause your children’s marriage to have issues because you don’t get along with their parents or with who they married,” Cradduck said.
Include others and let families build traditions
Ambrose encouraged families to combine gatherings when possible and include widows and others who may be left out of holiday meals.
“Be inclusive and let’s bring families together,” she said.
Cradduck said to let your children develop their own traditions.
“Allow your children to develop their traditions with their kids,” Cradduck said. “If those traditions are to follow yours, great. That’s fine, let them come on over and let them be part of that, but if they choose to stay away and to have traditions and time with just their children, go over and see them. Don’t exclude yourself because they want to do something different than you always did.”
Cradduck said not to make your angst someone else’s issue.
Key takeaways
- Grandparents don’t have to agree on politics or parenting, but the grandchild should never become the battleground.
- Focus on shared love for the child rather than being right.
- Establish clear ground rules that leave sensitive topics at the door.
- Keep disagreements between grandparents separate from the grandchild’s parents’ marriage.
- Split holidays when keeping the peace matters most.

title: Man in ICU after 7-foot plank flies off pickup, crashes through windshield
text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily/Gray News) - A Phoenix man has spent eight days in intensive care after a 7-foot wood plank flew off a pickup truck and crashed through his windshield on an interstate, his mother said.
Lisa Hughes said her 35-year-old son, DJ Hughes, was driving near Jackrabbit Trail around 1:20 p.m. Nov. 10 when the wood came from a white pickup truck hauling lumber on Interstate 10 in Buckeye.
The plank slid across the hood of his car before striking him in the face, she said.
Family seeks pickup driver
DJ Hughes’ family is looking for the pickup driver and hopes anyone who saw what happened or has information will come forward.
Injuries and surgeries
“Broke every bone in his, from his eyes down. Split his chin in half,” Lisa Hughes said.
She said her son’s skull was fractured in several places. He has undergone three surgeries and will likely need more, she said.
“It’s tough seeing your baby. I know he’s 35, but seeing him laying like that in pain,” she said.
Lisa Hughes described the incident as a near-death experience and said she has thought about what could have happened to someone else.
“Heartbreaking. In a way, I’m thankful that it was him and not a young kid or a young girl,” she said.
Recovery and securing loads
A GoFundMe campaign has been set up to support DJ Hughes’ recovery.
As DJ Hughes faces a long recovery, his mother hopes other drivers will take a moment to make sure their loads are secure.
“Just take the extra two seconds to secure it. It’s not that much time to save a life,” Hughes said.

title: Reporter who witnessed nearly 500 lethal injections says Texas execution was like no other he’s seen
text:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — After covering capital punishment for The Associated Press in Texas since 1983 — and witnessing nearly 500 lethal injections — I’ve become accustomed to a certain routine in the procedure, although I’m reticent to describe any execution as “routine.”
It was 6 p.m. Thursday — a bell from a nearby church tolling the hour — when I and other witnesses climbed the concrete steps into the more than century-old Huntsville Unit of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice. We were led into a reception office for what normally is a very brief period to await the short trek to the death chamber to watch condemned killer Reinaldo Dennes die.
A large state of Texas clock on a wall ticked off the moments. By about 6:20 p.m., we still hadn’t moved.
I knew one of two situations was likely: Dennes was resisting the execution team’s attempts to insert a pair of intravenous needles into his arms, or the execution team was having difficulty finding a suitable vein for the needles.
Thirty minutes later, as we were led into the chamber by corrections officers, Dennes appeared docile. His eyes were closed and his head was pointed toward the ceiling. His white prison garb was not disheveled and no additional restraints were applied to his head, meaning no evidence of a struggle.
Now I’ve seen over the years any number of final statements and reactions from condemned inmates who spoke in foreign languages, prayed, recited poetry, sang, cursed, expressed love, insisted on their innocence or acknowledged their crime and one who even told a joke.
Dennes was like no other.
Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Dennes talked about being “extremely blessed” by the love of “the father” and hoped his family and loved ones “get to know this great gift and great grace of God the father.”
He told the warden: “Go.” Almost immediately as the procedure began, his demeanor changed.
“The pain!” he exclaimed. “Go! Go!”
For nearly three minutes — and standing there furiously scribbling notes, I thought it seemed much longer — Dennes repeatedly moaned.
“Take me father! ... Take me into your arms! ... Take me father!” He occasionally interjected his cries with obscenities, a grunt and then groans. His right leg was “killing me,” he said, likening the sensation to a cramp.
“I don’t think this is normal,” he said at one point.
On that, he was right. I’ve heard inmates say the lethal drug was hot or cold, that they could smell or taste it, or that it hurt. No one I can recall went to such drama as Dennes.
At 7:08 p.m., after being examined by a physician, he was pronounced dead.
Texas prison officials said the execution team had difficulty finding suitable veins. Spokeswoman Amanda Hernandez said after repeated unsuccessful attempts — she couldn’t say how many — the technicians found a vein in Dennes’ left foot and another on the left side of his neck that were receptive to the IV needles.
I couldn’t see. His feet were covered by a sheet and only the right side of his neck was visible to those of us who were witnesses.
The injection sites were in line with the prison system’s procedures, Hernandez added. The alternate sites have been used in previous executions, although the need to do so is relatively rare.
Hernandez also suggested Dennes may have been faking, saying he had been complaining about pain from areas where no injections were attempted.
As a reporter, I’d like to find out the truth about the matter. But there’s no way to know for sure.
Dennes himself, as reporters are known to say, wasn’t available for further comment.

title: Letter: If you didn’t vote, don’t complain about the outcome
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
According to the Washington Post only 49% of the eligible voters voted in the latest midterm election. That was the highest for a midterm election since 1914! A staggering statistic in my opinion.
The top three states were Maine (65.7% turnout), Minnesota (65.2%) and Michigan (63.2%). Better than the national average but still not nearly enough.
How to improve this dismal performance is a good question. Why don’t eligible voters vote particularly since they have registered? I’m sure there are a multitude of reasons. A few might
be working, have no transportation to the polls, be sick, be a grandma or grandpa in a nursing home and have no idea of what day it is let alone for whom to vote, etc.
A possible way to improve the turnout could be to declare a national holiday, which could be expensive for many. Twenty two countries have mandatory voting. Should we? Some countries levy a modest fine for not voting) How would it be collected? If a fine were involved, there would need to be numerous exemptions — see grandma and grandpa above. We could have “no excuse” voting across the board and allow several days — maybe five to seven — after Election Day for mail-in ballots to be counted.
If you didn’t vote, stop complaining!
Tony Wilson
Camden

title: Bernie Kosar marks 1 year since liver transplant
text:
Former NFL QB Bernie Kosar marks 1 year since liver transplant
Bernie Kosar directed nine game-winning drives late in the fourth quarter at Cleveland Stadium during his nine seasons as quarterback of the Browns.
His greatest comeback continued on Wednesday, when he walked into the auditorium at the UH Cleveland Medical Center carrying his granddaughter, Alia Rose Kosar-Beck, 366 days after he had a liver transplant.
Video above: Sam Hartman named as next star on 'The Bachelor'
Kosar not only appears better physically, he is sharper mentally. Kosar and Dr. Zoe Stewart Lewis, chief of transplant and hepatobiliary surgery at University Hospitals, marked the one-year milestone with a news conference.
“I did kind of think that I’d be sitting here a year from now genuinely not feeling as good and maybe trying to put on my actor hat to project real health, happiness and healing. So I’m happily surprised, blessed that it really isn’t any attempt at acting, that it really is working and that I kind of yearn to get out and keep healing and keep getting stronger,” Kosar said.
Kosar revealed in 2024 that he had been diagnosed with cirrhosis of the liver and Parkinson’s disease. He went on the transplant waiting list in July 2024, but was hospitalized multiple times due to life-threatening complications before the transplant occurred on Nov. 17, 2025.
The 62-year-old from Youngstown played in the NFL for 12 seasons after leading the University of Miami to its first national championship during the 1983 season. He grew up rooting for the Browns, who selected him in the 1985 NFL supplemental draft.
Kosar played for the Browns from 1985-93, leading the franchise to three AFC Championship Game appearances (1986, ’87 and ’89), losing each time to the Denver Broncos. Kosar is third in franchise history with 21,904 passing yards.
After being released by the Browns, Kosar joined the Dallas Cowboys for the remainder of the 1993 season and got a Super Bowl ring. He played for the Miami Dolphins from 1994-96.
Kosar's new liver was donated by 21-year-old Bryce Dunlap, who died of a brain injury. Kosar has remained in contact with Dunlap's parents, Adam and Kimberly.
“I have this responsibility to keep carrying forward not only what I’m doing with this second and possibly third or fourth chance in life, but to inspire because of the unfulfilled life that Bryce wasn’t able to have,” Kosar said.
Kosar was also diagnosed with early stage dementia before the transplant. He had quit doing radio and television appearances due to midbrain paralysis and being delayed in his ability to have conversations.
“Now I’m borderline too chatty, but at least I’m able to respond and be cognitively present when I want to interact with people, whether it’s something like this or with your family,” he said.
Video below: How the marching band kept Baltimore's football dreams alive
Kosar's recovery regimen has also included some holistic methods, including partnering with the Crowley Center for Regenerative Biotherapeutics to improve brain health.
Stewart Lewis said the biggest immediate benefit after having a transplant is that patients' brains are working for them again after having thoughts clouded due to end-stage liver disease.
Kosar was taking as many as 50 pills daily after the transplant, but that number has been reduced significantly. He has blood tests every six weeks to make sure the liver is functioning properly.
Stewart Lewis called Kosar a model patient. Well, except for when he made an appearance at a wrestling show in April and entered the ring before striking someone with a steel chair.
“He’s one of the many examples with what happens with a transplant and how it can transform patients’ lives. Not just the physical way how they carry themselves, but it really restores them to their lives and families and to their grandchildren,” Stewart Lewis said.
Kosar, who turns 63 next Wednesday, said he will continue to be an advocate for organ donors while also helping former athletes affected by cognitive issues.
“I think we’ve been able to figure out a great way to give people second chances in life, and I really think it’s my responsibility to pass it forward,” he said. “I like to look into people’s eyes and give them the self-confidence and self-esteem that they really matter and it gives them the confidence to go forward.”

title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year as tech sell-off worsens
text:
S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year as tech sell-off worsens
A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.
The benchmark S&P 500 index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.
The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.
Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.
The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.
AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.
"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."
Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.
Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.
Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.
The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.
Anthropic's share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.
Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
Outside of tech, several companies managed to gain ground despite strong downward pressure on the market. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.
While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.
The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.
Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.
___
AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

title: Aging is normal. Planning ahead keeps it from becoming a crisis
text:
(Aging Untold) — Aging is a normal process, but families often treat it like a crisis when they’re caught off guard.
A fall, hospitalization, new diagnosis or sudden need for care can quickly expose the lack of conversations about money, housing, insurance, caregiving and independence.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing what families can do ahead of time to ease into the care that comes with aging.
Know that aging is going to happen
The first step is accepting that aging and the care that comes with it are ahead, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said.
“The biggest thing is know that it’s going to happen,” O’Rourke said.
She said many people think “you live and then you die.”
Clients often tell her they weren’t expecting a health change. She said she has heard that “thousands and thousands of times.”
“I meet with a client and they said, ‘I just wasn’t expecting this. I feel blindsided. I’m shocked,’” O’Rourke said.
O’Rourke said families should expect a period of time when they are providing care, getting care or both.
“So think ahead. Plan ahead. Money, care, etc.,” O’Rourke said.
Expect some decline
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said people know they will age but are not expecting a decline in health.
“People are looking at, they know they’re going to age. What they’re not expecting is that deterioration in health, and that’s what catches them by surprise,” Rogers said.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck compared it to driving a car with worn tires.
“It’s like driving your car with bald tires and being shocked when you get a flat,” she said. “You have to know that as we age, there’s going to be a certain amount of decline, no matter how well you take care of yourself.”
Planning is what keeps aging from becoming a crisis
Cradduck said aging is a process, not a sudden event.
“There is a declining process. And so we treat this like it’s a crisis, and it’s been happening every day since we were born. It’s not a crisis. So we have to plan or we will be in crisis,” she said.
Healthy aging starts with daily choices
Rogers also spoke to younger viewers.
“You’re going to age, and healthy aging isn’t something that just happens to you. It’s something that you can have a choice in, one day, one habit and one choice at a time,” she said.
Stay in control by letting people know
Cradduck said the way to remain in control and make decisions about your own care is to tell the people around you what you want.
“The only way you get to stay in control, the only way you get to be the one that’s making those decisions, or at least dictating those decisions, is to let people know. So you have to prepare. You have to get your paperwork in place,” she said.
O’Rourke said there are three categories to prepare for: legal, financial and care.
“Think about those categories and what plans you need to be put in place addressing those categories: legal, financial and care,” she said.
Key takeaways
- Expect it. Aging and the care that comes with it will happen, and families can plan for a period of giving and getting care.
- Plan ahead for money and care. Conversations about money, housing, insurance, caregiving and independence are easier before a fall, hospitalization or new diagnosis.
- Some decline is expected. The Aging Untold experts said a certain amount of decline happens no matter how well a person takes care of themselves.
- Healthy aging is built one choice at a time. Dr. Rhea Rogers said it comes down to one day, one habit and one choice at a time.
- Get paperwork in place. Amy O’Rourke said to organize plans in three categories: legal, financial and care.”
- Tell people your wishes. “Sam” Cradduck said letting others know is how you stay in control of decisions about you.

title: Hundreds mourn Fiona the hippo at Cincinnati Zoo as memorial grows
text:
CINCINNATI (WXIX/Gray News) - Hundreds of people visited the Cincinnati Zoo on Thursday night to mourn Fiona, the hippopotamus who died after ingesting a visitor’s hat that accidentally entered her habitat.
Flowers, handmade cards and stuffed animals were left at a growing memorial near a statue of Fiona.
“We love our Cincinnati Zoo. Fiona we will miss you always,” 10-year-old Mikey read from a card.
Fiona’s final days
Fiona ingested the hat on Nov. 8. Her care team worked around the clock in the days that followed, but she died despite their efforts.
“I can’t imagine what her caretakers are going through, everything they’ve done in the past 10 days,” one visitor said.
Fiona’s birth in 2017
Fiona captured the world’s attention in 2017 when she was born six weeks prematurely, weighing 29 pounds.
Millions followed her journey as she grew from a newborn into a hippo who drew families to the zoo.
“I remember when she was born. I remember the fight, all of the nurses from Cincinnati Children’s feeding her around the clock,” another visitor said. “I started buying our family season passes because of Fiona.”
For one parent, Fiona’s story was connected to memories of watching a child grow up.
“I watched him kind of grow with Fiona because I was staying at home with him, and she was born a month later,” the parent said.
Visitors remember Fiona
Another visitor reflected on Fiona’s fight to survive and the impact of her death.
“It’s just so sad with her story and how hard she fought and how long she made it and then to lose her tragically. It’s heartbreaking for us and the whole city,” the visitor said.
“We will miss her very much,” Mikey added.

title: Penobscot County County Commissioners must justify their budget to residents
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I am a third-term councilor and current council chair for the town of Hampden. I also served as an elected member of the Penobscot County Budget Committee and was one of five committee members who voted in opposition to the proposed budget.
In spite of municipal employees and fellow elected officials from Veazie, Carmel, Bradley, Bangor, and Brewer speaking out against the FY27 budget proposal, the Penobscot County Commissioners approved the 23.36% increase, with only District 1 Commissioner Dan Tremble voting no.
Any municipal budget is more than numbers. It should be about building communities. It should tell the story behind the numbers and not be a collection of financial information. It should present choices and practical options, not simply ask for approval of a collection of numbers. It should look beyond the next 12 months. And it should communicate with confidence, humanity, and humility.
Sadly, I believe these maxims were not honored in this budget process. Because county commissioners appear to be insulated from the regular interactions that county select boards and councils face from constituents, they have placed us in the unenviable position of making tough budget choices as we begin our respective budget discussions. This is a disservice to all of us serving at the local level.
I challenge our commissioners, in the interest of transparency, to speak publicly at their respective select boards and council meetings to tell the story behind the numbers and address the questions and concerns that are on the minds of municipal employees, elected officials, and our constituents.
Eric Jarvi
Hampden

title: Kaliyah Sain’s 15 overtime points lead UMaine women’s basketball to win over VCU
text:
Senior forward Kaliyah Sain scored 15 of the University of Maine’s 16 points in overtime to lead the Black Bear women’s basketball team to an 85-80 home win over Virginia Commonwealth University on Thursday night.
Sain, whose 2025-26 season was shortened to just eight games by a knee injury, scored a career-high 29 points as the Black Bears improved to 4-1. VCU fell to 2-2.
Sain scored six unanswered points in overtime to break a 71-71 tie and give UMaine a lead it would never relinquish.
Macy Spencer, last year’s Big South Player of the Year at High Point before transferring to VCU, pulled the Rams within four. But Sain answered with an and-one.
Spencer later hit a 3-pointer, then sank all three foul shots after being fouled on a 3-point attempt to make it 82-80 with nine seconds left. But Sain sewed up the win with two free throws three seconds later.
Sain added three rebounds and a steal to her game-high 29 points.
Lala Woods had 17 points, four rebounds and two assists for the Black Bears, and Maddie Fitzpatrick contributed 15 points, eight rebounds and a game-high eight assists.
Lizzy Gruber had a double-double with 14 points and a game-high 13 rebounds, plus five assists and a game-high four blocked shots. Alvarez had 10 points and four assists.
Spencer paced the Rams with 19 points, eight rebounds, three assists, a blocked shot and a steal. Ada Toribio, Nicole Torresani and Ann Zachariah each had 14 points. Toribio also had five rebounds and five assists, Torresani had six rebounds, and Zachariah had four rebounds and four assists.
UMaine will host Penn at 11:30 a.m. Sunday

title: Augusta Schools students to be released early every Wednesday for rest of academic year
text:
Augusta Schools students to be released early every Wednesday for rest of academic year in effort to reduce teacher burnout
In just over three weeks, the Augusta School Department will begin dismissing students early on Wednesdays in an effort to reduce teacher fatigue and burnout.
The Augusta School Board made the decision Thursday evening to have an early release every Wednesday for the remainder of the academic year, starting Dec. 9.
In a letter to families, Augusta Schools Superintendent Michael Tracy said the School Department has cut 39 positions over the last two years.
"We did this to operate efficiently and to limit the impact on city taxpayers, while still trying to meet the many different needs of our students. It was a thoughtful effort, but we have come to see that the reductions have stretched our staff very thin. Our teachers and staff care deeply about your children, and the demands on them are now leading to real fatigue and burnout," Tracy said in his letter. "Our teachers need our support to do their best work for your child, and the most meaningful way we can give it is by giving them more time: time to plan, to collaborate, and to meet the needs of every student in their classroom."
Tracy said school officials are sharing this information with families now so that they have as much time as possible to make arrangements.
"We understand that this change may create real challenges for some families, especially around work schedules and childcare," the superintendent said. "We appreciate your patience and your partnership, and we believe this change will benefit our students in the long run."

title: Thanksgiving get-togethers can reveal changes in older loved ones
text:
(Aging Untold) — Thanksgiving is a time for families to get together, celebrate and enjoy each other’s company.
But gatherings can reveal challenges that older loved ones are facing that are not apparent over the phone.
Problems not apparent by phone
“Thanksgiving is the number one holiday for families to get together and that spurs a huge crisis in the health care industry,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
She said people who may have been talking to their family every single day suddenly realize that things are not going as well as they thought.
Advice for the visit
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said sometimes family members arrive and find that things are not how they thought they would be with the older person.
“Stay out of judgment because it’s easy to do when you’re scared,” O’Rourke said.
She advises not to plan a lot of things so people can relax and be around each other.
Ambrose also said not to go into a holiday with a big agenda.
“Just observing and enjoying each other so you can kind of self-discover what is really going on and then you can make plans later,” Ambrose said.
Resources
Some older adults might hide that they are struggling from their loved ones. This can stem from a fear of losing independence.

title: Drake Maye doesn’t need surgery, could return this season
text:
Patriots quarterback Drake Maye suffered a fractured right fibula in Sunday’s loss to the Lions, sources told ESPN’s Adam Schefter and Mike Reiss.
Maye didn’t suffer any ligament damage and won’t require surgery, per ESPN. The injury is “expected to sideline him deep into the regular season, if he is able to return this year at all,” per ESPN.
The QB could potentially return late in the season if the 5-5 Patriots are still in playoff contention.
“I think he’s going to be unavailable for the short time and we’ll see how that goes down the road,” head coach Mike Vrabel said this week on Patriots.com. “But we’ll have to prepare to win without Drake in the short term and then how we handle and how we react to that, there’s a lot of things to be able to play for and compete for. Adversity strikes a lot of different teams in the National Football League, and I’m excited to see how we respond to it.”
The Patriots are currently on their bye week. They have winnable games left against the Chargers, Jets and Dolphins, then face four more difficult opponents in the Vikings, Bills, Chiefs and Broncos.
Tommy DeVito replaced Maye in Sunday’s 35-10 loss to the Lions and struggled. If DeVito plays like he did in that contest, then the Patriots have very little chance of being in playoff contention and could struggle even against their weaker opponents. It would not make sense to bring Maye back if the Patriots are out of the playoff race by the time he heals.
The Patriots also have rookie QB Behren Morton on their 53-man roster. Morton, a seventh-round pick out of Texas Tech, has spent all season as the Patriots’ emergency third quarterback.
The Colts announced Friday they are releasing starting quarterback Daniel Jones. The Patriots could elect to claim Jones off waivers by Monday at 4 p.m., though he comes with a $2 million salary and injury guarantees. If Jones clears waivers, he would become a free agent on Monday at 4 p.m.
Jones has experience playing in a system similar to the Patriots’ from his time under former Giants head coach Brian Daboll, an ex-Pats assistant.
The 2019 sixth overall pick has struggled this season while recovering from a torn Achilles. He’s completed just 58.4% of his passes for 1,974 yards with seven touchdowns and a league-leading 13 interceptions. He has just 98 rushing yards and one touchdown on 34 carries.
Ironically, DeVito took over for Jones as the Giants’ starting quarterback in 2023 and 2024.
The Patriots have not brought in any quarterbacks for workouts since Maye went down with his injury. They could elect to sign a quarterback off of another team’s practice squad to fill the third spot on their roster.
The Patriots also could decide to keep Maye on their 53-man roster and not move him to injured reserve. The Patriots get a maximum of eight designations to return from injured reserve, and they’ve already used five of them. They’ll need two more for left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker and wide receiver Romeo Doubs. Running back TreVeyon Henderson, outside linebacker Quintayvious Hutchins, linebacker Khalil Jacobs and safety Dell Pettus are also on injured reserve.

title: Trump administration use of encrypted messaging apps scrutinized by House Democrat
text:
Trump administration use of encrypted messaging apps like Signal scrutinized by House Democrat
A top House Democrat is demanding that multiple government agencies preserve communications created on nongovernment messaging apps and investigate whether any records related to official business have been deleted.
Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee and the panel's incoming chairman, said in a series of nearly identical letters made public on Friday that he was concerned that President Donald Trump's administration was circumventing record-keeping requirements by using apps like Signal that can be configured to automatically delete messages after a certain time period.
Raskin noted in the letters, which were sent to top officials at the FBI, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security, the Bureau of Prisons and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, that the agencies were legally required to preserve all records related to their official business, policies and decisions.
But he said: “There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records, seemingly with the express purpose of circumventing federal record preservation laws. This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials.”
The Maryland Democrat cited as an example a Signal exchange that he said he had obtained between the FBI’s top lawyer and an associate of the Republican president's oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., in which a potentially ongoing healthcare fraud investigation was discussed.
The Associated Press made multiple attempts to get comment from the agencies cited by Raskin but didn't receive any immediate responses.
Signal is an app that can be used for direct messaging and group chats as well as phone and video calls. It uses end-to-end encryption for its messaging and calling services that prevents any third party from viewing conversation content or listening in on calls.
Encrypted messaging apps are increasingly popular with government officials, an Associated Press review from last year found.
Their prevalence was demonstrated in vivid fashion last year when journalist Jeffrey Goldberg revealed that he had been inadvertently added to a Signal group chat of U.S. national security officials coordinating plans for airstrikes.
The White House and the Pentagon have said that disgruntled former employees were spreading false claims about the use of Signal, a commercially available app not authorized to be used to communicate sensitive or classified national defense information.

title: Wisdom Girls Finish Historic Season With First Soccer Gold Ball
text:
The Fall Five and Five No. 1: Wisdom Girls Finally Bring the Gold Ball Home
There really wasn’t much debate for me about what belonged at No. 1.
Wisdom had been here before.
The Lady Pioneers had reached the state championship three previous times, including 2025, when Bangor Christian beat them 3-0.
Then Bangor Christian beat Wisdom twice more during the 2026 regular season. Those were Wisdom’s only two losses all year So when the two teams met again in the state championship, there really couldn’t have been a more fitting way for Wisdom to finally finish the job.
One More Shot
Wisdom came into the state final at 15-2 after scoring goals at an incredible pace all season.
The Lady Pioneers finished the year with 102 goals, but Bangor Christian had been the one team they hadn’t figured out.
For a while, it looked like that might continue.
Bangor Christian led 1-0 at halftime in Presque Isle, leaving Wisdom 30 minutes away from another state-final disappointment.
Then the game changed.
Emma Soucy tied it in the second half, and Ellie Cyr scored twice late to give Wisdom a 3-1 lead.
When Cyr’s second goal went in with just 1:13 remaining, the Gold Ball was finally within reach.
Mikayl Michaud finished with eight saves, and Wisdom walked away with the first girls soccer state championship in school history.
A Long Wait Ends
That championship carried a little more history with it, too.
Wisdom’s girls had not won a state championship in any sport since the girls basketball team brought home the Class D Gold Ball in 1998.
Twenty-eight years later, another Wisdom girls team finally did it.
It was also the fourth state-final appearance for the girls soccer program, following trips in 1997, 2021 and 2025.
The fourth time was the one that ended with the Gold Ball. Wisdom finished 16-2, scored 102 goals and won four straight tournament games to close the season. And after losing three straight meetings with Bangor Christian going back to the 2025 state final, Wisdom finally beat them when there was no next game left.
That’s about as good an ending as you can ask for.
Family, Then Champions
Wisdom High School was named such in 1965. Sixty-one years later, the girls soccer program finally had its first Gold Ball.
And after hearing “1, 2, 3, family” at ever Wisdom game the better part of a year and a half, this group gets to add one more word to it.
Champions.
That’s why Wisdom girls soccer is No. 1 in my five moments that defined the fall of 2026.

title: Woman admits to using Meta glasses to secretly record witnesses in federal drug trial
text:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) — An Alabama woman who was upset about the prosecution of a now-convicted drug “kingpin” admitted Thursday that she used special glasses to secretly record witnesses who testified at the trial in January.
Tierra Shatalia “Badd Twin” Douglas, 35, of Mobile, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to retaliate against a witness.
Recording inside the courthouse
Recording devices are prohibited in federal court.
Douglas admitted that she used Meta glasses inside the courthouse to secretly record three witnesses during the January trial of Glennie “Little Man” McGee and his wife and sister-in-law.
Douglas also admitted that she communicated with co-conspirators to obtain personal information about the witnesses.
Harassment after the trial
Douglas’ written plea agreement indicates her harassment continued for months after the trial. In one case, according to the plea document, she asked ChatGPT in August to make a flyer identifying one of the witnesses as a “snitch.” The chatbot responded that it could not create a flyer accusing a real person of being a confidential informant but could produce an image that clearly was labeled as a fictional character or parody.
One of the witnesses reported that on Jan. 16, he received a video from a friend showing him exiting the courtroom, where he had just testified. Douglas admitted that she disseminated a flyer with a picture of the witness, labeling him as a “snitch.” She also admitted that she sent Discord messages identifying one of his minor children and where the child went to school.
In February, according to the plea agreement, Douglas sent text messages to the same witness. He was identified in her phone contacts as “The Rat.” She sent numerous messages taunting him for testifying.
Sentencing
Confronted with evidence that included internal surveillance video from the courthouse, Douglas confessed, according to the plea document.
A federal judge set Douglas’ sentencing for Feb. 19. The maximum sentence is life in prison, but prosecutors have agreed to recommend leniency.

title: Residents raise concerns after PFAS foam discharged in Owls Head
text:
OWLS HEAD, Maine (WABI) - Some Owls Head residents are calling for a cleanup after firefighting foam discharged near their properties tested positive for PFAS, a group of chemicals often referred to as “forever chemicals.”
A resident, who requested to stay anonymous, sent WABI video showing a South Thomaston firetruck at a hydrant and foam being flushed across the road mixed with water. The incident happened around 7 p.m. Nov. 2 at the intersection of North Shore and Ash Point drives.
The Maine Department of Environmental Protection tested the foam the following day and found PFAS.
Robert Banach, who has lived in his Owls Head home for seven years, said his property was among those affected. He said he learned about the incident the day after it occurred, while working the polls on Election Day, from Town Administrator Rodney Mason.
“The whole town of Owls Head is totally shocked that the South Thomaston Fire Department would come over here in the dark and pull this off,” Banach said. “Why did they have to come to a neighboring town to dispose these cancer-causing PFAS?”
In the South Thomaston Fire Department’s incident report, Chief David Elwell said remnants of PFAS-containing foam were accidentally activated during a truck check. Elwell said Maine Water advised the department to use the hydrant at the Owls Head intersection to refill the truck.
“The urgency of this response was based on the potential consequences of the two foam products mixing within the apparatus plumbing and pump system. Class A and Class B foam products can react when mixed, potentially creating a gel-like substance that can cause significant damage to the pump and associated plumbing,” Elwell wrote in the report. “The department has experienced a similar issue with this apparatus in the past, which resulted in repair costs totaling well into the tens of thousands of dollars.”
Elwell also reported that the DEP determined the amount of PFAS detected did not require cleanup.
But Banach said residents remain concerned: “When a DEP takes a test and says it’s positive, whether it’s a gallon or 1,400 gallons, something’s got to be done.”
Banach said with the Penobscot Bay less than 600 ft from the hydrant, he worries about wildlife, his property value and soil and water quality.
“My wife and I are concerned about a lot of things, not only the wildlife, because the geese come there and feed on the grass, and the deer come at this time of year and eat the apples. And I can’t walk my dogs there. I have to tell my landscape guy to not to cut the grass,” explained Banach. “We’re fortunate that we’re on municipal water. But most of the rest of the people around here are on wells. I’m not going to say it’s going to contaminate their wells, but it doesn’t need to be in the ground.”
Alongside cleanup efforts, Banach said he wanted an apology as an affected homeowner.
In a statement shared Monday with the Midcoast Villager, DEP Deputy Commissioner David Madore said, “DEP is evaluating next steps and determining whether any private drinking water wells in the area may be at risk.”
WABI reached out to the DEP for more information and has not heard back.

title: 82-year-old former history teacher preserves Vermont town’s past
text:
BRADFORD, Vt. (Aging Untold) — Larry Coffin is a former history teacher and, at 82, he continues to tell his town’s story and help preserve its history.
Writing local history
He writes about the history of Bradford and surrounding communities and serves as the curator of the Bradford Historical Society.
Coffin is working on an article about the history of veterinary medicine in the area. It will run in the local paper and on his blog.
“This will be about a 2,000-word article,” Coffin said.
He said he does this because it keeps his brain active.
“To me, is like he’s still teaching,” Carolyn, his wife of 57 years, said.
Teaching career
Coffin’s first classroom was at the old Bradford Academy. He arrived at the school in the fall of 1964 from Plymouth State College.
“I was very wet behind the ears,” Coffin said.
The school closed in 1971 to build Oxbow High School up the road. Coffin continued teaching there for 42 years.
The Bradford Academy building is now the town offices.
Coffin also served as town meeting moderator for 40 years.
“Listen to the word moderation. It’s part of the word moderator,” Coffin said. “I think people trusted me. I tried to be fair.”
Asked whether the building is a second home to him, Coffin said, “In many ways. Yeah.”
Bradford Historical Society
The third floor houses the Bradford Historical Society.
Bradford resident James Wilson, a farmer and blacksmith, made the first globe in the United States.
“Essentially, he was an uneducated person who did a great job,” Coffin said.
The Bradford Historical Society’s collection includes a globe dated 1810.
Asked whether he is the caretaker of Bradford’s history, Coffin said, “Well, I think in many ways that’s right.”

title: Man honored for finding missing toddler 2 miles from home, curled up in bush and shivering
text:
ELOY, AZ (AZFamily/Gray News) - A 2-year-old girl who went missing Tuesday night in Arizona was found 2 miles from her home.
Law enforcement, neighbors and family celebrated her safe return to her home in Eloy Wednesday.
A Pinal County Sheriff’s Office (PCSO) spokesperson said the 2-year-old wandered off from her family’s front yard around 5 p.m. Tuesday. She was wearing only a diaper.
A massive search effort launched, with 75 law enforcement officers, neighbors, and search-and-rescue volunteers helping the department.
After seven hours, around 12:15 a.m. Wednesday, Jay Stewart found the girl 2 miles from her home. She was curled up inside a bush and shivering.
“Can you believe this? That’s where she was at, right in that spot. I was just walking the ditch,” Stewart said in body-camera video released Wednesday evening.
“Are you OK? Are you so cold?” a deputy asked.
“She just jumped up and ran to me. She sounded like it came out of the bush,” Stewart said.
Standing on the side of the road Wednesday afternoon, Stewart became emotional as he thought back to Tuesday night and his part in getting the girl home safely.
“Everybody loved her, and we all did it for the same reason. We wanted her back,” Stewart said.
Stewart described how he found her.
“She was right in the middle of it. And when I picked her up to get my phone out, the bottom of her diaper had pebbles on it, so she had been sitting on pebbles,” he said.
They took the girl to the hospital to be checked out. She was back home Wednesday.
The sheriff’s office gave Stewart a certificate of appreciation for his dedication.

title: Housing markets can vary significantly by ZIP code, analysis finds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A new ConsumerAffairs analysis of more than 6,200 ZIP codes found the strongest buyer’s market among those studied in a Miami, Fla., neighborhood and the strongest seller’s market in a Rochester, N.Y., neighborhood.
Ella Gomes, a media relations specialist at ConsumerAffairs, said the results show how much the market can differ from place to place.
“Trends are shifting towards a buyer’s market nationally, but... the housing market is still so localized,” Gomes said. “You can have one ZIP code in a city that ranks top for buyers and one that ranks as top for sellers.”
Gomes and her team at ConsumerAffairs examined the housing market ZIP code by ZIP code. They used data from April through June of this year.
In the Miami neighborhood, the supply of homes for sale was enough to last more than 15 months at the current sales pace. Nationwide, the supply is about five months.
In the Rochester neighborhood, nearly 94% of homes sold above asking price during the study period.
Gomes said the report points to more housing supply and cooling demand.
“The South and areas like Miami had a significant amount of housing added in recent years. So in some markets, there are now more properties available relative to the number of people looking to buy. And that can translate into more choice and more negotiating room for buyers,” Gomes said. “And Florida is the clearest example of that pattern in our ranking.”
Gomes said the biggest takeaway for buyers is to look beyond national numbers and even citywide averages.
“If you’re shopping in a buyer-friendly zip code, you may have more time to compare properties, negotiate on price, or ask for concessions,” Gomes said. “And in a stronger seller’s market, you may need to be prepared for homes to move quickly and for competition above asking price.”
A buyer-friendly market does not necessarily mean homes are affordable. Even with more room to negotiate, buyers should make sure the home and financing still fit their monthly budget.

title: Another tech outage? Here's what to do
text:
Another tech outage? Here's what to do
From banking delays to a communications meltdown behind last week's nationwide ground stop, experts say don't panic. Here's what else to do in the event of a tech outage.
Another tech outage? Here's what to do
From banking delays to a communications meltdown behind last week's nationwide ground stop, experts say don't panic. Here's what else to do in the event of a tech outage.
From banking blackouts to inaccessible emails, tech outages over the past couple of weeks have disrupted millions of lives nationwide.
And, in an increasingly interconnected world, experts say AI integration could drive more outages. Now, they're stressing the importance of preparing before the next disruption hits.
"We're in an upgrade period right now. AI is changing things rapidly and we're trying to keep up," Chris Steinhauer from the National Cybersecurity Alliance said. "It's kind of like storm preparedness or disaster preparedness where you need to have extra water, extra food."
To stay ready, experts have several recommendations, including:
- Backing up essential files on external hard drives
- Keeping extra cash on hand
- Using backup accounts, like a second bank or cloud service, in case one goes down
- Printing useful phone numbers, medication lists and important documents
Writing down passwords is also a good idea, according to experts, who say the bigger threat today is online.
"Digital crimes don't rely on paper anymore for the most part," James Lee, president of the Identity Theft Resource Center, said. "You don't have to worry if you write down all your passwords. You can keep that in something folded up in your wallet or in your purse or your desk."
When an outage occurs, experts suggest verifying its legitimacy to avoid unnecessary actions like resetting passwords, which could lock you out of your account.
Keeping a record of transactions is also good practice, according to Lee.
"Go ahead and take a screenshot of what you did, so if you need it, when everything's back to normal, you can go to your customer service representative and say, 'Hey, I had this problem. I just want to confirm,'" Lee said.
After an outage, experts also advise reviewing what worked and what didn’t to improve your preparedness for the next disruption.
Scams are another concern during outages, as they tend to spike when people are anxious. Steinhauer warns against trusting incoming messages or calls without verification.
A general rule: trust no one and verify everything. And, if still unsure, look up the company’s official website, app, or phone number before contacting the company.
