title: Biddeford tech school aims to preserve Maine’s marine trades by acquiring Landing School
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Biddeford Regional Center of Technology will acquire The Landing School of Boatbuilding and Design in an effort to keep the tradition of marine trades alive in southern Maine.
The school, which is located in Arundel, announced its closure in May, citing a decline in student enrollment that created financial issues.
The Landing School was set to be auctioned off after a deal with a Massachusetts maritime school fell through, but now it will instead be sold to the Biddeford tech school — a deal that Superintendent Jeremy Ray described as exciting for the district.
“The interest is amazing from students,” he said. “It was such a once-in-a-lifetime deal. The opportunity knocked.”
The Landing School has been operating for nearly 50 years, preparing students for careers in the marine industry, including boatbuilding and marine systems. The school’s website describes it as the oldest operating institution of its kind in the United States.
That legacy will continue as the school becomes a part of BRCOT, Ray said. Students from Sanford Regional Technology Center will also have access to classes.
“We need the next level of people who will be our commercial fishermen,” Ray said. “You have to be able to fix your engine, do your own fiberglass, and understand the aquaculture and science behind it.”
BRCOT Director Paulette Bonneau said The Landing School will give students more opportunities and pathways that reflect their interests.
“Those pathways are also reflecting the workforce needs in the state,” she said.
WHAT COMES NEXT
Programming at the revived Landing School is expected to begin next fall. Several programs, including marine technologies, fiberglass boatbuilding, diesel mechanics, HVAC and veterinary care, have already been approved by the Maine Department of Education.
While the school’s legacy is in boatbuilding and marine trades, Bonneau said a recent survey of Biddeford high school students showed that many are interested in veterinary care.
“But they’re also interested in marine technology and diesel engine repair,” Bonneau said. “A number of the programs that have existed at The Landing School, students have shown interest in.”
The school will also offer commercial fishing and aquaculture courses, likewise after students expressed a desire to study those subjects.
“Those interests collided with our desire for more vocational programming,” Ray said. “The Maine economy is really built around the waterfront.”
While courses will initially only be offered to high school students, Ray hopes to one day expand into middle school and adult education, and professional development workshops.
At full capacity, about 200 students would be able to attend classes at the school.
The Landing School will be funded the same way BRCOT is, Ray added, using the Maine vocational center funding formula.
“Essentially, this will be no different than the vocational programs that we have here on campus,” Ray said. “It’s just an opportunity to offer more programming for students.”
‘THE STARS ALIGNED’
When Ray found out that The Landing School was going to auction, he immediately jumped into action.
He knew marine education would be an asset to BRCOT, which already offers vocational classes in culinary arts, plumbing and heating, automotive technology, and welding.
In order to purchase The Landing School, the Biddeford school district paid off the school’s $890,000 in debt using money from fundraising and excess funding. Ray said local business owners like Jim Godbout and Tim Spang — who own HVAC contracting and home repair businesses, respectively — were instrumental in the purchase.
“I think public schools can always rely on the local generosity of tradespeople in their communities,” he said. “They know how to move quickly, they know how to get it done and they’re passionate about trades.”
For Ray, keeping the mission of The Landing School — to train the next generation of boatbuilders and marine workers — alive and well is personal.
“I grew up in a fishing town. My grandfather loved nothing more than having lobster boats built,” Ray said. “It just means a little something extra.”
While Biddeford Regional Technology Center will be tacked on, The Landing School will keep its name.
The name is important to the Arundel community, Ray said: It carries decades of tradition and a legacy that the Biddeford school district is proud to inherit.
“I truly get to be captain of the ship a little bit,” Ray said.

title: Trump speaks after meeting with Xi, Putin at APEC summit
text:
SHENZHEN, China (AP) — Results matter in the international arena, but so do optics.
This week’s high-level meetings in China’s tech hub gave President Xi Jinping a win, reinforcing his image as a central player in global diplomacy and demonstrating the nation’s superpower status.
As host of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday and Thursday, Xi welcomed the leaders of 21 economies that account for about 60% of global economic activity. He also convened the first formal gathering of the three biggest nuclear powers: the United States, Russia and China.
“History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace, and when they engage in confrontation the world is thrown into turmoil,” Xi said Thursday before starting closed-door discussions with U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“Our three countries should set an example by working together to address global challenges, jointly safeguard world peace and stability and make greater contributions to human progress,” he added.
Summit images were a diplomatic win despite lack of substance
Although the trilateral meeting produced no major breakthroughs, the image of Xi, Trump and Putin seated at an enormous round table with Xi at the center will become part of diplomatic history.
“For most, the image was a suggestion that the world increasingly revolves around Beijing’s power and preferences,” Rush Doshi, director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in an article. “And for U.S. allies in particular, it was unsettling because it suggested that Washington will prioritize engagement with the other great powers over that with its own partners.”
“Xi’s clearest diplomatic gain in Shenzhen was bringing Trump and Putin to the same table,” said Yaqi Li, a Chinese foreign policy researcher at Singapore’s ISEAS — Yusof Ishak Institute.
China has positioned itself as a force for global stability in recent years. Xi started the meeting with Trump and Putin with a reminder of how the three countries fought together in World War II.
“History is the best textbook,” Xi said, presenting the talks as a way to push for peace for humanity. “We must remember history, learn from it and work together to shape the future.”
The meeting resulted in a joint declaration that was light on commitments and did not tackle major issues in a substantive way.
“They’re using this opportunity … to highlight that China is a great power, and they’re in a different status relative to other countries,” said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.
On Friday, meetings between Xi and other foreign leaders continued. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim congratulated him.
“You were successful in handling President Trump and President Putin together. That takes only President Xi, I don’t know anyone else who can do that,” he said.
Relationship with US appears stable but issues remain
Xi and Trump held their third meeting this year, highlighting the personal rapport they have built that both men said was important to the bilateral relationship between their nations. China’s government highlighted the “constructive strategic stability” of the relationship, while Xi commended the U.S. president for his role.
“The efforts you have made are there for all to see and will go down in history,” Xi told Trump.
There were no announcements about existing trade tensions between the countries, such as U.S. complaints that China has not fulfilled its commitment to buy from U.S. farmers and export more rare earth materials. Nor were there announcements about the Board of Trade and the expected framework to allow trade in nonsensitive goods worth $30 billion on each side.
It was unclear if officials taking part in a diplomatic channel to discuss artificial intelligence issues met in Shenzhen, said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
However, “AI seems to be the one area where some progress has been made, with China affirming its concerns about safety and security and welcoming bilateral work,” Cutler said.
Whether the personal rapport between Xi and Trump can persist will be tested soon, according to Craig Singleton, senior fellow and senior director of the China Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
“Xi treated Trump with respect in Shenzhen. He will test his resolve in Miami next month, when the bill for Beijing’s trade commitments comes due,” Singleton said in an email.

title: Volunteers finish 18-year restoration of Greenville Junction Depot
text:
GREENVILLE, Maine (WABI) - After 18 years of work, volunteers have finished restoring a historic depot in Greenville Junction. They are now preparing for the CPKC Holiday Train’s scheduled stop there Sunday night.
Depot restoration
Not long ago, the future of the building was uncertain.
“It was falling down. Raccoons were living in it, vagrants. When we came in here, it was pretty rotten,” said Cheri Goodspeed, secretary of Greenville Junction Depot Friends.
The nonprofit group spent 18 years restoring the depot. Goodspeed said the group raised the entire cost of the $1.3 million project. The work was made possible by volunteer hours.
The group celebrated the completed restoration in October.
“Now we can just go to having fun. Like we’re thinking maybe have line dances and movies and things like that,” Goodspeed said.
Holiday Train stop
The CPKC Holiday Train is scheduled to stop at the depot Sunday from 9 to 9:30 p.m.
Goodspeed said last year’s stop drew nearly 5,000 people and brought in almost $7,000 and several truckloads of food for local pantries.
“It gets people in our building and gets people to see all the hard work that we’ve done over the past 18 years. But most importantly we’re servicing the Greenville area with tons and tons of food and money to keep everybody going through the winter months,” Goodspeed said.
The event at the depot on Rockwood Road is free. People are encouraged to bring a nonperishable food donation.

title: Cross Country Impresses in Postseason, Earning At-Large Bids to NCAA Division III Championships
text:
The men’s and women’s cross country teams kicked off their postseasons at the NESCAC Championships on Saturday, Oct. 31, which were hosted by Middlebury College.
The women’s squad finished fourth out of eleven teams outrunning Connecticut College, Wesleyan, Colby, Bowdoin, Amherst, Trinity and Hamilton. Charlotte Crum ‘30 was the Bobcats’ top finisher on the women’s side coming in 12th out of 153 competitors. The men’s team also had a strong showing finishing in sixth place ahead of conference rivals Bowdoin, Hamilton, Colby, Connecticut College and Trinity. Max Hoffman ‘28 led the men’s team finishing 12th out of 155 runners.
Both teams carried this momentum with them to the NCAA Northeast Regionals in South Portland, Maine on Saturday, Nov. 14. The women’s team was once again led by Crum who came in first out of a field of 216 runners. When asked to reflect on her victory, Crum said, “It showed me that I can push my boundaries and proved that all the hard work my team and I have put in this season did make a difference.” She went on to add, “I was really proud of myself but more importantly my team and everyone who came to support us that day.”
Co-captain Leah White ‘27 also finished inside the top ten at regionals posting a sixth place finish. Zoe McCullough ‘30 trailed just behind White coming in tenth place overall. These results propelled the women’s team to a third place standing on the leaderboard, helping them earn an at-large bid to the NCAA Division III Championships, which are being held in Northfield, Minnesota at Carleton College on Saturday, Nov. 21.
When asked to reflect on the team’s success this season co-captain Gwen Anderson ‘27 said, “In August, we decided our team motto was going to be ‘that’s love’ and all throughout the season that message has carried through in every moment. In our hardest workouts and most important races, everyone was working hard for each other and fighting to make our goals a reality.”
White added, “When I think of the goals we set for ourselves this season and the way we have worked toward them, the possibility of us not competing on the big stage this weekend seems impossible.” The women’s race at the NCAA Championships will begin at 1 p.m. EST and can be watched on the live feed.
The men’s team also put on a stellar performance at regionals placing fourth in a field of 31 teams. They too received an at-large bid to the NCAA Division III Championships. On the individual side, Hoffman yet again led the Bobcats this time finishing eighth out of 214 runners. Other notable top twenty finishes from the men’s race included Nate Roberts ‘28 who came in 18th place and Nathaniel Aronson ‘27 who came in 19th place. Their NCAA Championship race will begin at 2 p.m. EST and can also be watched via the live feed.
The Bobcats have set a high bar for themselves at the NCAA Championships. Hoffman expressed, “I feel confident going into nationals and my goals are All-American, which is top 40, as an individual, and top 20 as a team.” Aronson also shared his thoughts on qualifying for the NCAA Championships with The Bates Student remarking, “Even though we are all ecstatic to have made it to the championship, we are coming into the meet ranked 21st and are hoping to have an incredible team performance. This team is the strongest it’s ever been, and I’m really pumped to see what we can do on Saturday.”
The Bobcats will compete on the biggest stage in Division III collegiate running tomorrow Saturday, Nov. 21 at 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. respectively.

title: Treasury secretary says no further restrictions are needed for Nvidia chip exports to China
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that no further restrictions on the sale of older Nvidia chips to China are needed following the Trump administration’s move earlier this week to block China’s remote access to the latest semiconductors.
The ability of Chinese tech firms to access Nvidia’s technology came under scrutiny after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down amid allegations of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that uses advanced chips to generate computing power that Chinese firms access remotely.
“The proper chip restrictions are in place,” Bessent said in an interview with CNBC after returning from a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump. “And the remote access has been curtailed.”
Bessent’s comments came a day after the House Foreign Affairs Committee released details of the Commerce Department’s approval of the sales of more than 850,000 chips from Nvidia and its competitor AMD to Chinese companies. The Pentagon has identified some of those companies as having ties to the Chinese military.
The report tracked applications from Nvidia to sell its H200 chips — one of its more powerful products, though not the most advanced — and AMD’s applications to sell its roughly comparable MI325X chip to companies that are either located or headquartered in China, or entities with parent companies based in China.
The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security approved the export, re-export, or transfer of 879,868 of these chips to companies with Chinese ties across 21 license applications as of May 11, 2026, the report said. Nvidia and AMD had requested to sell a cumulative total of more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese-tied companies across those applications, per the report.
The approvals, which don’t necessarily indicate completed sales, included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent and its subsidiaries, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, according to the report. Each of those companies has been identified by the Defense Department as having ties to the Chinese military.
The report shows the Commerce Department has a “long track record of transparency with Congress about licensing activity for the H200 and equivalent chips, including both approvals and rejections,” a spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security said in a statement Friday.
The spokesperson said the Commerce Department’s approach to H200 licensing is based on a rule in the Federal Register that was published in January. The rule imposes “significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial,” the spokesperson said.
An Nvidia spokesperson said in a statement Friday that the “limited shipments we made under the H200 program were legal and authorized” by the BIS. “The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes,” the company spokesperson said.
Earlier this week, Nvidia said it was no longer shipping H200 chips to China. The spokesperson said Friday that shipments had stopped despite prior approvals.
AMD said it complies with U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains “rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations” in a statement from a spokesperson Friday. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity,” the spokesperson said.
Chinese technology firms have been bracing for impacts on their ambitious AI development plans as scrutiny mounts on export controls in the U.S.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under intense scrutiny himself in the wake of the turmoil following the Huang affair. Last week, Bessent said he was frustrated with the Commerce Department’s delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed International, which is under investigation by the U.S. for potentially diverting restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. A former executive at the company who allegedly had an affair with Huang was reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being a spy for China.
In an unusually public rebuke of a fellow Cabinet member, Bessent said his department wanted to place export controls on Megaspeed, but Commerce was in charge of the matter.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump said he has “not lost confidence” in Lutnick. Calling him a “different kind of guy,” Trump said he “has a natural business instinct” and has “done a very good job.”
___
Huamani reported from Los Angeles. Associated Press writer Meg Kinnard contributed from Columbia, South Carolina.

title: Senate backs bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Senate backs bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs
The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation's energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.
The legislation's sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.
The vote sends the bill to the House and is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.
The bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.
Trump urged approval of the Senate bill, calling it a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE" in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, "lowering Energy Costs for American Families," Trump wrote.
Industry groups back bill, but environmentalists fear it would weaken safeguards
Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.
However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.
"Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.," said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.
Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill "a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America" and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.
Democrats push for amendments
A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands.
Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.
"Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn't tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that," Merkley said.
Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project's possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.
"In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build," said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. "Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years" as they await approval by the federal government.
"Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box" driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said.
The bill's four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation.
The four senators, who lead the chamber's energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.
Co-sponsor calls bill 'the floor, not the ceiling' for legislative action on climate
Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by longtime allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure is "the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations," adding that he hopes "to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities" over the next two years.
But Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill has been rushed and its impacts are not fully considered.
Cantwell, who met Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation's bodies of water, land and wildlife.
"Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process" to debate and amend the bill, she said. "Don't sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it's currently drafted, is not the answer."
Oneida Nation Vice Chairman Jameson Wilson said the bill threatens the tribe's ability to protect its sacred spaces, ancestors, traditional ceremonies and culture. "Any effort to accelerate development must strengthen, not diminish and erode tribal sovereignty and meaningful consultation," he said.
Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who led the agency in the Biden administration, said she understands those concerns, but believes recent changes by bill sponsors strengthen protections for tribal consultation and restore important state authority over water quality.
"A bigger Democratic majority can write a stronger bill," Granholm wrote in a social media post. "But it would still need this president's signature."
Lawmakers "have a bipartisan deal in front of us today that can get more clean power onto the grid and protect ratepayers," she said, urging them to take the opportunity.
___
Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, Rhode Island.

title: Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain
text:
Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain
Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour, as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital.
And once it began, he moaned repeatedly about pain, groaned several times and asked God to take him away from the pain. Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately.
Related video at the top: Florida seeks death penalty for quadruple murder in Brevard County
The execution followed renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee’s failed execution in September of Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.
Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, was the second person put to death in the country on the day, after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.
Dennes gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years “knowing the love of the father.” Then he told the warden: “Go, warden!”
Almost immediately he exclaimed: “The pain! Go! Go!” He uttered an expletive and implored “the father” to “take this pain.” “Let me go, father,” he said again and again. “Let me go. … I’m here. I’ve been your son all these years.”
Then he shouted: “My right leg is killing me!” and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, “I don’t think this is normal. Take me, father. Don’t let me suffer like this. C’mon.”
After three loud groans, Dennes began snoring sounds — eight of them — that progressively got quieter before a final loud snore. Then he began breathing quietly, about a dozen breaths, also getting progressively less pronounced.
The procedure was completed at 7:07 p.m., 63 minutes after he was strapped to the gurney. A minute later, after being examined by a physician, Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. at the penitentiary in Huntsville.
Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately. Spokesperson Amanda Hernandez acknowledged a number of unsuccessful attempts to find a suitable vein before the execution team managed to insert the needles in Dennes’ left foot and on the left side of his neck.
She did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but said the sites ultimately used were in accordance with the state’s procedures.
Hernandez also suggested that Dennes may have been exaggerating the pain, saying he began complaining before the drugs began to flow and also of pain in places where there was no IV.
Asked if he was faking, she replied, “I think, yeah, there were allegations. ... There was nothing abnormal on our part.”
“This isn’t the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It’s also not the first time we’ve had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately,” Hernandez said.
Witness Janice Copeland's husband, David, was a security guard shot during the robbery. He survived his wounds and died five years ago.
“David always felt Reinaldo would outlive him. Unfortunately he was right,” she said Thursday. “Finally after 30 years, justice has been served.”
Earlier in the day Florida carried out its execution of Overton, 71, who was convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband, Susan and Michael MacIvor, during a home invasion.
Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple’s home and attacking them, saying, “I never killed anyone.”
Florida has now carried out more than half the nation’s 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors.
DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who wait decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Florida still plans two more executions, in December.
Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.
The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population.
Florida husband and wife were strangled
In Florida, Overton was strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the death chamber curtain lifted at 6 p.m.
“I’ve never sexually assaulted anyone. I never killed anyone,” Overton said, denying ever having been in the MacIvors’ home or gated community. “I didn’t kill the MacIvors.”
The injection began immediately afterward with Overton panting and breathing heavily before all movement ceased. A warden then shook Overton and shouted his name without answer before a medic declared him dead.
The MacIvors' bodies were found in their Tavernier, Florida, home on Aug. 22, 1991, court records show. Autopsies determined they were strangled and that Susan MacIvor, eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.
Investigators collected DNA evidence but found no match with the state's database. But when Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors' home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996, his DNA sample matched one from the MacIvors' home.
Overton was subsequently convicted in 1999 of two first-degree murder counts and received a death sentence for each.
Michael MacIvor’s sister, two brothers and cousin witnessed the execution. The man's sister, Sharon MacIvor, said watching Overton die gave her a sense of relief but not satisfaction.
“One of the hardest things I have ever had to hear was how my brother Michael fought to stay alive,” Sharon MacIvor said. “Michael was my little brother. He was loved, he had a family, and he had a lifetime ahead of him.”
Diamonds missing in jeweler's killing were never recovered
Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes arranged for her to open the building’s back door after hours, allowing Dennes and his brother entry the night of the shooting. Records showed she also distracted the security guard at Dennes’ request.
The guard was shot twice but recovered and identified Dennes as his assailant.
Police found the jeweler's body in his office, but his safe was empty with no sign of the diamonds or some $200,000 in cash he supposedly kept there, court filings indicated. Authorities said the diamonds were never located.
Dennes’ attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove he killed Szucs.
A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.
___
Stengle reported from Dallas, and Fischer from Raiford, Florida.

title: Police find puppy in tied-up trash bag at Massachusetts apartment complex dumpster
text:
Police find puppy in tied-up trash bag at Massachusetts apartment complex dumpster
Criminal charges are pending after a puppy was found inside a trash bag in a dumpster outside a Massachusetts apartment complex.
Body camera video from a Rutland police officer showed the small puppy being removed from the dumpster.
See the body camera video in the player above.
According to police, someone reported that they heard the puppy's cries before alerting officers.
The Shih Tzu, which was found in a tied-up bag, was turned over to animal control.
Detective Jacob Deschamps said an officer and the chief used trial and error and focused on a specific black bag in the search for the dog.
"It was tied shut, but they were able to rip it open and find the small puppy," Deschamps said. "We actually found some children's homework, and with the help of the school, we were able to figure out who the child was because they had written their name on there, and from there we were able to find out who the parents were, and where they lived."
Police said a search warrant for a nearby residence was issued. Officers found five additional puppies, plus the puppies' mother. The suspect, who is the owner of the dogs, surrendered all the animals to police.
The puppy is happy and healthy, police said.
"This is just a reminder how vulnerable they are, and how much they rely on us," Deschamps said. "It was really heartbreaking to see video and I'm just happy they found a good home."
The suspect, who has not been identified, will face animal cruelty charges.

title: Capitol Christmas tree arrives in Washington after 2,500-mile journey
text:
Capitol Christmas tree arrives in Washington after 2,500-mile journey
Crews hoisted the 76-foot tree on Capitol grounds, marking another festive season in the nation's capital.
Capitol Christmas tree arrives in Washington after 2,500-mile journey
Crews hoisted the 76-foot tree on Capitol grounds, marking another festive season in the nation's capital.
The holiday season is officially underway in Washington. On Friday morning, crews hoisted the Capitol Christmas tree on the West Front Lawn of the Capitol, continuing a tradition that has lasted more than six decades.
This year’s tree is a 76-foot-tall and 30-foot-wide Engelmann spruce from the Nez Perce-Clearwater National Forest in Idaho.
"After being harvested on October 24, this tree on this beautiful truck made the 2500-mile journey, making stops in communities all across the country," Capitol Grounds and Arboretum Director Jim Kaufmann said. "We look forward to seeing the tree lit up in all its splendor and we're glad to have a beautiful tree that Idahoans and all Americans can be proud of."
The tree will be decorated with around 5,000 handmade ornaments and 6,000 LED lights, and it will also get a four-foot-tall star adorning its top.
Once an official lighting ceremony takes place, the tree will be lit from dusk until 11 p.m. through January 2027.

title: Trump defends calling Putin a friend but says he ‘can’t speak’ to whether he’s a friend to the US
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has defended calling Russian President Vladimir Putin a friend but says he “can’t speak” to whether the Russian leader is a friend to the U.S.
Trump raised eyebrows in China days ago with his warm welcome and repeated references to his Russian counterpart as his “friend,” and he did not back away from that in the briefing room on Friday.
The Republican president appeared to sidestep a question about whether he sees Putin as a friend to the United States.
“I can’t speak to America,” he said, without expounding before he shifted to his “very good” personal relationship with Putin and repeated his longstanding grievances over the extended federal probe into Russian attempts to influence U.S. voters in the 2016 presidential election.
“I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship (with),” Trump said. “It’s actually very good.”
Trump broadly praised Putin and China’s Xi Jinping after bilateral and trilateral meetings among the trio.
Putin, Trump insisted, would “love to end the war” in Ukraine but said both Putin and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy are “stuck in it.”
“You have two guys that don’t know how to end it,” he said. “We’re trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other.”
Trump insisted his relationships with the other world leaders is a key to an eventual peace.
“You know, you’re very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries,” he said.

title: 16-year-old boy accused of killing his twin brother, police say
text:
(Gray News) - A 16-year-old is accused of killing his twin brother in Washington, D.C., according to authorities.
Jamari Young was charged as an adult with second-degree murder in connection with the death of his twin, Jabrell Young, the Metropolitan Police Department said.
Jabrell died after he was shot on the morning of Oct. 25 on 46th Street Northeast, police said. Jamari turned himself in at a police station on Nov. 18.
Jamari appeared in court Thursday and was held without bond, 7News reported.
The judge said he did not believe Jamari intended to kill his brother but found probable cause for a second-degree murder charge, WJLA reported.
The teens’ mother, Chantel Poe, told police the brothers had been “tussling” after someone was heard yelling, “stop touching my stuff.”
Poe said she tried to separate them, but “the joint [gun] came up and it went off,” according to the affidavit. She told police the gun was in Jamari’s hand.
“I didn’t mean to, it just went off, I didn’t mean to, I’m sorry Ma,” Jamari said afterward, according to the affidavit.
Poe described the brothers as “thick as thieves” and pointed to their close relationship in saying the shooting was an accident.

title: Trump warns U.S. companies against building data centers overseas
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump warned U.S. companies that want to build data centers overseas that they will face what he called a “tremendous tax.”
Data centers have become one of the biggest hot-button issues in the country. Trump gave his support to data centers at a Friday press conference, amid protests against construction in many communities around the country.
“We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they’re great places. They have energy, and they have everything. They’re tremendous assets,” Trump said.
Trump also said he opposes any U.S. company building a data center overseas that uses AI chips.
“They can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them,” Trump said.
Numerous American-based tech companies, including Microsoft, Amazon and Oracle, have already built data centers in foreign countries. It is not clear if the president’s tax threat applies to them.

title: How did a hat get into Fiona’s habitat, and why wasn’t surgery an option?
text:
CINCINNATI (AP) — Fiona, the hippo whose premature birth and fight for survival at the Cincinnati Zoo turned her into a global sensation nearly a decade ago, died Thursday from complications after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure. She was 9 years old.
Fiona swallowed the hat about 12 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air. A ceiling fan caught and deflected the hat into the hippo enclosure through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows.
It was an accident, zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley said.
Before Fiona died, Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health, said veterinarians had sedated her twice to evaluate her condition.
An ultrasound on Tuesday showed some bunching of her intestines, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy using a 9-foot (2.7-meter) scope but were unable to detect anything, he said.
The Association of Zoos and Aquariums, the accrediting body for facilities, said in a statement Thursday that the Cincinnati Zoo provided “extraordinary 24/7 care for Fiona throughout this heartbreaking event.”
Surgery would have been challenging
Surgery would have been a major logistical challenge — multiple incisions would have been needed during a very long surgery, as hippos are notoriously difficult to anesthetize and have thick skin, said Jack Kottwitz, assistant professor at Michigan State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine.
The hat and its blend of fibers posed a particular danger despite its relatively small size.
Experts said hippos have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants, and the system makes for a very large gastrointestinal tract through which anything would have to travel.
Jan Hawkins, doctor of veterinary medicine at North Carolina State University, said Fiona’s situation was difficult because it would have been hard to tell where in her body the hat was.
“You can’t do the normal imaging and things that you can do in some of the smaller animals, or even horses,” Hawkins said.
Zoos around the world have warned for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats. Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.

title: Fiona the hippo's best moments: Remembering a global icon
text:
Fiona the hippo's best moments: Remembering a global icon
Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s cherished hippo who captured hearts worldwide, has died following a freak accident involving a knit cap thrown into her enclosure.
Fiona was born in 2017, arriving as a 29-pound preemie — 25 pounds lighter than any recorded birth for her species — and quickly became a symbol of hope and joy for animal lovers.
Her birth came just eight months after the death of Harambe the gorilla, offering a much-needed emotional lift to the zoo and its visitors. Millions watched online as Fiona learned to swim, reunited with her mother, Bibi, and father, Henry, and grew into an inspirational figure.
She quickly became not just a Cincinnati icon but an animal beloved by the world.
Fiona’s influence extended beyond the zoo. Statues of her are displayed around Cincinnati, and she inspired an annual Holiday Nutcracker performance. Graeter’s Ice Cream even created special orders in her honor. Her habitat became a place for visitors to escape heavy topics, offering moments of joy and distraction.
On Nov. 8, a child tossed a knit cap into the air, and an overhead fan flung it into Fiona’s enclosure. Fiona ingested the cap and was unable to pass it, leading to her illness. Zoo workers and veterinarians cared for her around the clock, trying everything they could, but their efforts were not enough.
For Fiona fans, this loss will feel like a painful punch to the heart.
Fiona, who would have turned 10 in January, will be remembered as a “perfect 10 in personality and presence” during a time when she was needed most.

title: Florida, Texas execute 2 men on same day; Florida sets yearly record
text:
RAIFORD, Fla. (AP) — Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year Thursday on a man convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion, while Texas put to death a man for a jeweler’s killing during a $3.6-million diamond heist.
Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. EST following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple’s home and attacking them, saying, “I never killed anyone.”
Soon after, Texas conducted the day’s second execution. Reinaldo Dennes, 70, became the ninth Texas inmate executed this year, receiving a lethal injection at the penitentiary in Huntsville. He was pronounced dad at 7:08 p.m. CST. The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population.
Overton was convicted of killing Michael and Susan MacIvor and their unborn child during an August 1991 break-in at their Florida Keys home. Dennes was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996.
Florida has now carried out more than half of the nation’s 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. The executions follow renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike in September.
DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who’ve waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. After a record-setting Thursday, Florida is planning two more executions in December.
Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.
Florida husband and wife were strangled
In Florida, Overton was strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the death chamber curtain lifted at 6 p.m.
“I’ve never sexually assaulted anyone. I never killed anyone,” Overton said, denying ever having been in the MacIvors’ home or gated community. “I didn’t kill the MacIvors.”
The injection began immediately afterward with Overton panting and breathing heavily before all movement ceased. A warden then shook Overton and shouted his name without answer before a medic declared the inmate dead.
The MacIvors’ bodies were found in their Tavernier, Florida, home on Aug. 22, 1991, court records show. Autopsies determined they were strangled and that Susan MacIvor, eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.
Investigators collected DNA evidence but found no match with the state’s database. But when Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors’ home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996, his DNA sample matched one from the MacIvors’ home.
Overton was subsequently convicted in 1999 of two first-degree murder counts and received a death sentence for each.
Michael MacIvor’s sister, two brothers and cousin witnessed the execution. The man’s sister, Sharon MacIvor, said watching Overton die gave her a sense of relief but not satisfaction.
“One of the hardest things I have ever had to hear was how my brother Michael fought to stay alive,” Sharon MacIvor said. “Michael was my little brother. He was loved, he had a family, and he had a lifetime ahead of him.”
Diamonds missing in jeweler’s killing were never recovered
Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes arranged for her to open the building’s back door after hours, allowing Dennes and his brother entry the night of the shooting. Records showed she also distracted the security guard at Dennes’ request.
The guard was shot twice but recovered and identified Dennes as his assailant.
Police found the jeweler’s body in his office, but his safe was empty with no sign of the diamonds or some $200,000 in cash he supposedly kept there, court filings indicated. Authorities said the diamonds were never located.
Dennes’ attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove he killed Szucs.
A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.
___
Corrects that the failed Tennessee execution was in September, not October.
___
Stengle contributed to this report from Dallas and Graczyk from Huntsville, Texas.

title: UMaine men’s basketball team held in lockdown after active shooter reported on Quinnipiac campus

After UMaine’s 69-67 win at Quinnipiac on Thursday night, the team was held in lockdown and told to shelter in place for nearly two hours immediately following the game.
Reports spread across social media of an alleged active shooter on the campus of Quinnipiac.
The lockdown at the York Campus (where Quinnipiac basketball’s M&T Bank Arena is located) was lifted around 10:45 p.m. The University of Maine men’s basketball team safely left campus.
“Following our game this evening, our team was required to shelter in place for approximately two hours due to a lockdown on the Quinnipiac campus. The lockdown has been safely lifted and we have safely left the campus,” the team posted on X on Thursday night.

title: Biden's fault? Trump's fault? Fact-checking the partisan blame game about the FAA ground stop
text:
Biden's fault? Trump's fault? Fact-checking the partisan blame game about the FAA ground stop
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
As airlines work to recover from the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, Democrats and Republicans are blaming each other for the interruption.
The rare nationwide freeze snarled air travel across the country. Trump administration officials have said a routine router upgrade — part of the FAA's system changes — overloaded the older system. The agency announced it was pausing router installation while it investigates the outage.
President Donald Trump, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and conservative critics accused former President Joe Biden's administration of mismanaging funds and failing to prioritize aviation infrastructure upgrades.
Democrats countered that the Trump administration was deflecting responsibility for a situation that occurred after nearly two years of uniform Republican control of the federal government, and after Congress had allocated billions of dollars for FAA upgrades.
However, blaming either political party ignores the full context. There's a paper trail dating back more than two decades documenting delays and other problems with modernizing the nation’s air traffic communications system — and these occurred during presidencies and Congresses controlled by both parties.
"Modernization programs can take years to move from planning and procurement through testing and deployment," said Mike O'Donnell, a former senior FAA official who is now a consultant and an adjunct professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Frequent turnover in leadership makes it hard to maintain priorities and accountability across programs, he said.
Trump says Biden administration misspent money, made things worse
About a day after the ground stop was lifted, Trump said the Biden administration's FAA was a "disaster."
"Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began," Trump wrote Nov. 15 on Truth Social. He told reporters that Biden's transportation secretary, Pete Buttigieg, "totally ruined it." Buttigieg pushed back on that criticism.
"The Democrats really — it's very old — but what they did really set back the system a long way," Trump said.
When PolitiFact contacted the White House for further details, a spokesperson referred us back to the president's comments.
Available public records, including audits and FAA investigations, do not substantiate Trump's claims that the Biden administration made the system worse or improperly wired copper into fiber.
This isn't the first time Trump has said the Biden administration wasted money in its FAA upgrade. After a Cabinet meeting in July 2025, he said the administration had hundreds of contractors hooking "copper into fiber, into steel" and other systems, spending "billions of dollars" that worsened things.
To attribute the outage to the Biden administration, O'Donnell said, "I'd want to see evidence that a specific decision affected the system that failed, its safeguards, or the FAA's ability to respond." That evidence hasn't surfaced, he said.
At the same 2025 Cabinet meeting, Duffy said Biden's FAA signed a 15-year contract with an American company "to fix the copper to fiber," and that "the system is failing today."
His comments referred to the agency's long-running initiative to replace its 1980s-era telecommunications network with a modern system, which includes swapping aging copper cables across thousands of facilities with fiber-optic wires.
A spokesperson for Buttigieg's political action committee, Win the Era, pointed PolitiFact to a 2023 contract the FAA signed with telecommunications company Verizon to lead the system's upgrade. The deal was a 15-year agreement valued at up to $2.4 billion, with the last five years structured as optional one-year renewals for maintenance and support.
The FAA under Trump restructured the contract in August, switching to AT&T as the lead project manager to speed up the system's deployment. Verizon assumed a supporting role.
The revamped contract started with an initial $74.3 million planning and development order, butthe FAA said it anticipates it to rise to a "multi-billion" contract for "a period of performance of up to 15 years." It's unclear how much money was already spent from the initial contract, or how much this one will cost once completed.
A long-running saga of delays
FAA's modernization struggles have spanned several Democratic and Republican administrations and Congresses, with aviation specialists noting issues stemming from the early 2000s, during President George W. Bush's first term.
- 2006: A Transportation Department inspector general report, published four years into an FAA upgrade, said the effort was "falling behind schedule" and was "not likely to be completed on time."
- 2008: A follow-up report again found that the upgrade wouldn't be completed on time, saying the "FAA will have to maintain existing equipment much longer than expected."
- 2010: In a letter to Congress, the inspector general's office reported its findings about a 2009 communications outage. It concluded that the FAA and Harris — the predecessor company of L3Harris, the contractor Duffy blamed for the recent outage — "acknowledged that there is still a risk of critical outages" because of the upgrade.
- 2023: An FAA-commissioned safety review warned that the agency's technology updates could cause air traffic disruptions and cited the need for old systems to be preserved during the transition period.
- 2024: The Government Accountability Office, Congress' investigative arm, reported that the FAA found 51 of its 138 systems were unsustainable because of outdated functionality, a lack of spare parts and other concerns, and that it had been "slow to modernize."
- 2026: In March testimony before the House, the Transportation Department's deputy inspector general, Mitch Behm, said, "Our work, over more than two decades and across 50 audit reports, has highlighted issues" with the upgrade's implementation "that led to cost increases, schedule overruns and delayed or reduced benefits and capabilities."
Congress has given the FAA billions, but not all funds were for system upgrades
Democrats have pointed to Trump's 2025 signature tax and spending legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, saying it provided the department with billions of dollars.
U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said in a Nov. 15 statement that the FAA has "received historical and monumental investments over the last two years, over $12.5 billion" and it "largely remains unspent."
DeLauro cited an accurate appropriation figure — but she exaggerated how much money is specifically for the communications upgrade.
Of the $12.5 billion provided in the law, $4.75 billion was earmarked for "telecommunications infrastructure modernization and systems upgrades." The rest of the money was for other purposes, including radar system replacements, runway safety technologies and construction of a new air route traffic control center.
The Transportation Department told PolitiFact that Duffy has consistently asked for funding for new software. In July 2025, Duffy said system upgrades are "a massive project" and that the sum provided by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act “is not enough."
The Office of Management and Budget and the Transportation Department told PBS that the FAA has enough funds today to complete the switch from copper to fiber, and that the transition is about 70% complete. Duffy said on CNN's "State of the Union" on Nov. 15 that "we are on track to have all of that $12.5 billion spent and deployed by the end of 2028."
Before he was Transportation secretary, Duffy questioned the need for more money. "They got billions of dollars, the FAA did, over COVID," Duffy, then a former member of Congress, said on Fox News in January 2023, shortly after an earlier FAA ground stop. "And now they're gonna come back and say, 'We want even more money to fix this crisis that we weren't able to handle when, you know, for what, three hours in the morning aircraft couldn't, couldn’t fly.'"
Experts said it's not unusual for money to be spent in increments rather than all at once, because projects may need to be completed in phases.
"While more money may be necessary, you don’t need it all at once — that is a recipe for waste," said Steve Ellis, president of Taxpayers for Common Sense, which tracks the federal budget. "It took a long time for these problems to develop, and it is going to take a while to fix them."
Did DOGE cuts affect the FAA?
Shortly after Trump began his second term in early 2025, his administration pursued a wide-ranging effort to cut government jobs and spending via the Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, led by billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk.
"You remember when Elon Musk was standing on a stage spinning his chainsaw around, cutting government willy-nilly?" U.S. Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., said Nov. 15 on CBS News' "Face the Nation." "Well, part of that chainsaw got 1,300 employees of the FAA to resign or to retire. They fired 400 probationary employees. … What you're seeing is the wages of what Elon did, where he just gutted an entity that — that affected millions of Americans last Friday."
Himes' count of employees fired is broadly in line with the numbers reported by media outlets. But drawing a straight line from those cuts to the ground stop is speculative at best.
The 400 employees who were fired in early 2025 were "the types of workers tasked with helping aircraft safety inspectors, repairing air traffic control facilities and updating digital maps that pilots use in flight," The Associated Press reported in February 2025.
It's unclear how many would have been involved in the communications upgrade, which was handled largely by contractors.
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Man honored for finding missing toddler 2 miles from home, curled up in bush and shivering
text:
ELOY, AZ (AZFamily/Gray News) - A 2-year-old girl who went missing Tuesday night in Arizona was found 2 miles from her home.
Law enforcement, neighbors and family celebrated her safe return to her home in Eloy Wednesday.
A Pinal County Sheriff’s Office (PCSO) spokesperson said the 2-year-old wandered off from her family’s front yard around 5 p.m. Tuesday. She was wearing only a diaper.
A massive search effort launched, with 75 law enforcement officers, neighbors, and search-and-rescue volunteers helping the department.
After seven hours, around 12:15 a.m. Wednesday, Jay Stewart found the girl 2 miles from her home. She was curled up inside a bush and shivering.
“Can you believe this? That’s where she was at, right in that spot. I was just walking the ditch,” Stewart said in body-camera video released Wednesday evening.
“Are you OK? Are you so cold?” a deputy asked.
“She just jumped up and ran to me. She sounded like it came out of the bush,” Stewart said.
Standing on the side of the road Wednesday afternoon, Stewart became emotional as he thought back to Tuesday night and his part in getting the girl home safely.
“Everybody loved her, and we all did it for the same reason. We wanted her back,” Stewart said.
Stewart described how he found her.
“She was right in the middle of it. And when I picked her up to get my phone out, the bottom of her diaper had pebbles on it, so she had been sitting on pebbles,” he said.
They took the girl to the hospital to be checked out. She was back home Wednesday.
The sheriff’s office gave Stewart a certificate of appreciation for his dedication.

title: Does mushroom coffee deliver on its health promises? Unpacking 5 selling points
text:
Does mushroom coffee deliver on its health promises? Unpacking 5 selling points
A warm, aromatic cup of coffee can be a reliable, flavorful pick-me-up. In recent years, online influencers have promoted pairing it with an unlikely counterpart: mushrooms.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
“I’m on a mission to stop getting that afternoon crash from coffee that makes me want a second cup,” said an influencer advertising mushroom coffee on Instagram in January. She extolled its purported virtues, saying, “it promotes gut health and your overall immune support” and blended mushrooms that are “really good for your focus and energy.”
Mushroom coffee can refer to a mixture of instant coffee and varying powdered mushroom extracts or powdered mushrooms with other ingredients and no coffee.
As for the taste of coffee combined with mushroom powder, “interestingly enough, mushroom coffee tastes pretty similar to regular coffee,” registered dietitian Beth Czerwony told the Cleveland Clinic.
Although people might not taste the mushrooms in the coffee, they could notice the difference in their wallets. A 7- or 8-ounce container of instant coffee typically sells for less than $10, and a similar amount of mushroom coffee generally costs $15 to $35.
For some people, paying extra is an easy trade-off for certain health benefits. But is mushroom coffee bringing those benefits?
Limited scientific research shows that consuming certain mushrooms might have health benefits. However, almost all of that research has been in labs or animals, rather than clinical experiments designed to evaluate the mushrooms’ effects on humans.
We found no studies evaluating mushroom coffee’s purported health benefits.
Nicholas Money, a Miami University biology professor who studies fungi, said he knows of no evidence that mushroom coffee has any positive effects on physical or mental health. For that reason, he said: “I don’t think it’s worth your time or money.”
But Toby Amidor, a registered dietician and nutrition expert, said there are no drawbacks to drinking mushroom coffee.
Most research showing health benefits from mushrooms looked at both the mushroom and its root-like structures. If buying “mushroom coffee,” Amidor recommended purchasing products that contain both.
Mushroom coffee can also fall into the loosely regulated category of dietary supplements, so there’s no way to know with certainty that you’re getting the mushroom extracts advertised on the packaging — or how much the product contains.
Here are some facts about the most-repeated mushroom coffee selling points.
Claim: Mushroom coffee prevents a caffeine crash.
Facts: Mushroom coffee can be decaffeinated, but it often contains some caffeine — just less than a standard cup of coffee because some of the brew is mushroom powder. Swapping standard coffee for mushroom coffee might help reduce or prevent caffeine crash-related headaches, fatigue or irritability, but there’s no clear evidence that any mushrooms in the blend would be responsible.
That caffeine reduction might help many people who are especially caffeine sensitive, Aisling Daly, a nutrition lecturer at Oxford Brookes University, said in 2024 on the BBC’s “Sliced Bread” podcast.
It’s possible the mushrooms themselves might have properties that reduce the effects of a caffeine crash, she said, but “we don’t know enough about what these mushroom powders can do.”
Claim: Mushroom coffee is good for gut health.
Facts: Incorporating mushrooms into a regular diet can change the composition of a person’s gut microbiome, research shows. The gut microbiome is the unique microscopic ecosystem of organisms including bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites in a person’s digestive system. It breaks down fiber and starch and synthesizes vitamins, amino acids and fatty acids that help prevent disease.
There’s a lot we don’t know about the gut microbiome, but some bacteria are known to be beneficial, and some research shows that whole mushroom powders can increase the gut microbiome’s population of bacteria with known health benefits.
This research wasn’t specifically on mushroom coffee, however.
“Promising research suggests that mushrooms may support gut health, but there is not yet sufficient evidence to say that drinking mushroom coffee improves gut health in humans,” Amidor said.
Claim: Mushroom coffee supports the immune system.
Facts: Mushrooms and mushroom extracts can influence immune reactions — some stimulate immune function while others suppress it, and some increase inflammatory responses while others decrease them.
Much of the marketing around mushroom coffee says it “supports” immunity, but doesn’t make clear, specific claims about how.
“Our bodies react to fungi if they’re present in our diet in any form,” Money said, so it’s unsurprising that people have an immune reaction to mushrooms. “But whether or not that plays any useful role in health and well being? That’s very questionable.”
Claim: Mushroom coffee is good for brain function and focus.
Facts: Some research has associated mushroom consumption with improved cognitive performance or with nerve cell growth.
A 2022 study found that older adults who reported higher mushroom intake scored better on cognitive function tests, signaling that regular mushroom consumption might benefit brain function.
Money said lion’s mane mushrooms produce a specific chemical compound that has been shown to speed up nerve cell growth when cells are grown in a petri dish in a lab. Other studies have shown that rats fed high doses of the compounds show brain chemistry changes, he said.
However, clinical studies on humans “really show no effect whatsoever” on focus and concentration or ability to complete intellectual tasks, Money said.
Also, there’s no research suggesting that mushroom coffee in particular can provide any cognitive benefits.
Claim: Mushroom coffee is safe.
Facts: There’s no reason to think mushroom coffee is unsafe when consumed in moderation.
At high doses, certain medicinal mushrooms might pose health risks, but mushroom extracts are typically present in small amounts when consumed in mushroom coffee, Money said. So if it seems to provide benefits that outweigh its higher price tag, mushroom coffee might be a useful purchase — even if it’s the power of the placebo effect, he said.
That said, there are some health considerations. Some mushrooms can raise the risk of bleeding or interact negatively with certain drugs. Mushrooms can also be high in oxalates, which can cause problems for people with kidney issues.
PolitiFact Staff Researcher Caryn Baird contributed to this report.

title: Trump defends calling Putin a friend but says he ‘can’t speak’ to whether he’s a friend to the US
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has defended calling Russian President Vladimir Putin a friend but says he “can’t speak” to whether the Russian leader is a friend to the U.S.
Trump raised eyebrows in China days ago with his warm welcome and repeated references to his Russian counterpart as his “friend,” and he did not back away from that in the briefing room on Friday.
The Republican president appeared to sidestep a question about whether he sees Putin as a friend to the United States.
“I can’t speak to America,” he said, without expounding before he shifted to his “very good” personal relationship with Putin and repeated his longstanding grievances over the extended federal probe into Russian attempts to influence U.S. voters in the 2016 presidential election.
“I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship (with),” Trump said. “It’s actually very good.”
Trump broadly praised Putin and China’s Xi Jinping after bilateral and trilateral meetings among the trio.
Putin, Trump insisted, would “love to end the war” in Ukraine but said both Putin and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy are “stuck in it.”
“You have two guys that don’t know how to end it,” he said. “We’re trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other.”
Trump insisted his relationships with the other world leaders is a key to an eventual peace.
“You know, you’re very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries,” he said.
