Motorcyclist killed in crash with a car in Alton, Maine
One person is dead after a crash between a motorcycle and a car in the Penobscot County town of Alton.
The Penobscot County Sheriff's Office says the crash happened at about 4 p.m. on Bennoch Road.
The motorcycle rider died at the scene. The driver of the vehicle was treated for minor injuries.
Police did not immediately release the names of either person involved in the crash because they were still notifying family members. As of Thursday evening, police were still investigating how the crash happened.

title: Recall roundup: Pastas, breakfast foods, whipped cream and more recalled across U.S.
text:
Recall roundup: Pastas, breakfast foods, whipped cream and more recalled across U.S.
Breakfast sandwiches, whipped cream and bicycle helmets are among the latest products recalled across the nation.
Several companies have pulled products from stores or warned consumers about potential safety risks, affecting everything from cars and SUVs, air-fryer ovens, children’s pajamas, infant bouncers and magnetic toys.
Related video above | Check your fridge: Recalled foods could already be in your home
Some involve undeclared allergens or bacteria that can cause serious illness. Others raise concerns about fires, burns, falls or entrapment.
Here’s what to know about the affected products recalled over the past few weeks, the risks and where they were sold.
FOOD ITEMS
- Whipped cream. A batch of Kirkland Signature Real Heavy Whipped Cream may contain a small amount of cleaning chemical; affected 15-ounce cans have a best-by date of April 2, 2027, and can timestamps from 00:35 to 02:45. Costco sold it in 12 states: Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Wisconsin. Click here to view the full recall
- Breakfast biscuit sandwiches. Grand Strand Sandwich Company recalled four Lunch Box varieties—bacon, egg and cheese; jumbo sausage; sausage, egg and cheese; and chicken sausage biscuits—because they may be contaminated with Listeria. They were sold in convenience stores, vending machines and prison canteens in North Carolina, South Carolina and Virginia. Click here to view the full recall
- Frozen dessert bars. Naia recalled Chocolate Banana Bar Sorbetto with specified date codes after some pistachio gelato bars were put in wrappers that did not declare pistachio, milk or egg. The bars were sold in Northern California and Reno, Nevada. Click here to view the full recall
- Refrigerated pasta. ALDI recalled Priano Protein Carbonara Tortelloni and Protein Herb & Cheese Tortelloni because they may have been kept at improper temperatures and could contain botulism-causing bacteria. The products were sold at ALDI stores in Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina. Click here to view the full recall
- Cheddar cheese. Family Farmstead Dairy recalled its raw mild cheddar cheese because it may be contaminated with E. coli. The affected cheese was distributed through retailers in Connecticut, Massachusetts, Maryland, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania and Virginia. Click here to view the full recall
- Breakfast biscuit sandwiches. Fresh & Ready Foods recalled Fresh to You sausage, egg and cheese biscuit sandwiches because they may be contaminated with Listeria. The recalled sandwiches were made at the company’s Longview, Texas facility; check the notice for the affected distribution details. Click here to view the full recall
MEDICATIONS
- Blood pressure medication. Breckenridge Pharmaceutical recalled one lot of 60-mg extended-release propranolol capsules because of possible metal contamination that could cause cuts to the mouth or digestive tract. The lot was distributed to wholesalers and pharmacies nationwide. Click here to view the full recall
- Dried herbal root. Larbi recalled three lots of Herb To Body Yellow Dock Root C/S in 4-ounce pouches because they may be contaminated with Salmonella. The product was sold nationwide through the company website, online marketplaces and retail stores. Click here to view the full recall
- Dietary supplement capsules. bioQuad Life Sciences issued an allergy alert for OsteoDenx capsules because the product contains undeclared milk, which may cause a serious reaction in people with milk allergies. Click here to view the full recall
- Medical beds and accessories. Medline’s recall and repair-or-replace program covers Medline-brand beds, rails, mattresses and accessories because electrical parts can overheat and cause fires, while some bed-and-accessory setups can create entrapment or asphyxiation risks. The products were distributed in the United States and Canada. Click here to view the full recall
EVERYDAY ITEMS
- Air-fryer ovens. Gourmia recalled its stainless-steel 9-slice digital air-fryer ovens, model GTF7530, because the glass doors can swing shut unexpectedly and burn someone retrieving food. The ovens were sold at Target stores nationwide and online. Click here to view the full recall
- Adult portable bed rails. Xentrawave recalled XT016 rails from all batches and XT026 rails from batch 20251212 because users can become trapped between a rail and mattress and suffocate; one death was reported. The rails were sold in the United States. Click here to view the full recall
- Bicycle helmets. Cipton recalled white youth-size helmets with built-in multicolored LED strips because they fail impact, stability and certification requirements and may not protect a rider in a crash. They were sold at Dick’s Sporting Goods and JCPenney stores nationwide and online. Click here to view the full recall
- Rechargeable battery packs. Ororo recalled PD10K-Pro lithium-ion packs because they can overheat and cause fires or burns; one overheating report was received. The packs were sold online at Ororowear.com and Amazon in the United States. Click here to view the full recall
- Magnetic robot toys. CHE-US recalled magnetic stick-figure robot toys sold in sets of five or 10 because magnets can come loose when the figures are pulled apart and pose a serious ingestion hazard. They were sold on Amazon.com in the United States. Click here to view the full recall
- Children’s pajamas. Qpancy recalled children’s pajama sets because they do not meet federal sleepwear flammability standards, creating a burn risk. The sets were sold online in the United States. Click here to view the full recall
- Waterproof dry bags. Fidlock recalled medium Hermetic dry bags because their adhesive closure strips can detach and release magnets that could be swallowed. The affected bags were sold in the United States. Click here to view the full recall
- Infant bouncers. Kidsview recalled khaki bouncers made in August, September or October 2022 because they can collapse during use and injure an infant. They were sold online in the United States. Click here to view the full recall
- Electric off-highway vehicles. Vanderhall recalled model-year 2024–2026 Brawley GTS vehicles because the brakes may engage while airborne and lock up when the vehicle lands, risking a crash and serious injury. The recall covers vehicles sold in the United States. Click here to view the full recall
- Lighted portfolios and measuring tools. Hultafors Group recalled select CLC portfolios, Johnson Level angle locators and calipers, and Calculated Industries calculators because button-cell batteries can be accessed, posing a risk of serious injury if swallowed. The products were sold in the United States. Click here to view the full recall
VEHICLES
- Cars, trucks and SUVs. Toyota is recalling more than 314,000 vehicles with passenger-side Takata airbags that may degrade and rupture, sending metal fragments into the cabin and potentially causing serious injury or death. The affected Toyota and Lexus models were sold in the United States; owner notices are expected to begin Dec. 28. Click here to view the full recall
- Luxury SUVs. Ford recalled about 36,994 model-year 2025–2027 Lincoln Navigators because the front passenger seat may move unexpectedly when the rear-seat “Chauffeur Seat” feature is activated, potentially striking passengers or putting the front occupant in an unsafe position. The recall applies to vehicles in the United States. Click here to view the full recall

title: Katahdin Trust to open bank branch in downtown Portland
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND – Katahdin Trust, a community bank established in 1918 with nearly $1.2 billion in assets, announced plans to open a full-service branch at 120 Exchange St. in downtown Portland to serve personal and business banking customers. It will be the bank’s 17th branch in Maine. Renovations will begin in early 2027, with the opening expected later in the year.
“Katahdin has been supporting Maine communities for more than 100 years, and for nearly two decades, we’ve been proud to serve customers and communities across southern Maine,” Jon Prescott, president and CEO of Katahdin Trust, said. “We’re excited to become part of the community and build new relationships in Portland. A downtown branch puts us closer to customers who live, work and do business in the area, making it easier for them to bank with us.”
The Portland branch will be Katahdin’s third location in southern Maine, joining a full-service branch and its heavy equipment financing affiliate, Maine Financial Group, both on U.S. Route 1 in Scarborough. Katahdin employs approximately 185 people statewide.
The new branch will offer in-person and drive-up teller service, a 24/7 ATM and private offices for one-on-one meetings. Customers will have access to a full range of personal and business banking services, including checking, savings, home loans, commercial lending and cash management, along with the convenience of online and mobile banking.
“Banking is still about relationships,” Prescott said. “Customers in Portland will be able to walk in, chat with a local banker, and get to know the people helping them reach their goals.”
Planning, approvals and hiring for the new branch are underway. Katahdin will share more details, including an opening date, as the project moves forward.
Founded in 1918, Katahdin Trust is a community bank serving individuals and businesses through 16 branches across Maine, as well as online and mobile banking. The bank also offers heavy equipment financing throughout New England through its affiliate, Maine Financial Group. Its parent company, Katahdin Bankshares Corp., is quoted on the OTCQX under the symbol KTHN. Learn more at katahdintrust.com.

title: Trump says he plans to penalize US tech companies that build AI data centers in other countries
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Trump says he plans to penalize US tech companies that build AI data centers in other countries
U.S. tech companies will face “a tremendous tax” if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries, President Donald Trump said on Friday.
Trump did not provide details and said he hadn’t yet told his own officials about his plan. The Republican president urged Americans to welcome data center construction in their communities and extract concessions from the developers, repeating a point he made before the midterm elections.
“You ought to take advantage of the data centers," Trump said in a White House press briefing. "Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off.”
Related video above | President Trump '100%' backs bill to make data centers pay more, potentially lower electricity costs
After a campaign season filled with outrage against AI data centers, the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.
A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if Trump — perhaps the industry’s biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown.
Despite backing from Trump, the data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom have become politically toxic.
The tech industry says it has gotten the message. Besides ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build.
Companies are also making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment and offering assurances that data centers will boost local property values — all while maintaining AI is a positive force for the American economy, despite its skeptics.
With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses.
The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train its best artificial intelligence models.

title: Midcoast bicyclist on a ‘ride to recovery’ after hit-and-run
text:
In the two weeks since being seriously injured in a Nov. 4 hit-and-run crash, Jaja Martin has undergone two surgeries and faces a long road to recovery, but she is not letting that stop her. Instead, she said, she is taking this next chapter in her life as a new adventure.
“I’m progressing forward,” Martin said. “I’m not looking back and, you know, all the trauma I left on the street behind me. I’m just going one way — forward — and I’m trying to make that forward and up.”
Martin was struck by a vehicle while riding her bicycle in Damariscotta and hospitalized until Nov. 11 when she returned home.
The driver — later identified as John Barczak, 67, of Rockland — fled the scene. He was arrested later that day and charged with three felonies: elevated aggravated assault, reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, and leaving the scene of an accident involving serious bodily injury.
Barczak was previously sentenced to 60 years in prison for the murder of two Sanford convenience store clerks but was released from prison in March 2024, decades before his sentence would have ended, after earning time off for taking part in work programs, the Bangor Daily News reported.
Martin’s daughter, Teiga Martin, started a GoFundMe, titled “Jaja’s Ride to Recovery,” to help with medical expenses and to support the family. Since its creation on Nov. 13, it has raised $60,623.
In the description, Teiga Martin said one of her mother’s biggest needs is dental care after her teeth were damaged in the crash. Other than immediate medical care, donations will go toward physical therapy and support Jaja Martin until she goes back to work, which her daughter said could be anywhere from six months to a year from now.
“If you know Jaja, you know how active she is and how much she loves being outdoors and living life to the fullest,” Teiga Martin said in the description. “It’s hard knowing that the road back to that life will take time.”
As Jaja Martin recovered in the hospital and now as she recovers at home, the surrounding community has come together to send thoughts and well wishes. Central Lincoln County YMCA Youth Programs Coordinator Sarah Glenn said the organization put together care packages to send to Martin while she was in the hospital. They included cards, silly sunglasses, and a disco ball for her hospital room.
Martin is an active member of the YMCA and one of the teachers for the gym’s summer sailing camps in Round Pond. Glenn described Martin as “magical” and said she hopes her recovery goes well.
“We’re very happy to help with the communitywide initiative,” Glenn said.
At Great Salt Bay Community School in Damariscotta, students in Kaity Newell’s strings program put together a card for Martin, who is a musician in the Seacoast Youth and Community Orchestra and volunteers with the class.
“She is just a wonderful person and she makes a difference to the school, a positive difference,” Newell said. “And the kids love her.”
When Newell heard about the crash, she and her junior high students decided to work together to design a card. Newell said a lot of her students have known Martin for a long time, especially from some of the crossover between strings and the sailing camps she teaches.
“All the kids were just very sad and wanted to send their love, so we made a card,” Newell said.
Every October, Martin is a familiar face during Damariscotta Pumpkinfest, usually found racing pumpkin boats alongside her family during the regatta. This year, her team themed itself and its pumpkin for the late Dolly Parton. When staff at Maine Medical Center discovered Martin was “Dolly,” she became somewhat of a celebrity in the hospital.
Pumpkinfest and Regatta Executive Director Jed Weiss said he hopes Jaja Martin has a speedy recovery and that he sees her in a pumpkin next fall.
“We wish her the best,” Weiss said.
Martin said she is overcome with emotion and that she feels like she has received a “huge, giant hug” from the whole community. She recalled the disco ball and other trinkets from YMCA made her hospital room more fun and that a video she received from the Seacoast Youth and Community Orchestra brought tears to her eyes.
“It has been overwhelming and just joyful, really joyful, and warm and fuzzy, and all those great things,” Martin said. “This is why we live here. Our community is incredible.”
For more information, go to gofundme.com/f/support-jajas-ride-to-recovery.
BDN writer Sabrina Martin contributed reporting.

title: Officials: Washington pulp mill violated safety standards before ruptured chemical tank killed 11
text:
SEATTLE (AP) — The Washington state pulp mill where a chemical tank ruptured in May, killing 11, had an extensive track record of egregious and willful safety violations, including failure to inspect or repair more than a dozen other tanks at the facility, state investigators said Friday.
Nippon Dynawave Packaging Co. faces more than $10 million in state fines, including the largest employer safety fine in state history, and investigators plan to refer their findings to prosecutors for possible criminal charges.
“Without repair or replacement, the tank walls were a ticking clock,” Dan Pitts, state Labor and Industries compliance manager, said during a press conference in Longview to announce the findings. “It was a question of time, and time ran out.”
Nippon did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment about the state’s findings.
Nippon plans to restart operations in December. Officials said the company has an obligation to fix any hazards that have been identified, and the state will be closely monitoring to ensure that happens.
Besides the 11 who were killed, 12 were injured on May 26 when the tank holding more than 900,000 gallons (3.4 million liters) of “white liquor,” a highly corrosive chemical used in paper manufacturing, ruptured. The flood of caustic material was powerful enough to blow out building walls and overturn pickup trucks at the site.
“Nippon’s decision to keep G-10 operating when they knew it was not safe contributed to the death of 11 workers,” said Labor and Industries Director Joel Sacks. “Because of that, we will be referring this case to prosecutors to consider criminal charges.”
The state Ecology department also announced that it has issued 34 violations that impacted air and water, and is seeking $961,000 in penalties and costs for responding to the emergency.
Most of the environmental violations were due to the impact of the white liquor that spread across the site, officials said. It reached storm drains and a wastewater treatment system, with some discharging into the Columbia River and a nearby ditch, killing fish.
State investigators said Friday the company failed to take appropriate action to address the issue in violation of state law, and similarly failed to inspect or address deficiencies in 13 other tanks at the site.
Officials also said Nippon’s emergency response and planning fell short of state requirements. The company had not effectively prepared its staff to respond to an emergency, and there was no employer-led incident command for several hours after the tank failed, Pitts said.
“We believe failures in the response were a contributing factor in serious injuries to four of 12 workers who were hurt that day,” Pitts said.
The state investigation mirrored an August report by the U.S. Chemical Safety Board that revealed inspectors hired by the company in 2025 found the tank that ruptured was “not fit for continued service” due to deteriorating thickness in the tank walls.
Records reveal a history of violations at the paper mill
An AP review of inspections and safety complaints at the plant prior to the tank collapse found that Labor and Industries had investigated more than a dozen safety complaints at the plant since 2018 and issued almost $7,000 in fines for violations. Ecology had issued 54 environmental violation notices against the company since 2016 and fined them $41,500 for eight serious offenses.
More than $2.4 million in workers’ compensation claims have been paid for 169 employees injured on the job since 2015, the agency reported, including for injuries related to exposure to caustic substances.
After the May tank collapse, the state’s Department of Ecology filed a violation notice against the company listing 35 citations.
Nippon Dynawave said in an email Wednesday that they have remained engaged with the government agencies that are investigating the tank collapse. They said the mill has hosted hundreds of visits by regulators and investigators.
“The full deconstruction, forensic examination and technical analysis needed to determine the root cause have not yet been completed,” the company said. “The tank is currently being deconstructed, with great care being taken to log and retain portions of the tank to determine the root cause.”
Among workers killed in the rupture were brothers Tyler and Brad Covington. Their mother, Sheri Lynn King, has filed a wrongful-death lawsuit against Nippon Dynawave, saying her sons were burned and crushed by the white liquor and debris. The lawsuit claims the company failed to maintain and inspect equipment, failed to properly train and supervise employees and failed to implement safety policies and emergency response procedures.

title: Father, son die in home explosion after trying to start wood-burning fireplace with gasoline, deputies say
text:
LINCOLN, Neb. (KOLN/Gray News) — A father and son died after an explosion at a home in Nebraska on Wednesday night.
Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office (LSO) deputies were called to the home near Lincoln shortly before 9 p.m. When they arrived, the house was in flames.
Three people, two men and a woman, suffered critical injuries in the fire. The sheriff’s office confirmed Thursday morning that the father and son, 54-year-old Jerad Nyhoff and 19-year-old Jaxsen Nyhoff, later died.
A 52-year-old woman was outside working when the explosion happened. Houchin said she suffered third-degree burns on her hands, wrists and face while trying to get Jerad Nyhoff and Jaxsen Nyhoff out of the fire. She was taken to the hospital.
LSO Chief Deputy Ben Houchin said a preliminary investigation shows that the two were in the living room when Jerad Nyhoff attempted to start their wood-burning fireplace with gasoline, resulting in an explosion.
Further information was not yet available.

title: Aging is normal. Planning ahead keeps it from becoming a crisis
text:
(Aging Untold) — Aging is a normal process, but families often treat it like a crisis when they’re caught off guard.
A fall, hospitalization, new diagnosis or sudden need for care can quickly expose the lack of conversations about money, housing, insurance, caregiving and independence.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing what families can do ahead of time to ease into the care that comes with aging.
Know that aging is going to happen
The first step is accepting that aging and the care that comes with it are ahead, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said.
“The biggest thing is know that it’s going to happen,” O’Rourke said.
She said many people think “you live and then you die.”
Clients often tell her they weren’t expecting a health change. She said she has heard that “thousands and thousands of times.”
“I meet with a client and they said, ‘I just wasn’t expecting this. I feel blindsided. I’m shocked,’” O’Rourke said.
O’Rourke said families should expect a period of time when they are providing care, getting care or both.
“So think ahead. Plan ahead. Money, care, etc.,” O’Rourke said.
Expect some decline
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said people know they will age but are not expecting a decline in health.
“People are looking at, they know they’re going to age. What they’re not expecting is that deterioration in health, and that’s what catches them by surprise,” Rogers said.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck compared it to driving a car with worn tires.
“It’s like driving your car with bald tires and being shocked when you get a flat,” she said. “You have to know that as we age, there’s going to be a certain amount of decline, no matter how well you take care of yourself.”
Planning is what keeps aging from becoming a crisis
Cradduck said aging is a process, not a sudden event.
“There is a declining process. And so we treat this like it’s a crisis, and it’s been happening every day since we were born. It’s not a crisis. So we have to plan or we will be in crisis,” she said.
Healthy aging starts with daily choices
Rogers also spoke to younger viewers.
“You’re going to age, and healthy aging isn’t something that just happens to you. It’s something that you can have a choice in, one day, one habit and one choice at a time,” she said.
Stay in control by letting people know
Cradduck said the way to remain in control and make decisions about your own care is to tell the people around you what you want.
“The only way you get to stay in control, the only way you get to be the one that’s making those decisions, or at least dictating those decisions, is to let people know. So you have to prepare. You have to get your paperwork in place,” she said.
O’Rourke said there are three categories to prepare for: legal, financial and care.
“Think about those categories and what plans you need to be put in place addressing those categories: legal, financial and care,” she said.
Key takeaways
- Expect it. Aging and the care that comes with it will happen, and families can plan for a period of giving and getting care.
- Plan ahead for money and care. Conversations about money, housing, insurance, caregiving and independence are easier before a fall, hospitalization or new diagnosis.
- Some decline is expected. The Aging Untold experts said a certain amount of decline happens no matter how well a person takes care of themselves.
- Healthy aging is built one choice at a time. Dr. Rhea Rogers said it comes down to one day, one habit and one choice at a time.
- Get paperwork in place. Amy O’Rourke said to organize plans in three categories: legal, financial and care.”
- Tell people your wishes. “Sam” Cradduck said letting others know is how you stay in control of decisions about you.

title: Judge says agriculture secretary's religious emails were unconstitutional
text:
Judge says agriculture secretary's religious emails were unconstitutional
Religious messages that U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins emailed to the agency's 100,000 employees were unconstitutional, and she must be careful to avoid proselytizing when communicating with workers, a federal judge ruled Thursday.
Video above: What's the deal with the first amendment?
Rollins sent the messages, which included Christian messages and images, from her official email account on holidays such as Independence Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter. She did not send messages commemorating holidays from other religions.
“And so, like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for,” Rollins wrote in an April 5 email marking Easter.
U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson in San Francisco said the emails violated the First Amendment's establishment clause, pointing to her position of authority, her use of an official email account and the messages suggesting that Christianity is the shared faith of USDA workers.
A USDA spokesperson called the ruling “a completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary" and said the agency is considering an appeal.
Employees cannot realistically opt out of reading emails from their agency director, and the messages could coerce them to hide their own faith or feel pressure to adopt Rollins' Christian faith, Thompson ruled.
When disseminating religious messages, Rollins must stop if a colleague asks her to stop, “cannot create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances” and “cannot use official authority to pressure subordinates,” Thompson ordered. Her commands were quoted directly from a USDA policy on workplace religious expression that Rollins herself adopted.
Rollins may discuss her faith with interested colleagues, share why her faith is meaningful to her, politely invite co-workers to religious events and express her views in appropriate conversations, Thompson ruled, again quoting directly from Rollins' policy.
Six USDA employees and the National Federation of Federal Employees, a labor union representing 19,000 USDA workers, brought the suit in May.

title: Maine plans to delay MaineCare work requirements until July 2027
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Maine plans to opt in to the federal government’s six-month “hold harmless” period before denying or ending MaineCare coverage solely because someone does not meet new work requirements, according to a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Health and Human Services.
The period would apply to people whose MaineCare applications or renewals are initiated from Jan. 1 through June 30, 2027. State officials say they could keep or receive coverage if they meet the program’s other eligibility requirements.
The federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced the optional period Nov. 13. States that opt in must still assess whether applicants and beneficiaries meet the requirements, but they cannot deny applications or end coverage solely for noncompliance during the period.
Maine plans to use the time to strengthen and extensively test its eligibility systems ahead of full implementation on July 1, 2027.
In July, Maine DHHS estimated that the new work requirements would lead to more than 31,000 people losing their health insurance coverage.

title: Oh! Let there be music
text:
To the Editor:
… and it came to pass
That on waking from rest of the Seventh Day,
A "Word," which was Music,
Waited. Filling God's heart and soul, and mind.
But no image of it could God find.
The only thing available to God was to think back
On what had already been done,
That Music might come into being.
A dotted whole note.
Mid winter ice facing a late dawn Sun.
A quarter notes.
A hiker just about back to his house.
Eighth notes:
A sand piper searching a well littered beach.
Sixteenth notes:
A gorilla beating its chest!
Volume variation:
An elephant resting on one side
And breathing deeply.
Thus, from, these simple beginnings,
Music was create from the Creation itself,
On the Eighth Day.
William F. Fuller
Bar Harbor

title: Festival of Trees in Houlton continues through Sunday with more than 50 trees available
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - The Health Services Foundation Festival of Trees is open through Sunday, Nov. 22, at the Big Red Barn in Houlton. A winner could take home a fully decorated Christmas tree. More than 50 trees are available.
How the festival raises money
Larry McGuire, a festival participant, put 20 tickets in a bucket for a chance to win a new golf set. Tickets cost $1 each.
“About every one I go by I put one in,” McGuire said. “They told me I bought the lucky tickets.”
The money raised goes toward equipment for local hospitals, clinics, first responders and schools, among other things.
“So we have a broad scope and we’re just very happy to be able to contribute,” said Lori Weston, an organizer of the festival.
Prizes
Besides toys, games and fully decorated trees, many prizes this year are things people need.
“There’s a lot of great trees here today, a lot with the gift cards and things that are necessities, I think, this year with everything that’s going on,” said Amee Gellerson, a festival participant.
Festival history and location
The festival has been a community tradition for more than 20 years. It started at the hospital, and Weston saw it was outgrowing its space. Five years ago, the festival moved to the Big Red Barn at Sunset Farm. Weston said she knew the area was perfect to host the festival as soon as she saw it.
“The amazing thing, someone gave me the name of Dave Benedict, who owns the property, and I came out and before he said one thing, we realized that every beam has an outlet, like it was made for the barn to plug in trees,” Weston said. “So it’s perfect.”
Weston said the barn is the draw, but people stay for a chance to win and a guarantee to help the community.
“This is a hard year for folks, and it’s not lost on us that we’re doing extremely well and we’re ahead of where we were last year at the same time,” Weston said. “So we’ll see how it comes out on Sunday afternoon, but it’s looking really, really great.”
Event details
The festival is open through Sunday at the Big Red Barn in Houlton. Doors close at 2 p.m. Sunday, followed by the ticket drawings.
Santa is at the barn until 8 p.m. Friday.

A CNN review of his posts to Reddit after that incident revealed he wrote that speed is not inherently dangerous and that excessive speed isn’t the same as distracted driving.

title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
text:
Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.
Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.
Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.
With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a "testament of the hard work" his team put into the case. He said he was "intimately familiar" with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.
Rinderknecht's attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.
"After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration," Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.
Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.
Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren't presented as evidence during the trial.
Juror says Rinderknecht's own testimony pointed to a guilty verdict
Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.
"It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise," he said. "After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he's guilty."
Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a "lack of information" presented to the jury about the technical review.
In the end, it was Rinderknecht's own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.
"Stating that he was up on the hill, didn't smell a fire, didn't see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night," Cameron said.
Prosecutors say Rinderknecht had been 'mad at everything'
During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht's state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by "societal revenge" like they previously did.
Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire's origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.
"He was mad at everything, and frustrated," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.
After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?"
These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.
They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.
Defense argues fire's origin is unproven
Haney cast doubt on the government's case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.
The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.
Prosecutors attacked the fire investigator during cross examination and at one point accused him of perjury, alleging he did not disclose all records related to the case. The judge ultimately rejected prosecutors' request to strike his testimony.
Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor's testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht's character, such as his angry text messages, because they were "evidence of the man, not evidence of the act."
Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.
In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

title: United States loses measles elimination status
text:
United States loses measles elimination status
United States loses measles elimination status
Measles is no longer eliminated in the United States, according to an announcement to the Pan American Health Organization Tuesday.
PAHO said the U.S. lost their elimination status because the same measles virus has circulated uninterrupted for more than a year in the country. The U.S. first received elimination status in 2000.
The CDC reported more than 5,400 cases in 2026 and roughly 2,200 cases in 2025.
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the CDC is working to close vaccination gaps and regain public trust.
“I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” Kennedy Jr. said.
In Maine, the state CDC has reported six cases of measles in 2026. Chief Health Improvement Officer at MaineHealth Dr. Dora Mills says vaccines can help eradicate the disease.
“I don't want to see anybody die of measles,” Mills said. “It's so preventable.”
Mills said vaccines can protect one’s own safety and the others around them.
“We're the oldest state in the country," Mills said. "We have a lot of people who are immunocompromised, not just because age, but because of the diseases that often increase with age."
If you’re not sure if you’re protected, the CDC says to check if you already have the vaccine or if you’ve already had measles.
If you’re unsure about whether you want to get vaccinated, Mills says to talk to your local provider about any concerns you may have.
Early symptoms include high fever, cough and red and runny eyes.
You can learn more about measles prevention here.

title: Could AI’s discovery of software flaws lead to more outages?
text:
Could AI’s discovery of software flaws lead to more outages?
Cybersecurity experts say AI is helping uncover software vulnerabilities — putting pressure on companies to patch systems without causing new disruptions.
Could AI’s discovery of software flaws lead to more outages?
Cybersecurity experts say AI is helping uncover software vulnerabilities — putting pressure on companies to patch systems without causing new disruptions.
Flights grounded. Email inboxes unavailable. Banking transactions delayed.
As technology outages pile up, cybersecurity experts say artificial intelligence may be adding pressure to the race between finding software vulnerabilities and fixing them. But they caution that there is no clear evidence linking the recent disruptions to one another.
“There’s nothing that we see that is necessarily linking these,” said cybersecurity expert Christina Powers. “But it could be tying back to just the pace of needing to stay on top of security fixes and upgrades to keep pace with the way that AI is exposing vulnerabilities in systems.”
A software patch is an update designed to fix a flaw or improve a program. Installing one is essential to protect systems from attackers, but changing one part of complex software can sometimes disrupt another.
Companies track known software vulnerabilities through records called Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVEs. More than 100,000 vulnerability records have been reported to the public database this year — more than double the total from all of last year.
That amounts to as many as 300 vulnerabilities a day for security teams to assess.
Darrell West of the Brookings Institution said artificial intelligence is a major reason for the increase in reported vulnerabilities.
“The big increase that we’ve seen over the past year is due in large part to AI finding those vulnerabilities,” West said.
Powers said AI can help identify weaknesses, but attackers can also use it to write code that exploits them. That creates pressure on organizations to address flaws faster, she said, even as they try to test updates carefully.
“Not only is there a much higher volume of vulnerabilities that organizations have to deal with, they also have to look to address them a lot faster because the attackers are able to exploit them a lot faster,” Powers said.
A Google Cloud report from Mandiant, M-Trends 2026, underscores how quickly that race can move. It estimates the mean time to exploit vulnerabilities at minus seven days — meaning attackers are often exploiting flaws before a patch is released.
West said companies should test software updates on a smaller scale before applying them across an entire system.
“Companies should do pilot testing of their software updates, as opposed to just rolling it out for the system as a whole and hoping that it works well,” he said.
The pressure to move quickly is unlikely to disappear. West described the contest over vulnerabilities as a “game of cat and mouse”: AI can help find weaknesses, while other actors may use AI to exploit them.
Powers said companies also need to understand how their systems depend on one another, so a technical problem in one part of a network does not spread into a wider disruption.
When asked if we are going to see an increase in outages, Powers said, "Potentially, we could see more outages as organizations are looking to move quickly to address known vulnerabilities, to apply patches, to try to just move faster than they have in the past."
Our partners at PolitiFact have advice to protect your personal devices and information before another outage occurs:
- Keep software updated.
- Use strong passwords and don't reuse them across websites. A verified password manager can help store passwords securely.
- Use multifactor authentication.
- Keep a data backup.

title: NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from an awe-inspiring one light-day away
text:
NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from awe-inspiring one light-day away
NASA's Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away, marking humanity's first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space.
Flight controllers received the spacecraft's call Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent. That's how long it took for the radio signal to traverse the more than 16 billion miles at the speed of light.
"Voyager 1 light-day distance confirmed ... Voyager 1 continues its journey into the unknown," controller Nshan Kazaryan announced to cheers and applause.
For a spacecraft already loaded with historic firsts, it was an especially momentous milestone.
"Once again Voyager breaking records, breaking boundaries and taking humanity on a voyage," NASA's science mission chief Nicky Fox said. "There's no end for the Voyager mission."
Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 swept past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, snapped the most distant photo ever taken of our "Pale Blue Dot" in 1990, became the most distant human-made object in 1998, and crossed from the sun's sphere of influence into the vast void between stars in 2012.
NASA could not confirm the newest distance record until the signal reached the control team at California's Jet Propulsion Laboratory via the deep space telescope near Madrid. But that didn’t stop the space agency from wishing everyone a "Happy Voyager light-day … day!" via social media on Wednesday.
Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, are NASA's longest-operating space missions, churning out data for nearly a half-century despite powering down most of their instruments to keep exploring.
Voyager 2 actually beat its twin into space by two weeks. But its route to Jupiter and Saturn, plus Uranus and Neptune, was slower and longer, and it did not reach interstellar space until 2018. It won't reach the one-light-day mark until 2035.
Both spacecraft are doing well for their 49 years of age, plowing through space at 38,000 mph with plutonium for power. Picture-taking ended long ago, but they typically send back bits of precious data almost every day on their never-before-explored environment.
Over the weekend, though, Voyager 1's stream of science and engineering data came to an abrupt halt. The carrier signal that normally conveys that data kept coming in strong and, along with flight path calculations, allowed the team to confirm the light-day milestone. Controllers are trying to figure out why the flow of science and engineering data stopped. A similar problem three years ago was traced to an onboard computer.
Each Voyager carries a so-called Golden Record brimming with the sounds of Earth. The project was led by the late Cornell University astronomer Carl Sagan, who also coined the phrase "Pale Blue Dot" for Voyager 1's farewell glimpse of Earth.
NASA expects the gold-plated phonographic records — time capsules for anyone or anything that might encounter them — to last more than 1 billion years.
"No matter how long it takes or how dark things get or what we think our limitations are, we should never stop shining and never stop reaching for the stars. For we never know how far we will go," said deputy project scientist Jamie Rankin of Princeton University. "Shine on, Voyager, shine on."

title: Aging Untold: How to keep the peace when grandparents don’t get along
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore how families can navigate conflict between grandparents on both sides, keep the peace and focus on what’s best for the grandchildren.
Then we look at how planning for aging can ease uncertainty and help protect independence.
Plus, we decode emoji and texting slang so parents and grandparents can better understand kids’ online conversations and support their safety.
When grandparents don’t get along, it can create tension, especially during holidays, birthdays and major family events.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said children learn from how adults behave around them. Families can manage those relationships by keeping the child’s well-being first, gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.
The Aging Untold experts are offering advice on how to do that along with setting ground rules for tough topics and showing children what respect looks like.
If conflict continues after families have tried to resolve it, aging expert Amy O’Rourke said separate arrangements can help.
Aging is normal. It is not a crisis, but it can become one without preparing for the help you or a loved one will need in the future.
The Aging Untold experts said everyone is aging, and a fall, hospitalization, new diagnosis or sudden need for care can quickly expose the lack of conversations about money, housing, insurance, caregiving and independence.
Learn what families can do ahead of time to ease into the care that comes with aging.
You might be familiar with LOL, BRB and many emojis, including hearts and thumbs-up. But some emojis and acronyms have hidden meanings that parents and grandparents might not know.
Jill Story said it is tough to stay on top of the abbreviated language her three daughters use.
“They have a whole language that they use that I’m constantly having to, like, figure out,” she said.
Story said some of the acronyms her daughters use are even more difficult to decipher.
The founder of For Working Parents, a former vice principal, detailed what he described as sinister emojis, symbols that could represent something different from what parents might think. The meanings range from drugs to sex to extremism.
Larry Coffin is a former history teacher. The 82-year-old is also a living link to the history of his town, Bradford, Vermont.
He serves as the curator of the Bradford Historical Society and writes about the history of the town and surrounding communities.
“To me, is like he’s still teaching,” Carolyn, his wife of 57 years, said.
Coffin said he does it because it keeps his brain active.

title: Sen. Warner links recent tech outages to AI, calls for more oversight
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), the Vice Chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said artificial intelligence is responsible for the recent surge in tech outages across the U.S. He said he wants more federal oversight of the industry.
Warner said companies are using AI to prevent AI hacks and are struggling to keep up with the speed of the programs. He said he believes the entire AI field needs more oversight.
Americans have seen tech systems go down over the course of one week, including ground stoppages, Microsoft Outlook and banks. Some Americans have grown suspicious of a cyber attack.
Warner said the Federal Aviation Administration issues had to do with replacing a router. He said the other outages share the same cause.
“All of these are related to AI,” he said.
Warner said the outages are coming from companies using similar software to perform preventative maintenance to avoid cyber attacks.
“AI tools, particularly Mythos that came from Anthropic, are finding a number of vulnerabilities,” he said.
Warner used a pipe leak analogy to explain how AI is shifting security.
“Where it used to be you’d have one leak a month or every three months, you may have 100 leaks in a single day,” he said.
Warner said he believes the government has been too hands off when it comes to the buildout of AI. He said he believes stronger oversight is needed given how large a bet the U.S. economy has made on the technology.
“We are flying blindly with trillions of dollars of investment without the kind of oversight from the regulatory agencies and from the investment community that’s needed,” Warner said.
He’s cosponsoring a bipartisan bill that would require more transparency on AI company investment. It also would require companies with significant AI exposure to provide more information on potential risks.

title: How we can pay for Medicare for All
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How can we pay for universal healthcare? By cutting the inefficiencies out of the system, like Medicare does. Medicare’s budget is about 2% for non-medical spending (the highest number I found for that expense).
In a commercial insurance company, about 8% goes to administrative costs (it costs a lot of money to deny care for so many evaluations, tests and procedures), 2% goes to taxes and fees, 3% goes to agents and brokers and 3% to 5% goes to investors. In other words, 16% to 18% goes for non-medical expenses.
Some 47% to 65% of Mainers (the number is very difficult to calculate) get health insurance from employers — virtually all of which is from commercial insurance companies.
To make the calculation simple and conservative, I will use 50% as the percentage of Mainers who get their healthcare insurance from their employer. That means that Mainers are sending 8% to 9% of their healthcare dollars to entities other than providers.
That is inefficient! And it could be fixed by some entity, the state of Maine or the U.S. government, providing healthcare coverage to everyone, like Medicare does.
It would be very easy to save that 8 or 9% and give everyone in the country health insurance. Why don’t we do it? I think everyone can answer that question for themselves. And we should all work to fix this.
Ben Lounsbury, MD
Auburn

title: Trump's pick to lead CISA says Jan. 6 was not an attack on the Capitol
text:
Trump's pick to lead CISA says Jan. 6 was not an attack on the Capitol
President Donald Trump's nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) faced tough questions from lawmakers about the Capitol attack and the 2020 election during his Senate testimony.
Trump's pick to lead CISA says Jan. 6 was not an attack on the Capitol
President Donald Trump's nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) faced tough questions from lawmakers about the Capitol attack and the 2020 election during his Senate testimony.
President Donald Trump's nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) faced scrutiny from lawmakers Thursday as the agency remains without a Senate-confirmed director for nearly two years.
Michael LoSapio, currently the chief information security officer at the artificial intelligence firm Palantir, is Trump's pick to head CISA, which protects critical infrastructure such as nuclear power plants, banks and elections.
During his testimony on Capitol Hill, Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked LoSapio to characterize the events at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.
"Was there an attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021?" Blumenthal asked.
"I, I, I don't know," LoSapio said.
"You don't know?" Blumenthal pressed.
"I, I, I don't know," LoSapio said. "I don't believe it was an attack, no."
Blumenthal responded, "You're giving us that answer?"
"I wasn't involved in politics," LoSapio said.
Blumenthal also asked LoSapio who won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election, referencing President Trump's false claims that he won. LoSapio declined to answer, saying he would not answer a question about an election six years ago.
Democrats also pressed LoSapio on whether he would reverse staffing and budget cuts at CISA to prevent outages. He largely avoided answering, stating he would report back after conducting an analysis on funding and gaps.

title: Court approves $7.25 billion settlement with Bayer over claims Roundup weedkiller caused cancer
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from U.S. cancer patients asserting the company should have warned people that its popular weedkiller Roundup could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved Friday by a Missouri judge.
The nationwide settlement applies both to Roundup users who already are ill and those who become diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in future years. Participants could get an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, depending on how they used the product, how old they were when diagnosed and the severity of their illness.
For Germany-based Bayer, which denies that Roundup causes cancer, the settlement provides some financial certainty against mounting litigation costs that have led it to contemplate pulling the product from U.S. agricultural markets.
Litigants also faced uncertainty. While the settlement was pending, the U.S. Supreme Court undercut one of the central arguments in the Roundup lawsuits. The high court ruled in June that Bayer cannot be sued in state courts on claims it failed to warn about cancer, because federal regulations don’t require a cancer warning label and states are forbidden from imposing additional labeling requirements.
Though some attorneys for cancer patients contend the settlement payouts are too small, others argue the deal is better than getting nothing — which became a heightened likelihood after the Supreme Court ruling.
In a written judgment granting approval, St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer said the average individual payouts are “fair and adequate” and the total dollar amount is “among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements.”
Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said in a statement that the court-approved settlement is “a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation.”
The decision could be appealed.
Roundup has been used on weeds for over 50 years
Missouri-based Monsanto debuted Roundup weedkiller in 1974 with the chemical glyphosate as its active ingredient. The product quickly became one of the most widely used herbicides in agriculture. Roundup is designed to be used with genetically modified seeds that can resist the weedkiller’s deadly effect, thus allowing farmers to produce more while conserving the soil by tilling it less.
The product also is commonly applied on lawns and gardens.
Bayer added Roundup to its portfolio when it acquired Monsanto in 2018. With it came a growing number of lawsuits alleging glyphosate causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. But that remains in dispute. The World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer classified the chemical as “probably carcinogenic” in 2015. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has determined that it’s not likely to cause cancer in humans when used as directed.
About 200,000 Roundup-related claims have been made against Bayer, many coming from people who used it on residential lawns and gardens. As a result, Bayer has removed glyphosate from its new versions of Roundup sold for residential markets.
The lawsuits have produced mixed results. Only a couple dozen cases have gone to jurors, some siding with Bayer and others with plaintiffs. In one case, a Georgia jury awarded plaintiffs $2.1 billion.
In the first Roundup verdict since the Supreme Court’s precedent-setting ruling, a Missouri jury in October sided with Bayer in a case alleging design defects, negligence and fraud. The verdict “should send a strong signal” that plaintiffs “will face significant challenges” pursuing Roundup-related cancer claims in the future, said Bill Dodero, Bayer’s U.S. general counsel and global litigation leader.

title: Maine plans to delay MaineCare work requirements until July 2027
text:
Maine plans to delay MaineCare work requirements until July 2027
Maine will delay implementation of MaineCare work requirements until July 2027, using a federal grace period to avoid cutting coverage solely for noncompliance.
Maine plans to delay MaineCare work requirements until July 2027
Maine will delay implementation of MaineCare work requirements until July 2027, using a federal grace period to avoid cutting coverage solely for noncompliance.
Maine plans to opt in to the federal government's six-month "hold harmless" period before denying or ending MaineCare coverage solely because someone does not meet new work requirements, according to a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Health and Human Services.
The period would apply to people whose MaineCare applications or renewals are initiated from Jan. 1 through June 30, 2027. State officials say they could keep or receive coverage if they meet the program's other eligibility requirements.
The federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced the optional period Nov. 13. States that opt in must still assess whether applicants and beneficiaries meet the requirements, but they cannot deny applications or end coverage solely for noncompliance during the period.
Maine plans to use the time to strengthen and extensively test its eligibility systems ahead of full implementation on July 1, 2027.
In July, Maine DHHS estimated that the new work requirements would lead to more than 31,000 people losing their health insurance coverage.

title: ‘This program saved my life’: veteran credits horse therapy
text:
Folsom, La. — Some veterans and first responders in Louisiana are finding peace at New Heights Therapy Center, the only equine-assisted therapy center of its kind in the state. Participants do not ride the horses. They groom and lead them, building trust, reducing stress and regulating emotions.
Coast Guard veteran Juliet LeBlanc, who says she struggles with PTSD, said horses were the key to her healing. “This program saved my life,” LeBlanc said. She has graduated from the program and still volunteers at the center.
Program Director Vicki Eiland said most people find the center through word of mouth. “So we saw that need and developed a program to help them build resilience and connect with other veterans,” Eiland said.
Adam Shields, a fire prevention captain with St. Tammany Fire District Five, said the program helps him reset without saying a word. “I’m not familiar with horses, but I’m much better now,” Shields said. Folsom police officer Patrick Fair said it took four weeks to get comfortable with the horses. He has since built a relationship with Pete.

title: 14-year-old’s death ruled homicide after alleged online manipulation and extortion, authorities say
text:
FORT WAYNE, Ind. (WPTA/Gray News) - The death of a 14-year-old Indiana girl has been ruled a homicide after authorities said she was subjected to psychological manipulation and extortion by an outside actor.
Brynlee Jo Stempa’s death was ruled a homicide following an autopsy, toxicology testing and an “extensive review of digital and investigative evidence,” according to the Allen County Coroner’s Office.
The coroner’s office said evidence provided by Fort Wayne police, the FBI and international law enforcement partners showed that Stempa’s death was “directly orchestrated and compelled through severe psychological manipulation and extortion by an outside actor.”
The office explained that, under forensic pathology standards, a homicide ruling means a death resulted from the intentional, coercive or culpable actions of another person.
The FBI said German authorities arrested a man in connection with her death. German broadcaster NDR reported that the suspect was 17 at the time of the alleged crime, according to the Hamburg Public Prosecutor’s Office.
Prosecutors said the suspect allegedly demanded that Stempa harm herself and later tried to obtain recordings of her death, NDR reported.
The broadcaster also reported that investigators found references to a group known as the “Nefarious Maniac Cult” in Stempa’s recordings.
Last month, Fort Wayne police warned families and educators about online networks that target children and other vulnerable people.
Police said perpetrators use platforms including Discord, Roblox and Telegram to build relationships with potential victims.

title: Fiona the hippo had hat lodged in small intestine, post-mortem exam shows
text:
Fiona the hippo had hat lodged in small intestine, post-mortem exam shows
Fiona the hippo had a hat lodged in her small intestine, a post-mortem exam shows.
The Cincinnati Zoo's beloved Nile hippopotamus died Thursday nearly two weeks after she swallowed a knit cap. She was 9 years old.
According to the zoo, a necropsy — a post-mortem surgical examination of animals — was done on Fiona and showed that the hat that she had swallowed was in the middle of her small intestine, located 25 feet beyond the final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines.
A hippo's intestinal tract is estimated to be over 100 feet long, with more than 70 feet in the small intestine alone.
Related video above | Fiona the hippo: Remembering the hippo who won our hearts
“Upper and lower GI endoscopy were unable to reach the object,” said Cincinnati Zoo’s director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger. “The location and anatomy made laparoscopic removal impossible. No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked."
Wenninger said surgery, such as an open incision surgery, would "have been a death sentence" for a hippo of Fiona's size.
"The only option we had was supportive care, and unfortunately that wasn’t enough for her," Wenninger said.
The hippo, who became an internet sensation after her premature birth, had been behind the scenes for the better part of two weeks after swallowing the hat.
Zoo officials say a bizarre series of events launched the cap into the hippo habitat.
It was tossed into the air in front of the zoo’s hippo enclosure, where it was caught by a massive ceiling fan and then was catapulted through a tiny 1-foot opening above the tank’s 12-foot-tall viewing windows.
“We probably couldn’t make it happen again if we tried,” a zoo spokesperson said of the incident.
Zoo officials said they tried everything in their power to help Fiona pass the hat through her system – including acquiring a nine-foot scope to attempt a colonoscopy, and providing laxative-like supplements to “push things through.”
The zoo provided 24-hour care, but said her condition worsened over time. Zoo officials ultimately announced her passing on Thursday saying, "Please keep her keepers and everyone who tried to help her in your thoughts as they try to navigate and come to terms with this shocking news. They are also, understandably, asking for space at this time."
Fiona’s story
Fiona weighed 29 pounds when she was born on Jan. 24, 2017, at the Cincinnati Zoo. She was six weeks premature and weighed about 25 pounds lighter than the lowest recorded birth weight for the species.
Hippos are generally born closer to 100 pounds.
Her tiny size made it difficult for her to stand and nurse, so zoo staff gave her round-the-clock care.
The world watched as caregivers helped her build strength with pool exercises, bottle feedings and plenty of close attention. Fiona steadily grew into a healthy young hippo, and her progress drew fans from around the world.
She became the zoo’s most famous resident, and one of the best-known hippos in the world. Visitors often recognized her by her lively curiosity — and by the way she can make even a routine swim look like a big event.
She became a big sister in 2022 when her mother, Bibi, gave birth to a healthy boy, Fritz.
Fiona and her family were among the zoo’s top attractions, delighting guests by swimming in their habitat known as Hippo Cove and snacking on hippo-appropriate treats like watermelons and, most recently, a whole pumpkin.
Fiona even had her own line of merch at the zoo’s gift shop.
The rest of the bloat
The zoo says that the rest of the hippo bloat—Tucker, Bibi and Fritz—are eating and behaving normally.
“It’s difficult to know how they’re feeling," the zoo's director of animal care Christina Gorsuch said. "But they appear to be their normal selves.”
The zoo says that keepers, vets, staff and volunteers are "shaken" and are trying to navigate the loss of Fiona.
"She meant a lot to a lot of people," the zoo said.
The zoo is remaining open, but the area around Hippo Cove will be closed through the weekend.
How you can help
The zoo says it has received many inquiries about how they can show their support.
In lieu of flowers, food and other material gifts, the zoo says they are asking "people honor Fiona by spreading love and cheer to those around you."
The zoo is accepting monetary memorial donations as well.

title: Formerly ‘dry’ coastal Maine town votes to allow on-site alcohol sales and consumption
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Voters in the town of Penobscot approved a measure that will allow a proposed local pub to get licensed to sell beer to its customers.
The vote at the special town meeting Friday night at the local fire station was split into two parts. The first vote was to allow on-premises alcohol consumption sales Mondays through Saturdays. The second vote was to allow them on Sundays.
Voters approved Sunday sales 187-102. They also voted 221-100 to allow sales the rest of the week.
The town has allowed local businesses to sell alcohol for customers to take home for several years, but selling open containers to allow people to consume on-site has not been allowed until now.
The local deliberations on the topic, which prompted letters published by local media outlets and debates among residents at local meetings, are a throwback to when many small towns in Maine and beyond were ‘dry’ towns that did not allow alcohol sales of any kind, either to consume on site or take home.
Many Maine towns, including Penobscot, first voted on specific liquor ordinances in a 1968 referendum. Some have remained dry because, in small communities with few local businesses, there’s simply been no reason to revisit the subject.
Several have loosened up laws in recent years, often holding votes at the requests of local businesses — though others have told the Bangor Daily News in the past that they’re happy to keep their restrictions, saying the bans suit the quiet natures of their towns.
Jamie MacNair, owner of the local Northern Bay Market who plans to open a pub behind the store, was the main proponent of throwing out Penobscot’s ban on selling alcohol for on-site consumption. She hugged supporters and cheered when the first vote came through heavily on her side.
“I think the overwhelming ‘yes’ was a message to the folks against expanding or change in Penobscot,” MacNair said. “I’m hoping I’ll win them over.”
MacNair said her store has been selling hard liquor to take home since 2019, when Penobscot took its first step to become a wetter town. Before then, she could only sell wine and beer for people to take home. She said that step went smoothly without causing any commotion.
“We’ve been very responsible with those,” she said. “The pub will operate the same way.”
BDN reporter Elizabeth Walztoni contributed to this story.

title: Former manager sentenced for contaminating coworker’s mug with bodily fluid
text:
PITTSBURGH, Pa. (WPXI) – A former healthcare company manager was sentenced Tuesday to one to two years in jail after pleading guilty to a stalking charge as part of a plea deal.
Prosecutors said Timothy Haver contaminated a Highmark Health coworker’s drink with his own bodily fluids.
Haver was taken out of the Allegheny County Courthouse in handcuffs.
Details of the case
Prosecutors said Haver put his bodily fluids into a female coworker’s mug at least five times.
Highmark detectives set up a sting to catch him on surveillance. When he was questioned, Haver told detectives he wanted to get close to the victim.
Victim impact statements
The victim and her husband each read victim impact statements Tuesday.
She told the judge it has been “the worst year of her life.” She said Haver was her direct manager.
The victim said she now suffers from PTSD and becomes anxious when accepting a cup of coffee from someone.
Her husband called Haver a criminal.
Defense attorney comments
Haver’s defense attorney, Casey White, spoke after the plea.
“He feels remorse for everyone involved, including his family, her family, and he’s hopeful she’s able to put this behind her,” White said.
White said the biggest goal for Haver was to keep him off the Megan’s Law registry.
“He’s sitting in the county jail, so it’s certainly not a win. Is it a win that he’s not going to be on the Megan’s Law registration? Yes, candidly, but he’s got a lot to deal with. Sitting at the county jail is certainly not sitting at a Hilton hotel for a year. He’s sitting in the county jail,” White said.
Haver’s statement in court
Before he was sentenced, Haver turned around to look at the victim and her husband and apologized.
“I wish I had an exact answer as to why I did this. Part of my brain didn’t signal that this was wrong,” Haver said.
During the hearing, the judge asked Haver how he would feel if someone did to his wife what he did to the victim.
“He’s been contrite. He’s upset. He still doesn’t understand why he did what he did. He’s embarrassed,” White said.

title: 'Taught me everything I know': Bruno Mars announces death of father
text:
'Taught me everything I know': Bruno Mars announces death of father
Singer Bruno Mars has announced that his father, Peter Hernandez, has died at the age of 74.
Related video above: Phil Collins at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony
The 41-year-old singer, born Peter Gene Hernandez, announced his father's death in a tribute posted to his Instagram feed on Thursday, Nov. 19. No cause of death has been listed.
"Last week I got to hug my father one last time," Mars wrote, alongside a photo of himself hugging his dad in a hospital bed.
"If you've ever seen me talk about him I've always said that he's the man that taught me everything I know, especially when it comes to music," Mars said. "He raised my four beautiful sisters, my brother, and me. In my eyes he was the greatest dad in the world, and I will miss him everyday until we meet again."
A musician in his own right, the elder Hernandez had spoken in the past about his musical upbringing.
"I lived 'West Side Story,'" he told MidWeek in 2014, referring to his Jewish and Puerto Rican heritage. "Without the dancing." He grew up accompanying his own father to performances, where his first musical influences — the Latin orchestra his father played in — began to take root.
He said he also grew up fascinated by doo-wop, rebranding himself as "Dr. Doo-Wop" at 13 years old, and later forming a band, the Love Notes, which numbered up to 18 people, in Hawaii. The band was inducted into the Doo-Wop Hall of Fame in 2014, according to the Boston Globe.
In a 2017 interview with Latina magazine, Mars credited his dad with inspiring his musical taste and his sense of style.
"My whole sense of rhythm is because my dad was teaching me bongos as a kid," he said. "He's an old-school working musician, so that's where the pinky rings come from, the patent-leather shoes, the suits, and the pompadour. It all stems from watching my father."
Mars, who just received six new Grammy nominations earlier this week, signed off his post with a heartfelt message to both of his parents.
"I Love you Pops. Kiss mom up there for me," he said, referring to his late mother, Bernadette San Pedro Bayot, who died from a brain aneurysm in 2013.

title: Vigil held for 17-year-old killed in Waldoboro hit-and-run
text:
NOBLEBORO, Maine (WMTW) - Dozens gathered for a vigil on Thursday to remember Brody Sawyer, the 17-year-old killed in a Waldoboro hit-and-run on Friendship Road. The crowd said prayers, shared memories, and called for justice.
“We have never seen anything like this here; I am just in shock,” said Jennifer Powers, a family friend and organizer of the vigil.
Sawyer was killed when Gifford Campbell, 53, veered into the right lane where Sawyer was walking, hit him, and sped away.
“I have a lot of memories that I can’t put into words right now without tearing up,” said Chris Collins, Sawyer’s grandfather.
Collins said he and his grandson loved to fish and hang out together, and got out on the water a few times this past summer. Collins also said Sawyer loved his family, girlfriend, and cat. Friends at the vigil also shared memories and how much Sawyer will be missed at school and around town.
“It’s worse when it is a child, and seeing his friends all so young saying this person was taken from the Earth way too soon,” Powers said.
Campbell has been charged with manslaughter, OUI, drugs resulting in death and leaving the scene of an accident resulting in death. He is being held at the Two Bridge Regional Jail and is scheduled to appear in court on Friday.
“I hope that guy gets what he deserves,” Collins said.
