title: Obituary: Carol A. Main
text:
PHIPPSBURG – We lost a true gem when Carol A. Main passed away Nov. 1, 2026, at age 88 as the result of a fall. She was born in Lynn, Mass., to Clifford and Mabel (McGill) Hogseth on July 10, 1938, and grew up in Saugus. Carol married Charlie Main in 1958. One of her favorite experiences was driving cross country to the national parks in a VW camper with their St. Bernard. When Charlie landed a career at BIW, they bought Butler Hill Farm in Phippsburg, the place Carol called home. She was a proud “Burger.” They were active with MOFGA, grew an enviable organic garden, and sold raspberries at the farm. They raised many animals – cows, pigs, chickens, goats and racehorses.
Carol had a lifetime career as an administrative assistant at the IRS in Boston, Millersville State College in Pennsylvania, the law office of Donald Spear in Bath, Flaherty Realty, and Chewonki until she opened Kennebec Office Services. For 17 years she managed rentals for the St. John cottages on Morse Mountain. In every role she made friends with both coworkers and customers. Many tenants of Morse Mountain stayed in touch for years because of the connection she made with them. Anyone who stopped by was welcomed with a visit and cup of tea.
Causes Carol believed in received her full energy and skills. In 1974 she was a founding member of the Phippsburg Land Trust and served as secretary of the board for years. She was active with the Phippsburg Historical Society and Albert F. Totman Library. She spent countless hours selling items for Midcoast Humane Society, volunteered at Paw in the Door cat rescue, and supported many animal rescue organizations with her donations.
After Charlie’s passing in 2022, Carol moved to the Plant Home in Bath, where she made friends with both residents and staff. She was known for her enviable sense of humor and quick wit; skills she carried until the end. Her life was celebrated at the Plant Home, and her ashes have joined Charlie’s at the Butler Hill Farm Cemetery in Phippsburg.
Donations in her memory to any of the organizations mentioned above
would be welcomed.

title: Man accused of calling, texting 911 more than 1,000 times in 3 days, police say
text:
SEATAC, Wash. (KOMO) — A SeaTac man was arrested for allegedly contacting 911 more than 1,000 times in three days, according to police.
Police said Subhan Mohammadi was upset about a court protection order.
Mohammadi was charged with telephone harassment and causing unnecessary emergency response.
Calls and texts came around the clock
April Colombo, a dispatch supervisor with King County 911, said the calls were continuous.
“I mean, it was around the clock. There was no break. It was constantly we would disconnect, he would call back,” Colombo said.
She said the caller used two cell phones and was texting and calling.
Colombo took over and sent officers to Mohammadi’s home.
Warning from police
Police said Mohammadi called 911 nonstop for three days. Body camera video shows SeaTac police warning him about the calls.
“I want to make sure you are abundantly clear, because if you continue this behavior, which is totally inappropriate, over 800 times you’ve called and texted over the last 24 hours, does that sound like harassment to you?” an officer said in the video.
Detectives said the calls resumed. They said dispatchers explained there was nothing they could do about his issue with the court.
Arrest
Sgt. Jason Houck of the King County Sheriff’s Office, SeaTac Precinct, said the number of calls reached about 1,400.
“It added up to right around that 1,400 times, and I was like, we need to go out and handle this by making an arrest,” Houck said.
Mohammadi was booked into jail for abusing the 911 system.
“We’ve never gotten to the point in my career – and I’ve been doing this 26 years – of actually charging somebody with abuse or harassment of 911 like that,” Houck said.
Police said the calls stopped after the arrest.
Dispatchers cite effect on emergency lines
Colombo said an incoming emergency call could be delayed while dispatchers handle repeated calls.
“It could be something medical or major in-progress call that’s coming in that needs to be handled,” Colombo said.
Dispatchers said non-emergency calls to 911 and harassment are becoming a frequent issue.
“We try to get them the correct resources so they will stop calling,” Colombo said.
Police said they will hold callers accountable when the calls don’t stop.
Houck said a delay in a call going through could affect the outcome of an emergency.
“It literally could be life or death a matter of seconds can make a difference if that call isn’t able to go through right away,” Houck said.

title: 16-year-old boy accused of killing his twin brother, police say
text:
(Gray News) - A 16-year-old is accused of killing his twin brother in Washington, D.C., according to authorities.
Jamari Young was charged as an adult with second-degree murder in connection with the death of his twin, Jabrell Young, the Metropolitan Police Department said.
Jabrell died after he was shot on the morning of Oct. 25 on 46th Street Northeast, police said. Jamari turned himself in at a police station on Nov. 18.
Jamari appeared in court Thursday and was held without bond, 7News reported.
The judge said he did not believe Jamari intended to kill his brother but found probable cause for a second-degree murder charge, WJLA reported.
The teens’ mother, Chantel Poe, told police the brothers had been “tussling” after someone was heard yelling, “stop touching my stuff.”
Poe said she tried to separate them, but “the joint [gun] came up and it went off,” according to the affidavit. She told police the gun was in Jamari’s hand.
“I didn’t mean to, it just went off, I didn’t mean to, I’m sorry Ma,” Jamari said afterward, according to the affidavit.
Poe described the brothers as “thick as thieves” and pointed to their close relationship in saying the shooting was an accident.

title: 'Still in disbelief': Fiona's caretaker reacts to beloved hippo's sudden death
text:
'Still in disbelief': Fiona's caretaker reacts to beloved hippo's sudden death
The death of Fiona the hippo is deeply affecting many who knew her, especially those closest to her throughout her remarkable life.
Senior keeper and one of Fiona's caretakers, Jenna Wingate, shared an emotional message to social media, mourning the loss of what she called "the most special, life-changing animal I've ever worked with."
"It feels like I've lost part of my identity, as well as the vessel that I was able to use to bring hope, joy and education to the world," Wingate penned in a message to her social media page.
"We lost her in the most horrific and tragic way....the unfairness of it all is hard to bear, we should have had her with us for another 40-50 years. We were already thinking of ways to celebrate her 10th birthday," Wingate said.
The beloved hippo was set to turn 10 in January, a milestone in her journey from preemie to growing hippo.
Fiona's story captured the hearts of millions across the world, especially those like Wingate, who became almost like a family member or friend.
"Fiona was a symbol of hope and inspiration for people all over the world. She became the most effective zoo ambassador I believe there has ever been. Gaining her in my life was life-changing, and losing her is also going to be life-changing," Wingate said.
"Losing any animal or loved one is heartbreaking, but her popularity and enormity make all of this almost too much to handle because there is no escape. She is all over my son's book shelf, the pictures hung in my home, the coffee mugs in my cabinets and t-shirts in my dresser. There's really nothing else like her."
"I'm not sure how to move on from this. She was magic wrapped in a hippo. She was a fighter. She brought people together. She was love. She was a conservationist. She was inspiration. She was our family. I love you Fiona and I am so sorry."

title: How conservation efforts helped bison recover from near extinction
text:
JAMESTOWN, N.D. (InvestigateTV) — More than 100 years of conservation efforts have helped keep bison from disappearing, and the population is now nearly half a million and growing, according to Ilana Xinos, executive director of the North American Bison Discovery Center.
Xinos called the story of American bison conservation is “the greatest success story.”
“Before the 20th century, right when bison got down to a population, I would say under a thousand, people went out to try to gather them up and save them,” Xinos said. “And there were ranchers. There were indigenous people. There were — one of them was a taxidermist, and he said, you know, these bison are going to go extinct, and I’m going on a journey to collect them for taxidermy so people can at least even know what they looked like. He changed his mind. He wanted to save them.”
Xinos said the story of American bison conservation is “the greatest success story.”
Bison are still considered “near threatened,” but enough exist that they can be found on dinner tables everywhere.
“They think, you know, if you eat a bison steak, like you’re contributing to their demise,” Xinos said. She said “people who are ranching bison love bison.”
Xinos said many people still think bison are extinct. Conservation of the national mammal can take different forms. “We don’t say your way is right, your way is wrong.”
She said the animal is meant to be wild, but human development makes that virtually impossible.
The animal’s spiritual importance to Native Americans, economic importance to ranchers and symbolic importance to the nation led to the National Bison Legacy Act of 2016, which made the bison the national mammal.
“This is an animal. It represents us. And look what it did and look how it keeps going,” Xinos said.
Yellowstone National Park is the only place where bison have lived continuously since prehistoric times, according to the National Park Service.
The National Park Service reports bison weigh more than 1,000 pounds, are agile and can reach speeds of up to 35 mph.
Bison can be aggressive, and rangers suggest staying at least 25 yards away. That is about two standard school bus lengths.

title: "Have a great day meow." New England flight delayed after cat gets loose
text:
"Have a great day meow." New England flight delayed after cat gets loose
A Delta Air Lines flight was delayed leaving Logan Airport in Boston due to an unusual issue in the cabin.
According to air traffic control audio, a cat got loose in the cabin.
Delta flight 2706 was taxiing to take off from Boston to go to Tampa, Florida, when the pilot can be heard on audio telling the tower that they had "a situation in the cabin" and needed to hold while the situation was addressed.
The plane was directed where to hold and the pilot was offered assistance, but the pilot said no assistance was needed.
After a few minutes, the pilot asked to get back in line for takeoff.
"Thanks for accommodating, we had a cat loose in the cabin," the pilot is heard saying on the air traffic control audio.
"That is a new one," the tower said. "You have a good day meow."
The flight was delayed by about 15 minutes as a result of the feline fiasco.

title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.
Rinderknecht, with little apparent reaction, gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. His father was present for the trial and as the verdict was read.
Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht’s first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial.
During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht’s state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by “societal revenge” like they previously did.
Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire’s origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.
After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?”
These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.
They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked. Jurors were instructed not to consider the Los Angeles Fire Department’s role in putting out the fire.
Rinderknecht’s defense attorney Steve Haney cast doubt on the government’s case and said that their evidence proves nothing.
Haney said the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was accessible to the public until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.
“Six days of anyone and everyone walking across the spot the government now calls a crime scene,” he said.
Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor’s testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht’s character, such as his angry text messages, because they were “evidence of the man, not evidence of the act.”

title: 82-year-old former history teacher preserves Vermont town’s past
text:
BRADFORD, Vt. (Aging Untold) — Larry Coffin is a former history teacher and, at 82, he continues to tell his town’s story and help preserve its history.
Writing local history
He writes about the history of Bradford and surrounding communities and serves as the curator of the Bradford Historical Society.
Coffin is working on an article about the history of veterinary medicine in the area. It will run in the local paper and on his blog.
“This will be about a 2,000-word article,” Coffin said.
He said he does this because it keeps his brain active.
“To me, is like he’s still teaching,” Carolyn, his wife of 57 years, said.
Teaching career
Coffin’s first classroom was at the old Bradford Academy. He arrived at the school in the fall of 1964 from Plymouth State College.
“I was very wet behind the ears,” Coffin said.
The school closed in 1971 to build Oxbow High School up the road. Coffin continued teaching there for 42 years.
The Bradford Academy building is now the town offices.
Coffin also served as town meeting moderator for 40 years.
“Listen to the word moderation. It’s part of the word moderator,” Coffin said. “I think people trusted me. I tried to be fair.”
Asked whether the building is a second home to him, Coffin said, “In many ways. Yeah.”
Bradford Historical Society
The third floor houses the Bradford Historical Society.
Bradford resident James Wilson, a farmer and blacksmith, made the first globe in the United States.
“Essentially, he was an uneducated person who did a great job,” Coffin said.
The Bradford Historical Society’s collection includes a globe dated 1810.
Asked whether he is the caretaker of Bradford’s history, Coffin said, “Well, I think in many ways that’s right.”

title: BC hockey shuts out UMaine
text:
ORONO, Maine — The Boston College Eagles scored a goal in each period and sophomore goalie Louka Cloutier made 33 saves as the Eagles earned an impressive 4-0 victory over the Black Bears at Alfond Arena on Friday night.
BC is now 5-5-2 overall and 4-2-1 in Hockey East and the Eagles have extended their unbeaten streak to four games (3-0-1).
UMaine fell to 6-6-1 and 2-4-1 and had its three-game unbeaten streak snapped (2-0-1).
The teams will play again on Saturday at 7.
Senior Albin Boija made 18 saves for the Black Bears, who have now scored just three goals in their last three games with one being an empty-netter.
UMaine has scored 10 goals in its last seven games.
Junior center Teddy Stiga scored a first-period goal and freshman left wing Alex Pelletier netted a second-period goal before junior center Dean Letourneau converted a breakaway and then added an empty net goal in the third period.
Stiga opened the scoring with 1:42 left in the first period.
Off a defensive zone faceoff, the Eagles broke out of their zone and created a three-on-three.
Carson Woodall fed the puck to Matias Vanhanen skating down the left wing into the offensive zone, and he made a nice pass to Stiga, who was trailing the play and was unattended in the inner half of the right faceoff circle.
Stiga took a few strides and snapped a wrister between the pads of Boija for his sixth goal of the season.
The Black Bears had a great opportunity to equalize shortly afterward when Oskar Komarov slid a pass from behind the net to a wide open Dante Siciliano in the low slot but Cloutier squeezed his pads to stop Siciliano’s one-timer.
Pelletier expanded the lead on the power play 1:02 into the second period.
Luka Radivojevic passed the puck to Oscar Hemming and he swept a waist-high one-timer toward the net.
Pelletier had his back to the net and was able to tip the puck downward past Boija for his second goal of the season.
The Black Bears had three power plays in the middle period but generated only two shots on goal and neither were of the high-percentage variety.
The three unsuccessful power plays extended UMaine’s power play drought to 0-for-18 since it last converted in the 7-2 loss to Boston University on Oct. 30.
UMaine had another power play midway through the third period but didn’t get produce a shot on goal.

title: Houlton police chief placed on administrative leave
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Breaking news
Our journalists are working right now to gather more details for you. The BDN publishes only verified information from trusted sources, so we don’t cite social media hearsay or police scanner chatter. Send a tip here.
Houlton Chief of Police Tim DeLuca was placed on paid administrative leave at 5 p.m. Thursday, pending an investigation, according to Town Manager Amber Jones.
Contacted Friday, DeLuca said he did not want to comment at this time.
Capt. Jasmine Cyr will serve as interim chief, Jones said.
There will be an internal investigation, although Jones declined to say what it relates to.
DeLuca came to Houlton as police chief in early 2017. Prior to that he was deputy chief at Old Orchard Beach Police Department, where he served in various roles for 33 years.
In November 2023, he was appointed interim town manager until a former town manager, Jeremy Smith, was hired six months later.
In the past year, the police department faced several challenges following former Town Manager Cameron Clark’s September 2025 arrest. In October 2025, the Maine Association of Police, Patrolman/Dispatcher and Command Unit Union delivered a letter of no confidence in town officials to the Town Council.
Since that time, there have been multiple resignations, leaving an already stretched department down five officers. Four of the five officers who resigned did so to take on higher paying roles with the Aroostook County Sheriff’s Office, according to DeLuca.
Until the new union contract was ratified at the end of September, the starting pay for an entry level officer in Houlton was $26.09 per hour as compared to the sheriff’s office at $35.20, Presque Isle Police at $30.37 and Caribou at $32.71, according to public records.
The contract raised pay $5 per hour, boosting an entry-level patrol wage from $26.09 to $31.09 per hour. Union employees will get an additional $1.50 per hour each year over the next two years of the contract.
“I am pleased the council recognized and supported a wage increase for our HPD officers and dispatchers to reflect increases throughout the region,” DeLuca said at the time. “This will allow us to recruit and retain the quality individuals required to be a Houlton police officer.”
DeLuca did not actively recruit while the contract was being negotiated, but after it was ratified with the bumped-up salaries, DeLuca said he was planning a big recruitment initiative.
Until new officers are hired and trained, DeLuca and Cyr have been working patrol shifts, DeLuca said last month.

title: InvestigateTV+: Protecting young athletes in the NIL era
text:
(InvestigateTV) — High school players are starting to cash in on Name, Image, Likeness (NIL) deals, and InvestigateTV+ explores how some states are trying to protect young athletes by regulating who gets a cut.
Then, we take an in-depth look at a tool some say can help protect people with dementia, when they wander off.
Plus, the biggest land animal in North America was once pushed to near extinction. We’ll explain how different communities fought to keep it part of our future.
Protecting young players
Name, image and likeness, or NIL, continues to dominate headlines and forever change the game for student athletes.
While the federal government tackles the college landscape, some states have enacted laws to protect high school students and their families.
In Louisiana, lawmakers recently passed legislation seeking to protect K-12 student athletes interested in signing NIL deals. Young players in the state can legally enter into big money contracts, but the new laws also look to add transparency and accountability.
Keeping track of family
Walking off alone can put people living with cognitive impairments in life-or-death situations.
Experts encourage families to make sure their loves ones have identifying information on them at all times. This can include caregiver contact and potentially GPS-enabled tracking tools.
In the summer of 2026, the Huntington Police Department rolled out the “Blue Lights the Way” program, aimed at protecting those who have a tendency to wander away from home.
Bison success story
Bison once roamed North America in the tens of millions. They became a critical part of Native American culture, which used the animal for food, shelter, tools, clothing and jewelry.
In the 1800s, the westward expansion of European settlers, along with railways, rifles and an international market for hides, led to the bison’s rapid decline.
Ilana Xinos called the story of American bison conservation is “the greatest success story.”
Supporting brides on a budget
Fighting human trafficking one wedding dress at a time. That is the mission of Adorned in Grace.
“We walk with young women, and we hope to show them that there are always opportunities for second chances and the story to continue,” said Kaitlin Berg.
The Bridal and Formalwear boutique is filled with donated dresses, some brand new from boutiques across the country, and others worn just once by another bride. All are under $1,000 with nearly 70% of every sale going directly to the mission – funding prevention, awareness, and survivor support.

title: ​​Missing Maine construction worker has been found
text:
A missing Maine construction worker has been found safe.
Alex Goncalves Dourado was reported missing after his family was unable to get in contact with him, according to the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office.
Dourado hadn’t been feeling well recently and didn’t have his own phone, complicating attempts to reach him.
He was working for a construction company in the Bethel area.
The sheriff’s office said late Thursday night that Dourado had been found safe.

title: Bicyclist suffered life-threatening injuries in Broadway collision
text:
A bicyclist suffered life-threatening injuries in a vehicle collision on Broadway in Bangor on Friday morning.
The bicyclist was hit about 5:30 a.m., according to Katy England, a spokesperson for the Bangor Police Department.
The crash happened near School Street.
The bicyclist, who hasn’t been publicly identified, was taken to the hospital with life-threatening injuries, England said in an email to the Bangor Daily News.
The crash closed Broadway near Walgreens Friday morning, prompting traffic to be detoured around the scene. The road has reopened.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: 2 women charged with murder after 3-year-old diagnosed with cancer did not see a doctor for 2 years, authorities say
text:
OZARK, Mo. (KY3/Gray News) — Two women have been charged in connection with the death of a 3-year-old boy who authorities said was diagnosed with cancer but was not taken to the doctor for treatment.
Police responded to a home in Ozark, Missouri, on July 31, where they found the boy dead. Officers wrote in court records that the child appeared undersized and severely malnourished.
Investigators learned the boy had been diagnosed with cancer as a baby but that he had not been seen by a doctor for two years before his death. According to investigators, the boy’s caregivers did not schedule follow-up appointments after he received his cancer diagnosis.
Investigators also described the home as cluttered with animal feces, urine and trash, according to the report.
A cause of death was not released.
The child’s mother, Destiny Schliefert, and another woman, Debbie Potter, who helped care for him, are charged with second-degree murder.
Both women are also charged with child abuse and endangering the welfare of a child.

title: Hampden waste facility gives new life to former Fiberight plant, with technology aimed at recovering more material
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HAMPDEN, Maine (WABI) - Years after the former Fiberight facility shut down, a waste-processing plant in Hampden is operating under a new name and using updated technology to sort material from communities across Maine.
Municipal Waste Solutions is receiving an average of about 600 tons of municipal solid waste a day, according to facility leaders. Over the past several months, the facility has added equipment and fine-tuned machinery that was used under its previous ownership.
“We’re servicing right now over 125 Maine municipalities, 115 of those are Municipal WasteHub members,” said Mike Carroll, CEO of Municipal WasteHub.
The Municipal WasteHub, represents communities that use the facility. Carroll said a second shift was added in early October and the operation now employs more than 40 people. He said many people have asked how they can become part of the facility.
How the sorting technology works
The facility is designed to sort mixed waste using equipment installed by CP Manufacturing. Belle Ryder, treasurer of the Municipal WasteHub board of directors, said that means participating residents do not have to separate their materials before disposal.
“Everything goes into one bag and the facility’s advanced equipment including optical sorters and robotic arms does the work,” Ryder said.
CP Manufacturing Systems Improvement Manager Alan Goode said newly installed artificial intelligence cameras can also monitor material leaving the back end of the system. That information can help operators see what might have been missed and look for ways to improve sorting.
“The new A-I camera, cameras, that we put in, it can actually visually see what is going out the backend and account for that as it’s going out so it can tell you that you’re losing 20% of this material or you’re losing 20% of that material and you can go back and look and see what you can do,” Goode said.
Goode’s percentages are examples of what the cameras can identify.
A goal of diverting waste from landfills
Facility leaders say the operation has added anaerobic digestion, a process in which microorganisms break down organic material without oxygen. They say the technology can help recover more material and divert up to 50 percent of waste that might otherwise go to a landfill.
Maine has set a goal of recycling 50% of its municipal solid waste; diversion and recycling are not necessarily the same measure.
“It helps control disposal costs, recovers valuable materials that would otherwise be wasted and gives our communities a more sustainable approach to managing waste,” Ryder said.
From Fiberight to Municipal Waste Solutions
The Hampden facility has a long history of delays and changes in ownership.
Fiberight operations stopped at the end of May 2020 amid financial problems. At the time, WABI reported that the operator was seeking financing for improvements and that member communities were diverting waste elsewhere.
Several attempts to find a buyer followed. In 2023, WABI reported that the MRC and Innovative Resource Recovery had signed an agreement to become co-owners of the facility under the Municipal Waste Solutions name.
The facility began receiving waste again in April 2025. At that point, officials said it would initially operate as a transfer station while they worked toward bringing the sorting equipment and anaerobic digesters online.
Carroll said proving the operation would work took time.
“Proving that it works, that took a lot of time. The due diligence just to make sure that we did it right took a long time,” he said.
Fire safeguards
Carroll also described a Fire Rover system that monitors the tipping floor, where waste is unloaded. He said thermal cameras analyze material for signs of smoldering or elevated temperatures and notify staff. If the temperature reaches a certain point, the system can deploy water and foam that does not contain PFAS onto the material
For Ryder, the work represents a new chapter for the facility and the communities it serves.
“I’m proud to have been a part of this project and see how far it’s come,” she said.

title: Family reburies relatives more than 2 years after hurricane washed out cemetery
text:
YANCEY COUNTY, N.C. (WLOS) — More than two years after Hurricane Helene washed away parts of a North Carolina cemetery, a family reburied two relatives whose remains were carried miles away by the storm.
Terry Miller said his grandmother and his aunt were laid back to rest in their original graves.
Miller said his mother, Glessie, has not been found.
“It’s been a long, hard two years,” Miller said.
Storm washed out cemetery
Hurricane Helene tore through Whitson Cemetery in Yancey County in September 2024. Floodwaters carried remains miles away and left the cemetery covered in debris.
“Everything was gone. All the tombstones, all the headstones in the whole cemetery were laying flat on the ground,” Miller said. “The area where my aunt and my mom and my grandparents were, everything was gone.”
Miller said crews had to haul in material to rebuild the cemetery.
“When we rebuilt the cemetery, it took 39 dump truckloads just to rebuild a small area back to the original size,” he said.
Remains found in Tennessee
Miller said answers came from Tennessee after more than two years of searching. He said he gave a DNA sample for a match.
“Finally, after digging through the rubble down in Tennessee, they were able to find my grandmother in Erwin,” Miller said.
His aunt was found in Jonesborough just over a week ago.
“I was happy because I was able to get closure on relocating them,” Miller said.
Miller said the East Tennessee State University forensic team played a significant role in identifying the family members.
Search for mother continues
“She was one of the last ones to wash out of the cemetery, and we still haven’t found her yet,” Miller said.
Miller said his mother, Glessie, remains missing.
“As they find any type of bone or anything, they can do a DNA and hopefully my mom, whether whatever can be found where, we can rebury her at the same time,” he said.
Miller said he hopes to rebury her at the same grave if remains are found.
“My mother, my grandmother, my aunt, they’re physically in heaven, but I’m glad that we can lay them back to rest in the original grave,” Miller said.

title: Man accused of calling, texting 911 more than 1,000 times in 3 days, police say
text:
SEATAC, Wash. (KOMO) — A SeaTac man was arrested for allegedly contacting 911 more than 1,000 times in three days, according to police.
Police said Subhan Mohammadi was upset about a court protection order.
Mohammadi was charged with telephone harassment and causing unnecessary emergency response.
Calls and texts came around the clock
April Colombo, a dispatch supervisor with King County 911, said the calls were continuous.
“I mean, it was around the clock. There was no break. It was constantly we would disconnect, he would call back,” Colombo said.
She said the caller used two cell phones and was texting and calling.
Colombo took over and sent officers to Mohammadi’s home.
Warning from police
Police said Mohammadi called 911 nonstop for three days. Body camera video shows SeaTac police warning him about the calls.
“I want to make sure you are abundantly clear, because if you continue this behavior, which is totally inappropriate, over 800 times you’ve called and texted over the last 24 hours, does that sound like harassment to you?” an officer said in the video.
Detectives said the calls resumed. They said dispatchers explained there was nothing they could do about his issue with the court.
Arrest
Sgt. Jason Houck of the King County Sheriff’s Office, SeaTac Precinct, said the number of calls reached about 1,400.
“It added up to right around that 1,400 times, and I was like, we need to go out and handle this by making an arrest,” Houck said.
Mohammadi was booked into jail for abusing the 911 system.
“We’ve never gotten to the point in my career – and I’ve been doing this 26 years – of actually charging somebody with abuse or harassment of 911 like that,” Houck said.
Police said the calls stopped after the arrest.
Dispatchers cite effect on emergency lines
Colombo said an incoming emergency call could be delayed while dispatchers handle repeated calls.
“It could be something medical or major in-progress call that’s coming in that needs to be handled,” Colombo said.
Dispatchers said non-emergency calls to 911 and harassment are becoming a frequent issue.
“We try to get them the correct resources so they will stop calling,” Colombo said.
Police said they will hold callers accountable when the calls don’t stop.
Houck said a delay in a call going through could affect the outcome of an emergency.
“It literally could be life or death a matter of seconds can make a difference if that call isn’t able to go through right away,” Houck said.

title: A 2nd federal judge blocks construction of Trump's memorial arch in DC
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A second federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump’s administration from building a 250-foot memorial arch in the nation’s capital, issuing an order on Friday that keeps the construction work on hold indefinitely, according to plaintiffs’ lawyers who sued to challenge the project.
U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema in Alexandria, Virginia, issued her order from the bench in a lawsuit brought by the Arlington County Board. Brinkema ruled two days after a different judge in Washington, D.C., extended a previous order that blocked the Trump administration from breaking ground on the arch on a more temporary basis.
The Virginia board claims Trump’s project will exacerbate traffic congestion and jeopardize public safety in the county, which is across the Potomac River from Washington.
“We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court,” plaintiffs’ attorney Kate Talmor said in a statement after Friday’s hearing.
On Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan in Washington agreed to extend a temporary restraining order keeping the project on hold until Dec. 3. The injunction issued by Brinkema doesn’t have a specified expiration date.
Chutkan initially blocked the arch’s construction on Nov. 5, shortly after a hearing of the National Capital Planning Commission ended with the Trump-heavy panel giving the arch its final approval in an 8-4 vote, despite dozens of witnesses who opposed the construction.
The case before Chutkan was filed on behalf of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian. Members of the Kennedy family filed a separate lawsuit last month, citing the impact the structure would have on Arlington National Cemetery, where family members are buried.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump, a Republican, has pushed in his efforts to leave a personal imprint on Washington’s historic landscape. At 250 feet, the arch would be twice the height of the Lincoln Memorial.
Brinkema was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Bill Clinton. Chutkan was nominated by Democratic President Barack Obama.

title: UMaine men's basketball team was at Quinnipiac during campus lockdown
text:
University of Maine men's basketball team was at Quinnipiac during campus lockdown
The University of Maine men's basketball team was playing a game at Quinnipiac University when a lockdown was issued Thursday night amid reports of a gunman on campus.
Hamden police said dispatchers received a call around 8 p.m. from a person who claimed to be armed and on the Quinnipiac campus.
The first alert, sent shortly before 8:35 p.m., said that all parts of the Quinnipiac campus were locked down and that members of the campus community should take shelter in a secure area until further notice.
That initial alert came during the second half of UMaine's game against Quinnipiac, which was played at M&T Bank Arena on the university's York Hill campus. The game was not interrupted, and the Black Bears won 69-67.
A UMaine spokesperson told Maine's Total Coverage that after the game, the team stayed in lockdown with the rest of the arena until just after 10:40 p.m., when the team was advised that it was safe to leave the York Hill campus and return to the hotel it was staying at.
The UMaine spokesperson said the team was already staying the night on Thursday ahead of its road game at the University of Massachusetts on Saturday, so the team's travel schedule was relatively unaffected by the Quinnipiac lockdown.
The lockdown continued at Quinnipiac's Mount Carmel campus until shortly before 2:30 a.m. Friday, when emergency response officials had completed a thorough sweep of all campus buildings and determined it was safe to resume normal activities.
"We are grateful to our community for the care, compassion and support shown to one another during last night's difficult events," Quinnipiac University said in a statement shared Friday morning. "This was a distressing experience. Counseling resources are available to students, faculty and staff. Thank you for looking out for one another."
Hamden police said the reports of a gunman on the Quinnipiac campus were determined to be "an apparent hoax." The university canceled Friday's classes.
Information from ABC affiliate WTNH was used in this report.

title: 3 Things To Remember As The Darkest Part Of The Year Settles In
text:
We're a couple of weeks out from the end of Daylight Saving Time, which wrapped up on November 1st this year. With that time change comes another change, a decrease in the number of daylight hours we're used to.
According to the Almanac, we've officially entered the "darkest" part of the year.
"Daylight drops fastest around the equinoxes and slows down as the winter solstice approaches."
The sun now sets earlier, and conditions stay dark longer. This has an impact on safety across the state, especially as it pertains to driving. Visibility becomes much more of an issue.
Read More: Broadway In Bangor Closed Friday Morning After Accident
And there are 3 factors you may want to keep in mind when it comes to safety in those darker hours; animals, delivery drivers and kids.
1.) Animals
Unaware of our implemented time changes, many animals use the cover of darkness to move from place to place.
Scanning the roadways for shadows or eye reflections, along with making sure you're alert are steps you can take to lessen your chance of colliding with an animal, big or small.
Aside from the morning commute, them majority of motorists are on the road between the hours of 3PM and 6PM. Taking extra care to stay aware of your surroundings as the sun goes down is key.
2.) Delivery Drivers
While you may not have thought anything of leaving your porch light or front door light off during the day before, it's important to consider that a number of your friendly, neighborhood delivery drivers work well into the evening, sometimes till 8 or 9 PM
If the sun goes down around 4 PM, and you don't get home from work till after 5 PM, there's a good chance whomever is brining that package to your house will be coming up an unlit driveway or stairwell.
Do your delivery person a solid and turn your outside lights on earlier. Light up your house for safety, not just the holidays!
And it's not just the UPS, FedEX or mail carriers you should consider, but those that deliver propane, oil and even doordashers.
Have their back, by lighting their way.
3.) Kids
After a long day in school, many kids head home to play.
Whether on their walk or bike back to the house, or their attempt to meet up with friends in their neighborhoods, it's likely that by the time they start their journeys for the afternoon, darkness will be setting in.
And sense safety isn't always front-and-center on the mind of a child, it should be in your mind.
Making sure your kids know to wear something light colored or even reflective is so important. Talking with your kids about staying out of the shadows, and near streetlights while they're moving from place to place is another things you can do to help keep kids safe.
Read More: Show Us Bangor + Eastern Maine Holiday Light Displays
Most important of all, in my opinion, would be to communicate to them that it's not only their own surrounding in space that they should be aware of, but where things like cars and cyclists are in the roadway.
It's also a good thing for drivers to approach any school bus, school zone, crosswalk or and residential sidestreet slowly and with caution this time of year after sunset.
The good news is the darkness doesn't last forever. There is light at the end of the tunnel, which we can wait out to enjoy, if we keep in mind these ways to keep ourselves and others safe this season.
Good luck!

title: Lala Woods suffers left knee injury in Maine’s 85-80 overtime win over VCU
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Lala Woods left Maine’s 85-80 overtime win over VCU midway through the fourth quarter with a left knee injury that occurred as she fell to the court chasing the ball into the backcourt along with a Rams player.
There was no post-game update to the severity of her injury after Kaliyah Sain helped lead the Black Bears to the win with 15 of her 29 points in overtime.
“Obviously, when you go down, your mind goes to the worst possible situation, or worst possible case. She has torn an ACL before, so of course her mind went there immediately. It’s just a matter of really trying to reframe her mind in the moment, just letting her breathe and relax, and we don’t know anything (on the severity of the injury),” said Amy Vachon, head coach.
“That’s really hard to watch one of your best players go down, but we did it for her. We knew that if we came out, played with our heart, played for her, that we would have a good turnaround, and we did,” said Sain, senior forward.
Maine returns to action when it hosts Penn on Sunday at 11:30 a.m.

title: By bungling Back Cove Music Festival, councilors let Portland down
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I almost bought the T-shirt.
If the Back Cove Music & Arts Festival was only going to happen once — as I assumed it would in the lead-up to the event two Augusts ago — I remember thinking I might want to have something to commemorate the experience.
I didn’t particularly like the shirt design, though, and was still trying to wrap my head around the $17 price tag on the giant White Claws being sold at the concession stands. Plus, by the time I got a look at the merch, I felt the festival was running smoothly, making its return seem more likely.
As I left Payson Park that Saturday night, after watching headliner Lord Huron play in front of Portland’s moonlit skyline, I was sure the festival would be back and that I would be, too.
With the announcement Tuesday that the festival won’t return, I’m having some Marden’s-style nonbuyer’s remorse about the shirt. Mostly, though, I’m disappointed that I won’t get to go again. And I’m perturbed that such a promising event met its end for seemingly preventable reasons.
To make the event financially viable, the festival’s organizers said its capacity would need to increase from 12,500 to 15,000 people. The city said it wasn’t likely to approve that change; the inaugural festival didn’t even reach the previously agreed-upon limit, with about 12,000 people attending each of the two days, according to organizers.
Based on the lack of lines and low-key nature of the festival, it seemed to me as though the park could handle the extra bodies — something the city might have been able to better evaluate, had the event been held this year.
That’s where the real issue lies.
People were skeptical at first, understandably, and not necessarily willing to risk $137 a day on an unproven concept (especially if they weren’t overly excited about the lineup, which included Jack White, Lucy Dacus and, originally, André 3000, who dropped out and was replaced by The Roots).
With the rave reviews this festival received, however, I have little doubt the following year would have been a sellout event.
We didn’t have a chance to find out because the Portland City Council’s Housing and Economic Development Committee spent too much time last fall scrutinizing the festival’s contract. As a result, organizers determined in January — as they had warned previously — that there wasn’t enough time left to pull off the event in 2026.
Mind you, there were no major problems with the three-year contract under consideration. Festival organizers already had agreed to give the city an increasing cut of ticket sales (up to $2 each) and pay $100,000 annually to the Portland Parks Conservancy. Money from the first event has gone toward safety improvements to Payson Park, including new bike lanes and speed bumps.
Changes made during the extended deliberations included increasing the noise deposit, from $1,000 to $5,000, and requiring council approval to transfer the festival agreement to another entity. There was nothing here worth thwarting what should have been a hallmark annual event for the city.
In the long run, the cancellation of this year’s festival might not have made a difference. The weekend could have been a washout, leaving the park torn up and attendees disappointed. A different lineup of artists could have brought out a more disruptive crowd, enraging the neighborhood. For any number of reasons, the city might never have approved the increased capacity. With all that said, a second festival would have given officials a better idea of what was feasible.
When the committee ultimately approved the three-year contract, outgoing Councilor Kate Sykes still wasn’t satisfied that the city was getting enough out of the agreement. Now, all we’re left with are memories. And, fittingly, a few new speed bumps.

title: Cruise ship tensions resurface at community forum
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BAR HARBOR — It was standing room only at the newly renovated Jesup Memorial Library on Wednesday as the Bar Harbor Chamber of Commerce hosted a community forum focused on cruise ship regulation. It's a topic that has recently been thrust back into the public discourse in a big way following the consequential decision by Judge Lance Walker earlier this month and the depletion of any larger cruise ships with "grandfathered" reservations heading into the 2027 summer tourist season.
The session began with the Chamber's executive director, Everal Eaton, providing some statistics from the 2026 season. According to Eaton, there were 12 "grandfathered" cruise ships with lower berth capacities exceeding the 1,000-passenger cap that called on Bar Harbor in September and October. There were also 55 of the smaller American Cruise Lines ships that visited Bar Harbor from May through October. Eaton said the town had seen a lower berth capacity baseline of 57,000, which is about 80% below the town's peak levels in 2022. There was also a decline in "total passenger days" from 204,000 in 2023 to about 57,000 in 2026.

title: 'She's a miracle': Ohio State marching band trumpeter takes center stage after beating rare cancer
text:
'She's a miracle': OSU marching band trumpeter takes center stage after beating rare cancer
Bengals fans were celebrating a massive win Sunday, but that wasn't the only triumph on the field for Ohio sports fans.
It also marked a major milestone for a Lebanon family whose daughter was told she'd never walk again after a cancer diagnosis.
Allison Morris was just six when doctors found a large tumor in her right hip, diagnosing her with Ewing Sarcoma bone cancer.
Despite hearing she might not walk again, she eventually marched to the tune of her own trumpet, making the Ohio State University Marching Band and performing during halftime Sunday at Paycor Stadium.
"I remember my high school band director showed Ohio State marching band videos in class, and I just thought it was like, the coolest thing ever," said Allison. "I was just excited about the idea of potentially joining the marching band."
Allison fought hard to be out on that field.
"My parents were told that I was never going to be able to walk again," she said.
To save her life, Allison went through major reconstructive hip surgery and more than a dozen rounds of chemotherapy.
"So, in place of my right pelvis, I have a metal claw that holds my femur in place," she said.
Her mom, Theresa Morris, remembers a time when she didn't know what Allison's future held.
"I remember the night before her surgery, videoing her dancing, thinking, this is the last time she'll do this ever," she said.
Cut to Sunday Night Football, Steelers versus Bengals, during a white-out at Paycor Stadium, Allison's dreams were shining bright on the biggest stage. 
"When I saw her march out for the first time, I just thought, like, I never would have thought this would have happened, and it's such a miracle. Cincinnati Children's Hospital is such a big part of that story," said mom, Theresa.
Allison is inspiring all those who helped her along the way, including the team behind her surgery at Cincinnati Children's.
"Her mom sent me a thank you letter; she attached a picture of her in her marching band uniform. I looked, and I was like, 'Oh my God, are you kidding me'?" said Dr. Joel Sorger. "Very, very happy and very proud."
Allison is also proud of how far she's come.
"I think it's super full-circle that I'm in the same place where I received all of my treatment, where I was able to learn how to walk again," she said.
This time, she's in Cincinnati to do what she loves most.
"I wish I could go back and tell like six-year-old Allison that it's all going to work out," she said. "Because this is not a moment I thought that I would get to experience."
Allison's folks still remember when Bengals players would visit her and other patients at Cincinnati Children's. For them to see her out there on that field, it meant everything.
Allison has now been cancer-free for 14 years.

title: This Maine island town’s plan to limit absentee vacation rental owners is working
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Three years after passing an ordinance to limit out-of-town ownership of short-term rentals, the island town of Stonington is seeing the results it hoped for.
As tourism increased and online bookings through sites such as Airbnb grew with it, residents worried that homes being bought as investment properties would hollow out its downtown and was hurting the housing prospects of year-round families and workers in the state’s top lobster port.
So, in March 2023, they approved by a 2-1 margin an ordinance requiring short-term rental owners to register with the town and limiting how such rentals could be operated, with a focus on regulating absentee owners.
The number of short-term rentals in Stonington owned by nonresidents listed has since dropped 14%, from 70 to 60, according to data from industry site AirDNA provided by the town. Overall, the number of short-term rentals is down from 140 in 2022 to 120 this year.
The limits are one part of a multi-pronged effort to address an acute housing shortage in the neighboring island towns of Deer Isle and Stonington that residents say seriously threatens its longevity as a year-round community. They’re trying to balance the tourism economy with the needs of its permanent workforce, a challenge particularly pronounced on the island but faced by communities across Maine.
“We are taking it seriously, and we think that all Maine towns need to take it seriously because otherwise, demographically, we are losing our workforce,” said Linda Nelson, the town’s economic and community development director. “…We are happy to be a poster child for being corrective of it.”
In 2023, Stonington had an estimated 145 short-term rentals, or 15% of its housing stock, the Bangor Daily News previously reported.
Increasing tourism was pushing it beyond the limits of its resources, particularly for drinking water, according to the town. It has had to haul in hundreds of thousands of gallons of water in recent summers, which the town’s water company has attributed to the new demand from rentals, not just drought conditions.
Especially in the densely built historic downtown, more short-term rentals created a situation like a resort without management, Nelson said: large groups and parties beyond occupancy limits and without building safety monitoring.
With vacation rentals growing from a home-based occupation of people renting out rooms into a larger commercial activity, regulations needed to catch up, according to Nelson.
“It’s government’s job to respond to markets and balance the market as best we can,” she said.
Officials hoped restricting that growth would make more of its housing stock available as year-round rentals and keep it affordable for locals. Workers pushed out by rising prices are in some cases driving an hour or more to work, and it’s a challenge for young families to find housing they can afford on the island.
The ordinance itself is similar to others enacted by coastal towns in response to increasing tourism, and out-of-towners purchasing homes as investment properties, since the pandemic and in the years just before it.
Stonington’s ordinance language frames the registry as a response to an erosion of local control over property, saying 55% of its downtown and 80% of its shoreline was owned by nonresidents.
It grandfathered all existing short-term rentals and separated them into those offered by year-round residents and nonresidents.
A person or entity can only register two short-term rental properties, followed by one more for every three local units they rent for year-round residential use. Registration fees are higher for nonresident owners and increase with every additional unit.
Short-term rental properties that aren’t also occupied by the owner cannot be within 1,000 feet of the property line of another, and the number of those units registered in a calendar year can’t be more than 1.5 times that of the year before.
The ordinance also sets safety standards, a minimum four-day stay length for units not occupied by the owner and fee penalties for not following it.
Registration doesn’t automatically transfer when a property is sold. Since 2023, 13 nonresident properties have dropped off the registry after selling, Nelson said.
Stonington is now seriously prioritizing opportunities for homeownership, according to Nelson. The island has also gained more than three dozen new year-round rentals in recent years from two privately funded projects.
In other Maine municipalities, residents have questioned whether restrictions would simply push the problem onto neighboring towns.
Deer Isle, the other town on the island, doesn’t regulate short term-rentals. The amount there has gone up by 23% in the same time period, according to AirDNA numbers.
Nelson said it’s hard to know whether that’s due to investors who would have bought in Stonington deciding to look one town over, or whether Stonington’s own numbers would have gone up without an ordinance.
“It’s really important for towns to think regionally on these things,” she said.
Deer Isle Town Manager Jim Fisher said his select board hasn’t asked for ordinances regulating them but may consider one in the future.
The town has a commercial site plan review ordinance, which hasn’t been used for short term rentals but could be a way to manage safety and environmental concerns, according to Fisher.
“Policies to discourage short-term rentals and/or seasonal housing have latent consequences, as would any policies that intervene in market systems,” he said. “…[Stonington] appear[s] to be happy with where they are headed.”
He added that Deer Isle hopes to create starter homes for year-round families, and that income needs to keep pace with markets through education, employment opportunities and the physical or online networks that allow people to get to them.
The two towns have recently hired a shared housing manager to work on numerous related plans to ease the housing crunch.

title: Federal judge orders ICE to release teenager arrested in Maine without a warrant
text:
A federal judge in Maine has ordered immigration agents to release an Ecuadorian teenager they arrested without a warrant this week.
According to court records, the 18-year-old, who’s identified by a pseudonym in the documents, entered the U.S. in 2024 as an unaccompanied minor.
He was later granted Special Immigrant Juvenile Status, which offers a pathway to citizenship for young people who’ve been abandoned, abused or neglected by a parent.
On Monday, he was detained at an unidentified location in Maine during a vehicle stop, even though agents did not have a warrant for him.
Judge Stacey Neumann ordered ICE to release him no later than Thursday morning.

title: Maine veterans receive Quilts of Valor for their service at State House
text:
Maine veterans receive Quilts of Valor for their service at State House
Eight Maine veterans received handmade Quilts of Valor during a ceremony at the Maine State House on Thursday, recognizing their service and sacrifice.
The ceremony, held in the Hall of Flags, was part of the 2026 Maine Veterans' Art Exhibition recognition event, which also honored 33 veteran artists whose work is featured in the exhibition.
Sharon Ann Paradis, with the Quilts of Valor Foundation, spoke about the meaning behind the quilts and the organization's mission to recognize veterans.
"Freedom is not free. The cost of our freedom is the dedication of lives of men and women like you, and this quilt is meant to say thank you for that sacrifice," Paradis said.
Since its founding, the organization has gifted more than 400,000 quilts.
The event also highlighted the creativity and experiences of Maine veterans through the 2026 Maine Veterans' Art Exhibition. Following the ceremony, attendees had the opportunity to walk through the exhibition at the Burton M. Cross Office Building and hear directly from the artists about the stories behind their work.

title: PCHC sells Belfast building to school district for bus garage
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Belfast-area school district on Wednesday bought a storage building that used to be part of the MBNA call center complex from Penobscot Community Health Center.
The property, located at 21 Schoodic Drive in Belfast, sold for $1.25 million, according to a real estate transfer tax document filed with the state. It includes two lots: a 45-acre lot of vacant land, and a 3.47-acre lot with a storage building.
The building will be used as a bus garage. The purchase was approved by district voters in a June 2025 referendum. Voters also approved $250,000 in spending to convert the building from a storage building to a bus garage.
It will take “a couple of years” before the bus garage is fully operational, superintendent Elizabeth Ridgeway said. The district has not made a decision on how to use the current bus garage once it is no longer needed.
The property is part of a 142-acre complex built by MBNA that PCHC bought from Stag Industrial Holdings in 2021. Stag bought the property from Bank of America in 2015, according to a 2021 Maine Biz story.
Penobscot Community Health Care, the parent company of the health center, did not respond to requests for comment about the sale.
Selling the property may be part of PCHC’s latest efforts to severely cut costs and stave off bankruptcy.
Penobscot Community Health Center said in August that it needed $3 million to avoid drastically cutting services or declaring bankruptcy. To narrow that gap, it sold an administrative building at 103 Maine Ave., in Bangor, to the city of Bangor for $1.35 million. It also conducted two rounds of layoffs in September, and has attempted to transfer some of its services to other organizations.

title: Housing markets can vary significantly by ZIP code, analysis finds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A new ConsumerAffairs analysis of more than 6,200 ZIP codes found the strongest buyer’s market among those studied in a Miami, Fla., neighborhood and the strongest seller’s market in a Rochester, N.Y., neighborhood.
Ella Gomes, a media relations specialist at ConsumerAffairs, said the results show how much the market can differ from place to place.
“Trends are shifting towards a buyer’s market nationally, but... the housing market is still so localized,” Gomes said. “You can have one ZIP code in a city that ranks top for buyers and one that ranks as top for sellers.”
Gomes and her team at ConsumerAffairs examined the housing market ZIP code by ZIP code. They used data from April through June of this year.
In the Miami neighborhood, the supply of homes for sale was enough to last more than 15 months at the current sales pace. Nationwide, the supply is about five months.
In the Rochester neighborhood, nearly 94% of homes sold above asking price during the study period.
Gomes said the report points to more housing supply and cooling demand.
“The South and areas like Miami had a significant amount of housing added in recent years. So in some markets, there are now more properties available relative to the number of people looking to buy. And that can translate into more choice and more negotiating room for buyers,” Gomes said. “And Florida is the clearest example of that pattern in our ranking.”
Gomes said the biggest takeaway for buyers is to look beyond national numbers and even citywide averages.
“If you’re shopping in a buyer-friendly zip code, you may have more time to compare properties, negotiate on price, or ask for concessions,” Gomes said. “And in a stronger seller’s market, you may need to be prepared for homes to move quickly and for competition above asking price.”
A buyer-friendly market does not necessarily mean homes are affordable. Even with more room to negotiate, buyers should make sure the home and financing still fit their monthly budget.

title: Smoldering wood blamed for fire that damaged Aroostook County home
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WABI) - A fire that started outside of a house in Aroostook County has been ruled accidental by the Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office.
It happened just before 5 a.m. Friday on New Sweden Road near Madawaska Lake.
Upon arrival, crews found fire along the backside of a house, with smoke coming from inside the home.
Officials said both people got out of the house and firefighters were able to rescue one cat.
Firefighters said the fire caused significant damage to the back of the home, including parts of the basement and attic.
Investigators from the FMO determined the fire started in shrubs and landscaping mulch along the outside of the home.
The investigation revealed that a homeowner had removed burned wood from the wood stove and discarded it outside.
The smoldering wood ignited yard, allowing the fire to spread to the house.
The Fire Marshal’s Office reminds residents to dispose of burned materials in covered metal containers outside away from buildings and anything flammable.

title: The Heart Gallery: Maine youth waiting for forever families
text:
What is a Heart Gallery? The Maine Heart Gallery is an online platform that gives you an opportunity to learn more about some of the children in our state who are waiting for a permanent, loving family through adoption.
By sharing their stories and helping connect children with prospective adoptive families, the Heart Gallery helps raise awareness about children in foster care who are still waiting to find their forever home. In Maine, A Family for ME manages our state’s Heart Gallery.
Until recently, the Maine Heart Gallery featured photos of youth waiting for adoption, along with additional information to help families learn more about them. Although some states still include children’s photos in their Heart Galleries, Maine has decided to take steps to protect the identities and privacy of youth in foster care by replacing those images.
Instead of photographs, the Heart Gallery now features creative graphics, including some designed by the children, such as poetry or artwork, and lists of their favorite things. This offers a glimpse into their unique personalities, talents and interests while providing a layer of privacy and protection.
For various reasons, not all children awaiting adoption are included in the Heart Gallery. Some children do not have guardian permission or consent to be featured. Some children may have a pending adoption plan. Some children simply prefer not to participate, and since this is their adoption journey, A Family for ME supports and respects how they want to move through it.
The Maine Heart Gallery typically features about 40 children and teens who are waiting for forever families, but there are even more youth in the program who are awaiting adoption.
According to the A Family for ME Adoption Matching Program (AMP) and DHHS, there are typically 70 to 100 children in the state who are enrolled in the Adoption Matching Program with A Family for ME and awaiting forever families. The children’s ages range from 6 to 17, with most being older youth and teenagers, and some are sibling groups.
AMP matching coordinators work tirelessly to recruit and support licensed families and help match them with youth in foster care who are waiting for adoptive families. To highlight youth waiting for adoption, AMP hosts events throughout the year for licensed and approved families, both in person and virtually. They work closely with caseworkers, foster families and other professionals and members of the children’s support teams to help create meaningful connections and support successful matches.
AMP staff also work closely with the A Family for ME recruitment team to find families for Maine youth waiting for adoption. They connect with licensed families, families who are working toward getting licensed and folks who are just beginning to think about becoming resource parents. Together, both teams help guide and support families as they move through the licensing process, helping them take each step with confidence as they prepare to welcome a child into their family.
Over the years, A Family for ME has highlighted success stories of youth who have found their forever families. These include Monique, who experienced multiple entries into foster care before being adopted as a preteen; Julianna, who spent her childhood in several foster homes before being adopted alongside her six siblings; Dmitry, a teenager with higher needs who found a loving family ready to embrace him; and Natalie, a teen who was initially resistant to the idea of adoption but ultimately found a family she didn’t know she wanted with parents who welcomed her with love and care.
When those families opened their hearts and homes, they provided stability, encouragement and support. Those children, like all the children in Maine awaiting adoption, have the simplest of hopes: to feel like they belong.
Every young person deserves the opportunity to find connection, permanence and a family who believes in their future. Could you be that family?
Learn more about Maine youth waiting for adoption and how you can help.
Visit the Maine Heart Gallery to learn about children waiting for forever families. Whether you’re already licensed, working toward licensure or just beginning to explore foster care and adoption, take the first step by completing the short interest form at afamilyformemaine.org.

title: Our first responders need far greater support
text:
Heidi Chadbourne lives in Manchester.
On a recent morning, we heard the sirens in great succession from the back porch as they passed through Augusta. I told my partner that EMS Chief Sarah Thompson must be returning to Searsmont after her long hospital rehabilitation; such celebration.
“No”, he replied, “That’s not the most direct route to Searsmont. And look, there’s a hearse in the procession.”
Sure enough, on the noon and 6 p.m. televised news, we learned why the honor guard was en route from Clinton to the Medical Examiner’s Office; a firefighter had taken her life. How indescribably sad. Kudos to both newscasts for highlighting the mental health help that many of our first responders need and aren’t getting.
I was an EMT once. I didn’t get much “time in the saddle” because we were summoned with pagers during that era (this was before cellphones). Many times, when my pager went off, I was working 40 or 60 miles away and could not respond in time. After missing so many calls, I was asked to turn in my pager and it was given to an EMT who lived closer to the firehouse. Frankly, I was relieved, even though some in that small Volunteer Fire Department viewed me as unreliable.
I’m shivering as I write this. It has nothing to do with the first flakes of snow forecast to fall on southern Maine in the next three hours. I can’t sleep until I get this written.
Yes, mental health care is important for so many who don’t receive it, despite the stoic front that many “tough guys” evidence in the line of duty, be they male or female. The lady who died had been in the fire department for two years. That’s not much time to learn how to repeatedly deal with inner turmoil, wishing that you had done more in a situation to prevent human (and pet) suffering and beseeching the universe why such accidents and anguishes happen.
As for me, while I strive to help people, I was never cut out to be an EMT. I learned that in hindsight, and was fortunate enough to find a good therapist who allowed me to explore outlets for my angst. One of my big “go-tos” is humor.
When in training for becoming an EMT, my instructor had a hugely offbeat sense of humor. It got him in trouble sometimes — people didn’t understand that it helped him blow off steam. His job was stressful, and he had to respond to emergencies quickly, efficiently, as best as he humanly could. Sometimes that was not enough to save the patient. As he watched the dying person “circle the drain” for the last time, after he had done all he could, he usually had to face a distraught family and a mountain of paperwork (this was before PCs).
Aside from what might seem like twisted humor, some EMTs would hit the bar once they were off shift. This was not a good option for many, including myself.
Those of us in EMT training had to spend at least two nights observing and helping in the hospital emergency room in Augusta (now the Ballard Center). One night, a man came in by ambulance. He was on a stretcher and had coded. I was asked to do CPR. Although I had passed my exam on the mechanical “Recessor Annie” doll, I had never performed CPR on a person.
I got into position, coached by the ER staff, and started. I was apparently doing such a good job that the man came around. I was elated. He took a direct look into my eyes. Then his pupils rolled back into his head. Professionals took over, but his time of death was shortly declared.
My excitement quickly changed to melancholy and feelings of inadequacy. The staff pointed out that he had arrived at the ER in poor shape and inebriated. We all are “called home” at a time and place not of our choosing. And then some wise-cracking intern said something like, “Maybe when he looked into your eyes he thought that he had already arrived in heaven.” Hardee, har! Still, it made me feel better and I will never forget it.
Some of us are not mentally strong. Some of us have undiagnosed mental illness. Some of us have seen much that we can’t grapple with mentally because we don’t have friends and relatives who deeply understand us, or our stressful paramedical careers. Some of us don’t have enough people in our lives to shield us from loneliness or people who truly love us. Some of us need a good group de-briefing after a traumatic incident. (Nonjudgmentally asking, what could have gone better? Or, is there a Volunteer Fire Department chaplain on staff?)
Some of us who have diagnosed mental illness are seeking the correct or updated medication that will keep us fully functional. This takes a dedicated personal general practitioner and good medical insurance. (Have you tried to find a good GP to align with lately, much less a quality counselor or therapist? Anybody not on Zoom?)
Maine lost a good person this November. I’m glad to share with you a couple ideas to explore so that it doesn’t happen again. My heart goes out to so many in Clinton and surrounding communities.

title: On Thanksgiving | Editorials
text:
Gratitude and fellowship are central Thanksgiving themes but for a while America was a nation divided on the subject of when to gather around the table.
In 1789, President George Washington issued a proclamation establishing a “day of public thanksgiving” on Thursday, Nov. 26 of that year. Subsequent Thanksgivings fell on different dates and not always in November. It was not until 1863 that President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed that Thanksgiving would fall on the last Thursday of November each year.

title: Judge refuses to dismiss Alex Murdaugh’s original indictments in killings of his wife and son
text:
COLUMBIA S.C. (AP) — A South Carolina judge on Friday refused to dismiss the original murder indictments against Alex Murdaugh in the killings of his wife and son.
Judge Debra McCaslin’s ruling came after a hearing on Nov. 13, when Murdaugh’s attorneys argued for nearly an hour that the chief investigator lied to a Colleton County grand jury in 2022 about blood spatter being found on Murdaugh’s T-shirt. Prosecutors say they have plenty of evidence supporting the charges.
The ruling clears the way for the disgraced lawyer’s April retrial on the murder charges. The South Carolina Supreme Court threw out his convictions and life sentence in May, ruling a court clerk improperly influenced jurors during his 2023 trial.
Chief investigator’s testimony led to indictment questions
The chief investigator in the case, former State Law Enforcement Division agent David Owen, was central to Murdaugh’s arguments.
McCaslin wrote in her order that any mistakes by Owen were not intentional and that other evidence was enough to support the indictments. Still, she said she was disappointed that Owen failed to read a report saying there wasn’t blood on the T-shirt before making his presentation to the grand jury.
“Law enforcement bears a fundamental duty to thoroughly review and accurately represent the complete evidentiary record,” the judge wrote. “Oversights of this nature undermine public confidence in the integrity of the criminal justice system.”
Any issues about inconsistencies in evidence are matters for the trial and cross examination, McCaslin said.
Prosecutors said Murdaugh, 58, killed his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, on their sprawling property in the South Carolina Lowcountry in 2021. Murdaugh is spending decades in prison for stealing millions of dollars from clients, and has admitted in court that he is a thief, insurance cheat, bad lawyer and longtime opioid addict. But he denies being a killer.
Defense questioned blood spatter conclusions
Defense lawyer Jim Griffin said at the Nov. 13 hearing that when prosecutors sought the indictments, Owen told the Colleton County grand jury that blood spatter was found on a T-shirt Murdaugh was wearing the night of the killings. An earlier report from state agents said there were no blood stains, and no such evidence was introduced at trial.
The false claim about the blood spatter was the only thing anyone heard that could link him to the place and time of the killings, Griffin said.
“A phone call doesn’t put him there. The video doesn’t put him there,” Griffin said. “The blood from his murdered son sprang through the air — it’s raining back on him — puts him there.”
Owen also told grand jurors that the same ammunition load of buckshot in one chamber and large birdshot in the other used to kill Paul Murdaugh was found loaded in weapons all over the Murdaugh property. This was not the case.
Prosecutors cited other evidence it said incriminates Murdaugh
Prosecutors wrote that “a single mistake is not bad faith” and that other evidence supports the charges.
Owen, who abruptly retired in 2024, told grand jurors about the video Paul Murdaugh recorded in which Alex Murdaugh’s voice could be heard at the scene, contradicting his denials. Owen also told them about the family’s mounting debts and how Murdaugh’s schemes to steal from clients and his law firm were close to being discovered.
Prosecutors said Murdaugh killed his wife and son because he thought the sympathy generated by the killings would buy him time to cover up his thefts.
