title: Bremen Bicyclist on a ‘Ride to Recovery’ After Hit-and-Run
text:
Since a hit-and-run crash left a Bremen bicyclist in serious condition, the surrounding community has come together to support her and her family through her recovery.
In the two weeks since the Nov. 4 crash, Jaja Martin has undergone two surgeries and faces a long road to recovery, but she is not letting that stop her. Instead, she said, she is taking this next chapter in her life as a new adventure.
“I’m progressing forward,” Martin said. “I’m not looking back and you know, all the trauma I left on the street behind me. I’m just going one way – forward – and I’m trying to make that forward and up.”
Martin was struck by a vehicle while riding her bicycle in Damariscotta on Nov. 4. She was transported by Central Lincoln County Ambulance Service to MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta for treatment. Due to the severity of her injuries, she was later transported to Maine Medical Center in Portland for further treatment. She arrived home on Nov. 11.
The driver – later identified as John Barczak, 67, of Rockland – fled the scene. He was arrested later that day and charged with elevated aggravated assault, a Class A felony; reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, a Class C felony; and leaving the scene of an accident involving serious bodily injury, a Class C felony.
Martin’s daughter, Teiga Martin, started a GoFundMe, titled “Jaja’s Ride to Recovery,” to help with medical expenses and to support the family. Since its creation on Friday, Nov. 13, the GoFundMe has raised $60,623.
In the description, Teiga Martin said one of her mother’s biggest needs is dental care after her teeth were damaged in the crash. Other than immediate medical care, the donation will go toward physical therapy and support Jaja Martin until she goes back to work, which Teiga Martin said could be anywhere from six months to a year from now.
“If you know Jaja, you know how active she is and how much she loves being outdoors and living life to the fullest,” Teiga Martin said in the description. “It’s hard knowing that the road back to that life will take time.”
As Jaja Martin recovered in the hospital and now as she recovers at home, the surrounding community has come together to send their thoughts and well wishes. Central Lincoln County YMCA Youth Programs Coordinator Sarah Glenn said the organization put together care packages to send to Jaja Martin while she was in the hospital. This includes cards, silly sunglasses, and a disco ball for her hospital room.
Jaja Martin is an active member of the CLC YMCA and one of the teachers for the gym’s summer sailing camps in Round Pond. Glenn described Jaja Martin as “magical” and said she hopes her recovery goes well.
“We’re very happy to help with the communitywide initiative,” Glenn said.
At Great Salt Bay Community School in Damariscotta, students in Kaity Newell’s strings program put together a card for Jaja Martin, who is a musician in the Seacoast Youth and Community Orchestra and volunteers with the class.
“She is just a wonderful person and she makes a difference to the school, a positive difference,” Newell said. “And the kids love her.”
When Newell heard about the crash, she and her junior high students decided to work together to design a card. Newell said a lot of her students have known Jaja Martin for a long time, especially from some of the crossover between strings and the sailing camps she teaches.
“All the kids were just very sad and wanted to send their love, so we made a card,” Newell said.
Every October, Jaja Martin is a familiar face during Damariscotta Pumpkinfest, usually found racing pumpkin boats alongside her family during the regatta. This year, her team themed itself and its pumpkin for the late Dolly Parton. Dave Martin said when staff at Maine Medical Center discovered Jaja Martin “was Dolly,” she become somewhat of a celebrity in the hospital.
Damariscotta Pumpkinfest and Regatta Executive Director Jed Weiss said he hopes Jaja Martin has a speedy recovery and that he sees her in a pumpkin next fall.
“We wish her the best,” Weiss said.
With the ongoing support and incoming gifts, Jaja Martin said she is overcome with emotion and that she feels like she has received a “huge, giant hug” from the whole community. She recalled the disco ball and other trinkets from YMCA made her hospital room more fun and that a video she received from the Seacoast Youth and Community Orchestra brought tears to her eyes.
“It has been overwhelming and just joyful, really joyful, and warm and fuzzy, and all those great things,” Jaja Martin said. “This is why we live here. Our community is incredible.”
For more information, go to gofundme.com/f/support-jajas-ride-to-recovery.

title: 3 Things To Remember As The Darkest Part Of The Year Settles In
text:
We're a couple of weeks out from the end of Daylight Saving Time, which wrapped up on November 1st this year. With that time change comes another change, a decrease in the number of daylight hours we're used to.
According to the Almanac, we've officially entered the "darkest" part of the year.
"Daylight drops fastest around the equinoxes and slows down as the winter solstice approaches."
The sun now sets earlier, and conditions stay dark longer. This has an impact on safety across the state, especially as it pertains to driving. Visibility becomes much more of an issue.
Read More: Broadway In Bangor Closed Friday Morning After Accident
And there are 3 factors you may want to keep in mind when it comes to safety in those darker hours; animals, delivery drivers and kids.
1.) Animals
Unaware of our implemented time changes, many animals use the cover of darkness to move from place to place.
Scanning the roadways for shadows or eye reflections, along with making sure you're alert are steps you can take to lessen your chance of colliding with an animal, big or small.
Aside from the morning commute, them majority of motorists are on the road between the hours of 3PM and 6PM. Taking extra care to stay aware of your surroundings as the sun goes down is key.
2.) Delivery Drivers
While you may not have thought anything of leaving your porch light or front door light off during the day before, it's important to consider that a number of your friendly, neighborhood delivery drivers work well into the evening, sometimes till 8 or 9 PM
If the sun goes down around 4 PM, and you don't get home from work till after 5 PM, there's a good chance whomever is brining that package to your house will be coming up an unlit driveway or stairwell.
Do your delivery person a solid and turn your outside lights on earlier. Light up your house for safety, not just the holidays!
And it's not just the UPS, FedEX or mail carriers you should consider, but those that deliver propane, oil and even doordashers.
Have their back, by lighting their way.
3.) Kids
After a long day in school, many kids head home to play.
Whether on their walk or bike back to the house, or their attempt to meet up with friends in their neighborhoods, it's likely that by the time they start their journeys for the afternoon, darkness will be setting in.
And sense safety isn't always front-and-center on the mind of a child, it should be in your mind.
Making sure your kids know to wear something light colored or even reflective is so important. Talking with your kids about staying out of the shadows, and near streetlights while they're moving from place to place is another things you can do to help keep kids safe.
Read More: Show Us Bangor + Eastern Maine Holiday Light Displays
Most important of all, in my opinion, would be to communicate to them that it's not only their own surrounding in space that they should be aware of, but where things like cars and cyclists are in the roadway.
It's also a good thing for drivers to approach any school bus, school zone, crosswalk or and residential sidestreet slowly and with caution this time of year after sunset.
The good news is the darkness doesn't last forever. There is light at the end of the tunnel, which we can wait out to enjoy, if we keep in mind these ways to keep ourselves and others safe this season.
Good luck!

title: How police are using this device to help track people with dementia
text:
HUNTINGTON, W.Va . (InvestigateTV) - Walking off alone can put people living with cognitive impairments in life-or-death situations.
For a person with dementia, any stage of the disease can be at risk for wandering, according to the Alzheimer’s Association. Many will do so repeatedly as symptoms include losing their ability to recognize familiar places and faces.
Families anywhere in Cabell and Wayne counties can apply to receive an AngelSense watch or fob tracking device for their loved one from HPD, free of charge.
“[Families] can set up a geofence that would let them know if the person has traveled outside of that area,” HPD Lt. Matt Null explained. “Or it can work like a two-way radio device that you could actually contact them, even has an SOS feature if someone was to fall.”
HPD is launching the program after a WSAZ investigation into Charles “Chuck” Carroll’s death. Carroll, who had dementia, was dropped off at Cabell Huntington Hospital on Dec. 30, 2021, before wandering off on his own.
Carroll was missing for 53 days before being found dead in an outbuilding blocks from the hospital.
“I was at home in Huntington and I started getting text messages from a lot of my classmates from Ravenswood, and they said Chuck is missing,” Caroll’s lifelong friend Debbie Holmes recounted. “And I said, ‘well, sometimes he’s always missing, because he kind of did his own thing and then he’d pop up every now and then.’ And so they said, ‘no, they have on WSAZ where he is missing from the hospital.’”
Caroll believes if Chuck had been wearing one of the devices now offered by HPD, he would have survived.
“I just couldn’t believe what had happened to him, that he was so close to the hospital,” she said. “He was so close to me, where I lived. He was pretty close to me. I wouldn’t have known to look for him there.”
Several changes have been inspired by Carroll’s death, including by the hospital and by Mingo Central students.
Lt. Dunn said the program, which is fully funded by a grant from the Department of Justice, is in the department’s mission to protect, serve, and better the community.
“Other than family, there’s very little that’s more important than that,” he said. “So if you’re already working through, if you have someone who’s having cognitive problems or they’ve been diagnosed with an illness, you’ve already got obstacles. If this can help alleviate some of those obstacles, and it’s exactly what we want to do. We want to make sure that everyone’s safe, that we don’t have any tragic stories.”
Holmes implored those with loved ones like Chuck to reach out for the program, so their loved ones can avoid what happened to Chuck.
“Don’t be apprehensive at all, because you’re saving a life,” she said. “Everybody’s family is going to be affected with dementia, one way or the other. My own family was. And it’s so sad to think that little things that we can do can make a difference. All it takes is effort.”
Lt. Null said there are only 100 devices available, and demand is already high, saying his phone has been “ringing off the hook.”
He also emphasized that the devices aren’t just for people with dementia, but can be used for people of any age with mental disabilities that might make them wander off, like autism.

title: Embden grow house owner had prior federal cannabis conviction, feds say
text:
Federal authorities charged three Cuban nationals Friday with conspiring to grow more than 100 marijuana plants at an Embden home owned by a company tied to a man previously convicted in a similar Colorado case.
The charges, filed in the U.S. District Court in Bangor, stem from an 11-month investigation that began earlier this year into the Barron Road home. The house has been used to grow marijuana since at least January, according to court records.
The charges are the latest in a string of federal cases over illegal marijuana grows in Maine. Jiamin Liao, a Chinese national, was sentenced in September to six months in prison for her involvement in a Norridgewock marijuana operation.
Homeland Security Investigations agents searched the home Thursday. They found more than 200 live marijuana plants in the basement, the garage and an outbuilding, according to an affidavit by Special Agent Pierre Mathieu. Inside the garage, agents also located about 120 pounds of processed marijuana, he said.
The three men — Lester M. Fuentes Gonzalez, 38, Hector A. Roque de Escobar, 60, and Osvaldo Guillermo Gamez Fernandez, 66 — were at home during the search and were arrested. Each is charged with conspiracy to manufacture more than 100 marijuana plants and manufacturing more than 100 marijuana plants.
Fuentes and Roque are lawful permanent residents of the U.S., according to court documents. Those documents didn’t specify Gamez’s immigration status.
Roque is the registered agent for a limited liability company that owns the Embden home, according to the affidavit. He also has a 2016 federal conviction in Colorado that resulted from a search of a marijuana grow house.
He and 13 other defendants were charged in that case with possession with intent to distribute and distribution of a controlled substance, according to court documents. He ultimately pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering, and the drug charges were dismissed at sentencing.
In 2018, Roque was freed from supervised release, roughly 17 months before his probation was supposed to end. He had complied with his conditions and had no reported violations, according to court records.
Gamez told the agents that he lived at the home as a caretaker and watered the marijuana plants when he was directed to do so. Gamez said he never left the property because he doesn’t have a valid driver’s license and gets all his food delivered. Messages on his phone indicated that he had lived there for more than a year, according to the affidavit.
Fuentes and Roque arrived at the home about before the search, Gamez told agents.
Before the Thursday search, an undercover agent visited the house and said he was looking for his dog. The agent later confirmed that Gamez was the man who answered the door.
Agents also found grow lights, heaters, cellphones and trash bags filled with stems, leaves and root balls from earlier harvests on the property.
Two electric accounts at the home have been in Fuentes’ name since 2024, according to the affidavit. Since January, one has used well above 8,000 kilowatt-hours a month. The other has averaged 5,515 kilowatt-hours a month, peaking at 10,164. The typical Maine household uses about 550 kilowatt-hours a month, according to the affidavit.
The Drug Enforcement Administration was also involved in the investigation, according to Andrew McCormack, a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Maine.
If convicted, each man faces a mandatory minimum of five years in prison and up to 40 years.
The three men are being held at the Somerset County Jail in East Madison.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Joel Casey, who is prosecuting the case, did not immediately respond to inquiries Friday. Roque’s lawyer, Kaylee Foster; Fuentes’ lawyer, Phil Noland; and Gamez’s lawyer, Donald Brown, also did not respond.

title: Foot and Paddle: Wind Song on Mount Blue
A new look: Portland Hearts of Pine introduce new kit for next season
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new look: Hearts of Pine introduce new kit for next season
The Portland Hearts of Pine have played two seasons, bringing sellout crowds to Fitzpatrick Stadium. Now, as the club looks to build a new stadium and is adding a women's club, it is getting a new on-field look.
The team introduced its new Woods & Water kit on Thursday that the team will wear for the 2027 season. Before the team's first official match in 2025, the original kit had already been sold in all 50 states and 30 countries.
The original Woods & Water jersey has become the best-selling kit in USL history and was named the No. 1 soccer kit of 2025 by Protagonist Soccer.
“When we first introduced Woods & Water, we wanted to create something that felt unmistakably Maine. What we couldn't have anticipated was how quickly people would make it their own,” said Gabe Hoffman-Johnson, Founder and Chief Community Officer of Portland Hearts of Pine.
"It's become more than a soccer jersey. It's a way for people to show their pride in Maine and feel connected to this community. We love the original design, and we know our supporters do, too. This refresh is about honoring what we've built together while continuing to make it better. We're not starting over. We're carrying something special forward."
The new kit
The new kit was unveiled during an event at the State Theatre, where the initial kit was introduced in 2024, and it builds on the original navy and green hoops, preserving the original design while introducing refinements in detail, construction and feel.
The club said the design is inspired by the layers of Maine's landscape and is a celebration of the Pine Tree State and all those who have their hearts in Maine, with a campaign inspired by Maine's familiar promise: The Way Life Should Be.
The kit itself is made of a new two-way stretch interlock knit fabric, resulting in a more substantial feel than previous Hearts kits, with a texture and character inspired by many classic kits of the 90s.
The club's motto, lead with your heart, is woven inside the neckline, while the club’s Dirigo Heart symbol – inspired by the Valentine’s Day Bandit and the Dirigo star on Maine’s state flag – is seen on a reflective hip tag.
The kit is produced in partnership with Danish sportswear brand hummel.
“We wanted to unveil this kit in a way that celebrates people, places, and community that make Maine such a special place to call home,” said Josh Lane, Vice President of Marketing for Portland Hearts of Pine.
“Maine is one big village. Like the craftspeople, establishments, community builders, and custodians of this state’s traditions featured in this campaign, Hearts exist to deepen the strength of that community. These hoops represent our landscapes, but together we’ve made this kit representative of all those who have their Hearts in Maine.”
Kit partners
L.L.Bean returns as the club's sleeve partner and the University of Southern Maine joins as the club's official education partner, with its logo featured on the back of the kit.
The partnership was celebrated during Thursday's unveiling with the premiere of a short film featuring students from USM's Promise Scholars program.
“Bringing our Promise Scholars together with Hearts of Pine is a natural fit,” said USM President Jacqueline Edmondson. “Both remind us of what's possible when passion and determination are met with opportunity and support. This partnership reflects our shared commitment to Maine and its people, and I'm proud to see USM represented on a jersey that means so much to this community.”

title: CMP cuts back tree trimming work amid financial pressures
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CMP cuts back tree trimming work amid financial pressures
The utility says it has reduced contractor crews delayed some scheduled maintenance into 2027
CMP cuts back tree trimming work amid financial pressures
The utility says it has reduced contractor crews delayed some scheduled maintenance into 2027
Central Maine Power is cutting back its scheduled tree trimming work as the utility faces growing financial pressures.
In a news release Friday, CMP said it reduced the number of contractor crews performing maintenance trimming from nearly 85 to approximately 35 beginning in November.
The company says the move represents a 20% reduction in work originally planned through early 2027.
"Trees are the leading cause of outages on our system, which is why vegetation management remains an important part of how we protect reliability for our customers," CMP President Linda Ball said.
CMP says its separate Hazard Tree Program will continue to address trees that pose risks to the electrical system.
The company cited inflation, increasing borrowing costs and rising labor expenses as reasons for the reductions.
In July, S&P Global Ratings revised CMP's financial outlook from stable to negative, citing the company's weakening financial position.
CMP also said that it has delayed some reliability projects, removed job postings from its website and paused a majority of its hiring while it evaluates its financial needs.
The utility will continue to evaluate its current and future workforce needs.

title: What is the Pownal cattle pound and why was it important?
text:
In our series AskME, we explore your questions about Maine's history, culture and customs. What have you been wondering? We’ll work to find an answer. Explore the questions, or submit your own, at pressherald.com/ask-me.
Along Route 9 in Pownal, just north of the entrance to Bradbury Mountain State Park, there’s an old granite structure that’s easy to miss but remarkable for the history it holds.
At first glance, driving by at 35 mph, it looks like the stone foundation of a house built by a town founder, whose bones and rafters turned to dust long ago.
A rustic brown sign off to the side explains that it’s a cattle pound, built in 1818, where stray farm animals were held until their owners came to pay a fine and take them home.
The Pownal Cattle Pound is one of seven former livestock enclosures in Maine that are listed on the National Register of Historic Places, along with similar structures in Charlotte, Greenwood, Jefferson, Otisfield, Turner and Waldoboro.
Maine State Historian Earle Shettleworth was the state historic preservation officer who sought national recognition for five of the cattle pounds listed in the early 2000s, including the Pownal site.
“Maine in the 18th and 19th centuries was heavily rural and a large number of communities were developing at that time,” Shettleworth said in a recent phone interview. “Farming was a primary occupation and, inevitably, cattle and other animals would go astray and become a nuisance by either destroying crops or wandering down country roads.”
More than 40 town pounds still exist across the state, according to the Maine Historic Preservation Commission. Made of stone or wood, some are in excellent condition, others are ruins.
They are remnants of a time when nearly every town had a pound to corral wayward cows, horses, pigs and sheep — and hold their owners accountable for crops eaten and other damage done.
MAINE’S FARMING HISTORY
Early colonists practiced mostly subsistence agriculture and couldn’t risk lost food production or property damage caused by roving livestock. In 1635, the Massachusetts Bay Colony ordered every town to build a cattle pound, according to the commission.
As the District of Maine developed in the late 1700s, communities here followed the Massachusetts law. The Maine Legislature adopted similar regulations soon after becoming a state in 1820.
Farms in Maine were often large and challenging to fence, whether with timbers or stones cleared from pastures. Livestock often got loose.
“At the earliest town meetings, there were angry demands for an end to damage by marauding cattle,” William Locke wrote in his 1994 history of Maine cattle pounds.
Town records for the Pownal Cattle Pound are remarkably complete, showing that residents voted to construct a pound, found an appropriate site less than a mile north of the town center and paid John Tylor (sic) $50 to build it, according to the 2004 national register application.
Constructed of dry stacked granite without a roof, the structure was 36 feet. The walls were 6 feet tall, 4 feet thick at the base and 18 inches thick at the top. A flat granite lintel measuring 7 feet 8 inches long spanned the entryway.
Nine-inch-square timbers ran along the top of the walls and the enclosure had “a good gate in frunt (sic) with iron hinges and a good lock,” town records state.
STACKED STONE AND TIMBER
The pound was built on property owned by the Cotton family, who worked the land on and around Bradbury Mountain from the late 1700s to the early 1900s. Thomas Cotton was elected the town’s first poundkeeper.
“The poundkeeper would be responsible for capturing the animal, securing it in the pound and identifying the owner, who would then have to pay a fine to bring the animal home,” Shettleworth said.
The owner was expected to compensate neighbors for any damage done by the animal, as well as the poundkeeper for feeding and caring for it. In 1835, Pownal selectmen adopted fees for every 24 hours an animal was impounded: horse, 25 cents; ox, 16 cents; cow, 13 cents; swine, 12 1/2 cents; sheep, 3 cents.
Town pounds were phased out of use in the 1870s following the invention and mass production of barbed wire, which made fencing exponentially easier.
The Pownal enclosure may have been used in later years as a feeding station for cattle being driven to market. The last poundkeeper served in 1891.
Now, more than 200 years after it was built, the Pownal Cattle Pound stands in good condition, according to the commission.
The wood timbers are gone. Some sections of the stone enclosure have settled, some have collapsed. The flat granite lintel that once spanned the entryway now rests on the ground just inside the pound.
“Some of the top stones were used in a local highway project in the 1950s, so the height of the structure now ranges between 4 1/2 and 5 1/2 feet,” according to the national register application.
Often it takes a while for old things to be seen as treasures.
Got a question you’d like answered? Ask it here:

title: Second federal judge blocks construction of Trump's memorial arch in DC
text:
Second federal judge blocks construction of Trump's memorial arch in DC
A second federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump’s administration from building a 250-foot memorial arch in the nation's capital, issuing an order on Friday that keeps the construction work on hold indefinitely, according to plaintiffs' lawyers who sued to challenge the project.
U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema in Alexandria, Virginia, issued her order from the bench in a lawsuit brought by the Arlington County Board. Brinkema ruled two days after a different judge in Washington, D.C., extended a previous order that blocked the Trump administration from breaking ground on the arch on a more temporary basis.
Related video above: Post-midterms, President Trump focuses on D.C. beautification projects
The Virginia board claims Trump’s project will exacerbate traffic congestion and jeopardize public safety in the county, which is across the Potomac River from Washington.
“We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court,” plaintiffs' attorney Kate Talmor said in a statement after Friday's hearing.
On Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan in Washington agreed to extend a temporary restraining order keeping the project on hold until Dec. 3. The injunction issued by Brinkema doesn't have a specified expiration date.
Chutkan initially blocked the arch's construction on Nov. 5, shortly after a hearing of the National Capital Planning Commission ended with the Trump-heavy panel giving the arch its final approval in an 8-4 vote, despite dozens of witnesses who opposed the construction.
The case before Chutkan was filed on behalf of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian. Members of the Kennedy family filed a separate lawsuit last month, citing the impact the structure would have on Arlington National Cemetery, where family members are buried.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump, a Republican, has pushed in his efforts to leave a personal imprint on Washington's historic landscape. At 250 feet, the arch would be twice the height of the Lincoln Memorial.
Brinkema was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Bill Clinton. Chutkan was nominated by Democratic President Barack Obama.

title: New video shows Brooklyn building collapse in real time
text:
NEW YORK (Gray News) – New video shows the moment a building in Brooklyn collapsed last week.
The video, provided by the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, was taken through a window of a New York City bus that was stopped at a red light.
Shortly after the light turns green, the building can be seen collapsing into a construction site.
Eight people were killed, including two children, ages 9 and 10, according to city officials. Another 18 people were injured, including four firefighters.
Many families were left homeless.
New York officials, from building inspectors to prosecutors, say they’re investigating what caused the three-story building to come crashing down as workers were digging at an adjacent construction site.
The city has ordered inspections at more than 160 sites in New York that are associated with six entities linked to the construction and demolition site next to the fallen building, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.
“I think it is always an outrage when eight New Yorkers lose their lives, when 18 New Yorkers are hospitalized, and when families are shattered as a result of all of this,” Mamdani said.
If investigators uncover “any evidence of criminality,” Mamdani said, “it is one that we follow through to the fullest extent of the law.”

title: School district to close after learning 500 employees didn’t undergo child protective services screenings
text:
ALBEMARLE COUNTY, Va. (WVIR/Gray News) - Citing a years-long issue with the background check process while hiring employees, a Virginia school district announced it would close temporarily.
Albemarle County Public Schools said that schools will be closed to students starting Thursday, November 19, and hopes to reopen after Thanksgiving break on Monday, November 30.
Acting Superintendent Dr. Chandra Hayes sent a message to Albemarle families saying that over the last three years, more than 500 people hired by the division passed their criminal background checks using the State Police criminal history database, but were not checked against the Virginia Department of Social Services’ Child Protective Services Central Registry.
In her message, Hayes said that schools must be closed until the issue is resolved and staff who work directly with children must have their Social Services screening completed before being able to work with students.
Dear Albemarle County Public Schools Community,
When I took on this role, I made a commitment to you to look closely at how our school division operates, to fix what needs fixing, and to tell you what we find. Some of what follows is difficult to share, but you deserve to hear it directly from me.
Immediate Issue Driving the Closure
Every new ACPS employee goes through a rigorous, fingerprint-based criminal background check using the State Police criminal history database. Virginia law and School Board policy also require that new hires be checked against the Child Protective Services Central Registry, which the Virginia Department of Social Services (VDSS) maintains, to confirm they have no founded complaints of child abuse or neglect.
During a review of onboarding procedures, we found that the criminal background checks were administered, but the personnel responsible for submissions to Child Protective Services did not consistently follow established processes. Specifically, over the past three years, there were more than 500 people hired by the division who passed their criminal background checks, but their information was never submitted for the Social Services registry review. We investigated the matter and took immediate action.
Families should not have to accept any uncertainty about the adults working with their children, and I will not risk the safety of our students. Because the affected employees work in schools and departments across the entire division, I made the decision that we must close all schools until we have this issue resolved. We shared our findings with the Virginia Department of Education and they agreed that staff who work directly with children must have their Social Services screening complete before being able to work with students.
What we are doing now
We are working with the Virginia Department of Social Services (VDSS) to complete the screening as soon as possible. Staff who work directly with students will be first to be processed, so that we can reopen schools quickly. The VDSS has prioritized these submissions, and I am grateful for their support.
If the VDSS review shows that any current employee is the subject of a founded complaint of child abuse or neglect, we will act immediately to protect students. School Board Policy GCDA requires that such an employee be dismissed once their appeal rights under state law have been exhausted, and it provides grounds for the division to recommend that the Virginia Board of Education revoke their teaching license.
We also checked whether anyone currently under investigation or facing charges related to abuse, neglect, or failure to report was among the employees not submitted. I can confirm that none of them were.
What families need to know during the closure
School Schedule Through Thanksgiving Break
Trust is built through honesty, especially when the news is hard. I’ll keep you informed as the checks are completed. I will receive a daily report from the Virginia Department of Social Services on the progress of the application review. This will allow me to confirm the reopening date by Nov. 27. With so little notice and the holiday season so close, I know this will be hard on many families, and I am sorry for that disruption. However, the safety of your children must always come first, and I believe this is a necessary action.
I will continue to review processes and procedures and make the changes needed to strengthen and restore Albemarle County Public Schools. Thank you for your continued support in those efforts.
Sincerely,
Chandra Hayes, Ed.D.
Acting Superintendent
Albemarle County Public Schools
Governor Abigail Spanberger said in a statement that Albemarle County Public Schools’ former leadership failed students and families by not conducting legally required background checks. She said state education leaders are assisting the school division’s interim leadership with corrective action, including hiring an outside investigator.
“Albemarle County Public Schools’ prior leadership failed the children and families they serve. They failed to follow the law by not conducting legally-required background checks, and they failed to uphold the trust our Commonwealth placed in them. Virginia Secretary of Education Jeffery Smith and Superintendent of Public Instruction Jenna Conway are assisting Albemarle County Public Schools’ interim leadership in taking swift corrective action, to include hiring an outside investigator. My administration is committed to the education and safety of every child in Virginia, and we will use every available tool to rectify this failure and ensure accountability.”

title: A decade after shooting Harambe, the Cincinnati Zoo is reeling from Fiona's untimely death
text:
CINCINNATI (AP) — Months of international backlash cast a shadow over the Cincinnati Zoo after workers decided to fatally shoot a beloved endangered gorilla named Harambe in response to a little boy falling into his exhibit in 2016.
That outrage faded the following year with the premature birth of an adorable hippo named Fiona, this time bringing positive attention to the reeling zoo, which shared her miraculous survival story in videos and blog posts. They showed her taking a bottle, splashing in a pool and learning to run. She captured hearts around the world and helped restore the zoo’s image.
Now, though, the zoo is dealing with another tragedy: Fiona died Thursday more than a week after eating a visitor’s hat.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.
Fiona’s death at age 9 led to an outpouring of grief as well as comparisons to the end of Harambe’s life, as both were untimely and involved zoo visitors. Some social media users were quick to condemn the zoo, saying it needs to better protect its animals. Others called for compassion.
“As devastated as we are, we cannot begin to fathom the grief that Fiona’s keepers, veterinary team, and the entire Cincinnati Zoo family are experiencing today,” Dino Buddies, a local wildlife outreach company, said in a statement. “We hope that everyone extends these incredible individuals the compassion, kindness, and grace they deserve as they mourn the loss of an animal they loved so deeply.”
After Harambe was killed at age 17, the zoo reopened its gorilla exhibit with a higher, reinforced barrier. Tongue-in-cheek online petitions circulated seeking to add his face to Mount Rushmore and the dollar bill. There was also a more somber “Justice for Harambe” petition that sought to hold the mother of the boy who fell into the enclosure responsible for the gorilla’s death. The county prosecutor determined there was no cause for charges.
Fiona swallowed the hat about 12 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air, it struck a ceiling fan and deflected into the hippo enclosure through a small opening above the viewing windows. It was an accident, a zoo spokesperson said.
She was not the first zoo animal to die from eating a non-food item that found its way into a pen. Zoos around the world have been warning for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats.
Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.
But the accidental nature of Fiona’s death hasn’t dampened the despair.
“The two saddest days in all my time here in Cincinnati come from the Zoo,” Facebook user Marianne King posted Thursday. The first was Harambe’s death and the second was Fiona’s, she said.
Joanne Prater, who lives in the Cincinnati suburb of Loveland, was attending a high school fundraiser Thursday evening and said every person she spoke to talked about how sad they were about Fiona’s death and compared it to Harambe’s.
“They are tokens of Cincinnati. You can’t say Fiona or Harambe without everybody knowing who that is here in Cincinnati,” she said. “I guess both of their deaths could have been prevented, but unfortunately accidents do happen.”

title: DHHS hosting public hearing on Prime Healthcare
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Central Maine Medical Center patients, staff voice safety concerns following Prime Healthcare takeover
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) held a public hearing on Friday to help determine whether Prime Healthcare Foundation, Inc., is in compliance with the terms of its acquisition of Central Maine Healthcare, including Central Maine Medical Center, Bridgton Hospital and Rumford Hospital, in February 2026.
Those terms include not making any reductions or changes in the level of essential services offered for at least five years, maintaining trauma hospital certification or accreditation for at least one year, and continuing to operate as critical access and general acute care hospitals for at least five years.
In the months since the acquisition, Prime Healthcare has been the focus of targeted complaints from patients and a newly formed nurses' union. State Rep. Julia McCabe requested the hearing after hearing from constituents in Lewiston and Auburn.
In a letter sent to DHHS commissioner Sara Gagné-Holmes, McCabe wrote, "The people of Lewiston deserve a hospital system that is safely managed and adequately staffed, that upholds the agreements entered into with the State of Maine, and that follows the laws of the state.
"Based on the many conversations I have had with healthcare providers and patients, it is my belief that Prime Healthcare is not currently abiding by their Certificate of Need agreement and is not providing the same level of healthcare as when they originally purchased the hospital system," McCabe added.
McCabe's letter detailed complaints of inadequate surgical sterilization equipment, non-compliance with the trauma certification requirements, staffing shortages, the termination of a contract with the emergency department physician group, high "left without being seen" rates in the emergency department, and staffing shortages.
McCabe also alleges there are more than 100 vacant positions, and according to the Maine State Nurses Association, 20 nurses were wrongfully fired or suspended in September 2026 over efforts to unionize.
McCabe wrote, "Prime Healthcare's degree of culpability for the decline in patient care at Central Maine Medical Center (CMMC) must be determined through the public hearing process. The people of Maine are owed as much."
During the hearing, which was held at Central Maine Community College's Kirk Hall Auditorium, Central Maine Medical Center patients and staff voiced their frustrations about a decline in care.
"In 50 years that I've been with CMMC, I've never seen this hospital in this bad of a condition," said patient Robert Hack. "I took my wife into the (emergency room). She was ultimately transferred to the (intensive care unit). My wife paid the ultimate price for poor healthcare and the cuts that CMMC has made."
"We started putting regular trash into the biohazard bin. There was no other place to put it," said Candy Gleason, another CMMC patient.
"I was fired by Prime Healthcare in September for speaking up for patient safety," said Katie Grinnell. "Nineteen of my nurse colleagues were suspended and terminated, as well."
Daniel Corriveau told Maine's Total Coverage that his wife and his mother have recently been treated at CMMC, and he described the hospital's conditions as unhygienic.
"Trash is running out of the trash bins in the emergency room. We've got black floors. We've got dried blood on the floor when my wife was brought in," Corriveau said.
Corriveau said that his wife was not properly cleaned when she arrived at CMMC, and that she has contracted sepsis.
"The hospital has gone to hell in a handbasket and, right now, I don't think they're saving people," he said.
Written comments will be accepted by mail or email through Nov. 30.
Prime Healthcare said it has invested approximately $26 million into Central Maine Healthcare since its acquisition of the network in February. When Prime took over, it said it would invest $150 million into CMMC. Central Maine Healthcare said it chose Prime as a parent company because of its commitment to investing in hospitals.
A DHHS spokesperson said everything from Friday's hearing will be considered in its investigation, but there is no specific timeline on when the investigation will move forward.

title: Court stay prevents US Army from detonating bomb-making chemicals in Iowa
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — A federal appeals court has granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit that cleared the way for the U.S. Army to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa.
The ruling came late Thursday, putting in jeopardy the military’s plans to deal with dozens of barrels of lead azide pending further direction by the court.
“The Army can’t detonate under the permit while the permit is stayed,” said Thien Chau, an attorney with Earthjustice, which filed a petition on behalf of Iowa groups calling for a review of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency permit.
The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals had yet to put out a schedule Friday for when it will issue a ruling on the groups’ emergency motion or even if there will be a hearing. Chau said attorneys expect the court will try to decide before Monday’s planned operation.
The Army did not immediately return messages seeking comment on how the court action would affect its plans.
The Army has said the chemicals are unstable, and the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop.
The detonation was initially planned for Friday, but the Army announced Thursday that it would push the operation back to Monday following an outpouring of public concern about the potential health and environmental consequences.
“This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material,” Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle had announced in a post on X.
The Army, the EPA and the federal Department of Health and Human Services followed up Friday with a joint statement saying they were working together to ensure the detonation is conducted in the safest way possible.
“Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” the statement read.
An inspection earlier this year at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant determined that the lead azide, which is used in munitions production, had started to degrade. The crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the Army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.
According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.
The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their petition that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public.
The Army detailed its plans during a public meeting in Middletown in October, but a public advisory Sunday was the first time other communities — some as far away as 100 miles (160 kilometers) — became aware of the potential impact.
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown — about 160 miles (257 kilometers) southeast of Des Moines — but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.
Some schools and businesses had planned to close, as the Army recommended that people stay indoors, bring their pets and livestock inside and keep their windows and doors closed. Officials also urged residents in the path of the predicted plume to clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces afterward.
“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory stated. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals.”
Lucy Giehl, her husband and two dogs live about 4 miles (6.4 kilometers) north of the ammunition plant. She said during an interview Thursday that she didn’t know if she needed to wear gloves to wipe down surfaces or to keep her dogs from drinking water in their pond.
“There’s just so many details that I feel like haven’t been addressed with the public.”
___
Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: Mild Fall Weekend Ahead! Tropical Moisture For Monday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Skies will stay mostly clear Friday night, with lows ranging from the upper 20s to the mid- and upper 30s. A weak cold front will pass through overnight. This will not bring any rainfall, but will shave temperatures down a few degrees for the weekend.
Saturday: Sunshine and mild temperatures
Saturday will be the pick of the weekend! Expect lots of sunshine, with highs reaching the 50s for most of Maine. A few spots in central and southern Maine could reach the low 60s. Southwest winds will average 10 to 20 mph.
Sunday: Clouds increase ahead of rain
Clouds will increase Sunday morning and thicken through the day. Highs will still reach the 50s, but the extra cloud cover should keep temperatures out of the 60s. Southwest winds will average 10 to 20 mph.
Rain is expected to move into southern Maine by Sunday evening and spread northeast across the state into early Monday.
Monday: Rain, then a sharp cooldown
Rain is expected across Maine Monday before ending by early afternoon. How much falls will depend on the storm’s track: A path farther offshore would mean less rain, while a track closer to the coast could bring higher totals.
Rainfall totals:
- South and east of the interstate: An average of 1 to 2 inches is possible, with locally higher amounts along the immediate coast.
- Foothills to the Interstate: 0.5 inches to 1 inch.
- Mountains and northern Maine: Less than half an inch.
A cold front moves through Monday night into early Tuesday, bringing much colder air. Any water left on roads or sidewalks could freeze quickly, creating slippery spots for the Tuesday morning commute.
Tuesday and beyond: Much colder
Highs from Tuesday onward will be mostly in the 30s, with a few spots reaching the low 40s. Overnight lows will fall into the teens and 20s.
We’re also watching another storm around Thanksgiving. It’s still VERY early, but just be aware that a wintry mix COULD be possible around Thanksgiving or after. Still plenty of time for the forecast to change.
First Alert 7-Day Forecast
TONIGHT: Mostly clear skies. Lows will range from the upper 20s to the upper 30s. NW wind 5-10 mph.
SATURDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 50s. A few low 60s possible. SW wind 10-20 mph.
SUNDAY: Increasing clouds with rain arriving in the evening. Highs in the 50s. SW wind 10-20 mph.
MONDAY: Rain likely with highs in the 50s.
TUESDAY: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 30s.
WEDNESDAY: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 30s.
THANKSGIVING: Mostly cloudy with a wintry mix arriving later in the day. Highs in the 30s and low 40s.

title: Obituary: Robert J. Robishaw Jr.
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND – Robert J. Robishaw, Jr., 80 years old, resident of South Portland, Maine, passed away on Nov. 16, 2026, after a long illness at the Veteran’s Home in Scarborough, Maine. He was surrounded by his loving family, friends, other residents, and caring staff of the Veterans Home.
Robert lived in South Portland for most of his life and graduated from South Portland High School. He also attended SMCC. He was an Army veteran, a volunteer fireman, a postal employee, and worked for the city of South Portland.
He will be remembered as a loving husband and brother, devoted father and grandfather, and as a kind-hearted man with a great sense of humor who loved his family and friends and always had time to help others. He videotaped the high school football games, set up a basketball court in the driveway and a pool in the back yard, and enjoyed camping with his family and friends.
Robert was predeceased by his father, Robert J Robishaw, Sr., his mother, Theresa Landry; his sister Anne, and his brother Roger.
He is survived by his wife, Deanna; his sons Jason, Lance and his wife Stephanie and Chad and his girlfriend Daisy; his brothers Danny and Ronald; his grandchildren Maria, Haley, Summer, Brandon, Corey, and Tony; and several nephews and nieces.
A graveside memorial services will be held on Saturday, November 21, at 1:00 pm, at Mount Pleasant Cemetery in South Portland.

memorial donations may be made to:
the Scarborough Veterans Home

title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.
Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.
Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.
With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a “testament of the hard work” his team put into the case. He said he was “intimately familiar” with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.
Rinderknecht’s attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.
“After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration,” Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.
Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.
Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht’s first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren’t presented as evidence during the trial.
Juror says Rinderknecht’s own testimony pointed to a guilty verdict
Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.
“It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise,” he said. “After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he’s guilty.”
Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a “lack of information” presented to the jury about the technical review.
In the end, it was Rinderknecht’s own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.
“Stating that he was up on the hill, didn’t smell a fire, didn’t see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night,” Cameron said.
Prosecutors say Rinderknecht had been ‘mad at everything’
During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht’s state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by “societal revenge” like they previously did.
Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire’s origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.
“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.
After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?”
These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.
They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.
Defense argues fire’s origin is unproven
Haney cast doubt on the government’s case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.
The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.
Prosecutors attacked the fire investigator during cross examination and at one point accused him of perjury, alleging he did not disclose all records related to the case. The judge ultimately rejected prosecutors’ request to strike his testimony.
Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor’s testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht’s character, such as his angry text messages, because they were “evidence of the man, not evidence of the act.”
Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.
In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

title: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
text:
A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company’s AI tool Claude.
It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.
Levent Alpöge, a member of the company’s technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.
“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”
Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.
Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about “my ability to announce,” as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.
A day after the company’s initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he’d solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge’s claim.
Alpöge released his and Claude’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University.
“Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that’s also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. And when you’re done, you should have a deep understanding of why something is true,” he said.
He said Claude followed that code and said the proof is true.
“Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there’s a very, very good chance you’re going to satisfy me too,” he said. “But I have to do the work.”
Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute’s website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.
The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.
“This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics,” he said in a statement. “But the journey from today’s announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult.”
Alpöge said he is “presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics.” He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.
In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.
“Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis,” said Kontorovich. “There’s some kind of out-of-body experience where I’m looking at myself saying, ‘Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,’ and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth.”
Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.
Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI’s future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.
___
AP Technology Writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed.

title: Improperly discarded wood sparks fire at Aroostook County home
text:
Improperly discarded wood sparks fire at Aroostook County home
Investigators say wood ignited landscaping before the fire spread to the house

A fire that caused significant damage to a home near Madawaska Lake Friday morning was caused by smoldering wood from a stove, according to the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office.
Firefighters responded to a home on New Sweden Road in Stockholm around 4:58 a.m.
Upon arrival, crews found flames along the rear exterior of the home and smoke coming from the inside.
Both occupants escaped and crews rescued a cat from the home.
The fire caused significant damage to the rear of the house, including sections of the basement and attic.
Investigators determined that a homeowner had removed burned wood from a wood stove and discarded it outside, where it ignited shrubs and landscaping mulch before spreading to the home.
The fire was ruled accidental.
The State Fire Marshal's Office reminds residents to place hot ashes and smoldering wood in covered metal containers, away from buildings and other flammable materials.

title: How much is the median income for households near you?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How much is the median income for households near you?
How much does the typical household make?
The median household income across the United States increased slightly in 2025 to an estimated $84,780. It's an increase of about 1.2% from $83,808 the year before.
The data released in October was a part of estimates calculated by the U.S. Census Bureau — but not part of its census every ten years. They also conduct the American Community Survey to collect social, economic, housing and demographic data about the people who live in the U.S.
One of these estimates is the median household income. This is calculated by taking the incomes of everyone age 15 and older in a household.
Washington, D.C., had the highest median household income in 2025 at about $109,505. Behind it were New Jersey and Maryland.
Mississippi had the lowest median household income at $59,346, with West Virginia and Louisiana above it.
There were 14 states that experienced a statistically significant increase from the year prior, and just one where median household income declined — California.
The other 14 states' median household incomes increased from the year prior.
Rhode Island saw the largest increase, going up 6%, followed by Virginia and New Hampshire.
The new estimates released also include data for metropolitan areas. Out of the 25 most populated areas, the San Francisco metropolitan area had the highest median household income at $136,020.
